terms.name: Laplacian matrix
terms.abstract: The Laplacian matrix of a weighted graph with n nodes is the n × n matrix L(G) = D(G) - A(G), the degree matrix minus the adjacency matrix of the edge weights. Its quadratic form xᵀ L(G) x is the sum, over the edges, of the edge weight times the squared difference of the two entries of x at the ends of the edge. The Laplacian matrix is therefore a symmetric matrix and positive semi-definite, the constant vector is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 0, and the multiplicity of the eigenvalue 0 equals the number of connected components of the graph. Two normalized variants divide the edge weights by the node degrees; they share their eigenvalues, which lie between 0 and 2. In machine learning, the quadratic form is the penalty term of Laplacian regularization, which makes the values learned at connected nodes similar and predicts the value at an unlabeled node as the weighted average of its neighbors. The eigenvectors of its smallest eigenvalues are the coordinates that spectral clustering feeds to k-means.
terms.description: Twelve weather stations around Krems an der Donau, from Melk and Zwettl in the west to Retz and Langenlebarn in the east, each recorded a mean temperature for the year 2024: 12.6 degrees Celsius at Krems, 9.6 on the Jauerling mountain. Two stations at most 35 km apart are joined by an edge whose weight decays with their distance, so the stations form a weighted graph G with 27 edges (Fig. 2(a)). How much does the temperature vary along the edges of G? One answer is the sum, over the edges, of the edge weight times the squared difference of the two temperatures at its ends. The Laplacian matrix of G is the matrix that computes this sum as a quadratic form in the vector of the twelve temperatures. Consider an undirected graph G = ( V,E ) with nodes V = 1, …, n and nonnegative edge weights Ai,i' = Ai',i, where Ai,i' = 0 when G has no edge i,i'. The edge weights are the entries of the adjacency matrix A(G) ∈ Rn × n, and the node degree d(i) := Σi'=1n Ai,i' of node i is the sum of the weights of its edges. The Laplacian matrix of G is the difference \begin{equation} {\mathbf L}^{(\mathcal{G})} := {\mathbf D}^{(\mathcal{G})} - {\mathbf A}^{(\mathcal{G})} \text{, with the degree matrix } {\mathbf D}^{(\mathcal{G})} := \operatorname{diag}\big\{ d^{(1)}, \ldots, d^{(n)} \big\} \text{.} \end{equation} The diagonal entry Gii of the Laplacian matrix Eq. (1) is the node degree d(i), and the off-diagonal entry Gii' is the negated edge weight -Ai,i', so every row sums to zero. Fig. 1 carries out the construction for a graph with three nodes and two edges. For the station graph, the edge between Krems and Langenlois, 8 km apart, has weight 0.92, the longest edges have weight 0.23, and Krems has degree 3.18 from its six neighbors. The Laplacian matrix is characterized by its quadratic form. For every vector x = (x1, …, xn)ᵀ ∈ Rn, one entry per node, \begin{equation} {\mathbf x}^{\top} {\mathbf L}^{(\mathcal{G})} {\mathbf x} = \sum_{\{i,i'\} \in \mathcal{E}} A_{i,i'} \big( x_{i} - x_{i'} \big)^{2} \text{.} \end{equation} The identity follows from expanding xᵀ D(G) x - xᵀ A(G) x = Σi=1n d(i) xi2 - Σi=1n Σi'=1n Ai,i' xi xi' and collecting the two terms of each edge. For the station graph and the vector of mean temperatures, the quadratic form Eq. (2) equals 26.9 squared degrees; the edge between Jauerling and Melk, with weight 0.79 and a temperature difference of 2.8 degrees, contributes 6.0 of it. Three properties of the Laplacian matrix follow from the quadratic form Eq. (2). First, L(G) is a symmetric matrix and positive semi-definite, since every term of the sum is nonnegative, so its eigenvalues are real and can be ordered as 0 ≤ λ1 ≤ λ2 ≤ … ≤ λn. Second, the constant vector 1 = (1, …, 1)ᵀ makes every term vanish, and L(G) 1 = 0 since every row sums to zero, so λ1 = 0 with the eigenvector 1. Third, the multiplicity of the eigenvalue 0 equals the number of connected components of G. A vector x with xᵀ L(G) x = 0 takes the same value at the two ends of every edge, so it is constant on each component, and the indicator vectors of the components span the nullspace of L(G). The station graph is connected, so λ1 = 0 is simple and λ2 = 0.25 is positive. Joining only stations at most 25 km apart leaves Langenlebarn without an edge and the graph with two components, and the limit 20 km leaves six components; the eigenvalue 0 then has multiplicity two and six (Fig. 2(b)). The second-smallest eigenvalue λ2 is the algebraic connectivity of G, and the eigenvector of λ2 is the Fiedler vector. The signs of its entries split the nodes into two clusters with few edges between them. For the station graph, the three stations more than 20 km east of Krems, Langenlebarn, Schöngrabern, and Retz, have negative entries and the other nine have positive entries. Two normalized variants of the Laplacian matrix divide the edge weights by the node degrees, \[ {\mathbf L}^{(\mathrm{sym})} := \big( {\mathbf D}^{(\mathcal{G})} \big)^{-1/2} {\mathbf L}^{(\mathcal{G})} \big( {\mathbf D}^{(\mathcal{G})} \big)^{-1/2} \text{ and } {\mathbf L}^{(\mathrm{rw})} := \big( {\mathbf D}^{(\mathcal{G})} \big)^{-1} {\mathbf L}^{(\mathcal{G})} \text{,} \] for a graph without isolated nodes. The first is a symmetric matrix whose quadratic form is the sum Eq. (2) with each xi replaced by xi / √(d(i)). The second is I - ( D(G) )-1 A(G), the identity matrix minus the transition matrix of the random walk on G that moves to a neighbor with probability proportional to the edge weight. The two variants have the same eigenvalues, which lie between 0 and 2; the eigenvalue 0 has the eigenvector 1 for L(rw) and ( D(G) )1/2 1 for L(sym), and its multiplicity again counts the connected components. For the station graph, the largest eigenvalue of L(sym) is 1.57. Which of the three matrices a method uses is a design choice: spectral clustering has been formulated with L(rw), with L(sym), and with L(G). In machine learning, the Laplacian matrix enters through its quadratic form Eq. (2) as a penalty term. Consider data points that are the nodes of G, which is then a similarity graph, with a label yi known only for the nodes in a subset A ⊂ V. Examples are the stations with a record, or the users of a social network who filled in a profile field. A hypothesis is a vector x ∈ Rn that assigns one value to every node, and the hypothesis space is Rn. Laplacian regularization adds the quadratic form to the average squared error loss on the labeled nodes, \begin{equation} \min_{{\mathbf x} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}} \frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}} \big( x_{i} - y_{i} \big)^{2} + \alpha {\mathbf x}^{\top} {\mathbf L}^{(\mathcal{G})} {\mathbf x} \text{,} \end{equation} with a hyperparameter α > 0. Adding a penalty term is one of the three routes that regularization distinguishes, and this one implements the assumption that nodes joined by a heavy edge carry similar values. The training error alone says nothing about a node outside A; the penalty term is the only term that constrains its value, so the generalization from the labeled to the unlabeled nodes comes from the edges. The objective Eq. (3) is convex and its minimizer solves a linear system, since the gradient of the quadratic form is 2 L(G) x. As α → 0, the minimizer pins xi = yi on the labeled nodes and minimizes the quadratic form over the remaining entries. The entry of L(G) x at an unlabeled node is then zero. Such a node takes the weighted average of its neighbors, xi = (1/d(i)) Σi'=1n Ai,i' xi', which is the harmonic solution of Zhu et al. (2003). Leaving each station of Fig. 2(a) out in turn and predicting its mean temperature by this average of its neighbors gives a mean absolute error of 0.86 degrees. Predicting the mean of the other eleven stations instead gives 1.12 degrees. The largest error is at Jauerling, 955 m above sea level, predicted at 12.3 degrees against 9.6 recorded. The edge weights encode distance but not altitude, so the penalty asks a mountain station to resemble the valley stations around it. The same quadratic form, with the model parameters of local models in place of the scalars xi, is the generalized total variation that generalized total variation minimization penalizes in federated learning. The eigenvectors of the smallest eigenvalues of a Laplacian matrix are the coordinates that spectral clustering hands to k-means.

terms.name: accuracy
terms.abstract: Accuracy is the fraction of correct predictions made by a hypothesis on a dataset with a finite label space, equal to one minus the average 0/1 loss. It is widely used as a single-number metric for classification methods. Accuracy is not suitable as an objective function for training, since the 0/1 loss is non-smooth and non-convex. Empirical risk minimization uses a surrogate loss instead, a convex or smooth upper bound on the 0/1 loss, and accuracy is reported on a validation set or a test set. On imbalanced data, accuracy alone cannot tell a classifier from a baseline that ignores the features, which calls for other means of evaluation such as the confusion matrix.
terms.description: A frost warning for Krems an der Donau is right on some days and wrong on others, and the fraction of days on which it is right is its accuracy. In general, accuracy is the fraction of correct predictions made by a hypothesis h: X → Y on a dataset D = (x(r), y(r) ) r=1m of feature vectors x(r) and labels y(r), each label a value y ∈ Y from a finite label space Y. With the 0/1 loss L(0/1)(z,h ), which is 1 for a wrong prediction on the data point z and 0 otherwise, accuracy is \begin{align*} \operatorname{acc}(h \mid \mathcal{D}) & := 1 - \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L^{(0/1)}\left(\big({\mathbf x}^{(r)}, y^{(r)}\big),h \right) & = \frac{1}{m} \Big| \Big\{ r \in \{1, \ldots, m\}: h\big({\mathbf x}^{(r)}\big) = y^{(r)} \Big\} \Big| \text{.} \end{align*} Accuracy ranges from 0 (no prediction is correct) to 1 (every prediction is correct). Equivalently, accuracy equals one minus the average 0/1 loss on the dataset. For example, in image classification with the label space Y = cat, dog, bird, the hypothesis assigns each image, represented by its feature vector x, a category h(x). Accuracy is then the fraction of images whose assigned category equals the true label y: 94 correct assignments among 100 images give an accuracy of 0.94. Fig. 1 compares two classifiers on the same training set D(train) of 60 data points, the dataset from which both were learned. The linear classifier h, whose decision boundary is a line, misclassifies three data points near that line. The nonlinear classifier h' curves around each of these data points and classifies them correctly. The classifier h' in Fig. 1 achieves the optimal accuracy of 1 on D(train): its decision boundary closely follows the positions of the individual data points that the linear classifier misclassifies. The classifier h' is therefore sensitive to small perturbations of the feature vectors, such as measurement noise. A slight shift in the feature vector of a data point near the decision boundary can flip the prediction. Optimizing accuracy on the training set therefore does not by itself ensure good generalization. Good generalization means a small loss on data points outside the training set. Accuracy is often used as a single-number metric to compare learned classifiers: on a validation set D(val), to select among candidate hypotheses during validation, and on a test set D(test), whose data points entered neither training nor selection, to assess the selected hypothesis. Accuracy could also be used as the objective function for training. However, accuracy is defined via the 0/1 loss, which is piecewise constant as a function of the model parameters and neither smooth nor convex, so accuracy is piecewise constant too: the gradient of accuracy is zero wherever it exists and therefore indicates no direction of improvement. Gradient-based optimization methods cannot maximize accuracy directly. Instead, empirical risk minimization-based methods use a surrogate loss that upper bounds the 0/1 loss and is chosen convex or smooth, so that those methods have a gradient to follow. Two examples for such a surrogate loss are the logistic loss, which is convex and smooth, and the hinge loss, which is convex but non-smooth: its one-sided derivatives at margin 1 are -1 and 0, so it is not differentiable there. Fig. 2 shows the three loss functions as functions of the margin, for binary classification with Y = -1, 1, where a real-valued hypothesis h predicts via the sign of h(x). Each loss function depends on the data point only through the margin y · h(x), which is how loss functions for binary classification are compared. The hinge loss lies above the 0/1 loss everywhere; the logistic loss equals ln 2 at margin 0, so it is the logistic loss scaled by 1 / ln 2 that lies above the 0/1 loss. Accuracy is the metric of choice when the classes are balanced and every error costs the same; on imbalanced data it is not. Consider a frost warning for Krems an der Donau (Austria): the features of a data point are the minimum and the maximum air temperature of one day, and its label indicates whether the minimum temperature of the following day falls below 0 ∘C. Frost days are the minority class: of a training set of 40 recorded days, only 6 are followed by frost. The constant prediction ``above zero'' (a baseline that ignores the features) is therefore correct on 34 of the 40 days, an accuracy of 0.85, and a classifier learned by logistic regression from the 40 data points reaches the same accuracy of 0.85. Both make the same number of errors, so accuracy cannot tell the two apart; they differ in where they are right, which calls for other means of evaluation such as the confusion matrix. The confusion matrices in Fig. 3 show that the learned classifier detects one of the six frost days and raises one false alarm, while the baseline detects none and raises none.

terms.name: artificial neural network (ANN)
terms.abstract: An artificial neural network (ANN) is a hypothesis space whose hypothesis maps are all built on one directed graph. Each hypothesis in this space is a map from the features of a data point to a prediction for the label, obtained for a particular choice of the learnable model parameters carried by the graph's edges (edge weights) and nodes (offset terms). Each node is an artificial neuron that applies an activation function to the weighted sum of its inputs plus its offset. The connectivity pattern, the architecture, is an important design choice: a feedforward network uses a directed acyclic graph, whereas a recurrent neural network allows a cycle. Depending on the connectivity, ANNs include deep nets, CNNs, RNNs, and transformer-based architectures.
terms.description: The face recognition of a smartphone camera and the speech transcription of a voice assistant are computed by ANNs whose connection strengths were learned from data. An ANN is a hypothesis space whose hypothesis maps are all built on one directed graph: its nodes are the artificial neurons, elementary computational units, and its weighted edges fix which artificial neurons feed which. The edge weights and the offset terms assigned to the nodes form the learnable model parameters w of an ANN, and a choice of w selects one hypothesis map h(w), from the features of a data point at the input to an output used as the prediction for the label. The learned hypothesis ĥ = h(ŵ) is one such choice, obtained by gradient descent on the training error with the gradient computed by backpropagation. Each artificial neuron applies an activation function σ(·) to the weighted sum of its inputs plus an offset term (Fig. 1). The activation function can itself carry model parameters (parametric activation functions), but it is customarily prescribed in advance, for example the rectified linear unit, so that only the node-wise offset and the edge weights are learned. The output of a neuron can be used either as the final output of the ANN or as an input to other neurons. The directed graph of the ANN records these uses: its nodes are the artificial neurons together with the input features, and each directed edge carries the output of one node to the input of another (Fig. 2). Which outputs are connected to which downstream neuron's inputs, the connectivity structure (or architecture) of the ANN, is therefore an important design aspect. Whether the graph is acyclic or contains a cycle separates the two broad families of ANN. The graph of Fig. 2 is acyclic, so this ANN is feedforward: the signal passes from the inputs to the output without returning to any node. One widely used type of ANN is deep nets where neurons form consecutive layers (Fig. 3). In a deep net, the outputs of neurons in a given layer are typically only connected to the inputs of the neurons in a consecutive layer. By contrast, in the general directed acyclic graph of Fig. 2 an output may feed any downstream neuron, and there x1 connects straight to the prediction. Each layer l then applies a feature transformation Φ(l) whose components are computed by the neurons of that layer (each as in Fig. 1), and the deep net computes the concatenation of these layer-wise maps. A shortcut or skip connection directly connects the outputs of neurons in one layer to the inputs of neurons in a nonconsecutive layer; Fig. 3 shows one as a dashed edge. With that edge removed, the network of Fig. 3 delivers the prediction h^{({\mathbf w})}({\mathbf x}) = {\mathbf \Phi}^{(3)}\Big({\mathbf \Phi}^{(2)} \big({\mathbf \Phi}^{(1)}({\mathbf x})\big)\Big) \text{.} Here, the input is the feature vector x = (x1, x2, x3)ᵀ. The two hidden layers compute Φ(1), Φ(2): R3 → R3, and the output layer computes Φ(3): R3 → R. The graphs seen so far are acyclic. A recurrent neural network instead includes a feedback edge, so its graph contains a cycle and is not a directed acyclic graph (Fig. 4): a self-loop feeds a neuron's output back to its own input. This feedback lets the network carry information across the steps of a sequence; unrolling the recurrence over the sequence, one copy of each neuron per step, recovers a directed acyclic graph. The networks of Figs. 2, 3, and 4 differ only in which nodes their directed edges join. This connectivity pattern names the common architectures. Feedforward networks have an acyclic graph, a directed acyclic graph (deep nets are the layered case), while CNNs are also feedforward but share weights across spatial positions. RNNs add feedback connections for sequence processing, and transformer-based architectures, which underlie modern LLMs, are likewise feedforward and use attention to connect every token to every other. Skip connections appear in these architectures as the residual connections of deep CNNs and transformers. Each architecture fixes a different hypothesis space, within which empirical risk minimization learns a single hypothesis ĥ = h(ŵ) by choosing the model parameters ŵ that minimize the average loss on a training set. The architecture also governs the generalization of the learned hypothesis to data points outside the training set, which is what the choice of an architecture is judged by. That choice need not be made by hand: neural architecture search learns a useful connectivity automatically.

terms.name: attention
terms.abstract: Attention is a mechanism that models the dependencies between the tokens that make up a data point, such as the words in a sentence or the pixel patches of an image. Attention represents the relationship between two tokens by a parameterized weight function whose model parameters are learned from a training set. An attention head then computes a new vector representation for each token as a weighted combination of the value vectors of all tokens. Like the weight function, the value vectors are learned. An attention head acts as a differentiable associative memory: a token uses its query vector to retrieve, through the key vectors of the other tokens, the values most relevant to it. Attention heads represent dependencies between tokens regardless of their positions within a data point, and they are a core component of modern LLMs.
terms.description: A sentence consists of words, an image of pixel patches, and a network of nodes: the data points of some machine learning applications are composed of smaller units, referred to as tokens. In general, the tokens that constitute a single data point are not independent of one another. Instead, the meaning of a token depends on a few other tokens of the same data point, which may lie far from it. The attention mechanism is a building block of ANNs that represents such dependencies between tokens regardless of their distance within a data point, and it is a core component of the LLMs built on the transformer. Probabilistic models represent and analyze such dependencies. Attention mechanisms instead represent these dependencies directly, without specifying a probability distribution over the tokens. They represent the relationship between a token with index i and a token with index i' by an attention weight f(w)(i,i'), a parameterized function whose model parameters w are learned from a training set. The attention weight measures how strongly token i attends to token i'. Practical attention mechanisms differ in their choice of the function f(w)(i,i') and in the empirical risk minimization variant used to learn w. The most widely used choice, described below, is scaled dot-product attention. Scaled dot-product attention derives three vectors from the embedding vector x(i) ∈ Rd of each token i via learned matrices. They are a query (vector) q(i) = WQ x(i), a key (vector) k(i) = WK x(i), and a value (vector) v(i) = WV x(i), with the matrices {\mathbf W}_Q, {\mathbf W}_K, {\mathbf W}_V \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} as model parameters learned during training. The query of a token determines which keys it matches, the key of a token determines which queries match it, and the value carries the information that is aggregated. The output of the attention mechanism for token i is a weighted sum of the values of all tokens, {\mathbf z}^{(i)} = \sum_{i'=1}^{n} \alpha_{i,i'} {\mathbf v}^{(i')} \text{.} Here, n denotes the number of tokens of the data point. The coefficient αi,i' is the attention weight, i.e., the scaled dot-product form of f(w)(i,i'). The attention weights are computed from the queries and keys in two steps. First, the attention score between tokens i and i' is s_{i,i'} = \frac{\big({\mathbf q}^{(i)}\big)^{\top} {\mathbf k}^{(i')}} {\sqrt{d}} \text{.} The inner product (also called dot product) (q(i))ᵀ k(i') measures how well the key of token i' matches the query of token i. Second, the attention weight αi,i' follows by applying the softmax function to the scores si,i' across all tokens i': \alpha_{i,i'} = \frac{\exp(s_{i,i'})} {\sum_{j=1}^{n} \exp(s_{i,j})} \text{.} The softmax function normalizes the scores. The attention weights αi,i' are nonnegative and sum to one across i' = 1, …, n, forming a probability distribution over the tokens. Dividing the inner product by √(d) in the attention score counteracts its growth with the dimension d. The score (q(i))ᵀ k(i') is a sum of d terms. Without the scaling, a large d would therefore push the softmax function into a region where its gradients nearly vanish. Fig. 1 illustrates scaled dot-product attention for an eight-token sentence. An attention head moves from a single token to the whole sequence of tokens. It is a parameterized function h(w) that maps the input embeddings to the output vectors, h^{({\mathbf w})}\big({\mathbf x}^{(1)}, \ldots, {\mathbf x}^{(n)}\big) = \big({\mathbf z}^{(1)}, \ldots, {\mathbf z}^{(n)}\big) \text{,} with model parameters w comprising the three matrices WQ, WK, WV. Collect the output vectors as the rows of a matrix Z, and the queries, keys, and values as the rows of Q, K, V. Then h(w) computes them in the compact form {\mathbf Z} = \operatorname{softmax} \left(\frac{\mathbf{Q} \mathbf{K}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}\right) \mathbf{V} \text{.} Here, the softmax function is applied independently to each row of Q Kᵀ/√(d), so that each row of the resulting matrix is a probability distribution over the n tokens. Since the queries, keys, and values are all derived from the same sequence of tokens, this construction is called self-attention. In practice, several attention heads, each with its own learned matrices WQ, WK, WV, operate in parallel; this is called multi-head attention, and each head can specialize to a different relation between tokens. Attention can be interpreted as a differentiable associative memory, i.e., a content-addressable store: the keys k(i') act as addresses, the values v(i') as stored contents, and a token i searches the other tokens with its query q(i). The inner product (q(i))ᵀk(i') measures how well the address i' matches the query, the softmax function turns the match scores into retrieval weights, and the output z(i) is the retrieved content. A classical dictionary data structure or hash table returns the single value stored at an exactly matching address. Attention instead returns a weighted average. Moreover, its output z(i) is a differentiable function of the matrices WQ, WK, and WV. In particular, the queries, keys, and values can themselves be learned via gradient-based methods for solving empirical risk minimization. The same retrieval principle, with a weighted average in place of a single best match, is used by k-nearest neighbors methods. Computing all pairwise scores si,i' requires n2 query--key inner products, one for each ordered pair of tokens. The retrieval principle also guides efficient implementations: locality-sensitive hashing restricts each query to nearby keys, reducing the cost of one attention head from n2 query--key comparisons to a constant multiple of n ln n, with n again the number of tokens. Because q(i) and k(i') are obtained from the different matrices WQ and WK, the attention weights are directed: in general, αi,i' ≠ αi',i, so that token i attending strongly to token i' does not imply the reverse. Fig. 2 visualizes the attention weights αi,i' that a single head learns on sentences from the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Trained to reconstruct each masked token from the others, the head gives many query tokens a weight concentrated on a few keys rather than spread uniformly, illustrating the associative-memory reading on this small corpus. The heat map also shows the directed nature of the weights discussed above: the query token ``rights'' places its full weight on the key token ``beings'' (α12,3 = 1.0), while the query token ``beings'' places no weight on the key token ``rights'' (α3,12 = 0.0).

terms.name: autoencoder
terms.abstract: An autoencoder is a machine learning method that learns an encoder and a decoder together. The encoder maps the feature vector of a data point to a new feature vector, referred to as code. The decoder reconstructs the original feature vector from the code. The code delivered by the encoder is typically much shorter than the original feature vector, so the code can retain only part of the information in the feature vector. Different autoencoders use different choices for the hypothesis spaces from which the encoder and the decoder are chosen. The special case where both are linear maps learns the same subspace as principal component analysis, and a deep autoencoder uses a deep net on each side.
terms.description: Three hundred points along a curve in the plane (Fig. 3) can each be stored as a single number from which the point is rebuilt almost exactly, and an image can likewise be stored as a short code from which a close copy is rebuilt. An autoencoder learns an encoder Φ from a hypothesis space H along with a decoder Φ* from a second hypothesis space H*. The encoder maps the feature vector x ∈ Rd of a data point to a code z = Φ(x) ∈ Rd'. The decoder maps the code back to a reconstruction x̂ = Φ*(z) of the original feature vector (see Fig. 1). The encoder and the decoder can be learned via empirical risk minimization with a loss that measures the reconstruction error x - Φ*(Φ(x)), such as the squared error loss, \begin{equation} \min_{{\mathbf \Phi} \in \mathcal{H}, {\mathbf \Phi}^{*} \in \mathcal{H}^{*}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\Big( {\mathbf x}^{(r)}, {\mathbf \Phi}^{*}\big( {\mathbf \Phi}\big( {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \big) \big) \Big) \text{,} \end{equation} The training set needs no labels: what the decoder has to reproduce is the data point itself, so an autoencoder is a form of self-supervised learning, as it does not require manual labeling. The length d' of the code is typically much smaller than the length d of the original feature vector, in which case the autoencoder is called undercomplete. The encoder then implements a form of compression that still allows the decoder to reconstruct the original feature vector with a small reconstruction error. The encoder map can afterwards be used as a feature transformation for learning tasks based on the same data points, which makes the autoencoder a feature learning and a dimensionality reduction method. The autoencoder is rarely used for the reconstruction itself: the decoder is dropped and the code kept, so that a later learning task learns a hypothesis with few model parameters on the code rather than on the raw features (see transfer learning). Different autoencoder methods are obtained by different choices for the hypothesis spaces H, H* and the loss function in the reconstruction error empirical risk minimization Eq. (1). The special case of linear maps for the encoder and the decoder, paired with the squared error loss, learns the same subspace as principal component analysis. At every minimizer of the reconstruction error empirical risk minimization Eq. (1), the composition Φ* ∘ Φ is the projection onto the span of the first d' principal components. The code itself can be the coordinates with respect to any basis of that subspace, not only the orthonormal one principal component analysis delivers. For some applications, nonlinear encoder and decoder maps represented by ANNs are more useful, and a deep autoencoder uses a deep net on each side (Fig. 2). On the curve of Fig. 3, a code of one number and one hidden layer on each side leave an average squared error loss of 0.003, against 0.457 for the best linear map with the same code. The gain is not the ANNs as such but the shape of the reconstruction: linear maps with a code of one number can only place the reconstructions on a straight line, and these data points do not lie on one.

terms.name: backpropagation
terms.abstract: Backpropagation is an algorithm that computes the gradient of the loss with respect to the model parameters of an artificial neural network. The algorithm consists of two consecutive phases, referred to as forward and backward pass. The forward pass evaluates, for the current model parameters, the activations and the resulting prediction errors on a given dataset. The backward pass then applies the chain rule to compute the partial derivatives of the average loss with respect to the model parameters. These partial derivatives constitute a gradient, which can be used in a gradient step to update the model parameters.
terms.description: Consider an artificial neural network with a billion model parameters and its prediction for a new data point. If this prediction is wrong, the model parameters can be updated by a gradient step. That update requires the partial derivatives of the loss on the new data point with respect to all model parameters. Backpropagation is an algorithm for computing these partial derivatives with as little duplicated computation as possible. More generally, it computes the gradient ∇ f(w) of an objective function f(w) with respect to the model parameters w of the artificial neural network. The model parameters consist of the edge weights and the offset terms at the nodes of the artificial neural network. The objective function is typically the average loss \[ f({\mathbf w}) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\left(\left( {\mathbf x}^{(r)},y^{(r)} \right),h^{({\mathbf w})} \right) \text{,} \] incurred on a dataset of m data points ( x(1),y(1) ), …, ( x(m),y(m) ). Backpropagation computes the partial derivatives of f(w) one layer at a time (Fig. 1). Its execution consists of two consecutive phases, the forward pass and the backward pass. In the forward pass, the artificial neural network is applied to each data point of the dataset: the neurons of each layer evaluate their activations from the activations of the previous layer. The final layer then produces the output, which is the prediction for the label of a data point with features x. The quality of this prediction is measured by a loss function L(( x,y ),h(w) ), where h(w) is the hypothesis map represented by the artificial neural network with model parameters w. In the backward pass, the partial derivatives of f(w) with respect to the edge weights of each layer are computed recursively, from the output back to the input. These partial derivatives form the whole gradient ∇ f(w). The backward pass requires about as much computation as the forward pass: its cost grows in proportion to the number of edges of the artificial neural network, one partial derivative, one multiplication, and one addition per edge. To illustrate the details of backpropagation, consider a simple artificial neural network: it consists of three layers with one neuron each. Its model parameters are the three edge weights w(1), w(2), w(3). The gradient of an average is the average of the gradients of its summands, so a dataset with a single data point already shows the recursion. The objective function f(w) is then the loss of that data point. Write a(0) = x for its feature. Layer ℓ = 1, 2, 3 computes \[ z^{(\ell)} = w^{(\ell)} a^{(\ell-1)} \text{,} \qquad a^{(\ell)} = \sigma\big(z^{(\ell)}\big) \text{,} \] with the activation function σ and no offset terms. The output is h(w)(x) = a(3). The edge weight w(3) enters f(w) only through z(3), w(2) through z(2) and then z(3), and w(1) through all three. The chain rule therefore gives \[ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial f}{\partial w^{(3)}} &= \frac{\partial f}{\partial a^{(3)}} \sigma'\big(z^{(3)}\big) a^{(2)} \text{,} \frac{\partial f}{\partial w^{(2)}} &= \frac{\partial f}{\partial a^{(3)}} \sigma'\big(z^{(3)}\big) w^{(3)} \sigma'\big(z^{(2)}\big) a^{(1)} \text{,} \frac{\partial f}{\partial w^{(1)}} &= \frac{\partial f}{\partial a^{(3)}} \sigma'\big(z^{(3)}\big) w^{(3)} \sigma'\big(z^{(2)}\big) w^{(2)} \sigma'\big(z^{(1)}\big) x \text{.} \end{aligned} \] Each line repeats the one above it and appends two factors. Evaluating the three lines separately would recompute the repeated factors twice over. Backpropagation computes them once, from the output backwards. The repeated factors form the partial derivative of f(w) with respect to z(ℓ). This partial derivative obeys its own recursion, \[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z^{(3)}} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial a^{(3)}} \sigma'\big(z^{(3)}\big) \text{,} \qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial z^{(\ell)}} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial z^{(\ell+1)}} w^{(\ell+1)} \sigma'\big(z^{(\ell)}\big) \quad \text{for } \ell = 2, 1 \text{.} \] Each edge weight then costs one multiplication, \[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial w^{(\ell)}} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial z^{(\ell)}} a^{(\ell-1)} \text{.} \] The backward pass is this recursion, and the activations a(ℓ) it needs are the ones the forward pass already computed. The partial derivatives delivered by backpropagation constitute the gradient used in a gradient step: \[ {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} = {\mathbf w}^{(t)} - \eta \nabla f({\mathbf w}^{(t)}) \text{, for } t = 0,1,\ldots \text{,} \] with step size η. Each gradient step requires a new run of backpropagation, since the model parameters change after each step. These partial derivatives are not only used for a gradient step. A class activation map explains a prediction of a convolutional neural network by weighting its feature maps with partial derivatives of the output.

terms.name: bagging
terms.abstract: Bagging is an ensemble method that uses randomly sampled subsets of a dataset as training sets for its base learners. Aggregating the predictions delivered by the base learners, by a majority vote in classification or by averaging in regression, yields the prediction of the ensemble method. A random forest is the instance of bagging whose base learners learn decision trees.
terms.description: On twenty-four days of 2020, twelve from winter and twelve from summer, the weather station Krems an der Donau recorded a minimum and a maximum temperature. Predicting the maximum temperature y of a day from its minimum temperature x is a regression problem, and a decision tree solves it by splitting the feature axis at a threshold and predicting the mean label on each side. Fig. 1 shows what happens when two decision trees are each learned from five of those days chosen at random: they place their threshold at 5.4 and 9.2 degrees Celsius, and their predictions differ by up to 22 degrees Celsius. This spread indicates a lack of stability of the base learner: it is too sensitive to the specific choice of training set, which in turn implies poor generalization. Bagging is an ensemble technique that suppresses this instability. Bagging executes its base learners in parallel, in contrast to boosting, which runs its base learners sequentially. The name is short for bootstrap aggregating. Bagging uses randomly sampled subsets of a dataset as training sets for its base learners. Given the original training set D, it generates perturbed copies D̃(1), …, D̃(M) (typically via bootstrap sampling) and trains one base learner on each, producing hypotheses ĥ(1), …, ĥ(M). The final hypothesis aggregates these by majority vote for classification (i.e., the class predicted by the most base learners) or averaging for regression, a task whose label space is R (see Fig. 2). Algorithm 1 states the method in full. Bagging methods differ in their choice of base learner. A random forest, for example, is the instance of bagging whose base learners learn decision trees. \begin{algorithm}[H] \caption{Bagging } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex Input: training set D = z(1), …, z(m), base learner, number M of base learners \For{ℓ = 1, …, M} \State draw the bootstrap sample D̃(ℓ): m data points from D, with replacement \State learn ĥ(ℓ) by applying the base learner to D̃(ℓ) \EndFor \Statex Output: ĥ(x) = (1)/(M) Σℓ=1M ĥ(ℓ)(x) for regression; the majority vote of ĥ(1)(x), …, ĥ(M)(x) for classification \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} Bagging reduces the variance of the machine learning method used for the base learners: each base learner is trained on a different resample, so their prediction errors are only partly correlated. In an idealized setting of bagging with M base learners that deliver uncorrelated predictions, each with variance σ2, the averaged prediction has variance σ2/M. In general the predictions are correlated. For M identically distributed predictions, each with variance σ2 and with pairwise correlation ρ, the averaged prediction has variance \rho \sigma^{2} + \frac{1-\rho}{M} \sigma^{2} \text{.} The second term vanishes as M grows, while the first does not: the correlation between the base learners sets a lower bound ρ σ2 that no number of base learners brings down. Fig. 3 shows, in a small numerical experiment, the estimated variance of the average of M bagged decision trees against the value this identity predicts from an estimated σ2 and ρ. The correlation ρ comes from the shared training set. The predictions of the base learners would be independent only if the training set were fixed and given, but it is itself modeled as a random variable, and every base learner is trained on a resample of the same m data points: a resample holds any one of them with probability about 1 - 1/e ≈ 63.2%, two resamples therefore share about (1-1/e)2 ≈ 40%, and all of them share the same empirical distribution. Bagging reduces only the variance of a machine learning method, not its bias. For the regression setting, the average and each of its members have the same expectation, so averaging leaves the bias of a member unchanged. Averaging also yields stability: the learned hypothesis depends only weakly on any single data point of the training set. Consider any machine learning method with predictions in [0,1] whose base learners are each trained on a share p of the m data points, drawn without replacement, and whose predictions are averaged over all such subsamples. Then, removing a single data point from the training set changes the prediction at a test point by more than ε for at most a δ-fraction of the removed data points, for every pair (ε, δ) with δ ε2 ≥ (1)/(4(m-1)) · (p)/(1-p). This guarantee holds for every training set and requires nothing of the base learner beyond the bounded predictions — the stability is created by the averaging itself. A random forest applies bagging to decision trees and, in addition, lets each split choose only among a small random subset of the features. The random choice reduces the correlation between the learned decision trees, and a lower correlation means a smaller variance of their average.

terms.name: base learner
terms.abstract: A base learner is the machine learning method that an ensemble method runs several times: an algorithm that reads a training set and returns a learned hypothesis. The ensemble method combines the learned hypotheses of its base learners into a single hypothesis. The main approaches differ in how they build the training sets and how they combine the results. Bagging trains its base learners in parallel on samples drawn by the bootstrap, and boosting trains them in sequence, each on a training set that the earlier results modify. Stacking instead treats their predictions as a feature transformation and learns an aggregation rule on the transformed features.
terms.description: An ensemble that predicts tomorrow's maximum temperature at Krems an der Donau averages the predictions of a linear model, a decision tree, and an artificial neural network, each learned on its own from the same training set. Each of the three is a base learner: a machine learning method used within an ensemble. Formally, it is an algorithm A that reads a training set D(train) and produces a learned hypothesis ĥ=A(D(train)). An ensemble method runs several base learners and combines their learned hypotheses into a more suitable hypothesis. The main approaches differ in how they construct the training sets and combine the results. Bagging trains base learners in parallel on samples generated by the bootstrap. Boosting trains them sequentially, using earlier results to modify the training set for the next base learner. Stacking uses their predictions as a feature transformation and learns an aggregation rule from the transformed features.

terms.name: baseline
terms.abstract: A baseline is a reference level against which the performance of a trained model is compared. The cheapest baseline uses no features at all and predicts the same value for every data point, e.g., the sample mean of numeric label values, or the most frequent label value in classification. Any useful method must beat that level. Baselines can be obtained from human performance, from an existing machine learning method, or from a probabilistic model. Given an accurate probabilistic model of the data generation, the smallest achievable risk is the Bayes risk, incurred by the Bayes estimator of the label given the features. In practice, however, the Bayes estimator is infeasible for at least two reasons. First, the probability distribution of the data generation process might be impossible to determine. Second, computing the Bayes risk might be computationally too expensive.
terms.description: On two days of 2024, a weather station Krems an der Donau (Austria) recorded the same minimum temperature of 11.8 ∘C, but a maximum of 13.2 ∘C on one day and 29.9 ∘C on the other. No hypothesis that predicts the maximum daytime temperature from the minimum can be right on both days. Whatever loss a hypothesis incurs on those two days is unavoidable, so a measured loss above zero is not by itself a sign of a poor machine learning method. More generally, consider a machine learning method that produces a learned hypothesis (or trained model) ĥ ∈ H. It is evaluated by computing the average loss on a test set. The question is whether the learned hypothesis is already close to optimal. If it is, little is gained by collecting more data or by spending more computation to improve it. Answering the question needs a baseline: a reference level for the average loss, either the smallest that any method can achieve or the level that any useful method must beat. Sometimes a baseline is computed from the dataset itself, as in the scatterplot of Fig. 1. The figure shows weather records of the station Krems an der Donau (Austria). Each of the 366 days of 2024 is a data point whose feature x is the minimum air temperature of the day and whose label y is its maximum air temperature. For the 15 data points whose x is between 11.5 ∘C and 12.5 ∘C, the corresponding label ranged from 13.2 ∘C to 33.4 ∘C. Two of these data points even share the same feature value x = 11.8, with labels 13.2 and 29.9. A hypothesis is a map, so it assigns both days the same prediction. On these two data points it therefore incurs an average squared error loss of at least (16.7/2)2 ≈ 69.7. The same holds wherever data points share a feature value: the spread of their labels determines an average loss that no hypothesis, however learned, can avoid. The gray strips of Fig. 1 collect data points with very similar feature values. Each strip holds at least four data points and is drawn over the range of labels those data points carry. A strip is therefore narrow where data points are dense along the feature axis and wide where they are sparse, and it is tall wherever those data points carry very different labels. Computing the sample variance of the labels within each strip and averaging the results across all strips yields 18.75 (in squared degrees Celsius). The resulting value, 18.75 squared degrees Celsius, is an estimate of the smallest average squared error loss any hypothesis can achieve on these data points. The hypothesis learned by linear regression, the solid line of Fig. 1, incurs an average squared error loss of 19.17, its training error. The training error lies within three percent of the baseline, evidence that little is left to gain. Baselines can provide lower bounds or upper bounds on the achievable average loss. The strip-wise estimate of Fig. 1 approximates a lower bound, the Bayes risk defined below: no hypothesis has a smaller risk. An upper bound, i.e., a baseline that any useful method should beat, comes from a trivial hypothesis map that does not depend on the features at all. For numeric labels, such a trivial prediction could be the sample mean of the labels in the training set. In classification, the constant prediction could be the label value of the majority class in the training set. Its accuracy is the share of that class, which on imbalanced data is already high. For the temperature dataset of Fig. 1, the constant prediction by the sample mean incurs an average squared error loss of 84.64, more than four times the above baseline value 18.75. A second source of a baseline is a probabilistic model, which provides a precise notion of a baseline that applies to any machine learning method. In particular, the Bayes risk is the risk of the optimal hypothesis: the Bayes estimator of the label y of a data point, given its features x. For the squared error loss, the Bayes risk equals the expectation of the posterior variance, taken over the features. The strip-wise estimate in Fig. 1 approximates the Bayes risk by local averaging: the sample variance of the labels within a strip around feature value x' approximates the conditional variance σ2y | x'. The average of the strip-wise sample variances approximates the expectation Eσ2y | x. This probabilistic interpretation also motivates the constant baseline above. The constant prediction of the majority class is itself a Bayes estimator for a probabilistic model P(y) that ignores the features of data points. Under the 0/1 loss, the Bayes estimator assigns the label with the largest posterior probability. For a probabilistic model that does not consider features, the posterior distribution equals the prior distribution of the label and, in turn, the Bayes estimator is the most probable label. The Bayes risk is then the probability that the label takes a value that is different from the most likely one. For a given choice of loss function, the Bayes estimator (if it exists) is fully determined by the probability distribution P. However, computing the Bayes estimator and Bayes risk presents two main challenges. First, the probability distribution P is unknown and must be estimated from observed data. Second, even if P were known, exact probabilistic inference can be computationally infeasible for general probabilistic models, such as multiply connected Bayesian belief networks. A widely-used probabilistic model for data points with numeric features and label is the multivariate normal distribution ( x,y ) ~ N(μ,C). Here, for the squared error loss, the Bayes estimator is the posterior mean μy|x := Ey | x of the label y, given the features x. The corresponding Bayes risk is the posterior variance σ2y|x (see Fig. 2). It is the baseline a trained hypothesis ĥ is compared against. Fig. 2 shows its prediction ĥ(x) beside the posterior mean. For the multivariate normal distribution, this posterior variance does not depend on x. More specifically, it is the reciprocal of the corresponding diagonal entry C-1, the inverse of the covariance matrix C: σ2y|x = 1 / [C-1]y,y. In practice, the mean vector μ and the covariance matrix C can be estimated from a dataset by the sample mean and the sample covariance matrix. The baselines so far are derived from the data or from a probabilistic model. Three further approaches to constructing a baseline use existing methods for determining predictions. First, a baseline might be obtained from human performance, e.g., the misclassification rate of dermatologists who diagnose skin cancer from images. Second, for LLMs, baselines are often obtained from a benchmark, i.e., a fixed collection of test problems together with an evaluation protocol. As an example, the benchmark GSM8K measures the ability of a large language model to solve grade-school mathematics word problems. A third source is an existing machine learning method that is unsuitable for the intended machine learning application, e.g., because it is computationally too expensive. The test set error obtained from such a method can still serve as a baseline.

terms.name: binary classification
terms.abstract: Binary classification refers to machine learning applications with a binary label space. The goal of binary classification is to assign each data point to one of two classes, each class represented by one of the two label values. Strictly speaking, a binary classifier is a hypothesis map from the feature space to a binary label space. However, it is customary to construct such a classifier by comparing the value of a real-valued hypothesis map against a threshold. Linear classifiers are obtained from the sign of a linear hypothesis map. A binary classifier partitions the feature space into two decision regions separated by a decision boundary, which is a hyperplane for a linear classifier. The natural loss function is the 0/1 loss, whose average over a dataset is 1 minus the accuracy. However, this loss function is hard to optimize for training methods, and its average on imbalanced data is dominated by the majority label value, so it does not indicate which of the two kinds of mistake a classifier makes. Practical methods therefore often use other loss functions for model training and validation.
terms.description: A frost warning answers one question: will the temperature in the coming night fall below 0 degrees Celsius? The answer is yes or no, nothing in between. Is an email spam? Will a credit applicant default on the loan? Does a biopsy image show malignant tissue? Binary classification is the machine learning problem behind all of these questions: predict, from the features of a data point, which of two values its label, a number y, takes. The label records the answer for one data point. It describes what the data point is asked about and not the data point itself: the label of a biopsy image says whether the tissue shown in the image is malignant. Binary classification is classification with a label space Y that holds two elements. Each data point carries one label, and that label takes one of the two values. The two values are usually written (or encoded) as Y = -1, +1 or Y = 0, 1. The choice of the two label values (the encoding) is a convention and irrelevant for the basic properties of binary classification methods. However, mathematical expressions about them often assume a particular encoding, such as -1, +1, and need to be modified accordingly if a different encoding, such as 0, 1, is used. Strictly speaking, a binary classifier is a hypothesis map that takes values in a binary label space Y. It is usually built from a real-valued hypothesis map h: X → R, which assigns the number h(x) to the feature vector x of a data point. Here, X is the feature space, the set of all possible feature vectors. The binary classifier compares that number against a threshold. For the label encoding Y = -1, +1 and the threshold 0, the predicted label value of the data point is the sign ŷ = sign(h(x)). The classifier partitions the feature space X into two decision regions, one per label value: the feature vectors with ŷ = +1 and those with ŷ = -1. The two decision regions are separated by the decision boundary, the set of feature vectors x with h(x) = 0. The product y · h(x) of the label y of a data point and the value of h at its feature vector is the margin of h on that data point. The margin is positive exactly when the prediction is right. For a linear classifier the real-valued hypothesis is h(x) = wᵀ x + w0. Its model parameters are the vector w, which holds one entry for each feature, and the number w0. The decision boundary is then the hyperplane wᵀ x + w0 = 0, a straight line when there are two features. The predicted label value is the side of that hyperplane on which x lies, and the distance of x from the hyperplane is |h(x)| / ‖ w ‖. If the model parameters are scaled so that ‖ w ‖ = 1, the margin of h on a correctly classified data point is that distance. A data point that lies on the side of the other label value is misclassified, and its margin is the negative of its distance from the hyperplane. The natural loss function for binary classification is the 0/1 loss: it assigns the loss 1 to a wrong label value and the loss 0 to a right one. Its average over a dataset is therefore the fraction of misclassified data points, and 1 minus that fraction is the accuracy. One of the 8 data points in Fig. 1 is misclassified, so the average 0/1 loss there is 1/8 and the accuracy is 7/8. The shape of the decision regions depends on the model. Fig. 2 shows three classifiers learned from the same training set of 30 days of weather recordings. The linear classifier divides the feature space into two half-planes and misclassifies three of the 30 days. The decision tree sends a data point through a sequence of splits, each of which compares one feature with a threshold and passes the data point to one of two branches. A split thus cuts a region along a line parallel to a feature axis, and the decision regions of the decision tree are unions of axis-parallel rectangles. A leaf is a node with no split below it, and it holds the label value predicted for the data points that reach it. Grown until every leaf is reached by data points of a single label value, the decision tree predicts the label value of every day in the training set correctly. The artificial neural network has a curve as decision boundary and also predicts every day of the training set correctly. The accuracies on the training set do not decide between the three classifiers. That decision needs validation, the assessment of a learned hypothesis on data points outside the training set it was learned from. On 170 further days, which form a validation set, the linear classifier is the most accurate of the three. The decision tree and the artificial neural network have adapted their decision regions to single days of the training set, which is overfitting. The average 0/1 loss is easy to compute for validation, but it is a difficult objective for training. Empirical risk minimization with the 0/1 loss results in computationally hard optimization problems. Practical methods therefore minimize a convex surrogate of the 0/1 loss. The hinge loss gives the support vector machine, and the logistic loss gives logistic regression. Fig. 3 shows the three loss functions as functions of the margin. The average 0/1 loss is not only challenging as an objective for training but can also be misleading. A high accuracy need not indicate a useful classifier. Of the 30 days of the training set and the 170 days of the validation set together, only 39 are followed by frost. These label values are imbalanced data, and the constant baseline that always returns the majority label value -1 reaches an accuracy of 0.805 on them. That baseline never warns of a frost: its recall, the fraction of the frost days it finds, is 0. The accuracy also does not indicate which of the two mistakes a classifier makes, a wrong +1 or a wrong -1, and the two mistakes differ in cost. For the frost warning, a wrong -1 leaves a fruit grower's blossoms unprotected in a frost, while a wrong +1 costs one night of covering or heating them. The two mistakes are therefore not interchangeable, and the classifier is chosen so that wrong -1 predictions are rare, at the price of a lower accuracy. The hidden imbalance and the hidden kind of mistake are the two reasons to report the confusion matrix, and the precision, recall, and F1 score computed from it, beside the accuracy.

terms.name: boosting
terms.abstract: Boosting is an ensemble method that sequentially combines simple base learners, also called weak learners. At each iteration, a base learner uses a modified training set constructed from the original training set and the current predictions. Gradient boosting replaces the labels by negative loss partial derivatives, while adaptive boosting retains the labels and changes the weights of the data points. The resulting hypothesis is an additive combination of the learned corrections.
terms.description: The weather station Krems an der Donau records the daily minimum and maximum temperature. Each day is a data point with the minimum temperature as its feature x and the maximum temperature as its label y (Fig. 1). The figure also shows a hypothesis learned by a depth-one decision tree. This tree is too simple to capture the relation between x and y. Boosting improves the hypothesis by adding another hypothesis that corrects its prediction errors. The two curves correspond to the first two iterations of this process. Boosting is an ensemble method that sequentially combines base learners to obtain a more accurate hypothesis. The base learners are typically simple models, such as shallow decision trees, and are also called weak learners. In contrast to ensemble methods such as bagging and stacking, boosting trains its base learners sequentially. At iteration t, a base learner learns a hypothesis ĥ(t) from a modified training set D(train)(t). This training set is constructed from the original training set D(train) and the predictions of h̃(t-1) (Fig. 2). Boosting methods start from an initial hypothesis h̃(0), which is iteratively improved by the update \begin{equation} \widetilde{h}^{(t)} = \widetilde{h}^{(t-1)}+ \eta^{(t)} \widehat{h}^{(t)}\text{,}\qquad t=1,\ldots,T\text{.} \end{equation} Here, η(t) is a learning rate and ĥ(t) the hypothesis of the t-th base learner (see Fig. 3). The additive updates Eq. (1) therefore form a sequence of aggregate hypotheses. Different boosting methods construct D(train)(t) differently. Gradient boosting replaces the label y of each data point (x,y) by the negative partial derivative of its loss with respect to the current prediction, \[ -\left. \frac{\partial L\left(({\mathbf x},y),z \right)}{\partial z} \right|_{z=\widetilde{h}^{(t-1)}({\mathbf x})}. \] These values are pseudo-labels, also called negative gradients. This construction applies when the loss function depends on the hypothesis through its prediction. For the squared error loss, the pseudo-labels are proportional to the prediction errors y-h̃(t-1)(x). Algorithm 1 summarizes a basic form of gradient boosting. \begin{algorithm}[H] \caption{Gradient boosting } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex Input: training set D(train) = (x(1), y(1)), …, (x(m), y(m)), base learner, loss function L((x,y),z ), learning rates η(1), …, η(T), iteration count T \State choose a constant hypothesis h̃(0) minimizing the training set loss \For{t = 1, …, T} \State compute the pseudo-labels ỹ(r,t) := -.∂ L((x(r), y(r)),z )∂ z |z=h̃(t-1) (x(r)) for r = 1, …, m \State learn ĥ(t) by applying the base learner to the feature vectors x(r) with ỹ(r,t) as labels \State update h̃(t) according to the additive update Eq. (1) \EndFor \Statex Output: h̃(T) \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} Gradient boosting can be viewed as an extension of gradient descent from updates of a finite-dimensional model parameter to updates in a hypothesis space. For the squared error loss and a base learner that uses linear regression, this connection is exact under the orthogonality and normalization condition stated below. At iteration t, Algorithm 1 learns a linear map that predicts the residuals y(r)-(x(r))ᵀ w(t-1), for r=1,…,m. If the feature matrix X=(x(1),…, x(m))ᵀ has full column rank, the model parameter of this map is the unique least-squares solution \[ \Delta{\mathbf w}^{(t)}= ({\mathbf X}^{\top}{\mathbf X})^{-1}{\mathbf X}^{\top} \big({\mathbf y}-{\mathbf X}{\mathbf w}^{(t-1)}\big). \] If the columns of X are also orthogonal and normalized such that XᵀX=mI, then \[ \Delta{\mathbf w}^{(t)}= \frac{1}{m}{\mathbf X}^{\top} \big({\mathbf y}-{\mathbf X}{\mathbf w}^{(t-1)}\big), \] which is the negative gradient, at w(t-1), of the scaled average squared error loss f(w) := (1)/(2m) ‖ y-Xw ‖22. The factor 1/2 cancels the factor 2 that differentiating the square produces. With matching initialization and learning rates, the boosting iterates satisfy h̃(t)= h(w(t)) and coincide with the gradient descent iterates. Adaptive boosting applies boosting to binary classification. Like gradient boosting in Algorithm 1, it uses the additive update Eq. (1). However, it uses a different construction for the training set D(train)(t): the prediction errors of h̃(t-1) determine weights, with larger weights assigned to misclassified data points. Algorithm 2 presents adaptive boosting.M1. \begin{algorithm}[H] \caption{Adaptive boosting.M1 } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex Input: training set D(train) = (x(r),y(r)) r=1m with y(r)∈-1,1, hypothesis spaces H(1),…,H(T) of hypotheses h: X → -1,1, iteration count T \State q(r) := 1/m for r=1,…,m \State h̃(0)(x):=0 \For{t=1,…,T} \State ĥ(t) ∈ h∈H(t) Σr=1m q(r) L(0/1)((x(r), y(r)),h ) \State ε(t) := Σr=1m q(r) L(0/1)((x(r), y(r)),ĥ(t) ) \State η(t) := (1)/(2)ln ( (1-ε(t))/(ε(t))) \State update h̃(t) according to the additive update Eq. (1) \State q(r) := q(r)exp (-η(t) y(r) ĥ(t)(x(r))) for r=1,…,m \State normalize the weights so that Σr=1mq(r)=1 \EndFor \Statex Output: ĥ(x) = sign ( h̃(T)(x)) \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} At the start of iteration t, the normalized weights satisfy \[ q^{(r)}= \frac{\exp \left(-y^{(r)} \widetilde{h}^{(t-1)} ({\mathbf x}^{(r)})\right)} {\sum_{r'=1}^{m} \exp \left(-y^{(r')} \widetilde{h}^{(t-1)} ({\mathbf x}^{(r')})\right)}. \] Since the normalized sample weights q(r) in the preceding display sum to 1, the quantity ε(t) defined in Algorithm 2 is the weighted average 0/1 loss of ĥ(t) on the training set used at iteration t. A single iteration of adaptive boosting reduces the average exponential loss, which is the empirical risk \[ \widehat{L}\big(\widetilde{h}^{(t)}|\mathcal{D}^{(\rm train)}\big) := \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \exp \left(-y^{(r)} \widetilde{h}^{(t)} ({\mathbf x}^{(r)})\right). \] Substituting the additive update Eq. (1) into this empirical risk gives \[ \widehat{L}\big(\widetilde{h}^{(t)}|\mathcal{D}^{(\rm train)}\big) =\kappa^{(t)} \widehat{L}\big(\widetilde{h}^{(t-1)}|\mathcal{D}^{(\rm train)}\big), \] where \[ \kappa^{(t)}=(1-\epsilon^{(t)}) e^{-\eta^{(t)}}+\epsilon^{(t)} e^{\eta^{(t)}} =2\sqrt{\epsilon^{(t)}(1-\epsilon^{(t)})}. \] Thus, if 0<ε(t)<1/2, then 0<κ(t)<1. For this iteration, scalar multiplication by κ(t) is a contractive operator on the average exponential loss. Since the 0/1 loss is bounded by the exponential loss, repeated contractions also reduce an upper bound on the training error. This argument concerns the empirical loss; it does not assert that the hypotheses themselves form a contractive sequence.

terms.name: bootstrap
terms.abstract: The bootstrap is a stochastic algorithm that generates perturbed variants, referred to as bootstrap samples, of a given dataset. Each bootstrap sample is obtained by randomly selecting data points, with replacement, from the original dataset. The bootstrap samples have the same size as the original dataset. However, they might repeat some of the original data points while omitting others. Several bootstrap samples allow the study of the properties of a machine learning method. For example, a robust machine learning method delivers similar model parameters for two datasets that differ only in the random fluctuations of the data generation. Bootstrap samples can also be used to estimate a confidence interval for a validation error. Another application of the bootstrap is bagging, where the hypotheses learned from the bootstrap samples are aggregated into one.
terms.description: Five days of weather recordings at Krems an der Donau are all the data there is. Each day is a data point, its feature the minimum temperature of the day and its label the maximum temperature of the same day (Fig. 1). This dataset is small: it does not allow the training of a high-dimensional model, and a hypothesis learned from it depends on which five days happened to be recorded. The bootstrap is a stochastic algorithm, stated as Algorithm 1, that generates additional datasets from the recorded one, the so-called bootstrap samples, and so makes that dependence measurable. Fig. 1 shows two bootstrap samples obtained from Algorithm 1. A bootstrap sample can contain a data point of D several times, so it is a list of data points rather than a set. The bootstrap is based on the independent and identically distributed assumption. \begin{algorithm}[H] \caption{The bootstrap } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex Input: dataset D = z(1), …, z(m), number B of bootstrap samples \For{b = 1, …, B} \For{r = 1, …, m} \State draw an index i uniformly at random from 1, …, m \State z̃(r) := z(i) \EndFor \State D̃(b) := (z̃(1), …, z̃(m)) \EndFor \Statex Output: bootstrap samples D̃(1), …, D̃(B) \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} Here, a dataset D = z(1), …, z(m) is interpreted as the realizations of m independent and identically distributed RVs with a common probability distribution P. That P is unknown and must be estimated from D itself. The bootstrap estimates it by the empirical distribution P(D) of D. For every event A, the fraction of the data points z(r) that fall into it approximates its probability by the law of large numbers, \[ \frac{1}{m} \big| r: {\mathbf z}^{(r)} \in \mathcal{A} \big| \approx \mathbb{P}\left(\mathcal{A}\right) \text{.} \] The empirical distribution P(D) is a fully specified probability distribution and can be sampled as often as wanted. As many data points and as many datasets as needed can therefore be generated from the collected dataset. The gain is copies, not information. Each copy keeps the size m of D, because the quantity being imitated is the spread of a dataset of that size drawn from P. Nor does a copy contain new data points: P(D) places all its mass on the m data points observed, so no draw can produce one that D does not already contain. A variant, the smoothed bootstrap, draws from a smoothed version of P(D) in which each data point is replaced by a small bump-shaped probability density function; it produces data points that D does not contain, which the bootstrap itself never does. Sampling m data points from P(D) is the same as drawing m times from D with replacement, which is what Algorithm 1 does: every draw is made from the whole of D, so a data point can be drawn twice and another not at all (Fig. 2). The number B of bootstrap samples is limited only by the computation they cost. A data point is left out of a bootstrap sample with probability (1 - 1/m)m, so it appears in one with probability 1 - (1 - 1/m)m, which approaches 1 - 1/e ≈ 0.63 as m grows, since (1 - 1/m)m converges to 1/e. The number of distinct data points in a bootstrap sample follows from that one probability alone. Write Ir for the random variable that takes the value one when z(r) appears in D̃(b) and zero otherwise. The count of distinct data points is Σr=1m Ir, so its expectation is \[ {\mathbb{E}} \Big\{ \sum_{r=1}^{m} I_{r} \Big\} = \sum_{r=1}^{m} \mathbb{P}\left(I_{r} = 1\right) = m \big( 1 - (1 - 1/m)^{m} \big) \approx 0.63 m \text{.} \] The Ir are not independent: a day drawn twice forces another to be left out. The expectation of a sum is the sum of the expectations nonetheless. A bootstrap sample therefore holds about 0.63 m distinct data points and overlaps D heavily. That overlap is what separates the bootstrap from k-fold cross-validation, which partitions D into blocks that do not overlap at all. Used naively to estimate the prediction error of a learned hypothesis, the bootstrap therefore evaluates it on data points that entered its own training, and the estimate comes out optimistic. Machine learning training methods can be applied separately to each bootstrap sample, giving the learned hypotheses ĥ(1), …, ĥ(B). A quantity computed from D̃(b) is a bootstrap replication, such as the hypothesis ĥ(b) learned by empirical risk minimization from D̃(b) or its prediction ĥ(b)(x) for a fixed data point. The spread of the B bootstrap replications estimates how much the output of the machine learning method changes due to random fluctuations in the data generation. Fig. 3 shows the bootstrap for learning a linear hypothesis from weather data recorded at Krems an der Donau during 2024, m = 366 days. Each dot is one data point, its feature the minimum temperature and its label the maximum temperature of the day; the figure draws 20 of them. The thick line is the hypothesis learned from all 366 by empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss. The thin lines show bootstrap replications ĥ(b), b = 1, …, B, learned by the same empirical risk minimization problem from bootstrap samples. Their spread is narrow here, and the 95% confidence interval for the slope is [1.05, 1.15]. While basic validation gives a point estimate for the risk of a hypothesis, i.e., the validation error, the bootstrap adds a confidence interval to this point estimate. A hypothesis ĥ is learned once from the training set D(train), and the validation set D(val) is resampled B times with replacement, each bootstrap sample of the size of D(val). Evaluating the same ĥ on each of them gives B estimates of the risk. The sample mean of these estimates is the risk estimate, and the square root of their sample variance is its bootstrap standard error. The estimate plus or minus a standard normal quantile times this standard error is a confidence interval. Bagging is the bootstrap put to a different use: instead of measuring the spread of ĥ(1), …, ĥ(B), it averages them into one hypothesis, which is how a random forest is built from decision trees.

terms.name: concept activation vector (CAV)
terms.abstract: A concept activation vector (CAV) is a direction in the activations of one hidden layer of a deep net that stands for a concept named by a user. The user supplies data points that carry the concept and data points that do not, and a linear classifier is trained to tell the two apart from their activations. The CAV is the direction perpendicular to the hyperplane that separates them, pointing to the concept side. Moving the activations of a data point a little along the CAV changes the score the deep net assigns to a label; the rate of that change is the sensitivity of the prediction to the concept. The fraction of data points with a positive sensitivity is the TCAV score. That score belongs to one layer and one label; it aggregates the per-data point sensitivities and thereby describes a whole class of data points rather than a single prediction.
terms.description: A deep net predicts from five consecutive days of weather at a station whether it rains on the sixth day. Whether it uses the notion of a heat wave, five hot days in a row, to arrive at that prediction cannot be decided by inspecting a single neuron. A heat wave is not a feature the network was built with, since its features are the daily temperatures and rain amounts. Nor need it be represented by any one neuron. A concept is a property that a user can name and exemplify but that the network was not built to compute, such as a heat wave. The concept is specified by examples instead: five-day windows that form a heat wave, the positive examples, and windows that do not, the negative examples. A CAV turns such a concept into a direction in the activations of one hidden layer, the direction along which the positive examples lie apart from the negative ones. Consider such a deep net, with several hidden layers, trained to predict the label of a data point from its feature vector; the trained network is the learned hypothesis ĥ. Fix one hidden layer and write z = f(x) for its activations, with f the function computed by the layers up to that point. The deep net is applied to the positive and to the negative examples of a concept C. A binary linear classifier g(z), whose features are those activations, is trained to tell the two apart. Its decision boundary is a hyperplane; the CAV for C is the normal vector ŵ of that hyperplane. A hyperplane has two normal vectors, one pointing to each side. The CAV is the one pointing towards the side that g(z) assigns to the concept class. Training g(z) with the positive examples as the positive class delivers this orientation, and when the two sets of activations are linearly separable, it is the side of the positive examples. In the terminology of mechanistic interpretability, this direction defines a feature of the trained deep net, the projection of the activations onto it: a human-interpretable concept represented by a direction in the space of activations. Fig. 1 draws the CAV of the heat-wave concept for a deep net with two hidden layers of 16 neurons, trained on the daily weather at Krems an der Donau of the training years 2000--2018 and tested on 2019--2024. A data point is a window of five days, its feature vector holds the daily maximum and minimum temperature and the rain amount of each day, and its label says whether at least 1 mm of rain fell on the sixth day. The concept is specified by 40 heat waves, windows with a daily maximum of at least 30 ∘C on all five days, and 40 windows that are not, drawn from the windows of the record. The plane drawn passes through the mean activation of the first hidden layer and is spanned by the CAV and the direction orthogonal to it along which the activations vary most. The concept hyperplane therefore meets the plane in a vertical line, and the CAV is its horizontal axis. Two classification problems appear in the figure. The first is the concept classification that g(z) solves on the activations. The second is the task the deep net is trained for, whose decision boundary on the plane is the solid line: rain is predicted to its right, where every heat wave lies. The CAV depends on the examples that specify the concept: training g(z) on all 9127 windows of the record instead turns it by 26 degrees. Like any explanation, a CAV must be understandable and faithful (see explanation). It is understandable by construction: the user supplies the examples that define the concept. Faithfulness is a separate question, because the concept is a direction in the activations whether or not the deep net responds to it. Testing with CAVs (TCAV) decides it. Write the trained deep net as a concatenation of two functions, the activations z = f(x) of the chosen hidden layer and a score s(z) that the remaining layers assign to one label. The conceptual sensitivity of a data point is the directional derivative of that score along the unit CAV v := ŵ / ‖ ŵ ‖, which for differentiable s equals the inner product of the gradient of s with v, \begin{equation} S({\mathbf x}) := \langle \nabla s\big(f({\mathbf x})\big), {\mathbf v} \rangle \text{.} \end{equation} It measures how much the score for that label moves when the activations move a little towards the concept. The orientation convention gives the sign its meaning: S(x) > 0 says the score rises towards the concept, and the opposite normal vector would flip every sensitivity. The sensitivity Eq. (1) delivers one number per data point. TCAV collects these numbers over one label: the TCAV score is the fraction of the data points carrying that label for which S(x) > 0. A random set of non-concept data points also yields a CAV, so a single such fraction is not evidence alone. A random concept is a set of data points drawn at random and labeled as if they carried a concept. It is as likely to raise the score as to lower it, so its TCAV score, the fraction of positive sensitivities, is one half on average. The CAV is therefore refitted against many fresh draws of non-concept data points, and the resulting TCAV scores are compared with those of random concepts: a concept the deep net responds to scores consistently away from one half, a random one does not. The explanation delivered is a single number attached to a concept, a label and a layer. Unlike the sensitivity S(x), which is defined for a single data point, it describes a whole class of data points rather than a single prediction. For the deep net of Fig. 1, moving along the heat-wave CAV raises the rain score at every test window followed by rain. A cold wave is five days with a minimum of at most -5 ∘C, and moving along its CAV lowers that score at every one of those windows. The record agrees: rain follows 30% of the heat waves and 16% of the cold waves, against 23% of all windows. Training the linear classifier g(z) and evaluating the sensitivity S(x) both read quantities inside the deep net: the activations f(x) of the chosen layer, and the gradient ∇ s(z) of the score with respect to them. A CAV is therefore unavailable for a system that returns predictions for submitted feature vectors and nothing else, such as a deep net served behind an interface or supplied by a vendor.
