An explanation produced by local interpretable model-agnostic explanations, by contrast, needs predictions and nothing else: its local approximation is fitted to predictions obtained by querying the learned hypothesis ĥ. A second consequence of reading the internals is that a CAV is not a property of ĥ alone: the split into f and s is a choice of layer, and two deep nets that deliver the same ĥ through different layers can have different CAVs. Both functions a CAV involves are defined on the space of activations: g(z) approximates concept membership there, and the sensitivity S(x) is a directional derivative of the score s on that same space. A CAV therefore concerns the interpretability of the deep net rather than its explainability; mechanistic interpretability studies such directions.

terms.name: classification
terms.abstract: Classification is the task of predicting a discrete-valued label for a given data point, based solely on its features. The label belongs to a finite label space: binary classification uses two label values, and multi-class classification more than two. A hypothesis whose predictions take values in the finite label space is a classifier; it partitions the feature space into decision regions separated by the decision boundary. A widely used construction compares a real-valued hypothesis against a threshold to obtain the predicted label. A natural quality measure is the 0/1 loss; since it is neither convex nor differentiable, training methods minimize surrogates such as the logistic loss or the hinge loss, and the learned classifier is judged by the accuracy and the confusion matrix on a test set. When the label space is continuous, the task is regression.
terms.description: A weather station records the minimum and the maximum air temperature of each day. From these two numbers, it must be decided whether the following day brings frost, that is, whether its minimum temperature falls below 0 ∘C. A library must file each incoming text into one of the subject categories mathematics, literature, or engineering. Both are classification problems: the task of predicting a discrete-valued label y of a given data point, based solely on its feature vector x, the vector of its features. The label takes values in a finite label space Y and names the category of the data point. Binary classification uses a label space with two label values, such as Y = -1, 1 with y = 1 marking a frost day; multi-class classification uses more than two label values, such as Y = mathematics, literature, engineering for the texts. When the label space is continuous instead, the task is regression: predicting tomorrow's minimum temperature is regression, predicting whether tomorrow brings frost is classification. Classification is also distinct from clustering: as a form of supervised learning, classification learns from data points whose labels are known, while clustering groups data points without any given labels. A hypothesis whose predictions take values in a finite label space is referred to as a classifier. A classifier partitions the feature space X into decision regions, one region per label value, separated by the decision boundary. All feature vectors in the same decision region obtain the same predicted label, so the decision regions determine the classifier completely (Fig. 1). A widely used construction of a classifier proceeds in two steps. First, a real-valued hypothesis h: X → R quantifies the confidence in one particular label value. Second, the confidence h(x) is compared against a threshold to obtain the prediction ŷ ∈ Y. Logistic regression, for the label space Y = -1, 1, uses a linear map h(x) = wᵀ x as the confidence in the label value 1. This confidence is compared against the threshold 0, \widehat{y} := \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } h({\mathbf x}) \geq 0\text{,} -1 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} The real-valued hypothesis h is not itself the classifier: the classifier is the thresholded map x ↦ ŷ, and calling h the classifier is a slight abuse of language. The two decision regions are then the halfspaces on either side of the hyperplane wᵀ x = 0, as illustrated in Fig. 1. A natural quality measure for a classifier is the 0/1 loss: its average over a dataset is the fraction of misclassified data points, and one minus that fraction is the accuracy. Even the best classifier cannot always achieve zero error: when data points with the same feature vector carry different labels, some misclassifications are unavoidable, and the smallest achievable risk is the Bayes risk. The 0/1 loss is rarely used as the objective function for training: it takes only the values 0 and 1, so it is piecewise constant, neither convex nor differentiable as a function of the model parameters, and its minimization is computationally hard. Practical methods therefore minimize the average of a surrogate loss over the training set: a loss function that approximates the 0/1 loss while having more convenient properties, such as convexity or differentiability. Logistic regression uses the logistic loss, which is convex and differentiable; the support vector machine uses the hinge loss, which is convex but not differentiable. Fig. 2 compares the three as functions of the margin y · h(x). The learned classifier is then judged by the accuracy and the confusion matrix on a test set.

terms.name: cluster
terms.abstract: A cluster is a subset of the data points of a dataset that are more similar to each other than to the data points outside the subset. The measure of similarity is a design choice, such as the Euclidean distance between feature vectors or the edge weights of a similarity graph. In a hard clustering every data point belongs to exactly one cluster; in a soft clustering it belongs to every cluster with a degree of belonging, and the degrees of belonging of one data point sum to one. A clustering method represents a cluster by an object that determines the membership of any data point. Three representations are in use: a cluster centroid, as in k-means; a probability distribution, as the multivariate normal distribution of one component of a Gaussian mixture model; or a densely connected subset of the nodes of a similarity graph, as in graph clustering. The number and the shape of the clusters depend on the method and its hyperparameters: k-means delivers convex clusters, a Gaussian mixture model ellipsoids, and density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise any shape that a chain of nearby data points can trace.
terms.description:
Consider the 366 days of one year at Krems an der Donau, each a data point with a feature vector x ∈ R2 that holds the morning minimum and the maximum daytime temperature of the day. A day in January, with a morning minimum near 0 and a maximum near 5 degrees, resembles the other days of January more than any day of July, whose temperatures lie some 20 degrees higher. A cluster is a subset of the data points of a dataset that are more similar to each other than to the data points outside the subset. Fig. 1(a) shows the two clusters that k-means finds among the days of 2024: 192 cold days and 174 warm days. Every day of January and February is a cold day, and every day of July and August is a warm day. Measured by the Euclidean distance between their feature vectors, two days of the same cluster are 8.0 degrees apart on average, a cold and a warm day 20.2 degrees, and for 364 of the 366 days the most similar other day belongs to the same cluster. The measure of similarity between data points is a design choice. For data points with numeric feature vectors x ∈ Rd, two data points are similar if the Euclidean distance between their feature vectors is small. Data points without numeric feature vectors, such as the members of a social network or the papers of a citation network, are the nodes of a similarity graph whose edge weights measure their similarity directly. Formally, consider a dataset D = x(1), …, x(m). A cluster is a subset C(c) ⊆ 1, …, m of the indices of the data points. A hard clustering into k clusters is a partition of the indices,  egin{equation} \mathcal{C}^{(1)} \cup \cdots \cup \mathcal{C}^{(k)} = \{1, \ldots, m\} \quad 	ext{and} \quad \mathcal{C}^{(c)} \cap \mathcal{C}^{(c')} = \emptyset 	ext{ for } c 
eq c' 	ext{,} \end{equation} so every data point belongs to exactly one cluster, and the hard clustering is recorded by the index of that cluster in 1, …, k. The two clusters of Fig. 1(a) form a partition Eq. (1) of the 366 days. A soft clustering replaces the index by a degree of belonging uc(r) of data point r to every cluster c = 1, …, k,  egin{equation} u_{c}^{(r)} \geq 0 \quad 	ext{and} \quad \sum_{c=1}^{k} u_{c}^{(r)} = 1 \quad 	ext{for } r = 1, \ldots, m 	ext{,} \end{equation} so the degrees of belonging of one data point form a vector in the probability simplex Δk-1. A cluster is then no longer a subset but the map r ↦ uc(r) that grades the membership of every data point. A hard clustering is the special case where every degree of belonging is 0 or 1: the cluster C(c) then consists of the data points with uc(r) = 1, and these clusters form a partition Eq. (1). A clustering method does not store a cluster as a list of indices. It represents the cluster by an object from which the membership of any data point follows, including a data point that does not belong to the dataset. This object is the hypothesis that the method learns, and generalization to new data points is what it is for. Three representations are in use (Fig. 1). First, a cluster centroid w(c) ∈ Rd is a single point of the feature space. It represents a cluster as the set of data points that are nearer to it than to any other cluster centroid,  egin{equation} \mathcal{C}^{(c)} =  ig\{ r: \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(c)} ightVert_{2} \leq \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(c')} ightVert_{2} 	ext{ for all } c' 
eq c  ig\} 	ext{.} \end{equation} This is the hard clustering delivered by k-means, whose cluster centroids minimize the clustering error, an instance of empirical risk minimization. The region of the feature space that satisfies the inequalities in the cluster Eq. (3) is an intersection of halfspaces, one for each other cluster centroid, and therefore convex. For the days at Krems and k = 2, the two cluster centroids are (1.5, 10.5) and (13.4, 26.1), and the boundary between the two clusters is the straight line through their midpoint at a right angle to their connecting segment (Fig. 1(a)). Second, a probability distribution represents a cluster. A Gaussian mixture model represents cluster c by a multivariate normal distribution with mean μ(c) and covariance matrix C(c), drawn with probability pc. The degree of belonging of a data point to cluster c is the posterior distribution of its cluster index given its feature vector, evaluated at c,  egin{equation} u_{c}^{(r)} =  rac{p_{c} \mathcal{N}\left({ oldsymbol \mu}^{(c)},\mathbf{C}^{(c)}ight)  ig({\mathbf x}^{(r)} ig)} {\sum_{c'=1}^{k} p_{c'} \mathcal{N}\left({ oldsymbol \mu}^{(c')},\mathbf{C}^{(c')}ight)  ig({\mathbf x}^{(r)} ig)} 	ext{.} \end{equation} The degrees of belonging Eq. (4) satisfy the constraints Eq. (2), so the result is a soft clustering. The level sets of the probability density function of a multivariate normal distribution are ellipsoids whose axes are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, so a cluster represented this way is an ellipsoid rather than an intersection of halfspaces. For the days at Krems, the covariance matrices learned by the expectation–maximization algorithm have a long axis 2.8 and 2.0 times the short one, tilted by 50 and 46 degrees, so each cluster is elongated along the direction in which both temperatures rise together (Fig. 1(b)). The larger of the two degrees of belonging names the k-means cluster for 335 of the 366 days, and 58 days have a degree of belonging between 0.2 and 0.8 to both clusters. Fig. 1(d) contrasts the two assignments over the year: the k-means index jumps between 0 and 1, while the degree of belonging to the warm cluster is 0 on every day from November to February and passes through intermediate values on days from March to October. Third, for data points that are the nodes V = 1, …, m of a similarity graph with edge weights Ar,r' ≥ 0, a cluster is a subset C ⊆ V of nodes that are densely connected among themselves and sparsely connected to the rest. Graph clustering methods measure this by the sum of the edge weights of the edges leaving the subset, divided by its size,  egin{equation}  rac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|} \sum_{r \in \mathcal{C}} \sum_{r' 
otin \mathcal{C}} A_{r,r'} 	ext{,} \end{equation} and a hard clustering into k clusters is good if the sum of the ratios Eq. (5) over its clusters, the ratio cut, is small. Spectral clustering minimizes the ratio cut approximately. For the days at Krems, the k-nearest-neighbor graph that joins each day to its 10 nearest neighbors, with unit edge weights, has 2209 edges; 2174 of them join two days of the same k-means cluster and 35 join a cold with a warm day. The ratio cut of the two clusters is 0.38, against 12.07 for the split of the days into those with an odd and those with an even index (Fig. 1(c)). Which subsets of a dataset are clusters therefore depends on the method and its hyperparameters, not on the dataset alone. The number k of clusters is an input to k-means and to a Gaussian mixture model, while density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise determines it from a distance threshold and a minimum cluster size. The shape of a cluster follows from its representation: an intersection of halfspaces for k-means, an ellipsoid for a Gaussian mixture model, and any shape that a chain of nearby data points can trace for density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise and for graph clustering. The same 366 days are split by a straight line in Fig. 1(a), while in Fig. 1(b) each day receives a degree of belonging to each of two tilted ellipses. The choice of representation is a choice of hypothesis space, and the number of clusters is chosen like any other hyperparameter, since the clustering error alone cannot choose it. Clusters serve as categories where no label provides them, the setting of unsupervised learning. An energy supplier can treat the cold days of Fig. 1(a) as the heating season and classify a new day by the side of the boundary line on which its feature vector falls. In image segmentation, a cluster of pixels with similar colors is one region of the image, and in customer segmentation a cluster of customers with similar purchase records is one market segment.

terms.name: cluster centroid
terms.abstract: A cluster centroid is a vector that represents a cluster of data points: among all vectors, it minimizes the summed loss over the data points of the cluster, where the loss measures how poorly a vector stands in for a data point. Under the squared Euclidean distance the cluster centroid is the mean of the feature vectors in the cluster, under the Euclidean distance their geometric median, and under the sum of absolute differences the median of each feature. k-means assigns a data point to its nearest cluster centroid, a rule that is a linear classifier whose decision boundary between two cluster centroids is the hyperplane through their midpoint and perpendicular to their difference. The averaging step of Lloyd's algorithm recomputes each cluster centroid as the mean of its cluster, and at a fixed point every cluster centroid is the mean of the data points nearest to it. The mean moves with every data point, so one outlier shifts it by the displacement divided by the size of the cluster, while the geometric median and the coordinate-wise median move little. A soft clustering method, such as a Gaussian mixture model, uses the mean weighted by the degrees of belonging as its cluster centroid. Replacing every data point by its cluster centroid compresses a dataset to k vectors and one cluster index per data point.
terms.description: Consider the 366 days of 2024 at Krems an der Donau, each a data point with a feature vector x ∈ R2 that holds the morning minimum and the maximum daytime temperature of the day. k-means with k = 2 decomposes these days into 192 cold days and 174 warm days, and it describes each cluster by a single vector: a typical cold day, (1.5, 10.5), and a typical warm day, (13.4, 26.1). Such a vector is a cluster centroid. A hard clustering method that represents each cluster c = 1, …, k by a cluster centroid w(c) ∈ Rd assigns a data point to the cluster whose cluster centroid is nearest, as Fig. 1(a) shows for the days at Krems. Which vector represents a cluster best is decided by a loss function L(x,w ) that measures how poorly a vector w stands in for the feature vector x of a data point. The cluster centroid of a cluster with index set C(c) ⊆ 1, …, m is a vector that minimizes the summed loss over its data points, \begin{equation} {{\mathbf w}}^{(c)} \in \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}} \sum_{r \in \mathcal{C}^{(c)}} L\left({\mathbf x}^{(r)},{\mathbf w} \right) \text{.} \end{equation} For the squared Euclidean distance L(x,w ) = ‖ x - w ‖22, the summed loss is a strictly convex quadratic function of w, and its unique minimizer is the mean of the feature vectors, \begin{equation} {{\mathbf w}}^{(c)} = \frac{1}{\big|\mathcal{C}^{(c)}\big|} \sum_{r \in \mathcal{C}^{(c)}} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \text{,} \end{equation} since the gradient of the summed loss vanishes exactly where the deviations x(r) - w sum to zero. The two cluster centroids of the days at Krems are the means Eq. (2) of the cold and of the warm days. Under the Euclidean distance itself, L(x,w ) = ‖ x - w ‖2, the minimizer of the summed loss Eq. (1) is the geometric median of the feature vectors. It has no closed form and is computed by Weiszfeld's fixed-point iteration, \begin{equation} {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} = \mathcal{F}\big({\mathbf w}^{(t)}\big) := \frac{\sum_{r \in \mathcal{C}^{(c)}} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \big/ \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {\mathbf w}^{(t)} \right\rVert_{2}} {\sum_{r \in \mathcal{C}^{(c)}} 1 \big/ \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {\mathbf w}^{(t)} \right\rVert_{2}} \quad \text{for } t = 0, 1, \ldots \text{,} \end{equation} a mean of the feature vectors weighted by the reciprocal of their distance to the current iterate. A fixed point of the iteration Eq. (3) that coincides with no feature vector is a point where the unit vectors towards the feature vectors sum to zero, which is the optimality condition of the geometric median, and the summed loss never increases from one iterate to the next. Under the sum of absolute differences, L(x,w ) = ‖ x - w ‖1, the summed loss separates into one problem per feature, so the cluster centroid holds the median of each feature over the cluster. For the warm days at Krems, the three choices give (13.4, 26.1), (13.5, 26.0), and (13.7, 26.1), within 0.3 degrees of each other; Weiszfeld's iteration started from the mean stops after 60 iterations. For a fixed cluster, the minimization Eq. (1) is empirical risk minimization over the hypothesis space of constant maps h(x) = w. The cluster centroid is the hypothesis that predicts one vector for every data point of the cluster, and the summed loss is its training error up to the factor 1 / |C(c)|. The k cluster centroids together are the model parameters of the hypothesis h(x) = w(c⋆(x)) learned by k-means, which sends a feature vector to its nearest cluster centroid, \begin{equation} c^{\star}({\mathbf x}) := \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{c = 1, \ldots, k} \left\lVert {\mathbf x} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(c)} \right\rVert_{2} \text{.} \end{equation} The average of the loss ‖ x - h(x) ‖22 over the dataset is the clustering error. The nearest-centroid rule Eq. (4) is a linear classifier. For two cluster centroids, a feature vector is nearer to w(1) than to w(2) if and only if \begin{equation} \big({{\mathbf w}}^{(2)} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(1)}\big)^{\top} {\mathbf x} \leq \frac{1}{2} \Big( \left\lVert {{\mathbf w}}^{(2)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} - \left\lVert {{\mathbf w}}^{(1)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \Big) \text{,} \end{equation} which follows from expanding the two squared Euclidean distances. The decision boundary of the linear rule Eq. (5) is the hyperplane through the midpoint of the two cluster centroids and perpendicular to their difference, the dashed line of Fig. 1(a). Each cluster is an intersection of halfspaces and so a convex region. The rule Eq. (4) also assigns a data point outside the dataset. A day with morning minimum 5 and maximum 18 degrees lies at distances 8.3 and 11.7 from the two cluster centroids of the days at Krems, so it is a cold day. The same rule serves classification when each class of a labeled dataset is represented by one or several cluster centroids and a new data point receives the label of the nearest one. Lloyd's algorithm for k-means alternates the assignment Eq. (4) of every data point with an averaging step that recomputes each cluster centroid as the mean Eq. (2) of the data points assigned to it. At a fixed point, each cluster centroid is the mean of the data points nearest to it. Two conditions then hold at the same time: each cluster centroid minimizes the summed loss Eq. (1) over its cluster, and each cluster consists of the data points nearest to its cluster centroid. For the days at Krems, started from the means of the colder and of the warmer half of the days, Lloyd's algorithm reaches this fixed point after 2 iterations. Changing the loss function changes only the averaging step: the geometric median gives k-medians, and restricting the cluster centroid to be one of the data points of its cluster gives k-medoids, which needs only the pairwise distances between data points. For a Bregman divergence as loss function, the mean Eq. (2) remains the cluster centroid. The mean Eq. (2) moves with every data point of its cluster: adding a vector to one feature vector adds the same vector divided by |C(c)| to the mean, whatever the other data points are. If the maximum temperature of the hottest warm day at Krems were recorded as 999.9, a value some archives use to mark a missing record, the mean of the 174 warm days would move by 965.6 / 174 = 5.5 degrees (Fig. 1(b)). The geometric median would move by 0.03 degrees and the coordinate-wise median not at all. The squared Euclidean distance gives the largest distances the largest weight, which is why cluster centroids built from an unsquared norm are less sensitive to outliers. A soft clustering method assigns each data point r to every cluster c with a degree of belonging uc(r) ∈ [0, 1], with Σc=1k uc(r) = 1. Its cluster centroid is the mean of all feature vectors weighted by their degrees of belonging, \begin{equation} {\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)} = \frac{\sum_{r=1}^{m} u_{c}^{(r)} {\mathbf x}^{(r)}} {\sum_{r=1}^{m} u_{c}^{(r)}} \text{,} \end{equation} whose denominator is the effective number of data points in the cluster. For a Gaussian mixture model, which represents the cluster c by a multivariate normal distribution with mean μ(c) and covariance matrix C(c), the degree of belonging is the posterior distribution of the cluster index, and the weighted mean Eq. (6) is the M-step of the expectation–maximization algorithm for μ(c). Hard clustering is the case uc(r) ∈ 0, 1, where the weighted mean Eq. (6) is the mean Eq. (2). For the days at Krems, the expectation–maximization algorithm started from the two k-means cluster centroids stops at the means (3.1, 12.4) and (14.2, 27.5), which lie 2.5 and 1.5 degrees from them. Of the 366 days, 58 have no degree of belonging above 0.8, and each of them is counted in part by both cluster centroids. Replacing every data point by its cluster centroid compresses a dataset to k vectors and one cluster index per data point, which is vector quantization. The 366 days at Krems become two typical days and one bit per day, and a photograph whose pixels are clustered by color becomes a palette of k colors and one palette index per pixel. The clustering error is the average distortion of this compression, and minimizing it over the cluster centroids is the task from which Lloyd's algorithm arose.

terms.name: clustering
terms.abstract: Clustering decomposes a dataset into subsets, called clusters, such that data points within the same cluster are more similar to each other than to data points in other clusters. Clustering methods differ in the measure of similarity between data points, in the representation of a cluster, and in whether each data point is assigned to exactly one cluster (hard clustering) or to several with varying degrees of belonging (soft clustering). k-means represents a cluster by a cluster centroid and a Gaussian mixture model by a multivariate normal distribution, so their clusters are convex regions and ellipsoids. Graph clustering represents the data points as the nodes of a similarity graph and uses its weighted edges to determine the clusters.
terms.description: A photograph taken in the Wachau shows sky, clouds, forested slopes, sunlit vineyards and rock (Fig. 1(a)). Cutting it into patches of 5 × 5 pixels gives 12288 data points, each characterized by a feature vector x ∈ R3 that holds the mean red, green and blue values of the patch. Clustering is the task of decomposing such a dataset into clusters, such that data points within the same cluster are more similar to each other than to data points in other clusters. Painting each patch in the mean color of its cluster divides the photograph into regions, an image segmentation. Fig. 1(b)--(f) shows the segmentations delivered by five clustering methods, k-means, a Gaussian mixture model, density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise, spectral clustering and convex clustering. The number k of clusters is either an input, as in k-means, or determined by the method from its other hyperparameters, as in density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise. Clustering methods differ in three design choices: \begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*)] \item the measure of similarity between data points, e.g., the Euclidean distance between their feature vectors, which makes the feature space a metric space, or the edge weights of a graph whose nodes are the data points; \item the representation of a cluster, e.g., a cluster centroid, a multivariate normal distribution, a set of data points connected by short hops, or a well-connected subset of the nodes of a graph; and \item whether each data point is assigned to exactly one cluster (hard clustering) or to several with varying degrees of belonging (soft clustering). \end{enumerate} Fig. 2 illustrates three families of clustering methods: hard clustering, such as k-means; soft clustering, such as a Gaussian mixture model; and graph clustering, where the data points are the nodes of a graph and a cluster is a densely connected subset of nodes. k-means represents a cluster by a point of the feature space, referred to as cluster centroid. Each data point is assigned to the cluster whose cluster centroid is nearest in Euclidean distance. The cluster centroids are chosen to minimize the average squared Euclidean distance between a data point and its nearest cluster centroid, which Lloyd's algorithm approaches by alternating assignment and averaging: each step lowers the average, and the iterates converge to a local minimum, not necessarily the global one. On the photograph, the five cluster centroids of k-means with k = 5 are five representative colors, and each cluster consists of the patches whose color is nearest to one of them: sky, cloud, shaded forest, sunlit slopes and rock (Fig. 1(b)). Painting each patch in the color of its cluster centroid also compresses the photograph to five colors. A clustering learned from one photograph is judged by how it assigns new patches: in k-means, a new data point joins the cluster of the nearest cluster centroid, so the cluster centroids are the learned hypothesis. A Gaussian mixture model represents each cluster by a multivariate normal distribution: a cluster index is drawn first, then the feature vector from that cluster's multivariate normal distribution. The degree of belonging of a data point to a cluster is the posterior distribution of its cluster index, and the expectation–maximization algorithm learns the model parameters by maximum likelihood. The result is a soft clustering whose clusters are ellipsoids, the level sets of a multivariate normal distribution; hard clustering is the extreme case in which every degree of belonging is 0 or 1, reached when all clusters share the covariance matrix ε I and ε → 0. On the photograph, each surface type becomes a multivariate normal distribution over colors, and the degree of belonging of a patch to the sky cluster is the probability that its color was drawn from the multivariate normal distribution of the sky. Painting each patch by the cluster with the largest degree of belonging gives Fig. 1(c); one in eight patches, mostly along the horizon and the cloud edges, has no degree of belonging above 0.8. Density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise defines a cluster through two hyperparameters, a distance ε and a minimum size m* of a cluster. A data point is a core point if at least m* data points lie within Euclidean distance ε of it. A cluster is a maximal set of data points that are connected through a chain of core points at most ε apart, and data points that are neither core points nor within ε of one are noise. A cluster can therefore have any shape that a chain of nearby data points can trace, and the number of clusters is an output, not an input. On the photograph, ε is a distance between colors. With the two hyperparameters of Fig. 1(d), the blue of the sky and the white of the clouds are joined by a chain of intermediate colors, so sky and cloud form one cluster and the land another. The patches along the horizon, whose mixed colors are rare, are noise (Fig. 1(d)). Graph clustering methods represent the dataset as the nodes r = 1, …, m of a graph whose edge weights express the similarity between data points, e.g., the k-nearest-neighbor graph that connects each data point to its nearest neighbors. The clusters are determined by the connectivity of the nodes: a cluster is a subset of nodes whose total edge weight to the rest of the graph, divided by the number of nodes in the subset, is small. The sum of this ratio over the clusters is the ratio cut that spectral clustering minimizes approximately. Spectral clustering computes the clusters from eigenvectors of the Laplacian matrix of the graph and flow-based clustering from network flows between selected nodes. There are also graph clustering methods that incorporate node-wise feature vectors x(r), r = 1, …, m: convex clustering combines the connectivity of the nodes with the node-wise feature vectors. Graph clustering methods suit data points without an obvious choice for numeric feature vectors: scientific papers connected by citations, users of a social network connected by friendships, or web pages connected by links. On the photograph in Fig. 1(a), the nodes are the patches and each patch is connected to the ten patches of most similar color; spectral clustering then separates the five surface types (Fig. 1(e)), since the patches of one surface type are neighbors in color. Fig. 3 arranges the methods by the representation of the data points, as Euclidean vectors or as the nodes of a similarity graph, and of a cluster; the penalty term of convex clustering is weighted by the edges of that graph. Convex clustering uses both representations of Fig. 3. It gives every data point x(r) its own cluster centroid w(r), which avoids the non-convexity of the clustering error. The method minimizes the convex objective function \[ \sum_{r=1}^{m} \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(r)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} + \alpha \sum_{1 \le r < r' \le m} A_{r,r'} \left\lVert {{\mathbf w}}^{(r)} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(r')} \right\rVert_{2} \text{.} \] The penalty term fuses cluster centroids with weights Ar,r' ≥ 0. The data points that share a cluster centroid at the unique minimizer form a cluster. At α = 0 every cluster centroid equals its data point, so distinct data points form m clusters. Once α is large enough, all cluster centroids of a connected component of the graph with the weights Ar,r' as its edge weights coincide, so the number of clusters is set indirectly through α. With the edge weights of a similarity graph as weights, the penalty term fuses only neighboring data points and the clusters follow the graph. On the photograph, with the edge weights of the color graph of the patches and the α of Fig. 1(f), the fused cluster centroids leave 65 clusters, four of them with at least 80 patches; like density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise, the method fuses sky with cloud along the gradual color transition (Fig. 1(f)). Beyond image segmentation, clustering is used for customer segmentation, for grouping documents by topic in natural language processing, for community detection in social networks, and for anomaly detection, where a data point that falls into no cluster or into a tiny one is an outlier. As a preprocessing step for supervised learning, clustering reduces a dataset to its cluster centroids as prototypes, or adds the distances of a data point to the cluster centroids as new features. It can also split the dataset so that a separate hypothesis is learned per cluster, e.g., one linear regression per cluster. For a large dataset, k-means is run on a coreset: a small weighted subset of the data points whose weighted average squared Euclidean distance to the nearest cluster centroid approximates that of the full dataset for every choice of the cluster centroids.

terms.name: clustering error
terms.abstract: The clustering error of a clustering is the average, over the data points of a dataset, of a loss that measures how poorly a data point is represented by the cluster it is assigned to. For hard clustering methods that represent a cluster by a cluster centroid, such as k-means, the loss is the squared Euclidean distance to the nearest cluster centroid. The Euclidean distance itself or the sum of absolute differences gives a variant whose best cluster centroids are medians instead of means and which is less sensitive to outliers. Soft clustering with a Gaussian mixture model uses the negative logarithm of the probability density function as the loss, so its clustering error is the negative log-likelihood function per data point. In every case the clustering error is the training error of a hypothesis, and minimizing it is empirical risk minimization. Lloyd's algorithm and the expectation–maximization algorithm never increase it but may stop at a local minimum. The clustering error is non-increasing in the number of clusters and vanishes when every data point is its own cluster, so it cannot choose that number.
terms.description: Consider the 366 days of one year at Krems an der Donau, each a data point with a feature vector x ∈ R2 that holds the morning minimum and the maximum daytime temperature of the day. A clustering method decomposes these days into a few clusters, and clustering methods differ in how they represent a cluster. One representation is a cluster centroid, a vector w(c) ∈ Rd for each cluster c = 1, …, k; each data point is assigned to the cluster with the nearest cluster centroid, which is the hard clustering delivered by k-means. A natural measure of how well the cluster centroids represent the dataset D = x(1), …, x(m) is the average, over the data points, of the minimum squared Euclidean distance to the cluster centroids, \begin{equation} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \min_{c = 1, \ldots, k} \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(c)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{.} \end{equation} The clustering error of k-means is the average Eq. (1). For two cluster centroids and the days at Krems, it is 42.0; Fig. 1(a) draws the distances it averages for some of the days. In the end, the clustering error Eq. (1) is the average of a loss, for a special choice of the loss function. The hypothesis learned by k-means is the map h(x) = w(c⋆(x)) that sends a feature vector to its nearest cluster centroid, with c⋆(x) = argminc = 1, …, k ‖ x - w(c) ‖2. The loss of a data point is \begin{equation} L\left({\mathbf x},h \right) := \left\lVert {\mathbf x} - h({\mathbf x}) \right\rVert_{2}^{2} = \min_{c = 1, \ldots, k} \left\lVert {\mathbf x} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(c)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{.} \end{equation} A data point carries no label here: the loss Eq. (2) compares the feature vector with the cluster centroid that stands in for it. The clustering error is the average of the loss Eq. (2) over the dataset, so it is the training error of the hypothesis h, and choosing cluster centroids that minimize it is empirical risk minimization over the hypothesis space of all maps of this form. The squared Euclidean distance in the loss Eq. (2) is one choice among several. Replacing the squared norm by the norm itself, L(x,h ) = ‖ x - h(x) ‖2, or by the ℓ1-norm ‖ x - h(x) ‖1, the sum of the absolute differences of the features, keeps the assignment of a data point to its nearest cluster centroid. It changes which cluster centroid is best for a given cluster. Under the squared Euclidean distance, it is the mean of the data points in the cluster, under the Euclidean distance their geometric median, computed by Weiszfeld's fixed-point iteration, and under the ℓ1-norm the median of each feature separately. A single far-away data point, an outlier, moves the mean of its cluster in proportion to its distance but moves either median little, so the clustering errors built from an unsquared norm are less sensitive to outliers. For the days at Krems and two cluster centroids, the three choices assign more than 99 percent of the days to the same cluster. Their clustering errors, 42.0, 5.8, and 7.6, are not comparable, since the first is measured in squared degrees and the other two in degrees. The squared Euclidean distance can also be replaced by a Bregman divergence, for which the mean remains the best cluster centroid. Another choice is used by soft clustering methods, which represent a cluster by a probability distribution rather than by a single vector and assign each data point to every cluster with a degree of belonging. A Gaussian mixture model represents a clustering by its model parameters: the cluster c is a multivariate normal distribution with mean μ(c) and covariance matrix C(c), chosen with probability pc. The clustering error of these model parameters is the negative log-likelihood function of the dataset per data point, \begin{equation} - \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \ln \sum_{c=1}^{k} p_{c} \mathcal{N}\left({\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)},\mathbf{C}^{(c)}\right) \big({\mathbf x}^{(r)}\big) \text{,} \end{equation} again the average of a loss, the negative logarithm of the probability density function at the feature vector. Minimizing the clustering error Eq. (3) is maximum likelihood estimation of the model parameters. The k-means clustering error is a limit of this choice: for equal probabilities pc = 1/k and covariance matrices C(c) = σ2 I, the loss of a data point in the clustering error Eq. (3) is, as σ → 0 and up to the factor 1/(2σ2) and an additive constant, the loss Eq. (2). Each of these clustering errors is a non-convex function of the cluster centroids or model parameters: with a single data point at x = 0 and two scalar cluster centroids w(1), w(2) ∈ R, the clustering error Eq. (1) is min(w(1))2, (w(2))2, which vanishes at (1, 0) and at (0, 1) but not at their midpoint. Lloyd's algorithm for k-means and the expectation–maximization algorithm for a Gaussian mixture model are fixed-point iterations that never increase the clustering error and stop at a fixed point, which can be a local minimum rather than a global one. They are therefore run from several initializations, keeping the run with the smallest clustering error. For the days at Krems, Lloyd's algorithm started from the means of the colder and of the warmer half of the days lowers the clustering error from 43.0 to 42.0 in two iterations. At the fixed point, 192 cold days share the cluster centroid (1.5, 10.5) and 174 warm days the cluster centroid (13.4, 26.1); every day of January and February is a cold day, and every day of July and August a warm day. The clustering error cannot choose the number k of clusters. An additional cluster centroid placed on any data point cannot increase it, so the smallest clustering error attainable with k cluster centroids is non-increasing in k, and it is zero at k = m, where every data point is its own cluster centroid. This is the training error of model selection in another guise: a larger hypothesis space never has a larger training error. Fig. 1(b) shows the curve for the days at Krems. With one cluster centroid the clustering error is the sum of the variances of the two features, 138.9; the second cluster centroid removes 96.8 of it, more than the next six cluster centroids together (32.9). Such a kink in the curve is the usual informal guide to k; otherwise k is a hyperparameter, chosen by a criterion that penalizes it or by the performance of a prediction task that uses the clusters.

terms.name: confusion matrix
terms.abstract: The confusion matrix of a hypothesis on a finite dataset with K label values is the K × K matrix whose entry in row y and column ŷ counts the data points with true label y and prediction ŷ. Its diagonal counts the correct predictions, and each off-diagonal entry counts one kind of misclassification. The accuracy, the precision, and the recall are obtained from the matrix by normalizing the diagonal, a column, or a row. On imbalanced data, the confusion matrix exposes failure on the rare class that the accuracy alone hides.
terms.description: The weather station in Krems an der Donau (Austria) records the minimum and the maximum air temperature of each day. A linear classifier is learned by logistic regression from a training set D(train) of 40 such data points from February and April 2024, and its decision boundary, a straight line, splits the plane of the two temperatures (Fig. 1). The features of a data point are the two temperatures of one day; its label indicates whether the minimum temperature of the following day stays above 0 ∘C or falls below it, a frost warning. Most days pose no risk: only 6 of the 40 following days bring frost. The constant prediction ``above zero'', a baseline that ignores the features, is therefore correct on 34 of the 40 days, an accuracy of 34/40 = 0.85, and the learned classifier reaches the same accuracy of 0.85. The single number cannot tell the two apart, nor reveal which mistakes either makes. A classifier with that accuracy might miss the frost days or raise false alarms. The confusion matrix breaks the count of predictions down by what was true and what was predicted (Fig. 2). The learned classifier detects one of the six frost days at the cost of one false alarm, while the baseline detects none and raises none. Consider a finite dataset with m data points, each characterized by a feature vector x and a label y from a finite label space Y = 1, …, K. For a given hypothesis h, the confusion matrix is a K × K matrix with one row per true label value and one column per predicted value. The entry in row y and column ŷ is the number of data points with true label y and prediction h(x) = ŷ. A diagonal entry is one with ŷ = y, where the prediction agrees with the label, so the diagonal counts the correctly classified data points, and the off-diagonal entries count each kind of misclassification separately. The standard classification metrics are ratios of entries of the confusion matrix. The accuracy is the sum of the diagonal divided by m. Normalizing a row by its sum yields the fraction of data points of that class that are detected (for the positive class, the recall), while normalizing a column yields the fraction of predictions of that class that are right, the precision. For the learned classifier of Fig. 2, with frost as the positive class, the recall is 1/6 and the precision is 1/2. The baseline has a recall of 0, and its precision is not defined at all, since it never predicts frost (pythondemos/cm.py). On imbalanced data, the confusion matrix exposes what a large accuracy can hide. A classifier that never predicts the rare class fills the row of that class with misclassifications while keeping most predictions correct. The always-above-zero baseline in Fig. 2 does exactly that (see baseline). All numbers above are computed on the training set D(train), the 40 days the classifier was learned from. A frost warning is judged on days that did not belong to D(train), so the confusion matrix, and every ratio taken from it, must be computed again on a validation set before one classifier is preferred over the other.

terms.name: convex
terms.abstract: A subset of the Euclidean space is convex if it contains the line segment between any two of its points. A function is convex if its epigraph is a convex set. A convex optimization problem is the minimization of a convex function over a convex set. Empirical risk minimization is a convex optimization problem whenever the hypothesis space is parameterized by a convex set of model parameters and the loss function is convex in those model parameters. Any local minimizer of a convex objective function is necessarily also a global minimizer, so a method that reaches a local minimum has solved the optimization problem.
terms.description: Learning a linear model by gradient descent moves the model parameters step by step, each iteration reducing the objective function within a neighborhood of the current model parameters. Many machine learning methods learn model parameters by such an iterative optimization method, with gradient descent and its variants the most widely used. These optimization methods are guaranteed to converge to a global minimum when the objective function is a differentiable convex function of the model parameters that attains its minimum and has a Lipschitz continuous gradient (see smooth), and the step size is chosen suitably. For a convex function every local minimum is necessarily a global minimum: any choice of model parameters at which no small change reduces the objective function already attains the smallest value that the objective function takes anywhere. The average squared error loss of linear regression is a convex function of the model parameters, and so is the objective function of the support vector machine. Empirical risk minimization over a hypothesis space parameterized by a convex set of model parameters, with a loss function that is convex in them, is a convex optimization problem: the minimization of a convex function over a convex set. Convexity is defined both for sets and for functions. For sets, the definition is geometric. A subset C ⊆ Rd of the Euclidean space Rd is referred to as convex if it contains the line segment between any two of its points. For w, w' ∈ C, that is \beta {\mathbf w} + (1-\beta) {\mathbf w}' \in \mathcal{C} \quad \text{for all } \beta \in [0,1] \text{.} Similarly, a function f: Rd → R is convex if its epigraph ( wᵀ,t )ᵀ ∈ Rd+1: t ≥ f(w) is a convex set, the epigraph being the set of points on or above the graph of f. Examples of a convex set and of a convex function are illustrated in Fig. 1. Two families of convex sets appear throughout machine learning. The first is the halfspace w ∈ Rd: aᵀ w ≤ b. It is determined by a nonzero normal vector a ∈ Rd 0, which fixes the direction of the bounding hyperplane, and an offset b ∈ R, which fixes its position. If two points satisfy the inequality, so does every point of the segment between them. The second is the convex hull of finitely many vectors x(1), …, x(m). It is defined as the set of all their convex combinations, \[ \operatorname{conv}\big\{ {\mathbf x}^{(1)}, \ldots, {\mathbf x}^{(m)} \big\} := \Big\{ \sum_{r=1}^{m} \beta_{r} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} : \beta_{r} \geq 0 \text{ for } r = 1, \ldots, m, \sum_{r=1}^{m} \beta_{r} = 1 \Big\} \text{.} \] It is the smallest convex set that contains these vectors. Every closed convex set is given by the intersection of all halfspaces that contain it \begin{equation} \mathcal{C} = \bigcap \big\{ H \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{d} : H \text{ is a halfspace}, \mathcal{C} \subseteq H \big\} \text{.} \end{equation} In general, intersecting a subset of the halfspaces containing a convex set yields a convex set that contains the original one, i.e., an outer approximation (see Fig. 2). The halfspace intersection Eq. (1) can be narrowed: it needs to consider only those halfspaces that are bounded by a supporting hyperplane. Every boundary point of a non-empty convex set carries such a hyperplane, and each point outside the set is already excluded by one of the halfspaces that these supporting hyperplanes bound: for a point x ∉ C and C closed, there is a unique nearest point p ∈ C to x. That nearest point is a boundary point of C, and therefore one of the points that carry a supporting hyperplane: a point of the interior could be moved a little toward x and would still lie in C, so it would not be the nearest one. The hyperplane through p with normal vector x - p, i.e., orthogonal to x - p, supports C at p, and the halfspace it bounds contains C but not x (see Fig. 3). Fig. 4 shows eight supporting hyperplanes of an ellipse. For the epigraph of a differentiable convex function f, the supporting hyperplane is determined by the gradient. At the boundary point (wᵀ, f(w))ᵀ, its normal vector is (∇ f(w)ᵀ, -1)ᵀ, since \[ \big(\nabla f({\mathbf w})^{\top}, -1\big) \left[ \begin{pmatrix} {\mathbf w}' t \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} {\mathbf w} f({\mathbf w}) \end{pmatrix} \right] \leq 0 \quad \text{for every } \big({\mathbf w}'^{\top}, t\big)^{\top} \in \operatorname{epi} f \text{.} \] This is the first-order condition f(w') ≥ f(w) + ∇ f(w)ᵀ (w' - w) written as a statement about the epigraph. At a point where the gradient vanishes, the condition gives f(w') ≥ f(w) for every w', which is the claim above that a local minimum of a convex function is a global one. The outer approximation of Fig. 2 is also used by approximate inference in probabilistic models defined over a graph. The set of achievable marginal distributions is a convex set described by a large number of linear inequalities. Message-passing methods optimize over an outer approximation of it obtained from a subset of those inequalities. Of the two families of convex sets introduced above, the convex hull is the one that characterizes the linear separability of data points with binary label values. Consider m data points with feature vectors x(r) ∈ Rd and labels y(r) ∈ -1,+1, for r = 1, …, m. These data points are linearly separable if some linear classifier predicts every label correctly, i.e., there are w ∈ Rd 0 and b ∈ R with y(r) ( wᵀ x(r) + b ) > 0 for r = 1, …, m. Linear separability holds precisely when the convex hull of the feature vectors labeled +1 and the convex hull of those labeled -1 do not intersect. Separability is therefore a property of two convex sets built from the data points. Convexity also appears in a widely used family of probabilistic models. An exponential family is constituted by the probability distributions whose probability density function has the form \[ p({\mathbf x}; {\mathbf w}) = h({\mathbf x}) \exp\big({\mathbf w}^{\top} \mathbf{t}({\mathbf x}) - A({\mathbf w})\big) \text{.} \] This probability density function is parameterized by the vector w and the sufficient statistics t(·). The log-partition function A is fully determined by requiring p(x; w) to integrate to one. Its Hessian is the covariance matrix of the sufficient statistics t(x) under p(x; w), \[ \nabla^{2} A({\mathbf w}) = {\mathbb{E}} \big\{ \mathbf{t}({\mathbf x}) \mathbf{t}({\mathbf x})^{\top} \big\} - {\mathbb{E}} \big\{ \mathbf{t}({\mathbf x}) \big\} {\mathbb{E}} \big\{ \mathbf{t}({\mathbf x}) \big\}^{\top} \text{,} \] which is positive semi-definite. A twice-differentiable function whose Hessian is positive semi-definite is convex, so A is a convex function on its domain. The convexity of A implies that the negative log-likelihood function of a training set, up to an additive constant that does not depend on w, \[ - \sum_{r=1}^{m} {\mathbf w}^{\top} \mathbf{t}\big({\mathbf x}^{(r)}\big) + m A({\mathbf w}) \text{,} \] is a convex function of w. Thus, for an exponential family, maximum likelihood estimation is a convex optimization problem.

terms.name: correlation
terms.abstract: Correlation measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two real-valued RVs. It is obtained by normalizing their covariance by their standard deviations, making it dimensionless and comparable across quantities measured on different scales. Its extreme positive and negative values characterize perfect increasing and decreasing affine relationships, while its central value characterizes uncorrelated variables. Independent RVs are uncorrelated, but uncorrelated RVs need not be independent, since correlation quantifies only linear dependence. The correlation between the predictions of the base learners of an ensemble bounds the variance reduction that averaging them can achieve.
terms.description: On a day with an unusually warm morning at Krems an der Donau, the afternoon tends to be unusually warm too. Fig. 1 shows a dataset of 1824 daily weather measurements at that station. Each data point represents a day, characterized by the air temperature at 06:00 and at 15:00 (UTC) as its feature vector x=(x1,x2)ᵀ. Selecting a data point from the dataset uniformly at random defines a random vector x. Correlation quantifies whether a day whose temperature at 06:00 is unusually high also tends to have an unusually high temperature at 15:00. More generally, for two real-valued RVs x and y on a common probability space with nonzero standard deviations σx and σy, their correlation is their covariance normalized by the product of these standard deviations, \[ \rho := \frac{{\rm cov}\left(x,y\right)}{\sigma_{x} \sigma_{y}} \in [-1, 1]\text{.} \] The value ρ is also referred to as the Pearson correlation coefficient. Unlike the covariance, correlation is dimensionless. Adding a constant to either random variable, or multiplying it by a positive constant, does not change ρ; multiplying one random variable by a negative constant reverses its sign. The extreme values ρ = 1 and ρ = -1 occur exactly when y is an increasing or a decreasing affine function of x with probability one. Indeed, |ρ| = 1 is the case of equality in the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for the centered RVs x - Ex and y - Ey, which holds exactly when one is a constant multiple of the other with probability one, and the sign of that constant is the sign of ρ. The sample correlation of two data vectors has the same property. The RVs are uncorrelated when ρ = 0. Independent RVs are uncorrelated, but uncorrelated RVs need not be independent, since ρ quantifies only linear dependence. For the random vector x obtained by selecting uniformly at random one of the daily temperature pairs shown in Fig. 1, the covariance between the two temperatures is 65.40 squared degrees Celsius, and their variances are 63.01 and 85.72 squared degrees Celsius. Thus, \[ \rho = \frac{65.40}{\sqrt{63.01\cdot85.72}} \approx 0.89\text{.} \] The correlation between the predictions of the base learners of an ensemble limits how much averaging them can help. An average of M identically distributed predictions, each with variance σ2 and pairwise correlation ρ, has variance ρ σ2 + (1 - ρ)σ2 / M. The second term vanishes as M grows, while the first remains, which is why bagging resamples the training set and a random forest randomizes the features at each split: both lower the correlation between their predictions.

terms.name: covariance matrix
terms.abstract: The covariance matrix of a random vector consists of the variances of the individual entries on its main diagonal and the covariances between different entries off the diagonal. Together with the mean vector, it represents the probability distribution of the random vector by its second-order statistics, which fix the spread of the probability distribution along every direction; for a Gaussian random vector, the two determine the probability distribution completely, and for a data point selected uniformly at random from a dataset, the covariance matrix is the sample covariance matrix of that dataset. Two uses follow from this representation. The inverse of the covariance matrix, the precision matrix, yields the smallest risk of predicting one entry from the others under the squared error loss: that risk is one divided by a diagonal entry of the precision matrix. For a Gaussian random vector, the precision matrix also yields the model parameters of the linear hypothesis that attains this risk. Whitening, a feature transformation built from the covariance matrix, standardizes the probability distribution to unit variances and zero covariances, which can speed up gradient descent.
terms.description: A warm morning at Krems an der Donau (Austria) usually comes with a warm afternoon, and the mornings vary less than the afternoons. Such informal claims can be turned into precise mathematical statements using a probabilistic model for the generation of data. Here, each daily weather observation amounts to observing a random vector x =(x1,x2)ᵀ that consists of the air temperature x1 at 06:00 and the air temperature x2 at 15:00 (UTC) of the day. The covariance matrix C(x) of a random vector x characterizes the spread of the probability distribution P(x). In particular, the entries of C(x) measure how much each entry of x varies and how strongly pairs of entries vary together. Different probability distributions can share the same mean vector and covariance matrix. For a Gaussian random vector (see multivariate normal distribution), however, the two determine the probability distribution completely. Formally, the covariance matrix of a random vector x ∈ Rd is defined as the expectation of the outer product of the centered vector x - Ex with itself: \[\mathbf{C}^{({\mathbf x})} := \mathbb{E} \bigg \{ \big( {\mathbf x} - \mathbb{E} \big\{ {\mathbf x} \big\} \big) \big({\mathbf x} - \mathbb{E} \big\{ {\mathbf x} \big\} \big)^{\top} \bigg\} \text{.}\] This expectation is well-defined whenever every entry of x has finite variance. The entry (C(x) )j,j' in row j and column j' is the covariance of xj and xj'. In particular, the diagonal entries ( C(x) )j,j are the variances of the individual entries of x. A covariance matrix can also be used to measure the spread of a dataset, such as the weather dataset of Fig. 1. Indeed, a dataset D induces a random vector x by selecting a data point from D uniformly at random. The resulting probability distribution P(x) is exactly the empirical distribution of D, the probability distribution that puts probability 1/m on each of its m data points. The corresponding covariance matrix C(x) is the sample covariance matrix of D. Fig. 1 depicts the mean vector Ex and the covariance matrix C(x) for this random vector. In particular, it shows the level set x: ( x - Ex )ᵀ ( C(x) )-1 ( x - Ex ) = 4. This level set is an ellipse with center Ex and axes along the eigenvectors of C(x). Its half-length along each axis is twice the square root of the matching eigenvalue, so the ellipse outlines the spread of the probability distribution. For every vector v ∈ Rd, the variance of vᵀ x is vᵀ C(x) v ≥ 0. A covariance matrix is therefore always positive semi-definite and, since it is also a symmetric matrix, admits a spectral decomposition \[\mathbf{C}^{({\mathbf x})} = \mathbf{V} \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \mathbf{V}^{\top} \text{.}\] Here, the columns of V are orthonormal eigenvectors and Λ = diag λ1, …, λd holds the nonnegative eigenvalues λ1 ≥ … ≥ λd ≥ 0. The covariance matrix C(x) is invertible, and then positive definite, exactly when all these eigenvalues are positive. Equivalently, no entry of x is, with probability one, an affine function of the other entries. Because the covariance matrix represents the spread of the probability distribution, it also determines the fundamental limit and the optimal method for predicting one entry of x from the others. The inverse of an invertible covariance matrix, referred to as the precision matrix, answers this task through its diagonal entry ( ( C(x) )-1 )j,j. The remaining features form the vector x-j := ( x1, …, xj-1, xj+1, …, xd )ᵀ ∈ Rd-1. For a Gaussian random vector x ~ N(μ,C(x)) (see multivariate normal distribution), the conditional probability distribution of xj, given x-j, is Gaussian with a variance that does not depend on the value of x-j. This conditional variance is 1 / ( ( C(x) )-1 )j,j. This conditional variance becomes a bound on every machine learning method once the data points can be approximated as realizations of independent and identically distributed random vectors x(r) ~ N(μ,C(x)). The conditional variance is also the smallest risk that any hypothesis can achieve under the squared error loss, \begin{equation} \min_{h: \mathbb{R}^{d-1} \to \mathbb{R}} \mathbb{E} \Big\{ \big( x_{j} - h\big({\mathbf x}_{-j}\big) \big)^{2} \Big\} = 1 \big/ \big( \big( \mathbf{C}^{({\mathbf x})} \big)^{-1} \big)_{j,j} \text{.} \end{equation} This smallest risk is the Bayes risk of the regression problem of predicting xj from x-j. It is attained by the Bayes estimator E xj | x-j, which depends linearly on x-j in the Gaussian case. For the weather measurements of Fig. 1, the best linear hypothesis predicting the temperature of a day at 15:00 from its temperature at 06:00 has the risk 17.8 squared degrees Celsius, against the variance 85.7 of the temperature at 15:00, which is the risk of the best constant prediction. Its two model parameters are computed from C(x) and Ex: the slope is the ratio of the covariance to the variance of the temperature at 06:00, and the intercept is fixed by the means of the temperature at 06:00 and at 15:00 (see linear regression). Under a Gaussian probabilistic model, this risk is also the Bayes risk. By the Bayes risk identity Eq. (1), the diagonal of ( C(x) )-1 yields a baseline. The spectral decomposition also yields a feature transformation that standardizes the represented probability distribution: it removes differences in scale and linear correlations between the entries of x. If C(x) is invertible, its inverse square root is \[ \big(\mathbf{C}^{({\mathbf x})}\big)^{-1/2} := \mathbf{V} \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2} \mathbf{V}^{\top}, \] where Λ-1/2 is obtained by replacing every eigenvalue with its inverse square root. The transformed feature vector \[ \widetilde{{\mathbf x}} := \big(\mathbf{C}^{({\mathbf x})}\big)^{-1/2} \big({\mathbf x}-\mathbb{E}\{{\mathbf x}\}\big) \] has zero mean and covariance matrix C(x̃)=I. Thus, its entries have unit variance and are mutually uncorrelated, as illustrated in Fig. 2. This transformation is known as whitening. By removing differences in scale and linear correlations between the features, whitening can improve the conditioning of optimization problems and thereby speed up gradient descent and related gradient-based methods. For linear regression with the squared error loss on centered features, the Hessian of the risk is 2 C(x), and one gradient descent step with an exact line search shrinks the gap to the smallest risk of a linear hypothesis by a factor of at most 1 - 1/κ (C(x)), where the condition number κ (C(x)) is the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue. After whitening, C(x̃) = I, this ratio is one, and a single step reaches the minimum. In practice, the mean and covariance matrix used for this transformation are estimated solely from the training set.

terms.name: data
terms.abstract: Data are representations of information, recorded in a form suitable for storage, communication and processing, and the word carries three technical senses in machine learning. In its general sense, it denotes recorded information in a form suitable for processing by machine learning methods. As a data point, it is an elementary information-carrying unit; as a dataset, it is an indexed collection of data points. A related regulatory term, personal data, is defined in the general data protection regulation and adopted by the EU AI Act.
terms.description: A weather station measures the temperature at its location and stores the value 23.4 ∘C together with a timestamp (see Fig. 1(a)). Such recorded values are data: representations of information, recorded in a form suitable for storage, communication, and processing by ML systems. Every machine learning method trains a model on data, and the usefulness of the hypothesis the method learns is limited by the quality and quantity of the available data. The word data is used in three technical senses, summarized in Fig. 1, and additionally in a legal sense. In its broadest use, data refer to recorded information. This sense applies when it does not matter whether a single data point or a collection of them is meant. Examples are raw sensor measurements such as the temperature reading in Fig. 1(a) and compound terms such as data parallelism, networked data, and data augmentation. As a formal unit, a data point is the fundamental information-carrying unit (Fig. 1(b)). Its information is contained in two types of properties: features, which are easy to measure or compute, and labels, which are difficult to measure or compute or need human annotation. The formal model of a domain set, a label set and a labeling function that assigns each domain point its label is given by Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David (2014, Sect. 2.1). As a formal collection, a dataset D = z(1), …, z(m) is the indexed collection of data points on which model training and validation are performed (Fig. 1(c)). The quality and the quantity of data that limit a learned hypothesis are properties of this collection: the labels of its data points and their number. The word data also carries a regulatory meaning. The general data protection regulation defines personal data as any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person. The EU AI Act adopts that definition and defines biometric data as personal data resulting from specific technical processing. Several regulatory obligations on ML systems, including the data minimization principle, the right to erasure, and the right to explanation, refer to data in this legal sense.

terms.name: data augmentation
terms.abstract: Data augmentation enlarges a training set with synthetic data points obtained from transformations or perturbations of existing ones. Typical examples are rotating or cropping an image and adding small perturbations to the features and labels of a measured data point. If the label does not change under a transformation, training on transformed copies makes the learned hypothesis vary little under it. Sensing devices measure with limited precision, so perturbed copies reflect the uncertainty interval around each recorded value. Data augmentation is a form of regularization, beside model pruning and adding a penalty term to the training error. For linear regression, perturbing the features with zero-mean noise whose covariance matrix is a multiple of the identity is, in expectation over the noise, equivalent to adding the ridge regression penalty term.
terms.description: Three measured days at Krems an der Donau are all a forecaster has to learn from. Each day is a data point, characterized by the maximum daytime temperature as its feature x, and the maximum daytime temperature of the next day as its label y (Fig. 1). The figure also shows a learned hypothesis map ĥ, obtained by empirical risk minimization using the polynomials of degree two as hypothesis space. The learned hypothesis achieves zero training error but delivers poor predictions outside the training set, which is overfitting. On a held-out set of 125 data points obtained from other days of 2024, whose feature lies inside the measured range, its average squared error loss is 256.2 squared degrees. One reason for the failure of ĥ is that the training set is too small. For almost every training set of sample size m = 3 there is one polynomial of degree two passing through its data points. Data augmentation enlarges a dataset with synthetic data points, obtained by perturbations of the features and labels of the measured ones. Sensing devices have imperfections such as thermal noise, so a reading x is one representative of an uncertainty interval U(x). Any other value from that interval could have been observed instead. Considering the weather data from Fig. 1, a temperature reading x carries U(x) = [x - 1, x + 1]. Each measured day ( x,y ) is replaced by 400 copies ( x + ε,y + ε' ), whose perturbations ε and ε' are realizations of RVs distributed uniformly on [-1, 1]. The augmented training set D̃ holds 1200 data points, none of which required a new temperature measurement. The width of the uncertainty interval used for the perturbation of the features and labels is a hyperparameter. One basic way to determine it is to try a few choices and compare the validation error of the resulting learned hypotheses. Fig. 1 also shows the polynomial of degree two ĥ' that empirical risk minimization learns using D̃ as training set. The hypothesis ĥ' no longer passes through the three measured days, but it delivers better predictions outside the training set. Its training error on them is 2.8 squared degrees, but its average squared error loss on the held-out data points falls to 24.7. The coefficient of x2 drops from ŵ2 = 0.71 for ĥ to ŵ2' = 0.06 for ĥ'. Enlarging D with perturbed copies is one basic form of regularization, beside model pruning, which shrinks the hypothesis space, and adding a penalty term to the training error. These different forms of regularization are sometimes equivalent in their effect on the learned hypothesis (Fig. 2). For linear regression, adding zero-mean perturbations with covariance matrix σ2 I to each feature vector yields the ridge regression solution, asymptotically in the number of copies. Its penalty term is σ2 ‖ w ‖22 for the weight vector w. Instead of adding noise to the features and labels, perturbations can also come from a transformation T of the feature space. A transformation known to leave the label alone is a symmetry of the learning task. A rotated or cropped image of a cat still shows a cat, while its feature vector, obtained by stacking the pixel color intensities, changes. The transformation must preserve the label, and a rotation does so only up to a point. Fig. 3 reduces images of the handwritten digits 6 and 9 to their first two principal directions (see principal component analysis) as features x1, x2. A small rotation T keeps an image of a 6 among the other 6s. However, rotating an image by 180 degrees carries it into the 9s, where the label has changed.

terms.name: data imputation
terms.abstract: Data imputation replaces missing attribute values of data points by estimates computed from the attribute values that were recorded. In tabular data a missing value is an empty cell of the table, and imputation fills the cell. It is one response to missing data, alongside discarding the incomplete data points. The filling is a machine learning problem: the missing value is the label of a data point, the recorded values beside it are its features, and the complete data points form a training set on which a hypothesis map (an imputer) is learned.
terms.description: The weather station Krems an der Donau records, for each day, the minimum temperature, the precipitation, and the maximum temperature. The year 2024 is therefore a table with one row per day and one column per quantity. This table is tabular data. A day on which the thermometer failed leaves the maximum-temperature cell of its row empty, while the table keeps its shape (Fig. 1). Data imputation fills such a cell: it replaces missing attribute values of data points, features or labels, by estimates computed from the attribute values that were recorded. It is one response to missing data, alongside discarding the incomplete data points or using a method that tolerates the gaps. The filling is a machine learning problem. The empty cell is the label of its row, and the recorded cells of the same row are its features. The complete rows form a training set, since each one supplies both a feature vector and the label that belongs with it. A hypothesis map, an imputer, is learned from them by empirical risk minimization. Applying that hypothesis to an incomplete row yields the estimate that fills its cell. The simplest imputation fills every empty cell of a column with the sample mean of the recorded cells of that column, which is the hypothesis that ignores the feature vector. A numerical experiment takes 15 days spread over the year and empties the maximum-temperature cells of 3 of them. From the 12 complete rows, it learns a linear regression hypothesis that maps the minimum temperature of a day to its maximum temperature. The emptied cells are then filled with its predictions, shown as a scatterplot in Fig. 2. The removed values are known, so the filling can be evaluated. The average squared error loss on the 3 cells, in squared degrees Celsius, is 17.6 for the learned hypothesis and 150.2 for the column average. A missing value can sit among other missing values, so that the feature vector of its row is itself incomplete. Rectangular patches lost from an aerial photograph are such a case. Each pixel is a data point, its features are the colors of the eight pixels around it, and its label is its own color, so a lost pixel inside a patch has lost neighbors as well. The filling then proceeds in sweeps: the missing values start at the sample mean of the recorded ones, and each sweep re-estimates them from the values that their neighbors currently hold, until the values no longer change. For a linear model, one sweep maps the vector x of missing values to M x + b, with a matrix M built from the weights of the hypothesis. Two runs started at x and x' differ after t sweeps by Mt (x - x'), so the sweeps converge from every start if and only if Mt → 0, i.e., if and only if the spectral radius ρ(M) is below one, and the limit is then the unique fixed point of the sweep. A numerical experiment fills the lost pixels by such sweeps. For the hypothesis learned from the intact pixels by least squares, ρ(M) = 2.72 and the sweeps diverge. The penalty term of ridge regression shrinks the weights: with the regularization parameter α = 0.03, the hypothesis learned by ridge regression gives ρ(M) = 0.84, and the sweeps converge. With that hypothesis, the average squared error loss on the lost pixels is half that of the baseline that fills every one of them with the average color, and the boundaries where the colors change sharply come out blurred. An imputed value is an estimate and not a measurement, and a method trained on imputed data points cannot tell the two apart. Part of the training set was produced by a hypothesis rather than observed, so a training error that averages over imputed cells scores a hypothesis partly against the predictions of the imputer rather than against measurements; for the imputer itself, every filled cell contributes zero loss. A single filled value also carries no information about the uncertainty of the estimate. Recording which values were imputed, and keeping them out of the test set, keeps the estimate of the risk free of values that a hypothesis produced.

terms.name: data leakage
terms.abstract: Data leakage arises when a machine learning method uses features that are available during training but not at prediction time. For example, in weather forecasting each data point covers a time interval, and one feature is the temperature one hour ahead of the forecast time. On historic data this later measurement is available, but when a forecast is actually computed it is not, so the feature leaks information. A leaked feature makes the loss on the training set and test set look near zero, yet the learned hypothesis fails after deployment, because the feature cannot be reproduced at prediction time. The term is also used, in a security sense, for the unintentional release of sensitive information.
terms.description: Consider a machine learning method trained on an hourly temperature sequence, where each data point is a sliding window of three consecutive hours (Fig. 1). The label is the temperature of the middle hour, and one of the features is the measurement one hour later. On historic data this later measurement is available, so the loss on the training set and test set looks near zero; but in real time the middle hour must be predicted before the next hour is measured, so the learned hypothesis is useless. The fault is data leakage: a feature used during training or evaluation is unavailable when a prediction must be delivered. More generally, a leaked feature is one whose value cannot be reproduced at prediction time, whether it is measured only later (as above) or computed from the label. Data leakage is formalized by Kaufman et al. (2012), who also give methods to detect and avoid it. Kapoor and Narayanan (2023) survey it as a cause of the reproducibility crisis in machine learning-based science. Test set contamination, the presence of test set data points in the training set, is a related form of data leakage: there, the information that should be unavailable at training time is the test set itself. The term data leakage is also used, in an unrelated security sense, for the unintentional release of sensitive information (data exfiltration from a trained system), a meaning distinct from the methodological one defined above.

terms.name: data point
terms.abstract: A data point is the elementary information-carrying unit on which machine learning methods operate. The properties of a data point fall into two categories: features, which are easily measurable or computable, and labels, which are higher-level facts that typically can only be determined using human expertise. Whether a given property is treated as a feature or a label is a design choice that depends on the machine learning application.
terms.description: An image of a cow herd (Fig. 1), a patient in a clinic, and a protein are objects that a machine learning method processes. A data point is an object that conveys information; such objects are the elementary units on which machine learning methods operate. Examples include students, radio signals, trees, images, RVs, real numbers, or proteins. Data points of the same type are described by two categories of properties. The first category includes features that are measurable or computable properties of a data point. They can be automatically extracted or computed using sensors, computers, or other data collection systems. The second category includes labels that are higher-level facts, or quantities of interest, that typically require human expertise or domain knowledge to determine rather than being directly measurable. Machine learning aims to predict the label of a data point from its features. Fig. 1 shows an image as an example of a data point. Several properties of the image can serve as features: the color intensities x1, …, xd of all image pixels, the timestamp xd+1 of the image capture, and the spatial location xd+2 of the image capture.
