Higher-level facts can serve as labels: the number of cows y1, the number of wolves y2, and the condition of the pasture y3 (e.g., healthy or overgrazed). For a data point that represents a patient, a feature could be the body weight, while the label could be the presence of cancer, the fact of interest. Determining this label requires a medical expert (or even a committee of experts) to examine the patient. A property treated as a label in one setting (e.g., a cancer diagnosis) may serve as a feature in another, where reliable automation (e.g., image analysis) allows the property to be computed without human intervention. Both kinds of properties are error-prone. For many machine learning applications, it is rarely possible to access the true labels. For example, a medical expert's diagnosis can be wrong, making it a noisy proxy for the patient's true condition. Errors of this kind, called label noise, arise whenever a label is only a proxy for the true quantity of interest, whether that proxy is produced by human judgment or by an automated system. Features are also a source of error within a machine learning method. A feature is obtained by measuring or computing a property of a data point. Physical and chemical sensing devices have a finite measurement uncertainty, and computing a feature on a finite computer introduces rounding errors. These imperfections make the recorded value deviate from the true feature value. This discrepancy is feature noise. Machine learning methods should be robust to both feature and label noise. Their predictions on new data points should not degrade sharply when some features or labels in the training set are corrupted. The EU AI Act reflects this concern: training data must, to the best extent possible, be ``free of errors'', and high-risk AI systems must attain an appropriate level of robustness. Robustness to feature and label noise can be improved by data augmentation, which deliberately perturbs the features or the label of a training data point (see Fig. 2). Training on such perturbed data points acts as regularization: for the squared error loss and small feature noise, it is equivalent to adding a penalty on the derivatives of the hypothesis with respect to the features.

terms.name: dataset
terms.abstract: A dataset is a finite collection of data points on which model training and validation are performed. Strictly speaking, a dataset is a set of distinct data points. With slight abuse of terminology, the term is also used interchangeably with sample, a finite sequence that may contain repetitions. Read as such a sequence, a dataset represents a probability distribution through its empirical distribution, in which a repeated data point counts as often as it is listed. The size of a dataset is measured most simply by its number of data points, which overstates what correlated data points carry and says nothing about how well they cover the feature space. In practice, machine learning methods do not access the data points themselves but a representation of them, such as a table of the relational model, which records their attributes and nothing about the dataset's fitness for a purpose.
terms.description: The cows of Fig. 2, or the rows of Table 1 that record them, form a dataset. A dataset is a collection D = z(1), …, z(m) of data points. Machine learning methods use a dataset for model training and validation. Strictly speaking, a dataset is an unordered collection of distinct data points, i.e., a set with no repetitions. In machine learning literature, however, the term is often used for a sample: a sequence of m data points, indexed by their position r = 1, …, m in the sequence, that may contain repetitions (see Fig. 1). Read as a list, a dataset also represents a probability distribution. Its empirical distribution P(D) assigns the probability 1/m to each entry of the list, so a data point that is listed twice receives the probability 2/m. A set, which cannot list a data point twice, has no such repetitions. The repetitions are therefore essential wherever a dataset represents a probability distribution. The bootstrap, e.g., draws new datasets from P(D) and so lists some data points several times. The size of a dataset has more than one measure. The most basic one is the number m of data points in the list. When the data points are realizations of correlated RVs, however, m overstates what they carry: the average over 30 consecutive days of a weather record scatters as much as the average over 7 days drawn at random from the whole record, because consecutive days are correlated (see sample size). The size of a dataset is then defined only relative to a probabilistic model of the data generation, as the number of independent and identically distributed data points that would carry the same information. A third measure asks how well the data points cover the feature space: the largest distance from a point of the region of interest to the nearest data point (see covering), which is small for a dataset whose features are spread out and large for one that leaves parts of the feature space empty, however many data points it holds. The notion of a dataset is broad: data points may represent concrete physical entities (such as humans or animals) or abstract objects (such as numbers). For illustration, Fig. 2 shows a dataset whose data points are cows. In machine learning applications, the dataset itself is often not accessible. For instance, accessing the dataset in Fig. 2 would require visiting the cow herd. What a machine learning method processes instead is a representation of the dataset within some data model, a formalism for representing and processing data. For example, the relational model organizes data as a collection of tables, or relations. A single table consists of rows and columns, where each row corresponds to a single data point and each column represents a specific attribute of a data point. The order of rows does not matter, and each attribute is associated with a domain that specifies its set of allowed values. Machine learning methods use these attributes as the features or the label of a data point, so the attribute domains correspond to the feature space and the label space. Table 1 shows an example obtained from the dataset in Fig. 2. A table records the content of a dataset, but not whether that content is appropriate for a given purpose. A dataset used in ethical and lawful ML systems must meet further requirements. For example, the EU AI Act requires that datasets on which high-risk ML systems are trained be ``sufficiently representative'' of the intended use cases. Trustworthy artificial intelligence also requires documenting how a dataset was assembled, for example through a datasheet that records the dataset's motivation, composition, and collection process. When the data points are personal data, this becomes a legal duty: under the purpose limitation principle, the general data protection regulation requires that such data be collected for ``specified, explicit and legitimate purposes''. These purposes are fixed at the time of collection.

terms.name: density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN)
terms.abstract: Density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN) is a clustering method for data points with numeric feature vectors that finds clusters of any shape and decides their number itself. Given a radius ε and a count m*, a data point is a core point if at least m* data points lie within Euclidean distance ε of it, and a cluster is a maximal set of data points connected through core points at most ε apart. Data points that lie within ε of no core point are noise and belong to no cluster. The clusters are the connected components of the ε-neighborhood graph on the core points, computed in a single pass, so DBSCAN iterates no operator and minimizes no empirical risk. Unlike k-means and a Gaussian mixture model, whose clusters are convex regions and ellipsoids, DBSCAN finds elongated and curved clusters, with the radius ε and the count m* as its hyperparameters.
terms.description: An aerial photograph of the Wachau, with Weissenkirchen, Rossatz and Duernstein along a bend of the Danube, is cut into square patches of 76 m, and the 1000 patches that lie mostly on vineyard parcels are data points, each characterized by a feature vector x ∈ R2 that holds its position: easting and northing in km (Fig. 1). The wine-growing areas that these patches form follow the river banks and the slopes. They are therefore elongated and curved, and their number is not known in advance. DBSCAN is a clustering method for data points with numeric feature vectors that finds clusters of any shape and decides their number itself: a cluster is a region in which data points lie densely, and data points that lie in no dense region are noise. DBSCAN clusters by density, not by shape, and leaves isolated data points as noise. It is a hard clustering method in the sense that every data point belongs to at most one cluster, but unlike a partition of the dataset it leaves the noise points outside every cluster. DBSCAN has two hyperparameters: a radius ε > 0 and a count m*. The ε-neighborhood of a data point is the set of data points within Euclidean distance ε of it, the data point itself included. A data point is a core point if its ε-neighborhood holds at least m* data points. It is a border point if it is not a core point but lies in the ε-neighborhood of one, and it is noise otherwise (Fig. 2). A cluster is a maximal set of data points that are connected through core points: two core points at most ε apart belong to the same cluster, and a border point belongs to the cluster of a core point in its ε-neighborhood. The clusters are therefore the connected components of the ε-neighborhood graph on the core points, the graph whose edges connect core points at most ε apart, with the border points attached. DBSCAN is a graph-based method. DBSCAN computes the clusters in a single pass over the data points. It picks a core point not yet assigned to a cluster, collects every data point reachable from it through core points at most ε apart, declares the collection a cluster, and moves on to the next core point not yet assigned. Algorithm 1 states the pass in full. \begin{algorithm}[H] \caption{DBSCAN } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex Input: feature vectors of the data points, radius ε > 0, count m* \State mark a data point as a core point if at least m* data points, itself included, lie within Euclidean distance ε of it \State mark every data point as unassigned \For{each unassigned core point} \State open a new cluster and assign the core point to it \While{the cluster holds a core point whose ε-neighborhood has not been collected} \State assign every unassigned data point of that ε-neighborhood to the cluster \EndWhile \EndFor \Statex Output: the clusters; every data point still unassigned is noise \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} No operator is iterated, so the fixed-point iteration view that applies to Lloyd's algorithm and the expectation–maximization algorithm does not apply here. A second pass over the result changes nothing, and the result depends on no initialization, so DBSCAN has no local optima to get trapped in. DBSCAN minimizes no empirical risk; it is defined by its notion of a cluster alone. On the vineyard patches with ε = 1.5 patch spacings and m* = 4, DBSCAN finds 934 core points, 40 border points and 26 noise patches, grouped into eight clusters, five of which hold at least 20 patches: the wine-growing areas of the strip (Fig. 1). The river, wider than ε, separates the areas on its two banks. The radius ε decides which structures count as clusters (Fig. 3). With ε = 1.1 patch spacings, so that only the four axis-aligned neighbors of a patch are within reach, the patches fall into 24 clusters with 6% noise, and several areas break along their thin stretches. With ε = 3 patch spacings, six clusters remain and no patch is noise. However, two areas that ε = 1.5 keeps apart are joined. The number of clusters and the noise share both fall as ε grows. A common way to choose ε is to place it where the sorted Euclidean distances of the data points to their m*-th nearest neighbor start to rise steeply. DBSCAN differs from k-means and from a Gaussian mixture model in three ways. First, a cluster of k-means is a convex region of the feature space and a cluster of a Gaussian mixture model is an ellipsoid, whereas a DBSCAN cluster can have any shape that a chain of nearby data points can trace. On the vineyard patches, k-means with five clusters splits one area and one of its clusters joins two areas, since an area that curves along the river is not convex. Second, the number of clusters is an input of k-means and of a Gaussian mixture model but an output of DBSCAN, at the price of the two hyperparameters ε and m*. Third, k-means and a Gaussian mixture model assign every data point to a cluster, whereas DBSCAN leaves outliers as noise. DBSCAN shares its graph-based view of a cluster with spectral clustering. That method builds a similarity graph, a graph whose edges connect similar data points, and clusters its nodes by the eigenvectors of the Laplacian matrix, a matrix that encodes the graph, instead of by the connected components of the ε-neighborhood graph.

terms.name: decision boundary
terms.abstract: The decision boundary of a classifier consists of the feature vectors that lie arbitrarily close to two or more decision regions. An arbitrarily small perturbation of such a feature vector can therefore change the predicted label. Many classifiers threshold a real-valued scoring function, and the decision boundary is then a level set of that function. Its shape depends on the model: a linear classifier has a hyperplane as its decision boundary, a decision tree one made of axis-parallel line segments, and logistic regression on polynomial features a curved one.
terms.description: A frost warning predicts from the minimum and the maximum air temperature of a day whether the following night brings frost. The pairs of temperatures at which the warning switches between frost and no frost form its decision boundary. In general, a classifier is a hypothesis h→Y with a finite label space Y. Its decision boundary consists of the feature vectors that are arbitrarily close to two or more of its decision regions. More precisely, x∈X lies on the decision boundary if every neighborhood of x contains feature vectors x' and x'' such that h(x')≠h(x''). An arbitrarily small perturbation of such a feature vector can therefore change the predicted label. In the notation of decision regions, each decision region Rŷ := x ∈ X: h(x) = ŷ is a subset of X = Rd. Its boundary ∂ Rŷ is the set of feature vectors such that every neighborhood contains elements of Rŷ and of its complement X Rŷ. The decision boundary is the union ŷ ∈ Y ∂ Rŷ of these boundaries over all label values. Many classifiers are built from a real-valued scoring function g→R: the predicted label depends on whether g(x) lies below or above a threshold c. If g is continuous, the decision boundary is the level set x:g(x)=c, provided that g takes values on both sides of c arbitrarily close to every point in this set. For a linear classifier with g(x)=wᵀx and w≠0, this level set is the hyperplane wᵀx=c, whose normal vector is w. Fig. 1 shows that the shape of a decision boundary depends on the model. A linear classifier has a straight decision boundary, a decision tree has one made of axis-parallel line segments, and logistic regression on polynomial features can have a curved one.

terms.name: decision region
terms.abstract: A decision region of a classifier is the set of all feature vectors that the classifier maps to one particular label value. The decision regions partition the feature space, one region per label value, and all feature vectors in the same region obtain the same prediction, so the decision regions determine the classifier completely. The union of the boundaries of the decision regions is the decision boundary. The shape of the decision regions depends on the model: a linear classifier has halfspaces, a decision tree has unions of axis-parallel rectangles, and logistic regression on polynomial features has regions separated by a curve.
terms.description: A frost warning predicts from the minimum and the maximum air temperature of a day whether the following night brings frost. Any rule that gives this warning splits the pairs of temperatures into two parts: the pairs for which it predicts frost and the pairs for which it does not. Each part is a decision region of the rule. In general, a classifier is a hypothesis hX → Y with a finite label space Y. Its decision region for the label value ŷ ∈ Y is the set of feature vectors that it maps to this value, \mathcal{R}_{\widehat{y}} := \big\{ {\mathbf x} \in \mathcal{X}: h({\mathbf x}) = \widehat{y} \big\} \text{.} The decision regions partition the feature space: every feature vector lies in exactly one of them, there is one region per label value, and a region may consist of several separate pieces. All feature vectors in the same decision region obtain the same prediction, so the decision regions determine the classifier completely. The boundary ∂ Rŷ of a decision region is the set of feature vectors such that every neighborhood contains elements of Rŷ and of its complement. The union of these boundaries over all label values is the decision boundary. The shape of the decision regions depends on the model. A linear classifier with h(x) = sign(wᵀ x + w0) has the two halfspaces on either side of the hyperplane wᵀ x + w0 = 0 as its decision regions. For more than two label values, a linear classifier predicts the value with the largest of K linear scores. Each decision region is then an intersection of K - 1 halfspaces and therefore convex. A decision tree compares one feature with a threshold at each split, so its decision regions are unions of axis-parallel rectangles. Logistic regression on polynomial features has decision regions separated by a curve, the level set of a polynomial. Fig. 1 shows the decision regions of three classifiers learned from the same data points with two features: a linear classifier, a decision tree, and logistic regression on polynomial features. A data point whose label differs from the label value of the region containing its feature vector is misclassified, and the fraction of such data points is the average 0/1 loss. The two label values are separated by a curve and not by any straight line, so the linear classifier misclassifies half of the data points, while the other two misclassify none.

terms.name: decision tree
terms.abstract: A decision tree is a flowchart-like representation of a hypothesis map: a root node receives the feature vector of a data point and evaluates a basic test on it. The test result selects a child node, which applies a further test, and the forwarding continues until the feature vector reaches a leaf node. A leaf node has no children and represents one specific function value, i.e., a prediction. The tree partitions the feature space into decision regions, one per leaf node, on which the represented hypothesis is constant. A maximum depth and a family of node tests define the model, the hypothesis space of all such trees, which has no vector of model parameters of fixed length and is therefore searched greedily rather than by gradient methods. Decision trees serve as base models of the random forest and of gradient-boosted decision tree methods. Small decision trees yield interpretable machine learning if the user can comprehend the tests executed at their nodes.
terms.description: A bank's loan approval can be written as a chain of simple tests on the applicant's features that ends in an ``approve'' or ``reject'' prediction. For example, is the income above a threshold? Is the credit score large enough? A decision tree is such a chain in general form: a flowchart-like representation of a hypothesis map h. More formally, a decision tree is a directed acyclic graph whose root node receives the feature vector x of a data point. The root node then forwards the data point to one of its child nodes based on some elementary test on the features x. If the receiving child node is not a leaf node, i.e., it has child nodes itself, it represents another test. Based on the test result, the data point is forwarded to one of its descendants. This testing and forwarding of the data point is continued until the data point ends up in a leaf node without any children, which carries the prediction ŷ = h(x) returned by the tree for this data point (Fig. 1). The leaf nodes partition the feature space into decision regions; in Fig. 1, each test compares an entry of x with a threshold, so the decision regions are rectangles. Next to each node, Fig. 1 highlights the part of the feature space that contains the feature vectors reaching that node. The depth of a decision tree is the number of tests on the longest path from the root node to a leaf node; the tree in Fig. 1 has depth two. Fixing a maximum depth D and a family of allowed tests defines the model: the hypothesis space H of all decision trees of depth at most D whose node tests belong to the family, for instance all threshold tests xj ≤ ε with j ∈ 1, …, d and ε ∈ R. A tree in H is specified by its shape, by the index j of the feature and the threshold ε that each test node compares, and by the value of each leaf node. This hypothesis space has no natural parametrization. The shape of the tree and the index j of the feature tested at each node are discrete choices, and how many of them a tree has depends on its shape, so H is not the image of a vector of model parameters of fixed length: there is no parameter space Rn on which the training error is a function. The thresholds form a vector once the shape and the tested features are fixed, but the training error is piecewise constant in each of them, since a data point changes child only when the threshold crosses its feature value, so the gradient is zero wherever it exists. Empirical risk minimization over H can therefore not use gradient descent, and a fixed point view of the training iteration does not apply: an iteration adds a node, it does not update a vector. Minimizing a bound that adds a size penalty to the training error is computationally hard, and the methods below search H greedily. Training a decision tree amounts to extending a leaf node by attaching another decision tree. In the simplest case, a leaf node is replaced with a test node whose children are new leaf nodes (Fig. 2). Widely used training methods for decision trees include classification and regression trees (CART), iterative dichotomiser 3 (ID3), and C4.5. Starting from a single leaf node, CART repeatedly replaces a leaf node with a test node. An impurity measure assigns a nonnegative number to a set of labels: it is zero when the labels agree, and it grows as they spread out. Among candidate tests that compare a single feature with a threshold, CART scores each test by the impurity of the two children, weighted by the fraction of data points routed to each of them, and greedily selects the test with the smallest score, i.e., with the largest reduction against the impurity of the parent node. Common impurity measures are the Gini index and the entropy for classification, and the squared error around the mean label for regression. The growth stops only when a leaf node contains too few data points, not when no candidate test reduces the impurity much, since a test that reduces the impurity little can enable a test with a large impurity reduction below it. The large tree is then pruned back by cost-complexity pruning, which removes the subtrees whose impurity reduction is smaller than the penalty for the leaf nodes they add. Fig. 3 shows, as a scatterplot, the result of this training on real data. Each day of 2024 at the Finnish Meteorological Institute weather station Helsinki Kaisaniemi is a data point, with the minimum temperature of the day as its feature and the maximum temperature as its label. The learned depth-2 tree is a piecewise constant hypothesis with four pieces, one per leaf node, each equal to the mean label of the days routed there. The tree was grown to depth two rather than until the stopping rule above applied, so that each of its four pieces is visible in the picture. Decision trees serve as base models of the random forest and of gradient-boosted decision tree methods. A decision tree with a small number of nodes is often considered interpretable: its computation can be traced by following the data point from the root node to a leaf node. Small decision trees are therefore a common choice in interpretable machine learning.

terms.name: decoder
terms.abstract: A decoder is a map that turns the code of a data point, the short vector an encoder computes from it, back into the space the data point itself lives in. The encoder and the decoder are learned together by empirical risk minimization, with a loss function that measures the reconstruction error between a data point and what the decoder returns for its code. In principal component analysis (PCA) both maps are linear and the decoder is the transpose of the encoder, so the reconstruction is the orthogonal projection of the feature vector onto the subspace spanned by the retained eigenvectors, and the average squared reconstruction error is the sum of the discarded eigenvalues. An autoencoder replaces both linear maps by ANNs, and its decoder is often discarded once the code is wanted for a later learning task. A decoder may return a probability distribution instead of a point: the decoder of a variational autoencoder (VAE) is a conditional probability distribution over feature vectors given a latent variable. The output step of a large language model (LLM) is a decoder as well, turning a vector into a probability distribution over the vocabulary, which is what lets text be generated one token at a time.
terms.description: The weather station at Krems an der Donau (Austria) records the lowest and the highest air temperature of each day, so a day is a point of the plane with these two features as its coordinates. Storing one number per day instead of two is possible, but that number is of no use unless some map turns it back into a pair of temperatures. A decoder is such a map. A decoder is a map Φ*: X' → X from a space X' of codes back to the feature space X that holds the feature vector x of a data point. Its counterpart is the encoder Φ: X → X', which computes the code z = Φ(x), a vector of d' numbers against the d numbers of the feature vector, with d' < d. The two maps form an autoencoder, and they are learned together by empirical risk minimization with a loss function that measures the reconstruction error x - Φ*(Φ(x)). No label enters this learning task: what the decoder has to reproduce is the data point itself. What the decoder returns need not be a point of X: it may be a probability distribution, over X or over a vocabulary of tokens. Fig. 1 shows the three shapes the decoder takes in principal component analysis, in a variational autoencoder, and in a large language model. Principal component analysis is the linear case. Its encoder is a matrix W ∈ Rd' × d with orthonormal rows, so the code of a feature vector is z = W x, and its decoder is the transpose Wᵀ of that matrix. The reconstruction Wᵀ W x differs from x by a vector orthogonal to the rows of W, and no other point of the subspace they span lies closer to x: the reconstruction is the orthogonal projection of x onto that subspace. The rows of W are the eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix Q̂ belonging to its d' largest eigenvalues. The eigenvalues of Q̂, in decreasing order λ1 ≥ ≥ λd ≥ 0, state what every code length costs. For a dataset D = x(1), …, x(m) of feature vectors with sample mean zero, the average squared reconstruction error is the sum of the eigenvalues the code drops, \begin{equation} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {\mathbf W}^{\top} {\mathbf W} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} = \sum_{j=d'+1}^{d} \lambda_{j} \text{.} \end{equation} The identity Eq. (1) holds at every code length d' = 1, …, d. The archive at Krems holds eight measurements per day: the lowest, highest and mean air temperature, the precipitation, the sunshine duration, the humidity, the air pressure, and the wind speed. Each of the eight is scaled to unit sample variance, because they are measured in different units. A code of two numbers then leaves 2.91 of the total 8, so the decoder recovers 64 percent of the total sample variance. Fig. 2 draws the decoder of a code of one number for the two temperatures, and both sides of the identity Eq. (1) at every code length. An autoencoder keeps the reconstruction error and replaces both linear maps by ANNs, so its decoder is a network that turns the code back into a feature vector. A denoising autoencoder changes what the decoder is asked for: the encoder reads a corrupted feature vector and the decoder has to return the clean one. After training, the decoder is often discarded and the code kept, so that a later learning task learns a hypothesis on the code rather than on the raw features. A decoder need not return a point. The decoder of a variational autoencoder is a conditional probability distribution pw(x | z) over feature vectors given a latent variable z, with model parameters w: given a code it returns a probability distribution over the feature vectors that could have produced it. Drawing z from a fixed probability distribution and then a feature vector from the decoder makes the pair a generative model. The two readings meet where that conditional probability distribution is Gaussian with mean R z, for a matrix R ∈ Rd × d', and a spread that does not depend on z. Its log-likelihood function is then a decreasing affine function of the average squared reconstruction error, so the matrix R that maximizes the one minimizes the other. The step that turns a vector into text is a decoder too. A large language model computes a vector z ∈ Rd from the tokens read so far. The decoder maps it to a probability distribution over the vocabulary V by a linear map followed by the softmax function. The rows of that linear map are a(1), …, a(|V|) ∈ Rd, and the decoder returns \begin{equation} \big( {\mathbf \Phi}^{*}({\mathbf z}) \big)_{v} = \frac{\exp \big( \langle {\mathbf a}^{(v)}, {\mathbf z} \rangle \big)} {\sum_{v'=1}^{|\mathcal{V}|} \exp \big( \langle {\mathbf a}^{(v')}, {\mathbf z} \rangle \big)} \quad \text{for } v = 1, \ldots, |\mathcal{V}| \text{.} \end{equation} Every value the quotient Eq. (2) assigns is nonnegative, and the values sum to one over v = 1, …, |V|, so the decoder returns a point of the probability simplex Δ|V|-1. Drawing one token from that probability distribution, appending it to the tokens read so far, and repeating is how text is generated one token at a time: without the decoder, the vector z names no token at all. A vocabulary of eight tokens is already enough to check the decoder Eq. (2) numerically. Cutting the highest temperature of each day at Krems into eight bins of about 45 days each, and choosing the rows a(v) by maximum likelihood, reproduces the observed frequencies of the next token to within 0.0014. A sequence of 20,001 tokens generated one at a time then matches the observed shares of the eight tokens to within 0.009. The reconstructions of a linear decoder lie in a subspace of dimension d', whatever the dataset looks like. The identity Eq. (1) says what that costs on average, and nothing about where the reconstructions land. Read back in the recorded units, the reconstruction of a day from a code of two numbers gives 128 of the 366 days a negative precipitation, down to -7.3 millimeters, and 17 days a negative sunshine duration. No day of the record takes a negative value in either measurement. A linear decoder learned with the squared error loss recovers the subspace principal component analysis finds, so only a nonlinear decoder places a reconstruction off a subspace, which is why the decoder of an autoencoder is an artificial neural network and not a matrix. What the linear decoder buys is a closed form: its eigenvectors come from the sample covariance matrix with no training run, and its eigenvalues state the error of every code length in advance. Curving the reconstruction set does not always lower the error: with the same code of one number, the average of the days in each of eight bins leaves 5.10 on days it was not learned from, against the 5.07 of the linear decoder. A decoder that returns a probability distribution rather than a point buys a probability for every reconstruction and the ability to generate, since a feature vector or a token can be drawn from what the decoder returns. The price is a probabilistic model that has to be learned and can be wrong, and a support fixed in advance. The Gaussian decoder above commits to a spread that does not depend on the code. The vocabulary of eight tokens resolves the maximum daytime temperature of a day only to its bin: 1.4 degrees in root mean square, and 10.3 degrees for the coldest token, which holds every day at or below 6.7 degrees. No sequence of these eight tokens tells two days of one bin apart.

terms.name: deep net
terms.abstract: A deep net is an artificial neural network whose hypothesis maps are compositions of several layers, each of which applies an affine map and then an activation function to every entry of the result. The number of layers that carry learnable model parameters is the depth of the net, and deep learning is the name of the machine learning methods that use a deep net as their model. The layers before the last one compute a feature transformation learned from the data, and the last layer applies a linear hypothesis to the activations they deliver. A deep net therefore makes the choice of features part of training instead of a design decision taken beforehand. Its model parameters, the weights and offset terms of every layer, are learned by gradient descent on the training error, with the gradient computed by backpropagation. Depth is a property of the net, not of a single hypothesis: adding layers enlarges the hypothesis space and lowers the training error, while beyond some depth the validation error rises again, an instance of overfitting. Depth is therefore a hyperparameter, and a feature transformation chosen beforehand can reach a lower validation error with far fewer model parameters.
terms.description: The daily maximum temperature at Krems an der Donau (Austria) rises from January to July and falls again towards December. The 365 days of 2023 form a training set D(train) and the 366 days of 2024 a validation set D(val), with the day of the year as the single feature of a day and its maximum temperature as the label. A hypothesis that is a linear function of the date can only rise or only fall over the year. Its training error, the average squared error loss over D(train), is 79.4 squared degrees, barely below the 83.4 of the constant hypothesis that always predicts the sample mean of the labels. A deep net replaces that single raw feature by features that it computes itself. A hidden layer of eight artificial neurons turns the date into eight activations, and a linear hypothesis of those eight numbers has a training error of 16.9 and a validation error of 23.7 on D(val) (Fig. 1(a)). A deep net is an artificial neural network whose hypothesis maps are compositions of L consecutive layers. Layer ℓ reads in the activations a(ℓ-1) of the previous layer, applies an affine map to them, and then an activation function σ to every entry of the result, \begin{equation} {\mathbf a}^{(\ell)} = \sigma\big( {\mathbf W}^{(\ell)} {\mathbf a}^{(\ell-1)} + {\mathbf b}^{(\ell)} \big) \text{ for } \ell = 1, \ldots, L-1 \text{,} \end{equation} starting from the raw feature vector a(0) := x of a data point. The last layer applies an affine map alone and returns the prediction \begin{equation} h^{({\mathbf w})}({\mathbf x}) = {\mathbf W}^{(L)} {\mathbf a}^{(L-1)} + {\mathbf b}^{(L)} \text{.} \end{equation} The number L of layers that carry learnable model parameters is the depth of the net, and the term deep learning comes from it. Deep learning covers the machine learning methods that use a deep net as their model. The activation function is prescribed rather than learned, most often the rectified linear unit σ(z) = max0, z. Without it, every layer would be an affine map, the layer recursion Eq. (1) and the output map Eq. (2) would compose to an affine map again, and the net would define the same hypothesis space as a linear model (Fig. 2). The composition splits at the last layer, and that split makes a deep net a feature learning method. The layers 1 to L-1 map the raw feature vector x to the activations a(L-1), a feature transformation learned from the data, and the output map Eq. (2) applies an ordinary linear hypothesis to these learned features. A deep net therefore makes the choice of features part of training instead of a design decision taken beforehand. A deep net whose last hidden layer has two artificial neurons turns the date at Krems into two learned features. Least squares on those two reaches a training error of 14.5, against the 14.6 of the net's own last layer and the 79.4 of least squares on the raw feature. A learned feature transformation is often useful beyond the learning task it was trained for, so the layers before the last are kept and only the last layer is learned again on a smaller dataset. The model parameters w collect the weights in every matrix W(ℓ) and the offset terms in every vector b(ℓ), and a choice of w selects one hypothesis h(w) of the net. They are learned by empirical risk minimization: gradient descent with a fixed learning rate lowers the training error L̂(h(w)|D(train)) by one gradient step after another. Each of them needs the gradient of the training error with respect to w, and backpropagation computes it one layer at a time. Depth is a property of the net, not of a single hypothesis in it, and what a larger depth changes is the size of the hypothesis space. Fig. 1(b) shows the training error at Krems falling from 79.4 at depth 1 to 12.0 at depth 5, every hidden layer eight artificial neurons wide. The validation error does not follow it down. It is smallest at depth 2, at 23.7, and rises to 29.5 at depth 5, an instance of overfitting. Depth is therefore a hyperparameter, chosen on D(val) rather than fixed beforehand. The depth-2 net lowers the validation error to 23.7 from the 88.2 of least squares on the raw feature. A feature transformation chosen beforehand reaches a lower validation error with a fifth of the model parameters. Least squares on the sine and cosine of the date at the annual period and at half of it needs five model parameters and has a validation error of 22.6, against the 23.7 of the net with its 25. Two further costs come with the net. Its training error is not a convex function of w and has many local minima. Gradient descent therefore returns a different hypothesis from every initialization: five initializations of the depth-2 net give training errors between 16.9 and 19.1, and four of the five end above the smallest of them. The learned features also carry no reading of their own, where the sine and cosine name the annual cycle. An explainable artificial intelligence method explains the trained net only by an approximation that cannot be fully faithful to it. A deep net is the answer where no such feature transformation can be written down beforehand: in image classification the first hidden layer delivers edges, the second corners and contours, and the third parts of objects.

terms.name: dimensionality reduction
terms.abstract: Dimensionality reduction uses a map Φ: Rd → Rd' to replace a raw feature vector x = (x1, …, xd)ᵀ by a shorter feature vector z = (z1, …, zd')ᵀ, with d' < d. Using fewer features lowers the effective dimension of a model, which reduces the probability of overfitting. Moreover, it lowers the amount of computation needed for model training and for inference. It also enables visualization: two features can be used as the coordinates in a scatterplot. Principal component analysis learns a linear map by minimizing the reconstruction error, while a random projection uses a linear map drawn at random, without any training. An autoencoder learns a nonlinear map represented by an artificial neural network.
terms.description: A square patch of the photograph in Fig. 2 is described by 48 numbers, and two numbers computed from them suffice to tell sky from vegetation. Dimensionality reduction uses a map Φ, a transformation Φ: Rd → Rd' to replace the raw feature vector x = (x1, …, xd)ᵀ of a data point by a shorter feature vector z = (z1, …, zd')ᵀ, with d' < d (Fig. 1). Using a shorter feature vector is beneficial in several ways: \begin{itemize} \item Statistical benefit: It typically reduces the probability of overfitting, as reducing the number of features often reduces the effective dimension of a model. \item Computational benefit: Using fewer features lowers the amount of computation needed for model training and for inference. For example, linear regression methods need to invert a matrix whose size is determined by the number of features. \item Visualization: A map can be learned that delivers two features z1,z2, which can then be used as the coordinates in a scatterplot. Each square patch of a photograph is first averaged down to a 4 × 4 grid of colors, still too many numbers to plot; Fig. 2 then places each patch at the two features that principal component analysis learns for it, which keep most of the variance of the raw feature vectors. \end{itemize} Dimensionality reduction methods differ in the hypothesis space used for the map, in the criterion they learn it by, and in whether the map is learned from data at all. Principal component analysis learns a linear map: the map is a matrix chosen so that the reconstruction error, the squared distance between x and the feature vector reconstructed from z by a second linear map, is minimal on average over the training set. An autoencoder learns a nonlinear map represented by an artificial neural network, under the same criterion. A random projection uses a random matrix without any training: by the Johnson--Lindenstrauss lemma, the distances between the feature vectors of the data points are approximately preserved. Nonlinear methods beyond the autoencoder include the manifold-learning family, among them t-SNE and UMAP, which are used mainly for visualization.

terms.name: distribution shift
terms.abstract: A data point carries features and a label, drawn together from one joint probability distribution. Distribution shift is a mismatch between that joint probability distribution during training and the one the learned hypothesis is applied to after deployment. The average loss on a test set estimates the risk under the training probability distribution, so a small test error is no evidence about the loss incurred after deployment. A joint probability distribution has two components, a marginal distribution and a conditional probability distribution, and the named special cases differ in which of them changes: covariate shift changes the marginal distribution of the features alone, label shift the marginal distribution of the labels alone, and concept drift the conditional probability distribution. Sample weighting corrects covariate shift when both probability distributions are known; online learning applies when they are not.
terms.description: The Finnish Meteorological Institute station Helsinki Kaisaniemi records the minimum and the maximum air temperature of each day. Every summer day is a data point: its feature is the minimum temperature of that day, its label the maximum. The generation of these data points can be approximately modeled as RVs with a joint probability distribution P of feature x and label y. A linear hypothesis ĥ, learned by linear regression from 62 of the 92 data points of June--August 2026, i.e., by minimizing the average squared error loss, reaches a training error of 5.0 and a test error of 6.5 on a test set that consists of the remaining 30 data points. The learned hypothesis ĥ is then applied to data points D' collected at the northernmost Finnish Meteorological Institute station, Utsjoki Nuorgam, during December 2025--February 2026. As with the training set, the generation of these data points can also be approximately modeled as RVs with some joint probability distribution P'. The resulting average loss on D' is 242.1, which is 37 times larger than the test error 6.5 of ĥ (Fig. 1). The reason for this discrepancy between test error and the performance on D' is a distribution shift. Distribution shift refers to a discrepancy between the probability distribution P underlying the generation of the data points used for training and the probability distribution P' underlying the generation of the data points to which the learned hypothesis is applied after deployment. A distribution shift cannot be detected from the test error when the test set is generated by P as well. The average loss of ĥ on such a test set is an unbiased estimator of the risk EP L(z,ĥ ) under P, which may differ substantially from the risk EP' L(z,ĥ ) under P'. The risk under P' is the one that matters after deployment, and no test set drawn from P measures it. A small test error is therefore no evidence about the loss incurred under P' ≠ P. Consider data points with a single feature x and a hypothesis that predicts by comparing x with a threshold (this is a simple decision tree). The two pdfs in Fig. 2, those of a standard normal distribution P and of a normal distribution P' with a larger mean and standard deviation, show the effect of replacing P by P' on a threshold chosen under P. The fraction of data points beyond the threshold rises from 14% to 88%, so the risk under P' exceeds the risk under P that the test error estimates. Three named special cases of distribution shift correspond to different origins of the shift from P to P'. These different origins correspond to the factors in the two factorizations of the joint probability distribution. Both hold for any joint probability distribution of a numeric feature vector and label, whether or not a probability density function exists, since the conditional probability distribution is then guaranteed to exist: \[ \mathbb{P}^{({\mathbf x}, y)} = \mathbb{P}^{({\mathbf x})} \cdot \mathbb{P}^{(y \mid {\mathbf x})} = \mathbb{P}^{(y)} \cdot \mathbb{P}^{({\mathbf x} \mid y)} \text{.} \] Covariate shift changes the marginal distribution P(x) of the feature vector (with P(y | x) unchanged), and label shift changes the marginal distribution P(y) of the label (with P(x | y) unchanged). Concept drift refers to a change in the conditional probability distribution P(y | x) (with P(x) unchanged) or P(x | y) (with P(y) unchanged). The two-station example from the beginning is not a pure case of any of the three, since every factor of both factorizations changes. The marginal distribution P(x) changes, as under covariate shift, since the winter data points have lower feature values. The conditional probability distribution P(y | x) changes as well, as under concept drift: a linear hypothesis learned from the 90 Nuorgam winter data points has slope 0.77, against the slope 0.48 of the hypothesis learned at Helsinki. A data point whose feature is one degree higher therefore has a label 0.77 degrees higher in winter, against 0.48 in summer. The marginal distribution P(y) changes too, as under label shift, and with it the class-conditional P(x | y), the second reading of concept drift. In particular, the two datasets have no label value in common, since every label at Nuorgam in winter is at most 4.6 ∘C and every label at Helsinki in summer at least 15.0 ∘C. Distribution shift is detected by comparing summary statistics of the features between the training set and the data points arriving after deployment, or by monitoring the incurred loss whenever labels become available. One mitigation of distribution shift is sample weighting which can be used when the probability distribution P and P' are known. Here, with p and p' the pdfs of P and P', each data point of the training set is weighted by the ratio p'(x)/p(x). This weighting corrects covariate shift under two conditions: P(y | x) is unchanged, and every feature vector occurring under P' also occurs under P, so that the ratio is defined. Under these two conditions, \[ p'({\mathbf x}, y) = p(y \mid {\mathbf x}) p'({\mathbf x}) = \big(p'({\mathbf x})/p({\mathbf x})\big) p({\mathbf x}, y) \text{, wherever } p({\mathbf x}) > 0 \text{.} \] Thus, the weighted loss has the same expectation under P as the loss has under P'. Another approach to mitigate distribution shift is to use online learning, which updates the hypothesis as data points from the changing probability distribution arrive. It needs their labels to become available after deployment, which sample weighting does not, and in return it needs neither probability distribution to be known.

terms.name: degree of belonging
terms.abstract: A degree of belonging is a number that indicates the extent to which a data point belongs to a cluster, one for each pair of a data point and a cluster of a clustering. In the most common formulation, the degrees of belonging of one data point are nonnegative and sum to one, so they form a vector of the probability simplex and a probability mass function over the cluster indices. Hard clustering is the special case in which this vector has one entry equal to one and all others equal to zero, as delivered by k-means. A principled construction of degrees of belonging strictly between zero and one is the posterior distribution of the cluster index under a Gaussian mixture model, which the expectation–maximization algorithm computes in its E-step. The degrees of belonging in turn determine the clusters: the mean of a cluster is the average of the feature vectors weighted by them, and with degrees of belonging of zero or one this weighted average is the averaging step of Lloyd's algorithm. As the common variance of the clusters of a Gaussian mixture model shrinks to zero, the degrees of belonging turn into zero or one and soft clustering turns into hard clustering.
terms.description: Consider the 366 days of one year at Krems an der Donau, each a data point with a feature vector x ∈ R2 that holds the morning minimum and the maximum daytime temperature of the day. A clustering method decomposes these days into a cold cluster and a warm cluster. A day in January is a cold day and a day in July a warm day, but 28 May 2024, with a morning minimum of 11.1 and a maximum of 21.3 degrees, lies between the two. A degree of belonging uc(r) is a number that indicates the extent to which data point r belongs to cluster c, for c = 1, …, k and r = 1, …, m. For 28 May 2024, the Gaussian mixture model of Fig. 2 delivers the degrees of belonging 0.50 to the cold and 0.50 to the warm cluster, while a day in January obtains 1.00 and 0.00. In the most common formulation, the degrees of belonging of one data point are nonnegative and sum to one, \begin{equation} u_{c}^{(r)} \geq 0 \quad \text{for } c = 1, \ldots, k \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sum_{c=1}^{k} u_{c}^{(r)} = 1 \text{.} \end{equation} The vector u(r) := (u1(r), …, uk(r))ᵀ then lies in the probability simplex Δk-1. It is the probability mass function of a random variable with values in 1, …, k, the cluster index of the data point. Possibilistic clustering drops the sum constraint of the simplex condition Eq. (1) and lets each degree of belonging vary in [0, 1] on its own. Fig. 1 sketches three data points and their degrees of belonging to two overlapping clusters. Hard clustering is the special case in which every data point belongs to exactly one cluster. With ĉ(r) the index of the cluster that data point r is assigned to, its degrees of belonging are \begin{equation} u_{c}^{(r)} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{for } c = \widehat{c}^{(r)} \text{,} 0 & \text{otherwise} \text{,} \end{cases} \end{equation} so the vector u(r) is a vertex of the probability simplex Δk-1. k-means delivers such a hard clustering: ĉ(r) is the index of the cluster centroid nearest to x(r) in Euclidean distance. For the days at Krems and two cluster centroids, k-means assigns 192 days to the cold cluster with cluster centroid (1.5, 10.5) and 174 days to the warm cluster with cluster centroid (13.4, 26.1). The dashed curve in Fig. 2(b) shows these hard assignments over the year: they jump between 0 and 1 from one spring day to the next. Soft clustering methods assign a data point to several clusters with degrees of belonging strictly between 0 and 1. A principled construction uses a probabilistic model for the data points, the Gaussian mixture model. Under it, the cluster index I(r) ∈ 1, …, k of data point r is an unobserved random variable with P(I(r) = c) = pc. Given I(r) = c, the feature vector x(r) is drawn from a multivariate normal distribution with mean μ(c) and covariance matrix C(c). The degree of belonging is then the posterior distribution of the cluster index given the observed feature vector, \begin{equation} u_{c}^{(r)} := \mathbb{P}\left(I^{(r)} = c \mid {\mathbf x}^{(r)}\right) = \frac{p_{c} \mathcal{N}\left({\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)},\mathbf{C}^{(c)}\right)({\mathbf x}^{(r)})} {\sum_{c'=1}^{k} p_{c'} \mathcal{N}\left({\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c')},\mathbf{C}^{(c')}\right)({\mathbf x}^{(r)})}\text{,} \end{equation} the responsibility of cluster c for the data point. The posterior degrees of belonging Eq. (3) are the probabilities of the k values of one random variable, so they satisfy the simplex condition Eq. (1) by construction. The model parameters pc, μ(c), and C(c) of the Gaussian mixture model are learned by maximum likelihood. This is an instance of empirical risk minimization: the loss of a data point is the negative logarithm of the probability density function of the Gaussian mixture model at its feature vector, and the clustering error is the average of this loss over the dataset. For the days at Krems, a two-component Gaussian mixture model learned by the expectation–maximization algorithm has the means (3.1, 12.3) and (14.2, 27.5) and the cluster probabilities 0.63 and 0.37. Under it, 58 of the 366 days have no degree of belonging above 0.8, 23 of them in May and none between November and February (Fig. 2). The degrees of belonging determine the clusters in turn. In the M-step of the expectation–maximization algorithm, the mean of cluster c is the average of the feature vectors weighted by the degrees of belonging. The cluster probability is the average of the degrees of belonging themselves. In formulas, \begin{equation} {\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)} = \frac{\sum_{r=1}^{m} u_{c}^{(r)} {\mathbf x}^{(r)}} {\sum_{r=1}^{m} u_{c}^{(r)}} \qquad \text{and} \qquad p_{c} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} u_{c}^{(r)} \quad \text{for } c = 1, \ldots, k\text{.} \end{equation} The covariance matrix C(c) is the covariance matrix of the feature vectors under the same weighting. A day with the degrees of belonging 0.50 and 0.50 counts half towards each mean. With the degrees of belonging Eq. (2) of a hard clustering, the weighted average Eq. (4) is the mean of the data points assigned to cluster c, which is the averaging step of Lloyd's algorithm for k-means, and pc is the share of data points in that cluster. The expectation–maximization algorithm alternates the posterior Eq. (3) with the weighted averages Eq. (4), so the degrees of belonging are recomputed in every iteration: they are not model parameters but a function of the model parameters and of the feature vector. At the fixed point of the expectation–maximization algorithm on the days at Krems, each mean equals the average of the days weighted by their degrees of belonging and differs from the k-means cluster centroid of the same cluster by at most 1.9 degrees. Hard clustering is also a limit of the posterior degrees of belonging Eq. (3). Fix every cluster probability at 1/k and every covariance matrix at σ2 I, a multiple of the identity matrix I with one common variance σ2. The posterior Eq. (3) then depends on x(r) only through its squared Euclidean distances to the means. As σ2 shrinks towards 0, it concentrates on the nearest mean: every degree of belonging tends to 0 or 1, and the expectation–maximization algorithm reduces to Lloyd's algorithm. For the days at Krems, with the two k-means cluster centroids as means and σ2 = 1, no day has both degrees of belonging above 0.2, and every degree of belonging is within 0.01 of its k-means value Eq. (2). With σ2 = 50, 16 percent of the days have both degrees above 0.2. With σ2 = 1000, every day has both above 0.2 and no degree of belonging exceeds 0.63. The degrees of belonging of a data point are the value of a hypothesis at its feature vector. The posterior Eq. (3) is a map h: Rd → Δk-1 determined by the model parameters of the Gaussian mixture model, and the assignment rule of k-means is a map from Rd to the vertices of Δk-1 determined by the cluster centroids. Either map applies to a day that did not belong to the dataset the clusters were learned from, which is how a clustering generalizes. A hard clustering is derived from degrees of belonging by assigning each data point to the cluster with the largest one, and 1 - maxc = 1, …, k uc(r) measures how uncertain that assignment is. For the days at Krems, the largest posterior degree of belonging names the k-means cluster on 91.5 percent of the days. In medical image segmentation, the degrees of belonging of a pixel to the tissue types let a pixel at the boundary between two tissues belong partly to both, where a hard clustering must pick one.

terms.name: edge weight
terms.abstract: An edge weight is a nonnegative number Ai,i' attached to the edge i,i' of a weighted graph that measures how strongly the two nodes it joins are connected. Collected in the weight matrix A, the edge weights of an undirected graph form a symmetric matrix with a zero entry for every pair that is not an edge. In machine learning, the nodes are often the data points of a dataset, and the weight of a pair is the Gaussian similarity of their feature vectors, a decreasing function of their Euclidean distance with a width σ as hyperparameter; an k-nearest-neighbor graph keeps only the weights of nearby pairs. Edge weights can also encode a relation given with the data, such as citations between papers or the collaboration between the devices of a federated learning network. Machine learning methods use the weights through weighted sums over the edges. The quadratic form of the Laplacian matrix is the weighted sum of the squared differences of a node signal, which for the indicator of a cluster is the total weight of the cut edges. The penalty term of convex clustering charges the distance between two cluster centroids in proportion to the weight of their edge. Edge weights are given before training and differ from the weights of an artificial neural network, which are model parameters.
terms.description: Consider eight days of 2024 at Krems an der Donau, every 46th day from 1 January, each a data point with a feature vector x ∈ R2 that holds the morning minimum and the maximum daytime temperature of the day. Two days with similar temperatures are similar data points. One way to record the similarity of every pair of days is a graph. The days are its nodes i = 1, …, n, here with n = 8, and an edge i,i' between two days carries a number that says how similar they are: the edge weight Ai,i' ≥ 0. In Fig. 1(a), a thick edge joins 1 January and 18 November, whose temperatures differ by less than two degrees Celsius, while no visible edge joins 1 January and 18 August. A weighted graph G = (V, E, A) consists of a node set V = 1, …, n, an edge set E, and an edge weight Ai,i' for every edge i,i' ∈ E. The weights of an undirected graph without self-loops are collected in the weight matrix A ∈ Rn × n. Its entries satisfy \begin{equation} A_{i,i'} = A_{i',i} \geq 0 \text{,} \quad A_{i,i} = 0 \text{,} \quad \text{and} \quad A_{i,i'} = 0 \text{ for } \{i,i'\} \notin \mathcal{E} \text{.} \end{equation} The first condition in the weight matrix Eq. (1) holds because the edge i,i' of an undirected graph is the edge i',i, so the weight matrix is a symmetric matrix. The third condition makes a zero weight and a missing edge the same thing, so the weight matrix determines the graph and is its adjacency matrix. An unweighted graph is the special case in which every edge has weight 1. The weighted node degree of node i is the row sum Σi'=1n Ai,i' of the weight matrix. In machine learning, edge weights come from two sources. The first source is the feature vectors of the data points: the m data points of a dataset become the nodes of a similarity graph, with n = m, and the weight of a pair is a decreasing function of the distance between their feature vectors. The usual choice is the Gaussian similarity \begin{equation} A_{i,i'} := \exp \Big( - \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(i)} - {\mathbf x}^{(i')} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \big/ (2 \sigma^{2}) \Big) \quad \text{for } i \neq i' \text{,} \end{equation} with a width σ > 0. The Gaussian weight Eq. (2) is 1 for identical feature vectors, exp(-1/2) ≈ 0.61 at Euclidean distance σ, and about 0.01 at Euclidean distance 3 σ. For the eight days and σ = 5 degrees, the weight is 0.95 for 1 January and 18 November, whose feature vectors are 1.6 degrees apart, and 6 · 10-7 for 1 January and 18 August, 26.8 degrees apart. Six of the 28 pairs weigh at least 0.5, and eight weigh below 0.01 (Fig. 1(b)). The width σ is a hyperparameter. With σ = 1, only two pairs weigh at least 0.01, so the graph falls apart into isolated days. With σ = 50, every pair weighs at least 0.87, so the weights no longer separate similar from dissimilar days. A width σ in the order of the mean distance of a data point to its k-th nearest neighbor is a common choice. The Gaussian weight Eq. (2) is positive for every pair, so every pair is an edge and the weight matrix has no zero off its diagonal. A sparse graph is obtained from the k-nearest-neighbor graph. The pair i,i' is an edge if x(i') is among the k nearest neighbors of x(i) or x(i) among those of x(i'). An edge keeps the Gaussian weight Eq. (2), and every other weight is set to zero. For the eight days and k = 2, ten of the 28 pairs are edges, and the graph is connected. The k-nearest-neighbor graph is not a threshold on the weights. It keeps 18 May and 18 August at weight 0.07, since 18 May is one of the two days nearest to 18 August. It drops 3 October and 18 November at weight 0.54, since each of the two has two closer days. Fig. 1(b) marks the kept pairs by filled circles and the dropped pairs by open squares. The k-nearest-neighbor graph therefore connects data points in sparse and in dense regions of the feature space alike, which is why it is the recommended first choice. The second source is a relation given with the data rather than computed from feature vectors: citations between scientific papers, friendships between the users of a social network, links between web pages, or the number of measurements that two weather stations share. In an image, the pixels are the nodes, and the weight of two pixels falls with the difference of their brightness and with their distance in the image, a construction used in image segmentation by normalized cuts. In a federated learning network, the nodes are devices, and the edge weight measures the extent of their collaboration, e.g., the capacity of the communication link between them or the statistical similarity of their local datasets. In transfer learning, the nodes are learning tasks, and the weight couples the tasks of nearby weather stations more strongly than those of distant ones. The edges of an artificial neural network also carry weights, and those are a different object: an artificial neural network weight is a model parameter, learned by training, and it can be negative. The edge weights of a weighted graph are nonnegative and are given before training starts; they belong to the data, not to the model. Edge weights enter machine learning methods through weighted sums over the edges. A node signal u = (u1, …, un)ᵀ ∈ Rn assigns one number to every node, such as a label or a prediction. The Laplacian matrix L(G) of the graph satisfies \begin{equation} \mathbf{u}^{\top} {\mathbf L}^{(\mathcal{G})} \mathbf{u} = \sum_{\{i,i'\} \in \mathcal{E}} A_{i,i'} \big( u_{i} - u_{i'} \big)^{2} \text{,} \end{equation} the Laplacian quadratic form. It is a weighted sum of squared differences. A heavy edge charges a difference between its two nodes more than a light edge, and the sum is zero for a signal that is constant on every connected component of the graph. For the indicator of a subset C ⊆ V of the nodes, ui = 1 for i ∈ C and ui = 0 otherwise, the quadratic form Eq. (3) is the total weight of the edges between C and the rest of the graph, the weight of the cut. For the eight days, the five days with a maximum temperature below 20 degrees cut edges of total weight 1.09, which is 15 percent of the total weight 7.44 of all pairs. Splitting the days into the first four and the last four of the year cuts 4.97, or 67 percent. Graph clustering methods seek clusters that cut little weight; spectral clustering approximately minimizes the cut weight divided by the size of the cluster through eigenvectors of L(G). Semi-supervised learning on a graph seeks a node signal that agrees with the labels of the few labeled nodes and makes the quadratic form Eq. (3) small. The weights then carry the labels from labeled to unlabeled nodes. They decide to which data points outside the training set a learned hypothesis is extended, which is the question of generalization. The generalized total variation replaces the squared difference in the quadratic form Eq. (3) by a measure of the discrepancy between the local models of the two nodes. Generalized total variation minimization adds it to the local training errors, as in federated learning and transfer learning. The network Lasso is the case of the unsquared distance between the model parameters of the two local models. Convex clustering uses the edge weights in its objective function. Every data point x(i) gets its own cluster centroid w(i), and the cluster centroids minimize \begin{equation} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(i)} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(i)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} + \alpha \sum_{\{i,i'\} \in \mathcal{E}} A_{i,i'} \left\lVert {{\mathbf w}}^{(i)} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(i')} \right\rVert_{2} \text{,} \end{equation} with a regularization parameter α ≥ 0. The first sum in the objective function Eq. (4) is the clustering error of the cluster centroids, the training error that empirical risk minimization minimizes; the second sum is a penalty term, so the method regularizes by loss penalization, one of the three routes that regularization distinguishes. The weights decide which pairs of cluster centroids are pulled together. A pair with weight zero is never charged, and a heavy pair is charged in proportion to its weight. For α large enough, the cluster centroids of a heavy pair coincide, which puts the two data points into one cluster. For a hard clustering in which every data point of a cluster shares one cluster centroid, the penalty term is the distance between the two cluster centroids times the cut weight. For the cold and the warm days above, it is 17.0, the distance 15.6 between their cluster centroids times the cut weight 1.09.

terms.name: effective dimension
terms.abstract: The effective dimension of a hypothesis space is its size as seen through the probability distribution of the features: the number of model parameters that make a difference on the data points the distribution produces. For a linear model it is the rank of the second-moment matrix of the feature map, estimated by the rank of the feature matrix, and it never exceeds the number of model parameters. Two hypothesis spaces that differ only outside the support of the distribution have the same effective dimension, and empirical risk minimization on them delivers the same predictions on the data. The same hypothesis space can have different effective dimensions under different data distributions. The Rademacher complexity is the distribution-dependent size measure of learning theory, while the Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension is its worst case over the whole feature space.
terms.description: Consider the 366 days of 2024 at the weather station Krems an der Donau, each a data point with the minimum temperature of the day as its feature x and the maximum temperature as its label y. Two hypothesis spaces are candidates for predicting y from x: the affine linear model H(1) = w0 + w1 x with two model parameters, and the linear model H(2) = w0 + w1 x + w2 max(0, x - 25) with three, whose third feature is a rectified linear unit hinge at 25 ∘C. The minimum temperature of the record ranges from -10.1 to 20.8 ∘C, so the hinge is zero on every day. On this record, every hypothesis of H(2) agrees with a hypothesis of H(1): the third model parameter changes no prediction that the data can test. The effective dimension deff ( H ) of a hypothesis space H is its size as seen through the probability distribution P(x) of the features: it counts the model parameters that make a difference on the data points the distribution produces, not the model parameters that are written down. For a linear model with feature map Φ, the effective dimension is defined as the rank of the second-moment matrix E Φ(x) Φ(x)ᵀ. A dataset estimates it by the rank of its feature matrix, which is the trace of the orthogonal projection that least squares applies to the label vector, the effective number of model parameters of a method whose predictions are a linear function of the labels. It never exceeds the number of model parameters, and it equals that number only when the features are linearly independent on the support of P(x). On the Krems record the feature matrix of H(2) has three columns and rank 2, since its hinge column is zero, so deff ( H(1) ) = deff ( H(2) ) = 2. Two hypothesis spaces that differ only outside the support of P(x) have the same effective dimension. The consequence for empirical risk minimization is visible in Fig. 1(a). Least squares on H(1) and on H(2) delivers the same prediction for every day of the record and the same training error of 19.2 squared degrees. The hinge coefficient w2 is not identifiable: every value gives the same training error, and the two learned hypotheses differ only for a minimum temperature above 25 ∘C, a region that no day of the record reaches. There the data say nothing, which is the generalization problem in its sharpest form: a hypothesis is tested only where the features lie. The effective dimension depends on the probability distribution, not only on the hypothesis space. Fig. 1(b) keeps H(2) and changes the feature to the maximum temperature of the day, with the maximum temperature of the next day as the label. The maximum temperature exceeds 25 ∘C on 97 of the 365 day pairs, the hinge column of the feature matrix is no longer zero, its rank is 3, and least squares on H(2) now reaches a smaller training error than on H(1), if only slightly. The same hypothesis space has effective dimension 2 under one data distribution and 3 under another. Beyond linear models, the size measures of learning theory also differ by whether they take a worst case over the feature space or an average over the data distribution. The Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension is a worst case over all datasets that the feature space admits, so it counts the hinge of H(2) whether or not the data ever reach it: for the classifiers obtained by thresholding a hypothesis at zero, three feature values with one beyond the hinge are shattered by H(2), since the three values of a hypothesis there are an invertible linear image of (w0, w1, w2), while every hypothesis of H(1) is monotone in x and so realizes no labeling that changes sign twice. The Rademacher complexity is an expectation over datasets drawn from P(x) and is therefore the effective size of H for the application at hand. For a method such as ridge regression, whose learned hypothesis is a linear function of the labels, the trace of that linear map is the effective number of model parameters: it decreases from the rank of the feature matrix toward zero as the regularization parameter α grows.

terms.name: eigenvalue
terms.abstract: An eigenvalue of a square matrix A is a number λ for which some nonzero vector x satisfies Ax = λx. Such a vector is an eigenvector of A. Multiplying an eigenvector by the matrix rescales it without moving it off the line it spans. The eigenvalues of a diagonalizable matrix form the diagonal factor of its eigenvalue decomposition. An iterative method that applies an affine update, such as gradient descent for linear regression, converges to the unique fixed point of the update, for every initialization, exactly when each eigenvalue of the update matrix has magnitude less than one. The second-smallest eigenvalue of the Laplacian matrix of an undirected graph measures how well the graph is connected and underlies spectral clustering.
terms.description: Whether gradient descent for linear regression converges is decided by the eigenvalues of a single square matrix. A square matrix A represents a linear map from Rd to Rd; the image of a vector x under this map is the product Ax. Multiplying a vector by a square matrix normally moves it off the line it spans. Some nonzero vectors are exceptions: each stays on the line it spans and is only rescaled. The factor by which such a vector is rescaled is an eigenvalue. Formally, a number λ ∈ R is an eigenvalue of a square matrix A ∈ Rd × d, one with d rows and d columns, if A x = λ x for some nonzero vector x ∈ Rd; such a vector is an eigenvector of A. For an eigenvector, the image Ax stays on the line x spans, pointing the same way when λ > 0 and the opposite way when λ < 0 (see Fig. 1). Arranging d linearly independent eigenvectors of a diagonalizable matrix as the columns of V, and the corresponding eigenvalues in a diagonal matrix Λ, yields the eigenvalue decomposition A = V Λ V-1. Eigenvalues can be used to study iterative machine learning methods with an update of the form \[ {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} = {\mathbf M} {\mathbf w}^{(t)} + {\mathbf b} \text{, for } t = 0,1,\ldots \text{.} \] An example is gradient descent for linear regression, whose update operator F(η): w ↦ M w + b is affine with iteration matrix M = I - (2η/m) XᵀX. Here, I is the identity matrix, η the learning rate, m the number of data points, and X the feature matrix of the training set (see linear regression). Such an iteration converges to the unique fixed point ŵ of F(η), for every initialization, if and only if the spectral radius ρ of M, the largest magnitude of an eigenvalue of M, satisfies ρ < 1. For a diagonalizable M, the eigenvalue decomposition shows why: in the basis of its eigenvectors, each iteration rescales the components of the error w(t) - ŵ by the eigenvalues, so the error shrinks exactly when every eigenvalue has magnitude below one. Beyond the convergence of iterative methods, eigenvalues are also used to measure the connectivity of an undirected graph G with the number of nodes n. The Laplacian matrix L(G) of G is positive semi-definite, with eigenvalues 0 = λ1 ≤ λ2 ≤ … ≤ λn. The second-smallest eigenvalue λ2, the algebraic connectivity of G, quantifies connectivity: λ2 > 0 if and only if G is connected, and λ2 close to zero indicates two clusters of nodes with few edges between them. Fig. 2 shows three edge sets on the same six nodes: adding edges increases λ2 from 0, for two clusters without a connecting edge, to 6, for the complete graph. The value 6 is the largest possible. For a graph with unit edge weights, the Laplacian matrix of G and that of the complement Ḡ, which has the edges G lacks, add to n I - 1 1ᵀ. A unit-norm eigenvector x of a positive eigenvalue is orthogonal to the constant vector 1, an eigenvector of the eigenvalue 0, so xᵀ L(G) x = n - xᵀ L(Ḡ) x ≤ n, since L(Ḡ) is positive semi-definite. For the complete graph the complement has no edges, so L(G) = n I - 1 1ᵀ and every eigenvalue other than λ1 = 0 equals n. The eigenvector corresponding to λ2, referred to as the Fiedler vector, can be used to partition G into two clusters: each node is assigned according to the sign of its own component of the Fiedler vector.

terms.name: eigenvector
terms.abstract: An eigenvector of a square matrix A is a nonzero vector x that A maps to a multiple of itself, A x = λ x. The number λ is the eigenvalue belonging to x, so multiplying by A keeps x on the line it spans and only rescales it. An eigenvector is determined only up to a nonzero factor: the eigenvectors belonging to one eigenvalue, together with the zero vector, form the nullspace of A - λ I, a subspace of Rd. For a symmetric matrix, the eigenvectors can be chosen to form an orthonormal basis, and collecting them as the columns of one matrix gives the eigenvalue decomposition. The eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix of a dataset are the directions that principal component analysis keeps and discards. Keeping those belonging to the largest eigenvalues leaves a reconstruction error equal to the sum of the eigenvalues left out.
terms.description: Every day of 2024 at the weather station Krems an der Donau (Austria) is a data point whose two features are the lowest and the highest temperature of that day in degrees Celsius. The sample covariance matrix Ĉ ∈ R2 × 2 of these m = 366 days sends most directions of the plane to a different direction. Two directions are exceptions: the matrix returns each of them rescaled and otherwise unchanged, and these two are its eigenvectors. The days scatter most widely along the line spanned by the eigenvector with the larger scaling factor, and Fig. 1 draws that line through the sample mean of the days together with the distance of each drawn day from it. Formally, a nonzero vector x ∈ Rd is an eigenvector of a square matrix A ∈ Rd × d if there is a number λ ∈ R with \begin{equation} {\mathbf A} {\mathbf x} = \lambda {\mathbf x} \text{,} \end{equation} and that number is then the eigenvalue belonging to x. The image A x is a multiple of x, so it stays on the line that x spans. The zero vector is excluded because it satisfies the defining equation Eq. (1) for every λ ∈ R and so singles out no direction. An eigenvector is determined only up to a nonzero factor: when x satisfies the defining equation Eq. (1), so does c x for every nonzero c ∈ R, with the same λ. The eigenvectors belonging to one eigenvalue λ, together with the zero vector, form the eigenspace of A for λ, which is the nullspace of A - λ I and therefore a subspace of Rd. Here, I is the identity matrix. Each eigenspace of the sample covariance matrix at Krems is a line through the origin, while the matrix 2 I has the single eigenvalue 2, whose eigenspace is the whole plane. An implementation therefore returns eigenvectors of unit norm, and even then their sign stays arbitrary. Symmetry restricts the eigenvectors further. For a real symmetric matrix, every eigenvalue is real and the eigenvectors can be chosen to form an orthonormal basis of Rd.
