Collecting such a basis as the columns of one matrix gives the eigenvalue decomposition of the symmetric matrix, which is then a spectral decomposition. The sample covariance matrix Ĉ is symmetric, which is why the two lines of Fig. 1 meet at a right angle. Without symmetry the eigenvectors need not be orthogonal: the matrix with rows (1.3, 0.8) and (0.4, 0.9) has the eigenvectors (2, 1)ᵀ and (-1, 1)ᵀ, whose inner product is -1. Eigenvectors are what principal component analysis computes. Principal component analysis, a method for dimensionality reduction, replaces the d features of a data point by d' < d numbers, chosen so that a linear map rebuilds the feature vector from them with the smallest average squared error loss over a dataset. That reconstruction error is the empirical risk of an instance of empirical risk minimization, and the eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix belonging to its d' largest eigenvalues attain its minimum, which equals the sum of the eigenvalues left out. For the two temperatures at Krems with d' = 1, the retained direction is the eigenvector u(1) drawn in Fig. 1 and the discarded eigenvalue is λ2 = 7.9 squared degrees, the average squared length of the dotted segments over all 366 days. The two eigenvalues add up to 138.9 squared degrees, so the retained direction keeps all but 5.7 percent of that total, while a line through the sample mean turned by 30 degrees away from u(1) would leave 38.7 squared degrees behind.

terms.name: expectation–maximization (EM)
terms.abstract: The expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm is an iterative optimization method for a particular class of maximum likelihood problems. In particular, EM is useful for probabilistic models that involve observed and unobserved (or latent) attributes of a data point. Each iteration of the EM algorithm alternates an E-step with an M-step. The E-step computes the posterior distribution of the unobserved attributes under the current model parameters. The M-step minimizes the negative log-likelihood of the complete data points averaged under this posterior distribution, which for many probabilistic models has a closed form. The EM algorithm is an instance of a majorize–minimize method. A canonical soft clustering method uses the EM algorithm to learn the model parameters of a Gaussian mixture model.
terms.description: The nightly minimum temperatures recorded over one year at the weather station of Krems an der Donau (Austria) scatter around two regimes, cold-season and warm-season nights. A probabilistic model for such data points has, besides the observed temperature, an unobserved attribute: the regime a night belongs to. Fig. 1 shows the histogram of the temperatures together with a Gaussian mixture model consisting of a separate normal distribution for each regime. The EM algorithm is an iterative optimization method for approximately solving maximum likelihood optimization problems for probabilistic models with an unobserved attribute. Consider a dataset D = x(1), …, x(m) whose data points are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs. The underlying probability distribution is a probabilistic model p(x',y')(x,y;w) for the observed feature vector x and an unobserved attribute y with values in a finite set Y. This probabilistic model is a family of probability distributions parameterized by model parameters w in a parameter space W. Maximum likelihood is an instance of empirical risk minimization: it minimizes the empirical risk \begin{equation} \widehat{L}\big({\mathbf w}|\mathcal{D}\big) := - \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \ln \sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}} p^{({\mathbf x}',y')}\left({\mathbf x}^{(r)},y;{\mathbf w}\right)\text{,} \end{equation} the average negative log-likelihood of the observed feature vectors. The sum inside the logarithm is what makes Eq. (1) hard to minimize directly: if the attributes y(r) were observed, the empirical risk would be an average of -ln p(x',y')(x(r),y(r);w), which for many probabilistic models, among them the Gaussian mixture model, has a closed-form minimizer. The EM algorithm solves the maximum likelihood problem Eq. (1) by alternating two steps, which together form one iteration. The E-step computes, for every data point, the posterior distribution of the unobserved attribute under the current model parameters ŵ, \begin{equation} p^{(y'|{\mathbf x}')}\left(y;\widehat{{\mathbf w}}\right) = \frac{p^{({\mathbf x}',y')}\left({\mathbf x}^{(r)},y;\widehat{{\mathbf w}}\right)} {\sum_{y'' \in \mathcal{Y}} p^{({\mathbf x}',y')}\left({\mathbf x}^{(r)},y'';\widehat{{\mathbf w}}\right)} \quad \text{for } y \in \mathcal{Y} \text{ and } r = 1, \ldots, m\text{.} \end{equation} These posterior distributions fix the surrogate that the E-step of Algorithm 1 forms, the empirical risk of the complete data points averaged under them, \begin{equation} Q({\mathbf w} \mid \widehat{{\mathbf w}}) := - \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}} p^{(y'|{\mathbf x}')}\left(y;\widehat{{\mathbf w}}\right) \ln \frac{p^{({\mathbf x}',y')}\left({\mathbf x}^{(r)},y;{\mathbf w}\right)} {p^{(y'|{\mathbf x}')}\left(y;\widehat{{\mathbf w}}\right)}\text{.} \end{equation} The M-step minimizes this surrogate over w ∈ W. Algorithm 1 states the method in full. \begin{algorithm}[H] \caption{Expectation-maximization } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex Input: dataset D, probabilistic model with parameters w ∈ W, initialization w(0), iteration count T \For{t = 0, 1, …, T-1} \State E-step: form Q(w | w(t)), the expectation of the complete-data empirical risk under the current parameters \State M-step: w(t+1) := argminw ∈ W Q(w | w(t)) \EndFor \Statex Output: w(T) \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} The EM algorithm is a majorize–minimize method: each iteration minimizes a surrogate Q(w | ŵ) of the empirical risk Eq. (1). The surrogate Eq. (3) has three properties (whose lower bound on the log-likelihood is this surrogate written for the negative log-likelihood;). First, it majorizes the empirical risk, Q(w | ŵ) ≥ L̂(w|D) for all w ∈ W, by Jensen's inequality applied to the concave logarithm. Second, it is tight at the current iterate, Q(ŵ | ŵ) = L̂(ŵ|D). Third, it is minimized exactly by the M-step. EM is not coordinate descent on the empirical risk Eq. (1). Coordinate descent minimizes the empirical risk itself over one block of the model parameters at a time, while the E-step varies no model parameter but builds the surrogate, and the M-step minimizes the surrogate. The two steps are coordinate descent only on the extended objective function that treats the posterior distributions of the unobserved attribute as a second block of variables beside the model parameters. Any model parameters w(t+1) that minimize the surrogate built at w(t) therefore satisfy L̂(w(t+1)|D) ≤ Q(w(t+1) | w(t)) ≤ Q(w(t) | w(t)) = L̂(w(t)|D): no iteration increases the empirical risk. The monotone decrease of the empirical risk Eq. (1) along the EM iterates yields a stopping criterion: the iteration stops as soon as the decrease of the empirical risk achieved by the last iteration falls below a given threshold. The empirical risk Eq. (1) is in general a non-convex function of the model parameters, and EM might converge to a local minimum. It is therefore typically run several times with different initializations, keeping the run with the smallest empirical risk. The EM algorithm is a fixed-point iteration ŵ(t+1) = F(ŵ(t)). The operator F maps the current model parameters ŵ to the result of one E-step followed by one M-step. The E-step Eq. (2) at ŵ builds the surrogate Q(· | ŵ), and the M-step Eq. (3) minimizes it, \mathcal{F}(\widehat{{\mathbf w}}) := \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathcal{W}} Q({\mathbf w} \mid \widehat{{\mathbf w}})\text{.} The fixed points of F are model parameters that minimize their own surrogate: there, the surrogate touches the empirical risk from above, so no further descent step is available. If the empirical risk and the surrogate are differentiable and the fixed point ŵ lies in the interior of W, the gradient of the empirical risk vanishes at ŵ. Indeed, the difference Q(w | ŵ) - L̂(w|D) is nonnegative for all w and zero at w = ŵ, so its gradient vanishes there, and the gradient of Q(· | ŵ) vanishes at its interior minimum ŵ. Under the conditions of Wu (1983, Thm. 2), every limit point of the EM iterates is such a stationary point of the empirical risk. EM is used to learn the model parameters of a Gaussian mixture model, where the unobserved attribute of a data point is its cluster index I(r) ∈ 1, …, k and the model parameters are the cluster probabilities pc, means μ(c), and covariance matrices C(c). The E-step Eq. (2) becomes the degree of belonging \begin{equation} u_{c}^{(r)} := \mathbb{P}\left(I^{(r)} = c \mid {\mathbf x}^{(r)}\right) = \frac{p_{c} \mathcal{N}\left({\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)},\mathbf{C}^{(c)}\right)({\mathbf x}^{(r)})} {\sum_{c'=1}^{k} p_{c'} \mathcal{N}\left({\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c')},\mathbf{C}^{(c')}\right)({\mathbf x}^{(r)})}\text{,} \end{equation} and minimizing the surrogate Eq. (3) yields the M-step in closed form. The cluster probability pc is the average of uc(r) over the data points, while μ(c) and C(c) are the mean and covariance matrix of the feature vectors weighted by uc(r). The learned degrees of belonging Eq. (4) constitute a soft clustering. Fixing every cluster probability at 1/k and every covariance matrix at σ2 I, a multiple of the identity matrix I with a common σ2 that shrinks towards 0 turns the degrees of belonging into 0 or 1, and EM reduces to Lloyd's algorithm for k-means. Consider next, as an illustration of the EM algorithm, the Gaussian mixture model of Fig. 1 for the temperature dataset. The feature of a data point is the nightly minimum temperature x ∈ R, and its unobserved attribute is the regime y ∈ cold, warm. The model parameters are the probabilities pcold, pwarm = 1 - pcold of the two regimes, the means μcold, μwarm and the variances σ2cold, σ2warm of the two normal distributions, so w = (pcold, pwarm, μcold, μwarm, σ2cold, σ2warm)ᵀ ∈ R6. The E-step Eq. (2) computes for every night the probability of the cold regime, and the M-step Eq. (3) recomputes w as averages weighted by these probabilities. On the 366 nights of 2024, EM learns pcold = 0.83, μcold = 5.1, μwarm = 17.2, σ2cold = 39.7, and σ2warm = 3.3. Fig. 2 shows the majorize–minimize view for this Gaussian mixture model as the cold-season mean μcold varies, while pcold, μwarm and σ2warm are fixed at their learned values and σ2cold is fixed at 16. The empirical risk is then a function of μcold alone, and so is each surrogate. Each surrogate lies above the empirical risk, touches it at its iterate, and its minimizer is the next iterate. Fig. 3 shows how the empirical risk decreases monotonically as the EM iterations proceed.

terms.name: encoder
terms.abstract: An encoder is a map that sends the raw feature vector of a data point to a shorter vector, a code of d' numbers with d' below the number d of raw features. Its counterpart is the decoder, which maps a code back to a vector of the original length, and the two are judged together: the decoder applied to the code of a data point should return approximately the feature vector the encoder started from. The average loss that remains, the reconstruction error, is what training minimizes. Principal component analysis uses a linear map as the encoder, a matrix whose rows are the eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix belonging to its largest eigenvalues. An autoencoder learns the encoder jointly with the decoder, so it can be a deep net rather than a linear map. A large language model begins with the token-to-vector encoder, which carries every token of a vocabulary to one row of an embedding matrix. The code length decides what the decoder can rebuild, and the code kept in place of the raw feature vectors is what makes an encoder a feature transformation for a later learning task. What a shorter code drops is beyond every decoder, so a code learned to reconstruct well need not serve that learning task well.
terms.description: The weather station at Krems an der Donau (Austria) records eight numbers for each day: the lowest, the highest, and the mean air temperature, the precipitation, the sunshine duration, the humidity, the air pressure, and the wind speed. Two numbers computed from the eight are enough to tell a day in January from a day in July, and a second map rebuilds the eight from the two with a small error. The map that delivers the two numbers is an encoder. It sends the raw feature vector x ∈ Rd of a data point to a shorter vector z ∈ Rd', its code, {\mathbf \Phi}: \mathbb{R}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{d'}: {\mathbf x} \mapsto {\mathbf z} := {\mathbf \Phi}({\mathbf x}) \text{,} with a code length d' below the number d of raw features. Its counterpart is the decoder Φ*: Rd' → Rd, which maps a code back to a vector with d entries. Encoders differ in the hypothesis space they are picked from. Principal component analysis picks a linear map: the encoder is a matrix W ∈ Rd' × d with z = W x, whose rows are the eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix of the feature vectors belonging to its d' largest eigenvalues, and the decoder is the transpose Wᵀ. An autoencoder picks the encoder from a hypothesis space of deep nets and learns it jointly with the decoder, so that neither map need be linear. A large language model begins with the token-to-vector step, an encoder on text. Every token of a vocabulary V carries one row of an embedding matrix E ∈ R|V| × d'. Picking the row of the token with index v is the linear map z = Eᵀ e(v) applied to the one-hot vector e(v) ∈ R|V| of that token. What makes a code useful is that the decoder can rebuild the data point from it. The reconstruction error of an encoder on a dataset D = x(1), …, x(m) of sample size m is the average loss between a feature vector and what the decoder returns for its code, \begin{equation} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\left({\mathbf x}^{(r)},{\mathbf \Phi}^{*} \big( {\mathbf \Phi} \big( {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \big) \big) \right) \text{.} \end{equation} A common loss function is the squared error loss ‖ x - Φ*(Φ(x)) ‖22, and minimizing the reconstruction error Eq. (1) over a hypothesis space of encoders and a second one of decoders is empirical risk minimization. No labels enter it: what the decoder has to reproduce is the data point itself, so the training of an encoder is a form of self-supervised learning. Each of the eight measurements of a day at Krems is scaled to zero sample mean and unit sample variance, so that they carry comparable weight. Over the 366 days of 2024, the principal component analysis encoder with d' = 2 then leaves a reconstruction error of 2.91 out of the total variance 8.00, and the eight reconstructed measurements of 1 January 2024 differ from the scaled originals by at most 0.80. Fig. 1(a) places 21 of the days at their two code numbers, split at the median of the maximum temperature, and Fig. 1(b) compares the reconstruction error of this encoder with what a random encoder with orthonormal rows leaves as the code grows. The code length decides what survives. On the days at Krems, the reconstruction error of the principal component analysis encoder falls from 4.38 at one number to 2.91 at two and 0.88 at four, and at every code length it equals the sum of the eigenvalues the code drops. A random encoder with orthonormal rows leaves 5.71 at two numbers, so which encoder is used matters beside how long its code is. Losing something is not inevitable: the token-to-vector encoder shortens a one-hot vector of length |V| to d' numbers and still loses nothing, since distinct tokens carry distinct rows of E and the nearest row therefore recovers the token. What training keeps is usually the encoder alone: the decoder is dropped and the code serves as the feature transformation of a later learning task, which makes an encoder a feature learning and a dimensionality reduction method. The code of two numbers leaves a reconstruction error of 2.91, and that loss is not spread evenly over the eight measurements. Of the unit sample variance of each measurement, the code keeps 96 percent of the mean temperature and 3 percent of the wind speed. What the dropped eigenvectors carried is beyond every decoder, not only the transpose Wᵀ. Of the 80 pairs of days whose codes lie closer than 0.1 together, 14 February and 22 November 2024 differ most in wind speed, 1.0 against 4.5 meters per second, and the decoder returns 1.76 meters per second for both. Whether the loss matters is decided by the later learning task and not by the reconstruction error alone. A day counts as windy when its mean wind speed lies above the median of the 366 values, which holds for 130 of them. A linear classifier learned by least squares has an accuracy of 98 percent from all eight scaled measurements and 66 percent from the two code numbers, against the 64 percent reached by calling every day calm. One new feature chosen from the labels instead of from the sample covariance matrix, the linear discriminant analysis direction, reaches 98 percent as well. A code learned to reconstruct well is therefore not a code learned to predict well, which is the difference linear discriminant analysis draws against principal component analysis. An encoder is also fixed once learned, and the dataset it was learned from decides how well it codes a later day. The principal component analysis encoder of the 183 days of January to March and of October to December leaves 1.93 on those days and 10.87 on the other 183, against 2.48 for the encoder of the whole year. What the code buys is its shortness: fewer numbers per data point to store and to hand to a later learning task, and at d' = 2 a plot of the dataset on two axes.

terms.name: ensemble
terms.abstract: An ensemble method combines several machine learning methods, each referred to as a base learner. Ensemble methods differ in how they construct the base learners and in how they combine their results. Bagging trains each base learner on a resampled copy of the training set. Boosting runs them sequentially, each one fitted to the errors of the previous ones. Stacking uses base learners to train different models on the same training set and learns an aggregation rule. For the squared error loss the gain is exact: the error of the average prediction is the average error of the base learners minus their average disagreement, so base learners that disagree are what makes an ensemble worth forming.
terms.description: Predicting the maximum temperature of a day at the weather station Krems an der Donau from the minimum temperature of the same day can be done with a linear model, with a decision tree, or with an artificial neural network. Fig. 1 shows all three learned from 244 of the 366 days of 2020. None of them is the best everywhere: the linear hypothesis misses the curvature at the cold end, the decision tree answers with a staircase, and the artificial neural network bends where the other two cannot. Model selection would keep one of them and discard the rest. Combining these base learners can do better than choosing one of them. Combining several machine learning methods into one predictor is an ensemble method: each combined method is a base learner. The base learners can be empirical risk minimization-based, using different choices for the loss, model, and training set. Of M base learners, base learner ℓ learns a hypothesis ĥ(ℓ) from its hypothesis space H(ℓ) and its, possibly perturbed, training set D̃(ℓ), and an aggregation rule φagg combines the outputs of these hypotheses into the final prediction. The aggregation can amount to averaging (in regression), as in Fig. 1, or to a majority vote (in classification); Fig. 2 shows the general shape. What the combination gains is exactly the disagreement among the base learners. For the squared error loss, the error of the average prediction is the average error of the base learners minus their average disagreement, where the disagreement of a base learner is the squared difference between its own prediction and the average one. The decomposition is an identity, not an approximation: on the held-back days of Fig. 1 the average member error 26.47 minus the average disagreement 0.52 is the 25.95 that the average prediction actually incurs. Two consequences follow. The average is never worse than its base learners are on average, since a disagreement cannot be negative. And base learners that agree everywhere gain nothing, which is why they are trained on different models or on different data points. Outperforming the best single base learner is a stronger claim, and one the identity does not guarantee: over 50 repetitions on random halves of the training set, the average did so 22 times. The same point in terms of variance: consider M base learners whose predictions are identically distributed, each with variance σ2 and pairwise correlation ρ. The average of these predictions has variance \rho \sigma^{2} + \frac{1-\rho}{M} \sigma^{2}\text{.} The second of these two summands vanishes as M grows, while the first, set by the correlation between the base learners, limits what averaging can achieve. Ensemble methods differ in how they construct the base learners and in how they combine their results. Bagging trains each base learner on a random resample of the training set and averages them; it reduces the variance of an unstable base learner such as a deep decision tree, while the systematic part of its error, the bias, is left unchanged. A random forest is bagging of decision trees with, in addition, a random choice of the features considered at each split, which lowers the correlation between the trees. Boosting runs the base learners sequentially, each one fitted to the errors of the previous ones. The number of rounds is a hyperparameter: the training error keeps decreasing while the validation error eventually rises, so boosting overfits when run for too long. Stacking trains the base learners on the same training set with different models and learns the aggregation rule itself by a second machine learning method. The second method is trained on predictions for data points that did not belong to the training sets of the base learners. Otherwise the base learners that fit the training set best are favored regardless of how they generalize.

terms.name: empirical risk minimization (ERM)
terms.abstract: Empirical risk minimization (ERM) selects a hypothesis by minimizing the average loss on a given training set D(train), the empirical risk. Machine learning methods aim at a hypothesis that incurs a small loss on any data point, and ERM replaces this unknown quantity by its average over the training set. Different machine learning methods arise from different choices of the model H and the loss function L, both of which depend on the feature space X and the label space Y of a given method.
terms.description: A weather forecaster predicting tomorrow's maximum daytime temperature is useful only if its predictions are accurate on the large majority of days, not only on the days it was trained on. This forecaster is a hypothesis: it maps a day's features to a prediction of tomorrow's temperature, and its loss quantifies how far that prediction lies from the measured value. More generally, machine learning methods aim to find a hypothesis that incurs a small loss for any data point. The phrase any data point is made precise by a probabilistic model for the generation of data points, as follows. If data points are assumed to be drawn from a probability distribution, then the risk of a hypothesis is defined as the expectation of its loss under that probability distribution. The ideal choice is then the hypothesis with minimal risk. However, in most machine learning applications, the underlying probability distribution is not known. Instead, only a finite training set D(train) of data points is available. ERM replaces the unknown risk with its sample-average surrogate, the empirical risk on D(train), and picks the hypothesis that minimizes this surrogate. For a fixed choice of loss function and hypothesis space, ERM is a map A that reads in a training set D(train) = z(r)r=1m of data points z(r) = ( x(r),y(r) ). The map returns a learned hypothesis ĥ = A(D(train)) ∈ H that minimizes the empirical risk on D(train), \begin{equation} \widehat{h} \in \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\left({\mathbf z}^{(r)},h \right) \text{.} \end{equation} The hypothesis ĥ in Eq. (1) is chosen from the underlying hypothesis space (or model) H. For an ERM-based method, model training is to compute A. Different machine learning methods arise from different design choices for the two components of the map A: the model H and the loss function L. Both depend on the nature of the data points, i.e., on the feature space X and the label space Y. For example, image data points with a high-dimensional feature space and a finite label space are typically handled by an artificial neural network together with the logistic loss. Conversely, data points with few real-valued features and a real-valued label often allow for a linear model together with the squared error loss. Fig. 1 illustrates ERM for a linear model on data points with a single feature x and label y. Each hypothesis is a linear map h(x) = w1 x + w0 with model parameters w0, w1. ERM picks the model parameters that minimize the empirical risk on D(train). In practice, the map A is computed by an iterative optimization method. Many of these optimization methods can be represented as a fixed-point iteration that starts with an initial hypothesis h(0) and then repeatedly applies an update operator F, h^{(t+1)} = \mathcal{F}\big( h^{(t)} \big) \text{, for } t=0,1,\ldots \text{.} The update operator F depends on the training set, the loss function, and the hypothesis space. It is chosen such that its fixed points are the stationary points of the empirical risk. The stationary points are its minimizers when the empirical risk is a convex function of the hypothesis, and need not be otherwise, e.g., for an artificial neural network. For ERM using a parametric model H, the fixed-point iteration can be formulated directly in terms of the model parameters w instead of the hypothesis h. In particular, starting with initial model parameters w(0), the update operator F is applied repeatedly to the model parameters, {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} = \mathcal{F}\big( {\mathbf w}^{(t)} \big) \text{, for } t=0,1,\ldots \text{.} One example of such a fixed-point iteration is gradient descent, which updates the model parameters in the direction of the negative gradient of the empirical risk (which needs to be differentiable). Two requirements delimit where ERM applies: full feedback on the loss and access to the whole training set at once. First, ERM presupposes that the loss L(z(r),h ) can be evaluated for every hypothesis h ∈ H and every training data point z(r). This full-feedback requirement is what distinguishes ERM from reinforcement learning algorithms, which use partial feedback. In particular, at each time instant t = 1, 2, …, a reinforcement learning algorithm chooses an action, the prediction of its current hypothesis ĥ(t), and observes only the loss incurred by that action. It has no information about the loss that would have been incurred by any other hypothesis h ∈ H ĥ(t). Second, ERM uses the whole training set at once. This requirement can be relaxed: ERM can also be implemented as an online algorithm, which is useful when the data points in D(train) can only be accessed sequentially. Such sequential access arises, for instance, when memory limits prevent loading the entire training set at once. The canonical online form of ERM is the Follow-The-Leader algorithm, which, at every round, solves a partial ERM problem on all data points seen so far. Assuming that the data point z(t) arrives at time instant t=1,2,…, Follow-The-Leader updates the learned hypothesis ĥ(t) by \widehat{h}^{(t)} \in \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \frac{1}{t} \sum_{r=1}^{t} L\left({\mathbf z}^{(r)},h \right) \text{.} Implementing this partial ERM separately for each time instant can become computationally expensive (and wasteful), as it does not exploit the similarity between consecutive partial ERM problems. This similarity can be exploited by online gradient descent, which performs a single gradient descent step on the new data point z(t) at every time instant t.

terms.name: eigenvalue decomposition (EVD)
terms.abstract: An eigenvalue decomposition (EVD) of a square matrix breaks the linear map it represents into elementary operations: expanding a vector in the eigenvectors of the matrix, multiplying each expansion coefficient by the corresponding eigenvalue, and summing the scaled terms up again. A matrix that has an EVD is called diagonalizable; symmetric matrices and matrices with distinct eigenvalues are diagonalizable. A dataset with numeric feature vectors can be characterized by the EVD of its sample covariance matrix. The EVD can be used to speed up computations such as the gradient step of gradient descent methods. For linear regression, each gradient descent iteration then reduces to element-wise operations. The EVD of the Laplacian matrix of an undirected graph is used by spectral clustering.
terms.description: Each day of 2024 at the weather station Krems an der Donau (Austria) is a data point recorded with two features, its lowest and its highest temperature, stacked into a feature vector x = ( x1, x2 )ᵀ ∈ R2. Fig. 1 shows 20 of the m = 366 days x(1), …, x(m) as a scatterplot together with an ellipse that is computed from their sample mean and sample covariance matrix. The sample mean of the days is \[ \widehat{\boldsymbol \mu} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \text{,} \] and their sample covariance matrix is \[ \widehat{{\mathbf C}} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big( {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - \widehat{\boldsymbol \mu} \big) \big( {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - \widehat{\boldsymbol \mu} \big)^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2} \text{.} \] The shape of the ellipse, which outlines the dataset, is determined by an EVD of the sample covariance matrix Ĉ, whose eigenvectors are the axes of the ellipse. An EVD for a square matrix A ∈ Rd × d is a factorization of the form \[ {\mathbf A} = \mathbf{V} {\boldsymbol \Lambda} \mathbf{V}^{-1} \text{.} \] The columns of the matrix V = ( v(1), …, v(d) ) are eigenvectors of the matrix A. The diagonal matrix Λ = diag λ1, …, λd contains the eigenvalues λj corresponding to the eigenvectors v(j). Multiplying the factorization by v(j) gives A v(j) = λj v(j): each eigenvector is a direction that A only scales, by the factor λj; a single such pair satisfies A x = λ x, and the EVD collects d of them, indexed by j. The EVD breaks the linear map u ↦ A u into three elementary operations. A vector u is expanded in the eigenvectors, u = Σj=1d βj v(j) with the expansion coefficients β = V-1 u; each coefficient is multiplied by its eigenvalue; and the scaled terms are summed up again, A u = Σj=1d λj βj v(j). Unlike the singular value decomposition, which exists for every matrix, square or not, the EVD is defined for square matrices only, and it need not exist. Moreover, the same matrix might allow for different EVDs: any nonzero linear combination of eigenvectors with the same eigenvalue is again an eigenvector with this eigenvalue. The geometric multiplicity of an eigenvalue is the maximum number of linearly independent eigenvectors with this eigenvalue. Matrices that allow for an EVD are called diagonalizable. One example of a diagonalizable matrix is \[ {\mathbf A} = \begin{pmatrix} 1.3 & 0.8 0.4 & 0.9 \end{pmatrix} \text{.} \] Fig. 2 illustrates its EVD. Two sufficient conditions for a real-valued square matrix to be diagonalizable are that it is a symmetric matrix or that its d eigenvalues are distinct. For a real-valued symmetric matrix, the EVD has additional structure: the eigenvectors can be chosen to form an orthonormal basis, i.e., the matrix V in the factorization can be chosen to be orthogonal. The condition that is both necessary and sufficient is that every root of the minimal polynomial of the matrix is simple. For a complex-valued matrix, the first condition is that it is Hermitian; a complex symmetric matrix need not be diagonalizable. The matrix A of Fig. 2 is not symmetric, since its off-diagonal entries 0.8 and 0.4 differ, but its two eigenvalues 1.7 and 0.5 are distinct, so it has an EVD. When neither condition holds, an EVD may not exist: the matrix \[ {\mathbf N} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \] is not symmetric and has the eigenvalue 0 twice, since the eigenvalues of a triangular matrix are its diagonal entries. The eigenvectors of N are all located on the line (a, 0)ᵀ: a ∈ R, so there is no invertible matrix V whose columns are eigenvectors of N. The ellipse in Fig. 1 is the set of feature vectors x for which the quadratic form (x - μ)ᵀ Ĉ-1 (x - μ) equals 4. This set can be characterized more conveniently using an EVD of the sample covariance matrix Ĉ. The matrix Ĉ is symmetric, so it has an EVD Ĉ = V Λ Vᵀ with an orthogonal matrix V that contains the eigenvectors in its columns. Transforming the feature vector x of a day according to x̃ := Vᵀ (x - μ) turns the quadratic form into \[ ({\mathbf x} - \widehat{\boldsymbol \mu})^{\top} \widehat{{\mathbf C}}^{-1} ({\mathbf x} - \widehat{\boldsymbol \mu}) = \widetilde{{\mathbf x}}^{\top} {\boldsymbol \Lambda}^{-1} \widetilde{{\mathbf x}} = \frac{\widetilde{x}_{1}^{2}}{\lambda_{1}} + \frac{\widetilde{x}_{2}^{2}}{\lambda_{2}} \text{,} \] since Ĉ-1 = V Λ-1 Vᵀ. The ellipse is therefore the set where x̃12/λ1 + x̃22/λ2 = 4, with half-axes 2√(λ1) and 2√(λ2) along the coordinate axes of x̃, that is, along the eigenvectors. The transformed days have the sample covariance matrix Vᵀ Ĉ V = Λ: the two new coordinates have sample covariance zero, and the eigenvalues are their sample variances. Replacing each day by its first coordinate x̃1 alone keeps the direction of largest variance, which is the idea of principal component analysis. Besides describing the shape of a dataset, the EVD can be used to speed up the implementation of a machine learning method. Consider gradient descent for linear regression, with the update w(t+1) = w(t) - (2η/m) Xᵀ ( X w(t) - y ) for t = 0,1,…, with the feature matrix X and label vector y of the training set (see linear regression). The matrix XᵀX is symmetric, so it has an EVD XᵀX = V Λ Vᵀ with an orthogonal matrix V. In the transformed coordinates w̃(t) := Vᵀ w(t), the update decouples into \[ \widetilde{w}_{j}^{(t+1)} = \big( 1 - (2\eta/m) \lambda_{j} \big) \widetilde{w}_{j}^{(t)} + (2\eta/m) \big( \mathbf{V}^{\top} {\mathbf X}^{\top} {\mathbf y} \big)_{j} \text{.} \] After the one-time computation of the EVD, each iteration is an element-wise multiplication and addition of vectors of length d (pythondemos/evd.py). Another application of the EVD in machine learning is the clustering of graph-structured data. Consider data points represented as the nodes i = 1, …, n of an undirected graph G, e.g., the users of a social network with edges given by friendships. The Laplacian matrix L(G) of the graph G is symmetric and positive semi-definite. It has an EVD L(G) = V Λ Vᵀ with an orthogonal matrix V and nonnegative eigenvalues. If the graph G is connected, the EVD has additional structure: the eigenvalue 0 has multiplicity one, with the all-ones vector as its eigenvector. Moreover, there is then a distinguished eigenvector, called the Fiedler vector: an eigenvector of the smallest nonzero eigenvalue, the algebraic connectivity of G. The Fiedler vector can be used for clustering the nodes of the graph, which is the idea of spectral clustering. Fig. 3 shows the Fiedler vector of a connected graph with six nodes: two clusters of three nodes and a single edge joining the two clusters.

terms.name: explainability
terms.abstract: Explainability is the property of a machine learning method whose explanations let a human user anticipate the predictions it delivers. The method delivers an explanation along with every prediction, and that explanation is effective if it lets the user anticipate the prediction made for a data point; comprehending the explanation is not required for this test. Explainability is always relative to a specific user or group of users: an explanation can be effective for one and useless for another. Explainability can be measured by comparing the predictions of a learned hypothesis to the anticipations of a user before and after they are provided with an explanation.
terms.description: A radiologist who is shown which pixels of a scan led an image classifier to its prediction can tell, for the next scan, what the classifier will say. A machine learning method is explainable for a human user if the explanations it provides let the user anticipate the predictions it delivers. Explainability thus includes the notion of an explanation: each prediction is delivered with an explanation for this specific prediction (see Fig. 1), such as the feature values that contributed most to it or, for image data, the relevant pixels. In the figure, the explanation for the prediction at a data point with feature vector x is a linear map that approximates the learned hypothesis near x. The definition asks for the existence of an explanation, not for a particular one: explainability is certified by exhibiting one explanation that works, and one explanation the user cannot follow does not show that the method is unexplainable. Explainability is relative to a specific user or group of users: the same learned hypothesis can be explainable for one user and inscrutable for another. The usefulness of an explanation can be measured by how much it enables the user to anticipate the predictions on a curated test set: the user states an anticipation for each data point in the test set. If the user comprehends the explanations, these anticipations should be close to the predictions of the learned hypothesis. A measure of this form is referred to as predictability. As with interpretability, predictability is weaker than comprehension of the explanations: anticipating the predictions does not require comprehending the provided explanations. A second measure of this predictability uses the conditional differential entropy, which is defined for RVs. If the data point is modeled as the realization of a random variable, the prediction and the anticipation of the user are RVs too, and their joint probability distribution yields the conditional differential entropy of the predictions given the anticipations. The conditional differential entropy quantifies the uncertainty that remains about the predictions once the anticipations are known, so a smaller value means that the anticipations determine the predictions more tightly. In practice, this conditional differential entropy is unknown and must be replaced by an estimator. One such estimator bins the predictions and the anticipations on a test set, and takes the fraction of test data points that fall into each pair of bins as the joint probability distribution. A related measure, the mutual information between a selected subset of the features and the prediction, is maximized by the explainer of Chen et al. (2018, Sect. 2.1). An explanation raises explainability when the user can reason with it. Fig. 2 illustrates this for a user who reasons in terms of linear maps and anticipates the predictions of an opaque hypothesis (Gaussian kernel ridge regression, a kernel method). Without explanations, the user anticipates by a single linear map fitted to a few predictions, and the anticipations deviate strongly from the predictions. The explanation for a test data point with feature value x0 is a local linear approximation of the hypothesis around it (cf. local interpretable model-agnostic explanations), a slope and an intercept that the user evaluates at x0. With this explanation, the anticipations match the predictions almost exactly. The example presupposes that the user knows how to apply a linear approximation: the anticipations improve only because the user can evaluate the explanation for a data point. A user who cannot gains nothing from it. An explanation can also mislead. A computed explanation can be unfaithful to the learned hypothesis, so that anticipations based on it are confidently wrong. Saliency maps, intensity maps over the pixels of an input image (see explainable artificial intelligence), barely change for some methods when the trained deep net is replaced by one with random weights. The predictability test detects such an explanation: anticipations drawn from it deviate from the predictions. The international terminology standard for artificial intelligence defines explainability as the property of an artificial intelligence system to express important factors influencing its results in a way that humans can understand. An explanation is intended to answer the question of why the artificial intelligence system produced a result, without arguing that the result was optimal. The AI Risk Management Framework of the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) ties explainability to a representation of the mechanisms underlying the operation of an artificial intelligence system. NIST reserves interpretability for the meaning of the output in the context of the designed purpose. The two documents thus divide the terms differently. The expressed factors influencing a result, which the terminology standard places under explainability, are close to the NIST notion of interpretability; the NIST notion of explainability is instead close to interpretability as comprehension of the computation of the method. Regulation treats explainability as a component of transparency. The EU AI Act requires that high-risk AI systems are sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system's output and use it appropriately. For individual automated decisions, the right to explanation entitles an affected person to a clear and meaningful account of the role that an artificial intelligence system played in the decision. The Colorado Automated Decision-Making Technology Act of 2026 requires that the deployer give the affected consumer a plain-language description of the decision and of the role the technology played in it, together with the means to request further information. What counts as an automated decision is drawn widely: the Court of Justice of the European Union held that a credit information agency computing a person's ability to meet future payments already makes one, when a third party draws strongly on that value.

terms.name: explanation
terms.abstract: An explanation accompanies a prediction delivered by a machine learning method and states which properties of the data point led to that prediction. Explanations can be a textual description, a feature importance score, an approximation of a hypothesis map, or a heat map. An explanation of local or global scope can be learned as a simple hypothesis that reproduces the predictions of the learned hypothesis on a probing set of feature vectors. On the one hand, an explanation must be faithful: it must reflect the computation by which the learned hypothesis arrives at the prediction. On the other hand, it must be understandable: its user must be able to anticipate, from it alone, how the prediction changes when the features change.
terms.description: A weather service forecasts frost for the coming night at Krems an der Donau (Austria) and adds which of the recent measurements weighed most. That addition is an explanation: it is provided alongside the prediction delivered by a machine learning method to increase its transparency for its human user. Explanations can take different forms. For instance, they may consist of human-readable text or quantitative indicators, such as feature importance scores. Fig. 1 illustrates two types of explanations, both for the same learned hypothesis ĥ(x) of a single feature x. The first explanation approximates ĥ(x) around a specific feature value x' by a linear function g(x). The weight of g(x), its slope, serves as a feature importance score. The second explanation type is a small set of predictions ĥ(x(1)), ĥ(x(2)), ĥ(x(3)) at selected feature values, possibly chosen by the user. Another form of explanation is a heat map, also called an intensity map or, for images, a saliency map. Such a map assigns each region of an image a score for how much that region contributed to the prediction and indicates these scores by color intensities overlaid on the image itself. For a convolutional neural network, the scores can be computed from its activations, which is what a class activation map does; Fig. 2 shows one. Besides their form, explanations also differ in their scope with respect to the feature space. The local linear approximation of local interpretable model-agnostic explanations delivers a local explanation for a learned hypothesis ĥ around a specific feature vector x ∈ X. Another example of a local explanation is a counterfactual for a classifier ĥ. For a given feature vector x, a counterfactual states a (small) modification x ↦ x' such that the prediction changes, ĥ(x) ≠ ĥ(x'). The Court of Justice of the European Union has named such information as an appropriate explanation of an automated decision: the extent to which a variation in the personal data would have led to a different result. In contrast to a local explanation, a global explanation of ĥ approximates it across the entire feature space. Such an approximation can be obtained by training a model, such as a decision tree, to reproduce the predictions ĥ(x(r)) for feature vectors x(1), …, x(m) that cover the entire feature space well. Algorithm 1 states this construction: the feature vectors form a probing set, each labeled with the prediction of ĥ, and the explanation g is learned via empirical risk minimization over a hypothesis space H' of candidate explanations. The scope is fixed by the probing set alone. The same algorithm delivers the local explanation of local interpretable model-agnostic explanations when the probing set consists of feature vectors drawn around the one x to be explained; the linear function g of Fig. 1 is its output for a probing set near x' and H' the linear model. \begin{algorithm}[H] \caption{Explanation by a surrogate model, following Ribeiro et al. (2016, Sect. 3.2) } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex Input: learned hypothesis ĥ to be explained; probing set of feature vectors x(1), …, x(m); hypothesis space H' of understandable hypotheses; loss function L(·,· ) \For{r = 1, …, m} \State y(r) := ĥ(x(r)) \Comment{the prediction to be explained serves as label} \EndFor \State g ∈ argminh ∈ H' (1)/(m) Σr=1m L(( x(r),y(r) ),h ) \Comment{empirical risk minimization} \Statex Output: the explanation g and its training error on the probing set \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} Explanations of (the predictions obtained from) machine learning methods should be (i) understandable and (ii) faithful. Understandable means that the user can work with the explanation on their own: from it alone, they can anticipate how the prediction changes when the features change. In Algorithm 1, this requirement falls on the choice of H', which must consist of hypotheses the user can comprehend, such as linear maps or shallow decision trees. Faithful means that the explanation reflects the computation the learned hypothesis carries out. For the output g of Algorithm 1, the training error on the probing set measures how faithfully g reproduces ĥ there, and nowhere else. An intensity map over the pixels of an image is faithful when manipulating a few of the pixels it highlights changes the prediction, while the same manipulation of pixels it leaves dark does not. Understandability and faithfulness can be contradictory requirements. An unfaithful explanation can be understandable while carrying no information about the computation. For some saliency methods, the map computed from an artificial neural network with random weights is nearly the same as the map computed from the trained artificial neural network. Such a map traces the edges of the input image and carries nothing about the prediction, yet it looks like a plausible explanation. An explanation that agreed with the learned hypothesis everywhere would be that hypothesis again, which might be incomprehensible for a user, so a simpler explanation may have to give up faithfulness somewhere. Fig. 2 illustrates the understandable part of an explanation for a prediction made from weather radar. The features are the hourly precipitation over a 120 km box around Krems an der Donau, given on a grid of cells of 2 km by 2 km, the pixels of the radar image. The prediction is whether it will rain at Krems two hours after the hour shown. A convolutional neural network trained on these images is explained by a class activation map, shown in panel (b). A second explanation, in words, is printed below the panels, and its construction is described after the faithfulness test. These two explanations might be considered understandable by a non-expert user of a weather app. Their faithfulness, however, has to be verified by a perturbation test. For the hour drawn in Fig. 2(a), the convolutional neural network assigns rain a probability close to one, and the class activation map in panel (b) scores the bands of precipitation highest south and south-east of the town rather than on the rain already overhead. Faithfulness is tested by perturbing the radar image. Setting the precipitation to zero in the 360 cells with the highest class activation map scores lowers the logit of rain, the number that the sigmoid function turns into the predicted probability, by 1.57, while zeroing the 360 cells with the lowest scores lowers it by only 0.26. The same ordering holds for 63 of the 72 hours of the test set, the last 30 percent of the recorded hours, which were not used to train the convolutional neural network. Fig. 2 also depicts an explanation in the form of text, the sentence printed below the panels. A fixed rule turns the class activation map of panel (b) into that sentence: it collects the 360 cells the map scores highest, the same cells the perturbation test above sets to zero, and computes two quantities from them. The first is the radius around Krems that holds nine in ten of these cells, rounded up to a multiple of 5 km. The last tenth sits in the far corners of the box and is left out, since it would stretch the radius over the whole box. The second is the compass direction in which these cells lie, seen from the center of Krems: their average position, each cell weighted by its class activation map score, rounded to one of 16 compass sectors. Because the rule is fixed, the sentence is exactly as faithful as the map it summarizes, whose faithfulness the perturbation test above checks. The sentence can also be compared with the radar image in panel (a).

terms.name: fairness (machine learning)
terms.abstract: Fairness (machine learning) is the property of a learned hypothesis, or of the decision rule built on it, to treat data points with different values of a sensitive attribute, such as gender or age, in a comparable way. A counterfactual criterion requires the prediction to be unchanged if the sensitive attribute had taken another value. An individual criterion requires similar predictions for data points that are similar under a task-specific metric. Group criteria equate a measure across the groups: the approval rates (demographic parity), the true-positive and false-positive rates (equalized odds), or the probability of the label given the score (calibration). The criteria are incompatible in general: calibration and equalized odds cannot both hold when the groups differ in their share of positive labels. A chosen criterion is met by a design choice for a component of empirical risk minimization: excluding the sensitive attribute and the features correlated with it from the model, adding a penalty term or a constraint to the loss function, or resampling the training set.
terms.description: Consider a bank that approves a loan when the creditworthiness predicted by a learned hypothesis ĥ exceeds a threshold τ. The feature vector x of an applicant collects the income, the gender, and further attributes, and ĥ was learned from the training set D(train) of five completed loans. An applicant with feature vector x' obtains ĥ(x') = 2.94, below τ = 3.8, and is rejected. The same applicant with only the gender flipped, x⋆, obtains ĥ(x⋆) = 3.93 and is approved. Whether this system is fair has several precise answers, and they cannot all hold at once. Fairness in machine learning is the property of a learned hypothesis, or of the decision rule built on it, to treat data points with different values of a sensitive attribute s, such as gender, race, or age, in a comparable way, in addition to making accurate predictions. It is one of the key requirements for trustworthy artificial intelligence. Three families of fairness criteria are distinguished. A counterfactual criterion requires that the prediction for a data point would not change if its sensitive attribute had taken another value, under a causal model of how s affects the other features (see causality). An individual criterion requires that data points that are similar under a task-specific metric, such as one that ignores s, receive similar predictions. A group criterion requires equality of some measure across the groups defined by s. Demographic parity equates the approval rates, \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{h}({\mathbf x}) \geq \tau \mid s = 0\right) = \mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{h}({\mathbf x}) \geq \tau \mid s = 1\right) \text{,} \end{equation} where the data point is modeled as the realization of a random variable. For a binary label y ∈ 0,1, such as whether a loan was repaid, equalized odds equates the true-positive rate and the false-positive rate across the groups, and calibration equates P(y = 1 | ĥ(x) = c, s) across the groups for every score c. Fig. 1 shows the credit-scoring example. The horizontal axis is a one-dimensional sketch of the feature vector; the gender flip moves the applicant from x' (open square) to x⋆ (open triangle). The gap ĥ(x⋆) - ĥ(x') = 0.99 (double arrow) is caused by the gender alone, so ĥ fails the counterfactual criterion. It fails the individual criterion under a metric that ignores s as well: x' and x⋆ are then the same data point, yet they receive predictions on opposite sides of τ. The group criteria cannot be checked from five loans. They compare the predictions of ĥ over the population of applicants, which the probability distribution of the demographic-parity condition Eq. (1) describes. The criteria are mutually incompatible in general. Kleinberg et al. (2017, Thm. 1.1) and Chouldechova (2017, Eq. (2.6)) show that calibration and equalized odds cannot both hold when the fraction of data points with y = 1 differs between the groups and ĥ is not perfect. Fairness in machine learning is therefore not a single property to be optimized but a choice among criteria. The choice depends on the application: on the harm caused by a wrong prediction, and on the applicable law. Two examples are Art. 22 of the general data protection regulation on automated decisions and the duty under the EU AI Act to examine the training set of a high-risk artificial intelligence system for biases that lead to discrimination (see data governance). Once a criterion is chosen, it is met by a design choice for one of the components of empirical risk minimization. The model can exclude the sensitive attribute; x' and x⋆ then coincide and the gap in Fig. 1 vanishes. Excluding s alone does not suffice, since features correlated with it, such as the postal code, carry the same information. The loss function can carry a penalty term for the gap, or the gap can be a constraint of the constrained optimization problem that replaces empirical risk minimization. The training set can be resampled so that the groups are represented equally (see imbalanced data). Each choice lowers the gap of the chosen criterion, at a cost. The hypothesis learned with a penalty term or a constraint has an average loss on D(train) at least that of the empirical risk minimization solution, since empirical risk minimization minimizes this loss over all of H. Lowering one gap can also raise the gap of another criterion: a score that is calibrated within each group and gives the positive class, and likewise the negative class, the same average score in both groups exists only when the groups share the fraction of data points with y = 1 or the score predicts perfectly.

terms.name: feature learning
terms.abstract: Feature learning is the task of learning, from a dataset, a feature transformation that turns the raw features of a data point into new features that make a subsequent learning task easier. A feature learning method is specified by the two feature spaces, by a hypothesis space of candidate feature transformations, and by a quantitative measure of how useful a feature transformation is, computed from a dataset that need not carry labels. Principal component analysis learns a linear feature transformation to fewer features, judged by the linear reconstruction error, and an autoencoder obtains a nonlinear one by the same criterion. The hidden layers of a deep net form a chain of feature transformations learned jointly with the output layer, so that each layer builds its features from those of the previous one. Pretraining an encoder on unlabeled data points learns features that are reused across learning tasks. In weather forecasting, forty measurements from the five days before are turned into two learned features from which linear regression predicts the maximum temperature of the next day.
terms.description: Consider the task of forecasting the weather of tomorrow at a weather station from the measurements of the previous five days. Each day is a data point, and its label is the maximum temperature of that day. Its raw features are eight daily measurements: the lowest, highest and mean air temperature, the precipitation, the sunshine duration, the humidity, the air pressure and the wind speed. Taken over each of the five previous days, that is a list of forty numbers. A point with forty coordinates cannot be drawn in a scatterplot. A feature transformation that delivers two new features from the forty raw ones places every day in a scatterplot (see Fig. 1), in which the days whose label lies above the median of all labels separate from the others, and a linear model of the two new features may already predict the label. Feature learning is the task of learning such a feature transformation from a dataset instead of designing it by hand. Feature learning is the task of learning a feature transformation {\mathbf \Phi}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}', \qquad {\mathbf x} \mapsto {\mathbf z} := {\mathbf \Phi}({\mathbf x}) \text{.} The transformation maps the raw feature vector x ∈ X of a data point to a new feature vector z from a new feature space X'. A feature learning method is specified by three design choices: the two feature spaces X and X', a hypothesis space H of candidate feature transformations, and a quantitative measure of how useful a specific Φ ∈ H is. The measure is computed from a dataset, which need not carry labels, and it need not be the dataset of the learning task at hand. A useful feature transformation is one that makes a subsequent learning task easier: the data points become separable by a linear model, fewer features suffice, or the features learned once serve several learning tasks. In the weather example, the learned features are judged afterwards by the validation error of linear regression on them. A measure of usefulness can be built from a second map. The feature transformation is then read as an encoder, and a decoder Φ*: X' → X rebuilds the raw feature vector from the new one. What the encoder kept is then measured by how well the decoder rebuilds the data point from it, the reconstruction error \[ \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\Big( {\mathbf x}^{(r)}, {\mathbf \Phi}^{*}\big( {\mathbf \Phi}\big({\mathbf x}^{(r)}\big) \big) \Big) \text{.} \] The loss function L penalizes a rebuilt feature vector for differing from the original. A common choice is the squared error loss. The dataset it is computed on needs no labels: what the decoder has to reproduce is the data point itself. The decoder may be learned alongside the encoder. The measure is then the minimum of the reconstruction error over a second hypothesis space of decoders. It may instead be fixed, and the encoder alone must then supply what the decoder cannot. Restricting the decoder therefore decides what the new features have to carry. Principal component analysis is this construction with X := Rd, X' := Rd' for some d' < d, and the hypothesis space of linear maps, \mathcal{H} := \big\{ {\mathbf \Phi}: \mathbb{R}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{d'}: {\mathbf x} \mapsto {\mathbf W} {\mathbf x} \text{ with some } {\mathbf W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d' \times d} \big\} \text{.} The decoder is linear too and is learned alongside the encoder W. The usefulness of a specific Φ(x) = W x is therefore the minimum of the reconstruction error over the reconstruction matrices R. On the dataset D = x(1), …, x(m), that minimum is \min_{{\mathbf R} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d'}} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {\mathbf R} {\mathbf W} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{.} For feature vectors with zero sample mean, a best W has as rows the d' eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix with the largest eigenvalues. Only the row space of W matters: replacing W by T W with an invertible T ∈ Rd' × d' and R by R T-1 leaves the product R W, and so the reconstruction error, unchanged. An autoencoder keeps the same criterion and replaces both linear maps by ANNs, so that the new features come from a nonlinear feature transformation. With a linear decoder and the squared error loss, it spans the subspace principal component analysis finds. Applied to the weather example, principal component analysis delivers the two learned features of Fig. 1. The forty raw features of the 361 days of 2024 at Krems an der Donau are turned into two learned features. Each raw feature is first scaled to zero sample mean and unit sample variance, because temperatures, precipitation and pressure carry different units. Warm and cold days separate along the first learned feature: 89 percent of the warm days have a positive z1 and 92 percent of the cold days a nonpositive one. Linear regression on the two learned features is trained on the days from January to August. It then predicts the maximum temperature of the days from September to December with a validation error of 13.5 squared degrees Celsius. Linear regression on all forty raw features reaches 10.2, and predicting the sample mean of the training labels reaches 110.9. The two learned features therefore retain most of the predictive content of the forty raw ones. A deep net learns a chain of feature transformations. Each hidden layer ℓ = 1, …, L is a feature transformation Φ(ℓ) that reads in the activations z(ℓ-1) of the previous layer, with z(0) := x. The features delivered to the output layer are the composition z(L) = Φ(L) ∘ ∘ Φ(1) (x) (see Fig. 2). The feature transformations are learned jointly with the output layer by empirical risk minimization with the loss of the final prediction, so the usefulness of the learned features is measured by how well the output layer, typically a linear model, predicts the label from z(L). The chain is useful because each layer builds its features from those of the previous one, so the feature transformations Φ(ℓ) ∘ ∘ Φ(1) grow deeper with ℓ. In image classification, early layers deliver edges, later ones corners and object parts, and the features at the last hidden layer separate the classes by a linear surface. Pretraining an encoder on a large dataset of unlabeled data points, with a loss constructed from the data points themselves (see self-supervised learning), learns features that are reused across learning tasks. A new learning task appends a task-specific hypothesis with few model parameters to the learned Φ and adapts it by fine-tuning on its own dataset. The dataset used to learn Φ can then be much larger than any labeled dataset, because unlabeled data points are cheap to collect. Alternative constructions of a feature transformation do not learn Φ. A kernel method fixes Φ through the choice of a kernel, with X' the reproducing kernel Hilbert space Hk and z = k(x,·), the kernel with its first argument fixed, never evaluated explicitly, and learns only a linear hypothesis on X'. A hand-designed Φ encodes domain knowledge instead of a dataset.

terms.name: feature
terms.abstract: A feature of a data point is one of its attributes that can be measured or computed easily, without human supervision. The features of a data point are collected into a feature vector, which a hypothesis map reads to predict the label of the data point. The red-green-blue (RGB) pixel intensities of a digital image or the signal values of an audio recording are typical features. Which attributes of a data point serve as features, rather than as labels, is a design choice within a machine learning application.
terms.description: A digital photo of a cow is a grid of pixels, and the red, green and blue intensity of each pixel is a number that a computer obtains without any human looking at the photo. Such a number is a feature of the data point: an attribute of the data point z that is measured, or computed, without human supervision. The features of a data point are assembled into a feature vector x = Φ(z) by a feature transformation, a function Φ: Z → X, viewing the data point itself as its raw features from which the computed features are obtained. A hypothesis map takes the feature vector as input and outputs a prediction of the label of the data point. Besides the red-green-blue (RGB) intensities of the pixels of a photo, Fig. 1 shows another example of features: the d signal values of a finite-duration audio signal, used as its features x1, …, xd. Whether a given attribute is treated as a feature or a label is not inherent to the data point. It is a design choice that depends on the machine learning application and the resources available for determining each attribute. An attribute should be used as a feature only if its value can be determined for every data point at the time the prediction is needed; an attribute that becomes known only afterwards is a candidate for the label instead. Once the features are chosen, new features can be constructed by transforming existing ones. Such a transformation can be an arithmetic computation applied to the existing features. For example, if a data point has a numeric feature x ∈ R, the quantities x2, exp(-x), and 3x can also be used as features of the data point. Instead of its raw signal values, the audio signal in Fig. 1 can be described by the magnitudes of its discrete-time Fourier transform (DTFT). These features describe the frequency content of the signal and are unchanged by time shifts, since shifting the signal by n0 samples multiplies its DTFT by exp(-j ω n0), a factor of modulus one. This invariance is useful for a stationary signal, one whose statistical properties do not change over time. Another example is the activation of a neuron within an artificial neural network: it is a new feature derived from the input features by a sequence of basic computations performed by the artificial neural network. Using activations as features underlies a second, narrower use of the word feature in mechanistic interpretability: a feature is a human-interpretable concept encoded inside a trained artificial neural network, such as a curve detector or the presence of a wheel. The activations of a subset of d neurons (for example, a whole layer, or the neurons that an analyst selects for study) form a vector in a Euclidean space Rd. Whereas the broader sense above treats a single neuron activation as one feature, here a feature is obtained as a function of this whole activation vector a. One such function is the projection of the activation vector a onto a one-dimensional subspace spanned by a unit vector (or direction) u. This unit vector can be obtained as the unit normal u of a hyperplane separating data points that express the concept from those that do not (see Fig. 2). Another construction of an activation-based feature is based on regions instead of directions in the activation space. In either case, constructing the function that maps the activation vector to the feature requires a set of data points labeled as representing the concept or not. Beyond their construction, regulation constrains which features may be used and how accurate they must be. The EU AI Act requires the training data of high-risk ML systems to be relevant, sufficiently representative, and, to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete. When features are personal data, the general data protection regulation adds the data minimization principle and the accuracy principle. Conversely, deliberately perturbing the features can be useful: adding small perturbations to the features of data points during training is a form of data augmentation that acts as regularization. For example, the ridge regression penalty equals the average loss under Gaussian feature perturbations: for a linear model with model parameters w, adding zero-mean Gaussian noise of variance α to each feature raises the expected squared error loss by α ‖ w ‖22, the ridge penalty.

terms.name: feature importance
terms.abstract: Feature importance scores measure how strongly a learned hypothesis relies on individual features. Such scores can be obtained from the weights of a linear hypothesis, learned either from a training set or as an approximation of a given hypothesis. The weights of a linear model describe the prediction change per unit of a feature. Another construction uses the effect of perturbing the value of one feature. Such a perturbation can be implemented by adding random errors or by permuting the feature values across the data points of a dataset. Feature importance scores measure primarily the reliance of a trained model on a feature. These scores might not reflect the relevance of the feature for the learning task itself. In particular, a trained model might ignore a relevant feature, which results in a low importance score.
terms.description: The weather station Krems an der Donau (Austria) records six observations of each day: the maximum and the minimum air temperature, the mean air pressure, the mean relative humidity, the sunshine duration, and the precipitation. These raw observations are used in a machine learning application where data points represent daily weather. The label of such a data point is the maximum daytime temperature which is to be predicted from twelve features x1,…,x12. These features are the six observations of the day before and the six observations of two days before. Fig. 1 depicts observed maximum daily temperatures along with their predictions obtained from a hypothesis ĥ learned via linear regression. Each prediction (or forecast) ĥ(x) for a data point is computed from its feature vector x = (x1,…,x12 )ᵀ. A feature importance score quantifies how strongly this prediction relies on a particular feature of the data point. It assigns a number to each feature of a data point: a large number marks a feature that strongly affects the prediction, while a number near zero marks a feature that barely affects it. Which of the twelve features the predictions of Fig. 1 rely on is what the importance scores of Fig. 3 quantify. Machine learning methods compute feature importance scores for different purposes. As an explanation in explainable artificial intelligence, a score describes how much a learned hypothesis relies on individual features of a data point. During model selection, importance scores can guide the choice of a subset of the features of the data points, after which a new hypothesis is learned using that subset. Consider a linear model with the learned hypothesis \[ \widehat{h}({\mathbf x}) = \sum_{j=1}^{12} \widehat{w}_{j} x_{j} \text{.} \] A natural choice of feature importance scores are its weights ŵj. Increasing the j-th feature of a data point by one unit changes the prediction by ŵj. The sign of ŵj says whether the prediction rises or falls with the feature, and the magnitude |ŵj| says by how much. A feature xj with a large magnitude |ŵj| can then be considered important. One challenge of using the weights ŵj delivered by linear regression as feature importance scores is their dependence on the scale of the feature values. As a case in point, replacing the feature x1 by 103 x1 makes linear regression learn a weight ŵ1 that is smaller by the factor 103, while every prediction stays the same. By rescaling a feature, or changing its measurement unit (e.g., millimeters instead of meters), its importance can therefore be made arbitrarily large or small. This dependence is avoided by applying linear regression to standardized features (see feature standardization): each column of the feature matrix is centered by its sample mean and divided by its standard deviation, so that ŵj becomes the prediction change per standard deviation of the j-th feature. Algorithm 1 summarizes the construction of feature importance scores by applying linear regression to the standardized feature values of a given dataset with feature matrix X = (x(1),…,x(m) )ᵀ ∈ Rm × d and label vector y = (y(1), …,y(m))ᵀ. Algorithm 1 can also be used to compute feature importance scores for a given learned hypothesis (or trained model) ĥ that might be nonlinear. Here, the label vector fed into Algorithm 1 contains the predictions of ĥ, y = ( ĥ(x(1)), …,ĥ(x(m)) )ᵀ, so the weights are those of a linear approximation of ĥ on the given dataset. \begin{algorithm}[H] \caption{Feature importance from linear regression on standardized features } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex Input: feature matrix X = (x(1), …, x(m))ᵀ ∈ Rm × d with entries xj(r), label vector y = (y(1), …, y(m))ᵀ \For{j = 1, …, d} \State μ̂j := (1)/(m) Σr=1m xj(r), \quad σ̂j := √((1)/(m) Σr=1m (xj(r) - μ̂j)2) \State replace every entry xj(r) of column j by (xj(r) - μ̂j) / σ̂j \Comment{standardize} \EndFor \State ȳ := (1)/(m) Σr=1m y(r); replace y by y - ȳ 1 \Comment{center the labels} \State ŵ := argminw ∈ Rd (1)/(m) ‖ y - X w ‖2 \Comment{linear regression} \Statex Output: importance scores Ij := |ŵj| for j = 1, …, d \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} Another construction of a feature importance score does not learn a hypothesis at all. Its input is a hypothesis ĥ already learned by some machine learning method, and its output scores how strongly ĥ relies on each feature. This construction, introduced for random forests under the name variable importance, measures the change of the average loss when the values of a single feature are replaced by random values. For a random forest, each decision tree is scored on the training data points that were not in its own resampled training set, and the score is the relative increase of the misclassification rate. Algorithm 2 summarizes the method in a form that applies to any learned hypothesis. Fisher et al. (2019, Sect. 3) introduce this form under the name model reliance, for a fixed hypothesis, and show that the score can be estimated on the training set itself. The input of Algorithm 2 is a dataset, characterized by a feature matrix X ∈ Rm × d and a label vector y ∈ Rm, and a learned hypothesis (or trained model) ĥ. This dataset is referred to as the scoring dataset. It should have the same statistical properties as the training set used to learn ĥ: ideally, the data points of both are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs. For the j-th feature, Algorithm 2 delivers a score Ij that compares the average loss of ĥ on the dataset (X, y) with its average loss on a perturbed dataset with the same y but a different feature matrix \[ \widetilde{{\mathbf X}}^{(j)} = \big(\widetilde{{\mathbf x}}^{(1)}, \ldots, \widetilde{{\mathbf x}}^{(m)}\big)^{\top} \text{.} \] The perturbed feature matrix is obtained by permuting the entries of the j-th column of X across its rows, with every other column unchanged (Fig. 2). The permutation importance of the j-th feature is the increase of the average loss that this exchange causes, \[I_{j} := \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\left(\left( \widetilde{{\mathbf x}}^{(r)},y^{(r)} \right),\widehat{h} \right) - \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\left(\left( {\mathbf x}^{(r)},y^{(r)} \right),\widehat{h} \right) \text{,} \] where y(r) is the label of data point r. The permutation is random, so Algorithm 2 averages Ij over B independent permutations of the j-th column of X. \begin{algorithm}[H] \caption{Permutation importance (variable importance), similar to Fisher et al. (2019, Sect. 3) } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex Input: scoring dataset with feature matrix X = (x(1), …, x(m))ᵀ and label vector y = (y(1), …, y(m))ᵀ; learned hypothesis ĥ; loss L(·,· ); number B of permutations \State L̂ := (1)/(m) Σr=1m L(( x(r),y(r) ),ĥ ) \Comment{average loss on the dataset} \For{j = 1, …, d} \For{b = 1, …, B} \State X̃(j) := X with the entries of column j permuted uniformly at random across the rows; denote its rows by (x̃(r))ᵀ \State L̃(b) := (1)/(m) Σr=1m L(( x̃(r),y(r) ),ĥ ) \EndFor \State Ij := (1)/(B) Σb=1B L̃(b) - L̂ \EndFor \Statex Output: importance scores I1, …, Id for each feature x1,…,xd \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} Fig. 3 plots Ij computed by Algorithm 2 with B = 20 for the weather data points of Krems an der Donau. The scoring dataset consists of the 92 data points whose label is the maximum temperature of a day from October 1 to December 31, 2024, so their features are the observations of September 29 to December 30. The linear hypothesis of Fig. 1 was learned on the training set of the 272 data points whose label days run from January 3 to September 30. The maximum temperature of the day before obtains the largest score, while the minimum temperature of the day before obtains a score near zero. That minimum temperature is not useless: its correlation with the label on the scoring dataset is 0.69, as strong as that of the minimum temperature two days before. The score Ij primarily reflects how much ĥ relies on the feature xj, which can be different from its relevance for the label of a data point. Algorithm 2 requires a choice of the loss function as input. For the squared error loss and a linear hypothesis, permuting the j-th column of X replaces xj by a value with the same variance drawn independently of the data point. If the prediction error y-ĥ(x) has expectation zero given x, the expected loss increase is 2ŵj2 var(xj), so the score satisfies \begin{equation} I_{j} \approx 2\widehat{w}_{j}^{2} \operatorname{var}\left(x_{j}\right) \text{.} \end{equation} For standardized features, var(xj) = 1 and the approximation Eq. (1) becomes Ij ≈ 2 ŵj2: the score of Algorithm 2 is, up to the square, the score of Algorithm 1. For the maximum temperature of the day before, the weight of the hypothesis of Fig. 1 times the standard deviation of that feature on the scoring dataset is 4.96, and √(Ij/2) = 4.96.
