Both algorithms access ĥ only through its predictions and therefore apply to any learned hypothesis. They differ in what they score: Algorithm 1 scores a linear approximation of ĥ, whereas Algorithm 2 scores ĥ itself, so its scores are meaningful also when no linear approximation is accurate. Fig. 4 shows the scores delivered by Algorithm 2 for a random forest, an ensemble of decision trees, learned on the same training set and evaluated on the same scoring dataset as the linear hypothesis of Fig. 3. Both reach almost the same average squared error loss on the scoring dataset, 8.2 in squared degrees Celsius, but they rely on the features differently.

terms.name: feature matrix
terms.abstract: The feature matrix of a dataset collects the feature vectors of its data points as its rows, one row per data point and one column per feature. Its two most basic properties are the number of rows, which is the number of data points in the dataset, and the number of columns, which is the number of features of each data point. More properties of a dataset follow from the singular values of its feature matrix. The number of nonzero singular values is the rank, and a rank below the number of features leaves linear regression with infinitely many solutions. The ratio of the largest to the smallest nonzero singular value is the condition number of the feature matrix. The condition number determines the number of gradient descent steps required by linear regression and its robustness against perturbations of the features and labels in the training set.
terms.description: A weather station at Krems an der Donau records eight measurements on each of the 366 days of the leap year 2024: the lowest, highest, and mean air temperature, the humidity, the wind speed, the precipitation, the sunshine duration, and the air pressure. Writing the eight measurements of one day as a row, and placing the rows of the 366 days under one another, gives a two-dimensional numeric array with 366 rows and eight columns. That array is a matrix, the feature matrix of the dataset whose data points are the 366 days, and each of its rows is the feature vector of one day. The feature matrix is the form in which machine learning software expects a dataset, and properties of the machine learning methods applied to the dataset, such as whether linear regression has a unique solution or how fast gradient descent converges, are determined by it. In general, consider a dataset D of m data points with feature vectors x(1), …, x(m), each in Rd. Stacking the feature vectors row-wise yields the feature matrix: {\mathbf X} := \big({\mathbf x}^{(1)}, \ldots, {\mathbf x}^{(m)}\big)^{\top} = \begin{pmatrix} x^{(1)}_{1} & x^{(1)}_{2} & \cdots & x^{(1)}_{d} x^{(2)}_{1} & x^{(2)}_{2} & \cdots & x^{(2)}_{d} \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots x^{(m)}_{1} & x^{(m)}_{2} & \cdots & x^{(m)}_{d} \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d} \text{.} The feature matrix is of size m × d, i.e., it has m rows and d columns. Each row is the transposed feature vector of one data point, and each column holds the values of one feature for all data points (see Fig. 1). Many properties of a dataset, and of the learning tasks built from it, are computed from X. The most basic ones are the numbers of rows and columns, m and d. The feature matrix also defines a linear map. A linear model with model parameters w from the parameter space Rd predicts wᵀ x(r) for the r-th data point, so the m predictions are the entries of X w. The feature matrix therefore maps each w ∈ Rd to the vector X w ∈ Rm, which is compared with the label vector y = (y(1), …, y(m))ᵀ ∈ Rm. Linear regression on a training set with feature matrix X and label vector y is the search for a vector w whose image X w is close to y in Euclidean norm. Linear regression has a unique solution only when X has full column rank, which requires m ≥ d (see normal equations). A rank below d leaves infinitely many parameter vectors w with the same training error, and the one a method returns can have a large loss outside the training set. Using more features than data points (i.e., d > m) forces this case, since then X has fewer rows than columns, which rules out full column rank. More properties of a dataset follow from the singular values of its feature matrix X. The singular value decomposition can be written as {\mathbf X} = \sum_{j=1}^{\min\{m, d\}} \lambda_{j} {\mathbf v}^{(j)} \big({\mathbf u}^{(j)}\big)^{\top} \text{,} where the vectors v(1), …, v(minm, d) ∈ Rm are orthonormal among themselves, the vectors u(1), …, u(minm, d) ∈ Rd are orthonormal among themselves. The singular values are ordered as λ1 ≥ … ≥ λminm, d ≥ 0. The number of nonzero singular values is the rank of X. A rank below d means that some feature is a linear combination of the others and adds no information beyond them. A small but nonzero singular value is the approximate form of such a dependence. When m ≥ d, the d right singular vectors form an orthonormal basis of Rd, and the smallest singular value is the smallest Euclidean norm of a linear combination of the feature columns with unit-norm coefficients, \[ \lambda_{d} = \min_{{\mathbf u} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}, \Vert {{\mathbf u}} \Vert = 1} \Vert {{\mathbf X} {\mathbf u}} \Vert \text{,} \] attained at the right singular vector u(d). The identity holds since a unit-norm u = Σj=1d cj u(j) gives ‖ X u ‖2 = Σj=1d cj2 λj2, a weighted average of the squared singular values. When d > m, a unit-norm u orthogonal to all m right singular vectors gives X u = 0, so the minimum is 0. A small singular value therefore says that some combination of the feature columns with unit-norm coefficients is nearly the zero vector: the features are nearly collinear, and the right singular vector names the combination. For the weather year of Fig. 1, with every measurement scaled to zero sample mean and unit sample variance, the smallest singular value is 0.05 against a largest of 36.4. Its right singular vector places all of its weight on the lowest, the highest, and the mean temperature, with coefficients -0.37, -0.46, and 0.81, because the mean temperature of a day is the midpoint of its lowest and its highest up to a residual with standard deviation 0.03 degrees. Dropping the mean temperature raises the smallest singular value to 4.19 (pythondemos/featuremtx.py). The size of a singular value depends on the units of the columns, which is why the scaling to unit sample variance comes first. The squares of the singular values are the eigenvalues of Xᵀ X, which for features with zero sample mean is m times their sample covariance matrix. The same eigenvalues and eigenvectors of Xᵀ X determine principal component analysis. Its dimensionality reduction keeps the eigenvectors of the largest eigenvalues as the new features, and the sum over the data points of the squared errors of reconstructing the feature vectors from them is the sum of the eigenvalues dropped. Another important property of a feature matrix is the condition number κ (X) = λ1 / λrank(X), the ratio of the largest singular value to the smallest nonzero one. For full column rank, it is the ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value. The condition number enters linear regression twice: through the number of gradient descent steps, and through the robustness of the learned model parameters against perturbations of the training set. The number that matters in both is its square κ (X)2. The objective function f(w) = (1/m) ‖ X w - y ‖2 has the constant Hessian (2/m) Xᵀ X, whose eigenvalues are the squared singular values of X scaled by 2/m. The condition number of Xᵀ X is therefore \begin{equation} \kappa \left({\mathbf X}^{\top} {\mathbf X}\right) = \kappa \left({\mathbf X}\right)^{2} \text{.} \end{equation} The square Eq. (1) determines the convergence speed of gradient descent on the empirical risk minimization problem of linear regression. One step with an exact line search multiplies the gap between f(w(t)) and the minimum f(ŵ) by at most 1 - 1/κ (X)2. The number of steps that reaches a given gap therefore grows in proportion to κ (X)2. Fig. 2 shows this for two feature matrices built from the weather measurements of Fig. 1. The features are the relative humidity and the wind speed, the label is the highest temperature, and each has its sample mean removed. In the recorded units the condition number is 14.5. After scaling each feature to unit sample variance, it is 1.45. Gradient descent starts at the point at distance ‖ ŵ ‖ from ŵ for which it is slowest, where the gap shrinks per step by exactly the factor in Eq. (2), \begin{equation} f\big({\mathbf w}^{(t+1)}\big) - f\big(\widehat{{\mathbf w}}\big) = \Big( \frac{\kappa \left({\mathbf X}\right)^{2} - 1} {\kappa \left({\mathbf X}\right)^{2} + 1} \Big)^{2} \Big( f\big({\mathbf w}^{(t)}\big) - f\big(\widehat{{\mathbf w}}\big) \Big) \text{.} \end{equation} From no start does the gap shrink by less, since this factor bounds the shrinkage of every exact-line-search step on a quadratic objective function. A gap of 10-6 of the initial one then takes 731 steps in the recorded units and 7 after the scaling. The condition number κ (X) also governs the robustness of the model parameters ŵ delivered by linear regression against perturbations of the training set. Let X have full column rank. Linear regression delivers the model parameters ŵ = X+ y with the pseudoinverse X+ = (Xᵀ X)-1 Xᵀ. They are the unique solution of the normal equations Xᵀ X ŵ = Xᵀ y, which state that the gradient of f vanishes at ŵ. Consider perturbations of the training set that change X to X + δ X and y to y + δ y, with X + δ X still of full column rank, and let ŵ + δ ŵ be the model parameters learned by linear regression on the perturbed training set. They solve the normal equations of the perturbed training set, ({\mathbf X} + \delta {\mathbf X})^{\top} ({\mathbf X} + \delta {\mathbf X}) \big(\widehat{{\mathbf w}} + \delta \widehat{{\mathbf w}}\big) = ({\mathbf X} + \delta {\mathbf X})^{\top} ({\mathbf y} + \delta {\mathbf y}) \text{.} Moving the terms with ŵ to the right side and using Xᵀ r = 0 for the least squares residual r = y - X ŵ, which is the normal equations of the unperturbed training set, gives the exact equation ({\mathbf X} + \delta {\mathbf X})^{\top} ({\mathbf X} + \delta {\mathbf X}) \delta \widehat{{\mathbf w}} = ({\mathbf X} + \delta {\mathbf X})^{\top} \big(\delta {\mathbf y} - \delta {\mathbf X} \widehat{{\mathbf w}}\big) + \delta {\mathbf X}^{\top} {\mathbf r} \text{.} Solving for δ ŵ applies the pseudoinverse of X + δ X to the noise in the labels and to the noise in the features acting on ŵ, and the inverse of (X + δ X)ᵀ (X + δ X) to the noise in the features acting on the residual. The largest singular value of X+ is 1 / λd, and that of (Xᵀ X)-1 is 1 / λd2. The same holds for X + δ X with its own smallest singular value. Let the largest singular value of δ X be at most ε λ1 and the Euclidean norm of δ y at most ε ‖ y ‖, with ε κ (X) < 1. The smallest singular value of X + δ X is then at least λd - ε λ1, and taking Euclidean norms in the exact equation gives the perturbation bound \begin{equation} \Vert {\delta \widehat{{\mathbf w}}} \Vert \leq \frac{\varepsilon \kappa \left({\mathbf X}\right)} {1 - \varepsilon \kappa \left({\mathbf X}\right)} \Big( \frac{\Vert {{\mathbf y}} \Vert}{\lambda_{1}} + \Vert {\widehat{{\mathbf w}}} \Vert \Big) + \frac{\varepsilon \kappa \left({\mathbf X}\right)^{2}} {\big(1 - \varepsilon \kappa \left({\mathbf X}\right)\big)^{2}} \frac{\Vert {{\mathbf r}} \Vert}{\lambda_{1}} \text{.} \end{equation} The bound Eq. (3) holds for every perturbation with ε κ (X) < 1. The bound Eq. (3) carries over to the prediction for any given feature vector x, such as that of a test data point. The learned linear model predicts xᵀ ŵ before and xᵀ (ŵ + δ ŵ) after the perturbation. The prediction therefore changes by xᵀ δ ŵ, and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality bounds this change by \begin{equation} \big| {\mathbf x}^{\top} \delta \widehat{{\mathbf w}} \big| \leq \Vert {{\mathbf x}} \Vert \Vert {\delta \widehat{{\mathbf w}}} \Vert \leq \Vert {{\mathbf x}} \Vert \Bigg( \frac{\varepsilon \kappa \left({\mathbf X}\right)} {1 - \varepsilon \kappa \left({\mathbf X}\right)} \Big( \frac{\Vert {{\mathbf y}} \Vert}{\lambda_{1}} + \Vert {\widehat{{\mathbf w}}} \Vert \Big) + \frac{\varepsilon \kappa \left({\mathbf X}\right)^{2}} {\big(1 - \varepsilon \kappa \left({\mathbf X}\right)\big)^{2}} \frac{\Vert {{\mathbf r}} \Vert}{\lambda_{1}} \Bigg) \text{.} \end{equation} The change of the prediction is therefore at most ‖ x ‖ times the right-hand side of the bound Eq. (3), and grows with the norm of the feature vector. Fig. 3 shows the robustness of ŵ against perturbations on a related but different and smaller dataset, the first days of the twelve months of 2024, twelve of the rows of Fig. 1. Each day has the feature vector x = (1, x)ᵀ with x its lowest temperature, and its highest temperature as the label. A hypothesis of the linear model then has intercept w1 and slope w2, and the feature matrix has a column of ones and the column of the lowest temperatures. Its condition number is 14.9, and the least squares residual is 0.20 times the norm of y. Two constructions of a perturbation of relative size ε = 0.01 are compared. The first is chosen adversarially, to make the change of the model parameters learned by linear regression as large as possible: δ X = -ε λ1 v(2) (u(2))ᵀ and δ y = ± ε ‖ y ‖ v(2), with the sign for which ŵ moves more. It changes ŵ by norm 2.23, which is 64 percent of the right-hand side of the bound Eq. (3). The second construction uses 100 realizations of random δ X and δ y. They are generated with independent and identically distributed Gaussian RVs as their entries and then normalized so that the largest singular value of δ X is ε λ1 and the Euclidean norm of δ y is ε ‖ y ‖. The largest change among the 100 realizations is 1.17, which is 34 percent of the right-hand side of the bound Eq. (3). For a day with lowest temperature x the feature vector (1, x)ᵀ has norm √(1 + x2). By the prediction bound Eq. (4) the prediction therefore changes by at most √(1 + x2) times the right-hand side of the bound Eq. (3): 3.5 degrees at x = 0 and 69 degrees at x = 20. The two dotted curves in Fig. 3(a) trace that bound and leave the plotted range. The hypotheses learned from the random perturbations stay within 1.6 degrees of the learned hypothesis over the plotted range, and the hypothesis after the adversarial construction within 3.1 degrees. Panel (b) repeats the comparison for ε from 5 · 10-4 to 5 · 10-2. The adversarial construction reaches more than half of the right-hand side of the bound Eq. (3) up to ε = 0.02, the random construction less than half at every ε.

terms.name: feature space
terms.abstract: The feature space of a machine learning application is the set of all values that the feature vector of a data point can take. It is the range of the feature transformation that maps a data point to its feature vector. For data points with d numeric features the feature space is usually the Euclidean space Rd, whose Euclidean distance and inner product are what nearest neighbor methods and linear models use. The same data points placed in two feature spaces have different nearest neighbors and yield different hypotheses, so the choice of the feature space is part of the model, and dropping a feature is model pruning. A feature space can also be a finite set, such as the months of a year, or a set of strings or graphs, which a kernel makes accessible. A kernel brings a second feature space with it, a Hilbert space of possibly infinite dimension in which the kernel is the inner product and which a kernel method uses without ever forming its elements.
terms.description: A day at Krems an der Donau can be described by a single number, its morning minimum temperature, or by two numbers, that minimum and the maximum temperature of the previous day. The first description turns every day into a point of the real line R, the second into a point of the plane R2. The set of all values that the feature vector of a data point can take is the feature space X of a machine learning application. A feature transformation \begin{equation} {\mathbf \Phi}: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}, \quad {\mathbf x} = {\mathbf \Phi}({\mathbf z}) \text{,} \end{equation} maps a data point z from the set Z of all data points of the application to its feature vector, and the feature space is the range of this map. The two descriptions of a day are two feature transformations Eq. (1) of the same data points, with the feature spaces R and R2. For data points with d numeric features, the default feature space is the Euclidean space Rd. The word space, rather than set, says that X carries structure that a machine learning method uses: the Euclidean distance ‖ x - x' ‖2 makes Rd a metric space, and the inner product xᵀ x' makes it a Hilbert space. The k-nearest neighbors method uses the distance: the nearest neighbor of a data point with feature vector x in a training set with feature vectors x(1), …, x(m) is x(r⋆) with \begin{equation} r^{\star} := \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{r = 1, \ldots, m} \left\lVert {\mathbf x} - {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \right\rVert_{2} \text{,} \end{equation} and the label of that neighbor is the prediction for x. A linear model uses the inner product: its hypotheses are the maps h(x) = wᵀ x + b with model parameters w ∈ Rd and b ∈ R. Which feature space the 366 days of 2024 at Krems are placed in changes what both methods deliver. The label of a day is its maximum daytime temperature. On 22 May 2024 the morning minimum was 14.4 degrees Celsius, the maximum of the previous day 22.7, and the maximum of the day itself 22.4. In the feature space R, the nearest neighbor Eq. (2) of this day among the other 365 days is 4 September, with the same morning minimum 14.4 but a maximum of 34.1. In R2 it is 11 June, with the feature vector (14.5, 22.7)ᵀ and a maximum of 20.2 (Fig. 1). The prediction by the nearest neighbor misses the label by 11.7 degrees in the first feature space and by 2.2 degrees in the second, and 346 of the 366 days have a different nearest neighbor in R than in R2. A linear model learned by least squares from all 366 days has a training mean squared error of 19.2 in R and of 9.2 in R2. The choice of the feature space is therefore part of the model. A hypothesis space is a set of maps h: X → Y into the label space Y, so changing X changes which maps it contains. The hypotheses h(x) = w x + b on R are, read as maps of the pair (x1, x2)ᵀ, the hypotheses w1 x1 + w2 x2 + b on R2 with w2 = 0. Dropping a feature thus shrinks the hypothesis space, which is model pruning, one of the three routes that regularization distinguishes: the training error of empirical risk minimization cannot fall (19.2 against 9.2), while the smaller hypothesis space may generalize better. Feature learning methods and feature standardization change the feature space in the other direction, by learning or rescaling the feature transformation Eq. (1). Rescaling one feature changes the distances in the nearest neighbor rule Eq. (2), and with them the nearest neighbors. A feature space need not be a Euclidean space. Describing a day by its month gives the finite feature space X = 1, …, 12. A hypothesis on it is a table of 12 values, and the table that minimizes the training mean squared error holds the monthly means of the maximum temperature, with a mean squared error of 17.0. One-hot encoding (see feature vector) maps the 12 months to the 12 unit vectors of R12, and on these every table is a linear model: least squares learns the same 12 means. Under the discrete metric, which is 0 for two equal and 1 for two different months, each of the 30 other days of May is a nearest neighbor of 22 May. Other feature spaces without arithmetic are the strings over an alphabet, for text documents and DNA sequences, and the graphs, for molecules. A method then accesses the feature space through a kernel that measures the similarity of two of its elements. The hours of a day, placed on a cycle graph, are the feature space of kernel ridge regression. A kernel brings a second feature space with it. A kernel k: X × X → R is an inner product of transformed feature vectors φ(x) in a Hilbert space H, k(x,x') = φ(x)φ(x')H, and H is also called the feature space of the kernel. For the polynomial kernel of degree two on R2, this space is explicit, \begin{equation} k\big({\mathbf x},{\mathbf x}'\big) = \big(1 + {\mathbf x}^{\top} {\mathbf x}'\big)^{2} = \phi({\mathbf x})^{\top} \phi({\mathbf x}') \text{,} \end{equation} with the feature transformation φ(x) = (1, √(2) x1, √(2) x2, x12, √(2) x1 x2, x22)ᵀ ∈ R6, so a linear model on the transformed feature vectors is a quadratic hypothesis on the original feature space. The 366 × 366 matrix of the polynomial kernel values Eq. (3) of the days at Krems has rank 6, the dimension of R6. The feature space of the Gaussian kernel exp(-‖ x - x' ‖22 / (2 σ2)) has infinite dimension: for σ = 1 degree, the matrix of its values on the 366 days has rank 366, so no feature space of smaller dimension produces these values. A kernel method never forms the transformed feature vectors; it uses the feature space H only through kernel values, which is what makes a space of infinite dimension usable. Fig. 2 draws three further shapes of a feature space: the real line, a bounded convex subset of the plane, and the nodes of an undirected graph. The second is the feature space of a sensor with a bounded range, and in the third the distance between two feature vectors is the length of the shortest path between their nodes.

terms.name: feature transformation
terms.abstract: A feature transformation is a function that maps the feature vector of a data point to a new feature vector, so that a machine learning method runs on the new features in place of the raw ones. What is learned is then the composition of the transformation with a hypothesis on the new feature space, which is why a linear model of the new features is not a linear model of the raw ones. Methods differ in where the transformation comes from: principal component analysis obtains it from the raw features alone, linear discriminant analysis uses the labels as well, a random projection draws it at random, and an autoencoder learns it with an artificial neural network. Each hidden layer of a deep net is one more feature transformation, and a kernel method fixes one through the choice of a kernel without ever evaluating it. The number of new features sizes the hypothesis space of the method that runs on them, so keeping it small is model pruning, one of the three routes that regularization distinguishes. For the maximum daytime temperature at Krems an der Donau (Austria), the first five powers of the day of the year turn a nearly flat hypothesis into a curve that follows the seasons and cut the validation error from 88.2 to 23.6 squared degrees. The choice matters as much as the count: the three odd powers of the day leave the validation error above that of the constant hypothesis, which is why the transformation is often learned from the dataset rather than chosen by hand.
terms.description: A weather station at Krems an der Donau (Austria) records the maximum daytime temperature of every day of 2023 and 2024. Each day is a data point, its label is that temperature, and its single raw feature x is the position of the day in the year, rescaled to the interval [-1, 1]. The 365 days of 2023 form the training set D(train) and the 366 days of 2024 the validation set D(val). Linear regression on x learns a nearly flat hypothesis from D(train) by least squares: it rises by 6.9 degrees from the first day of the year to the last, against a label range of 38.4 degrees. Its training error is 79.4 squared degrees and its validation error 88.2, above the 84.9 of the constant hypothesis that always predicts the sample mean of the labels in D(train). Replacing x by the five numbers x, x2, …, x5 and running the same method on them gives a curve that follows the seasons, with a validation error of 23.6. Fig. 1(a) draws the two learned hypotheses over the days of D(train). A feature transformation is a function \begin{equation} {\mathbf \Phi}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}', \qquad {\mathbf x} \mapsto {\mathbf \Phi}({\mathbf x}) \text{,} \end{equation} which carries the feature vector x of a data point from its feature space X to a new feature vector in a new feature space X'. For a single raw feature, the powers of the opening example are the transformation \begin{equation} {\mathbf \Phi}(x) := \big( x, x^{2}, \ldots, x^{d'} \big)^{\top} \text{,} \end{equation} which delivers d' new features. A machine learning method then runs on the new features in place of the raw ones, and it delivers a hypothesis h' on X'. What is learned overall is then the composition \begin{equation} h = h' \circ {\mathbf \Phi}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}, \qquad {\mathbf x} \mapsto h' \big( {\mathbf \Phi}({\mathbf x}) \big) \text{.} \end{equation} The composition Eq. (3) is why a linear model of the new features is not a linear model of the raw ones. With the powers Eq. (2), the learned h is a polynomial of degree d' in x, which is polynomial regression. Methods differ in where Φ comes from. Principal component analysis obtains it from the raw features alone, as the linear map of a given rank whose reconstruction error is smallest. Linear discriminant analysis uses the labels as well, projecting onto the subspace spanned by the class centroids. A random projection draws Φ at random instead of learning it, and an autoencoder learns a nonlinear Φ with an artificial neural network. Each hidden layer of a deep net is one more feature transformation, learned jointly with the output layer. A kernel method fixes Φ through the choice of a kernel, which returns the inner product of two transformed feature vectors. Such a method uses the transformed feature vectors only through those inner products, so Φ is never evaluated. A transformation that delivers fewer new features than the data point has raw ones is dimensionality reduction, and obtaining Φ from a dataset rather than by hand is the subject of feature learning. The number d' of new features in the definition Eq. (1) sizes the hypothesis space of the method that runs on them. For the powers Eq. (2), every hypothesis available at d' is available at d' + 1 as well, so the training error, the average squared error loss over D(train), cannot rise with d': it falls from 79.4 to 13.2 squared degrees as d' grows from 1 to 14. The validation error on D(val) behaves differently. It is smallest at d' = 5 with 23.6 squared degrees and rises again to 27.9 at d' = 14, the overfitting that a large hypothesis space brings. Fig. 1(b) draws the two errors. Keeping d' small therefore shrinks the hypothesis space, which is model pruning, one of the three routes that regularization distinguishes. Two other names are in use for the function Eq. (1). The kernel method literature calls it a feature map, and the statistical learning literature a basis expansion. The two senses of feature map are distinct: a feature transformation is the map between feature spaces of the definition Eq. (1), while a feature map is the grid of activations delivered by one channel of a convolutional layer. Since the training error cannot rise with d', it cannot report the cost of a transformation that delivers too many new features, so d' is a hyperparameter and is chosen on held-out data points by validation. The count is not the whole choice, since a transformation fixed before the labels are looked at can discard what the label depends on. The three odd powers x, x3, x5 leave the validation error at 86.7 squared degrees, above the 84.9 of the constant hypothesis, while the two even powers x2, x4 alone give 22.0. Every odd power is antisymmetric about x = 0, the middle of the year, and the maximum daytime temperature at Krems is nearly symmetric about that point. The composition Eq. (3) also changes what a weight means: a weight of a linear model on the new features multiplies one of them, at Krems a cube of a rescaled calendar position, and not a quantity the station recorded. In return, least squares on the new features reaches hypotheses that no linear model of the raw feature contains, at Krems a curve that follows the seasons where a straight line is of no use. Two alternatives avoid the choice of Φ by hand. One keeps the raw features and takes a method whose hypothesis space is not a linear model of them, such as a decision tree. The other obtains Φ from the dataset, which is feature learning, with an autoencoder or the hidden layers of a deep net.

terms.name: feature vector
terms.abstract: A feature vector is a list of numbers describing a data point, with one entry for each of its features. A feature is an attribute of the data point that is measured or computed without substantial human supervision. The precise specification of these measurements defines a feature transformation, the function that maps the data point to its feature vector in the feature space. A hypothesis map is applied to the feature vector to predict the label. The feature space is usually a Euclidean space whose dimension is the number of features. Nonnumeric features are encoded as numbers, a binary attribute as 0 or 1 and a categorical one by one-hot encoding. The domain of the feature transformation varies between applications: a data point can be a record of attributes, a text, a digital image, or an audio recording. More generally, the feature space can be any Hilbert space, and a kernel method uses such feature vectors without ever forming them, through their inner products alone.
terms.description: A machine learning method can represent a day at Krems an der Donau (Austria) by four numbers. They are the air temperature at 06:00 and at 15:00 (UTC) of that day, and the same two readings of the previous day. For 16 July 2024, these are 24.6 and 30.8 degrees Celsius, and 22.2 and 31.5 the day before. Stacking these measurements into a vector (24.6, 30.8, 22.2, 31.5)ᵀ ∈ R4 gives a feature vector that characterizes this day. In general, the entries of a feature vector x = (x1, …, xd)ᵀ are the features x1, …, xd of a data point: attributes measured or computed without substantial human supervision. A precise specification of how these attributes are measured defines a feature transformation \[ {\mathbf \Phi}: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}, \quad {\mathbf x} = {\mathbf \Phi}({\mathbf z}) \text{.} \] The function Φ maps a data point z ∈ Z to its feature vector x ∈ X (Fig. 1). Computing it is the preprocessing step also called feature extraction. A hypothesis map takes the feature vector as input and outputs a prediction of the label of the data point. One widely used choice for the feature space is a Euclidean space Rd of fixed dimension d. For the weather example above, the feature space is X=R4. The feature space Rd is the choice for machine learning applications whose features are numeric quantities, such as the four temperatures above. Nonnumeric features can also be entries of a feature vector, once their values are encoded as real numbers. A binary feature, such as whether there was rainfall during the day, is encoded as 0 or 1. A categorical feature with K possible values, such as the season (winter, spring, summer, or autumn), is one-hot encoded. It occupies K entries of the feature vector, all equal to 0 except for a single entry equal to 1, whose position names the value. On 16 July 2024, 18.7 millimeters of rain fell, and the season is summer, so the two features are encoded as the entries 1 and (0, 0, 1, 0), respectively. Stacked under the four temperatures, they give the feature vector x = (24.6, 30.8, 22.2, 31.5, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0)ᵀ ∈ R9 of the day. While the range of the feature transformation Φ can often be chosen as Rd, its domain Z varies widely among machine learning applications. For example, each element of Z can be a text document, with its feature vector consisting of word occurrence counts. In computer vision, the elements of Z are digital images, each an array of pixels. The feature vector then lists the red-green-blue (RGB) intensities of those pixels, one entry per intensity (Fig. 2). The feature vector of an audio recording typically consists of signal values at a sequence of time instants, one entry xj for each instant j=1,…,d (Fig. 3). The notion of a feature vector can be generalized by replacing the feature space Rd with an arbitrary Hilbert space H. Here, a feature vector is the image of a feature transformation \[ {\mathbf \Phi}: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{H} \text{,} \] and any Hilbert space can serve as the feature space. One construction of such a feature vector uses a kernel k: Rd × Rd → R. The kernel assigns to each z ∈ Rd the function k(z,·): Rd → R, whose value at z' ∈ Rd is k(z,z'). That function is itself a vector in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space H, a Hilbert space whose elements are functions on Rd. A kernel method uses elements of H as feature vectors without ever forming them explicitly. Many machine learning methods use feature vectors only through their inner products, which the reproducing property reduces to kernel evaluations, k(z,·)k(z',·)H = k(z,z').

terms.name: fine-tuning
terms.abstract: Fine-tuning continues the training of a model on a task-specific dataset, starting from model parameters obtained by pretraining on a larger dataset. It solves an empirical risk minimization problem over a small training set under the constraint that the model parameters stay close to the pretrained ones. One form of fine-tuning runs a few gradient descent steps on the small training set, started at the pretrained model parameters. Forcing the model parameters to stay close to the pretrained ones is a form of regularization, since it limits the effective hypothesis space that is searched during fine-tuning. For a linear model, the generalization gap grows in proportion to how far the model parameters may move from the pretrained ones, which is why a small training set suffices.
terms.description: Consider daily weather at Krems an der Donau. A linear model that predicts the maximum daytime temperature from the morning minimum is trained on 360 days of one year, which yields a pretrained hypothesis. The task-specific datasets are the temperature measurements of a single month, and one task is to learn a forecaster tailored to that month. For a single month, thirty gradient descent steps on that month's 30 days adjust the model parameters, starting from those learned on the whole year (Fig. 1). Fine-tuning is this second step: it continues the training of a model on a task-specific dataset, starting from model parameters obtained by pretraining on a larger dataset. Formally, let f(w) denote the average loss on the task-specific training set D(train) = z(r)r=1m, \[ f({\mathbf w}) := \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\left({\mathbf z}^{(r)},{\mathbf w} \right) \text{.} \] Fine-tuning solves the empirical risk minimization problem for f not over the whole hypothesis space but under the constraint that the model parameters stay within a radius B of the pretrained ones ŵ(pre), \[ \widehat{{\mathbf w}} \in \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{{\mathbf w} \in \overline{\mathcal{B}}_{B}(\widehat{{\mathbf w}}^{(\mathrm{pre})})} f({\mathbf w}) \text{.} \] Here, B̄B(ŵ(pre)) := w: ‖ w - ŵ(pre) ‖ ≤ B is the closed ball of radius B around ŵ(pre) (see Fig. 2). The radius B is what makes a small training set enough. Consider a linear model, whose hypotheses are h(w)(x) = wᵀ x. Let the feature vectors have norm at most R, and let the loss be ρ-Lipschitz in the prediction and bounded by c on the ball, as the hinge loss is. Let the data points be realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs. Then, with probability at least 1 - δ, every w ∈ B̄B(ŵ(pre)) satisfies \[ \bar{L} \big( h^{({\mathbf w})} \big) \leq f({\mathbf w}) + \frac{2 \rho B R}{\sqrt{m}} + c \sqrt{\frac{2 \ln(2/\delta)}{m}} \text{.} \] This is the bound of Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David (2014, Thm. 26.12) for model parameters of norm at most B, applied to the shifted model parameters w - ŵ(pre). The shift adds the fixed number (ŵ(pre))ᵀ x to the prediction for each data point, which the contraction step of the proof allows, as it admits a separate ρ-Lipschitz function per data point. The second term follows from the Rademacher complexity of the ball, which is at most B R / √(m). The generalization gap between risk and training error f(w) therefore grows in proportion to the radius B and not with the number d of model parameters. A gap of at most ε is guaranteed by m = (2 ρ B R + c √(2 ln(2/δ)))2 / ε2 data points, a number that falls with B. The constraint restricts the model the method searches, which is what regularization achieves by pruning a hypothesis space. The difference is that the pruned set is centered at the pretrained model parameters instead of at an arbitrary initialization. Gradient descent with few steps and a small step size, started at the pretrained model parameters, implements this constraint without enforcing it explicitly. Each step moves the model parameters by η times the norm of the gradient. After T steps with step size η, started at w(0) = ŵ(pre), \[ \Vert {{\mathbf w}^{(T)} - \widehat{{\mathbf w}}^{(\mathrm{pre})}} \Vert \leq \eta \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \Vert {\nabla f({\mathbf w}^{(t)})} \Vert \leq \eta T G \text{,} \] where G bounds the norm of the gradient along the iterates. The iterate therefore lies in the ball of radius B = η T G around ŵ(pre). Limiting the number of iterations is thus a form of regularization: it limits the effective hypothesis space that is searched during fine-tuning, with the step size and the iteration count in the role of the radius. Fine-tuning is useful when the task-specific dataset is small. A hospital has a few hundred annotated scans and needs a tumor detector. Training a deep net from an arbitrary initialization on that many labeled data points usually ends in overfitting; starting from model parameters already learned from millions of unrelated photographs achieves a lower validation error. LLMs are adapted the same way: one pretrained on unlabeled text is fine-tuned on each task it is wanted for. A common variant freezes some layers and adapts only the remainder; parameter-efficient fine-tuning restricts the update to a low-dimensional set of new model parameters while leaving ŵ(pre) untouched. The experiment pythondemos/finetuning.py measures the effect on synthetic data for linear regression with m = 15 data points and d = 30 model parameters. Gradient descent started at the pretrained model parameters with step size η = 0.02 falls to a validation error below twice the noise level after T = 16 steps. It has then moved the model parameters a distance 0.32, inside the ball of radius η T G = 0.72. The same iteration from an arbitrary initialization drives the training error to zero yet ends with a validation error more than four times larger, having moved a distance 2.6. Fig. 3 sketches the same effect on a schematic task-specific dataset of four data points.

terms.name: Gaussian random variable (Gaussian RV)
terms.abstract: A Gaussian random variable (Gaussian RV) is a real-valued random variable whose probability density function is proportional to the exponential of a negative quadratic. The probability density function is determined by two numbers, the mean μ and the variance σ2 of the random variable; the probability distribution with these two parameters is denoted by N(μ,σ2). The standard Gaussian random variable is the special case μ = 0 and σ2 = 1; a general Gaussian random variable is obtained from it by scaling and shifting. A Gaussian random vector is an affine transformation of independent standard Gaussian RVs. Gaussian RVs arise as limits of averages of many independent RVs through the central limit theorem. Among all random vectors with a given covariance matrix, the Gaussian random vector maximizes the differential entropy.
terms.description: The measurement error of a sensor, such as a thermometer, is usually modeled as a Gaussian random variable. A real-valued random variable z is a standard Gaussian random variable if its probability density function is \[ p^{(z)}\left(\eta\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp (-\eta^2/2) \text{.} \] Given a standard Gaussian random variable z, a general Gaussian random variable x with mean μ and variance σ2 can be constructed via x := σ z + μ, so that the probability distribution of x is the normal distribution N(μ,σ2), denoted by x ~ N(μ,σ2). The probability density function of x is, for every η ∈ R, \[ p^{(x)}\left(\eta\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}} \exp\Big( -\frac{(\eta-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}} \Big) \text{.} \] The standard Gaussian random variable is the special case μ = 0 and σ2 = 1. The two parameters of N(μ,σ2) act separately on the probability density function, as shown in Fig. 1: the parameter μ is the mean of x, and the parameter σ is its standard deviation, the square root of the variance σ2. Adding μ to the scaled random variable σ z shifts the probability density function along the horizontal axis by μ, without changing its shape. For σ>0, multiplying z by σ stretches the probability density function horizontally by a factor of σ and lowers its peak by the same factor, so the area under it remains 1. Two ways to generate a Gaussian random variable from other sources of randomness are in common use. For exact generation, let U be a random variable uniformly distributed on the open interval (0,1) ⊂ R and let Φ be the cumulative distribution function of a standard Gaussian random variable. Then μ + σΦ-1(U) ~ N(μ,σ2), the same probability distribution as x but obtained from a different source of randomness. For approximate generation, let m be a positive integer and let v(1), …, v(m) be independent and identically distributed RVs, not necessarily Gaussian, with mean 0 and finite, nonzero variance τ2. Then the normalized sum \[ \frac{1}{\tau\sqrt{m}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}v^{(i)} \] converges in distribution to a standard Gaussian random variable as m increases. Thus, the central limit theorem makes a Gaussian approximation appropriate for averages of many independent contributions, which is why the measurement error of a sensor is usually modeled as Gaussian, although a finite sum need not be Gaussian. Fig. 2 shows both halves of that statement for coin flips, each taking the values +1 and -1 with probability 1/2. The probability mass function of the normalized sum of m = 8 of them already follows the shape of the standard Gaussian probability density function, and the sum still takes only 9 values. Convergence in distribution is convergence of the cdfs, so the largest gap between the cumulative distribution function of the normalized sum and that of a standard Gaussian random variable measures how far the approximation still is. It is 0.137 for m = 8 and 0.050 for m = 64. A Gaussian random vector x ∈ Rd with covariance matrix C and mean μ can be constructed as \[ {\mathbf x} := {\mathbf A} {\mathbf z} + {\boldsymbol \mu} \text{.} \] Here, z := ( z1, …, zd )ᵀ is a vector of independent and identically distributed standard Gaussian RVs. The matrix A ∈ Rd × d is a matrix square root of C, i.e., any matrix with A Aᵀ = C (a Cholesky factor, for instance). The probability distribution of a Gaussian random vector is referred to as the multivariate normal distribution, denoted by N(μ,C). A Gaussian random vector need not have independent components; its components are independent exactly when its covariance matrix is diagonal. A Gaussian random vector x=(x1, …, xd)ᵀ can be interpreted as a stochastic process indexed by the finite set 1, …, d. More generally, a Gaussian process is a stochastic process over an index set I whose restriction to every finite subset of I is a Gaussian random vector. A standard Gaussian random variable z obeys the Gaussian tail bound P(|z| ≥ t) ≤ 2 exp(-t2/2) for every positive number t. That bound also controls functions of independent and identically distributed RVs. Consider a standard Gaussian random vector z ∈ Rd and a function f: Rd → R that is Lipschitz with constant L, i.e., | f(z) - f(z') | ≤ L ‖ z - z' ‖ for every pair of vectors z, z' ∈ Rd. The deviation of f(z) from its expectation is then a sub-Gaussian random variable with parameter at most L. For every positive number t, \[ \mathbb{P}\left(\big| f({\mathbf z}) - \mathbb{E}\big\{ f({\mathbf z}) \big\} \big| \geq t\right) \leq 2 \exp\Big( \frac{-t^{2}}{2L^{2}} \Big) \text{.} \] The number d of arguments does not appear in this concentration inequality: the bound is the same for two arguments and for a thousand. It constrains the tails of f(z) and does not state that f(z) has a normal distribution. The Euclidean norm is an example with L = 1: the length ‖ z ‖ has expectation at most √(d) and deviates from it by more than t with probability at most 2exp(-t2/2), however large d is. Among all random vectors with a given covariance matrix C, the Gaussian random vector x ~ N(μ,C) maximizes the differential entropy. This property is one reason why additive Gaussian measurement noise is a widely used probabilistic model in the statistical analysis of machine learning methods: when only the variance of the noise is known, a Gaussian is the least restrictive assumption.

terms.name: gradient descent (GD)
terms.abstract: Gradient descent (GD) is an iterative algorithm for minimizing a differentiable function f: Rd → R. Each iteration updates the current estimate by a step along the negative gradient, scaled by a step size η. Such a gradient step can be interpreted as the application of an operator that is parameterized by the step size and the underlying function. GD and its variants are widely used to train parametric models in deep learning.
terms.description:
When training a deep net for image recognition, the average loss incurred by the network on a training set of labeled images is a function f(w) of the vector w ∈ Rd of its model parameters, and training means minimizing that function. Many machine learning applications amount to such an optimization problem: an objective function f: Rd → R measures the quality of the model parameters w, which are the optimization variable. Minimizing f on the training set is a proxy: the goal is a small loss on data points outside it (see generalization). In many cases, the objective function is differentiable: at every point w there exists a gradient ∇ f(w) ∈ Rd, the vector of partial derivatives of f at w, which determines a local linear approximation of f (see differentiable). GD uses this local linear approximation to improve the current choice of the model parameters iteratively. Starting from an initialization w(0), it generates a sequence of estimates w(0), w(1), w(2), … that ideally converge to a minimum of f. At each iteration t, GD refines the current estimate w(t) by stepping in the direction of steepest descent of the local linear approximation to f at w(t). This direction is the negative gradient ∇ f(w(t)), giving the update  egin{equation} {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} = {\mathbf w}^{(t)} - \eta 
abla f({\mathbf w}^{(t)}) 	ext{,} \end{equation} where η > 0 is a step size; the update is a gradient step with step size η. For a sufficiently small η, each step decreases the function value, f(w(t+1)) ≤ f(w(t)), with strict decrease whenever ∇ f(w(t)) ≠ 0. GD and its variants are the standard solvers for model training in deep learning. Fig. 1 illustrates a single GD step. Algorithm 1 states the method in full.  egin{algorithm}[H] \caption{Gradient descent }  egin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex Input: objective function f, step size η > 0, initialization w(0), iteration count T \For{t = 0, 1, …, T-1} \State compute the gradient ∇ f(w(t)) \State w(t+1) := w(t) - η ∇ f(w(t)) \EndFor \Statex Output: w(T) \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} With a constant step size η, held fixed across iterations, a single step is described by the GD step operator F(η)(w) = w - η ∇ f(w), so GD is the fixed-point iteration w(t+1) = F(η)(w(t)). Its fixed points, where F(η)(w) = w, are exactly the stationary points ∇ f(w) = 0. For convex f, these are the minima according to the zero-gradient condition. The convergence of the fixed-point iteration w(t+1) = F(η)(w(t)) is governed by the properties of the GD step operator F(η). Assume f is convex and its gradient is L-Lipschitz continuous, i.e., \Vert {
abla f({\mathbf w}) - 
abla f({\mathbf w}')} \Vert \le L \Vert {{\mathbf w} - {\mathbf w}'} \Vert \quad 	ext{for all } {\mathbf w}, {\mathbf w}' \in \mathbb{R}^{d} 	ext{.} For 0 < η ≤ 1/L, the operator F(η) is then a non-expansive operator with respect to the Euclidean norm ‖ · ‖: it does not increase distances between any two points w, w', \Vert {\mathcal{F}^{(\eta)}({\mathbf w}) - \mathcal{F}^{(\eta)}({\mathbf w}')} \Vert \le \Vert {{\mathbf w} - {\mathbf w}'} \Vert 	ext{.} Non-expansiveness alone does not guarantee a unique fixed point. Assume, moreover, that f is μ-strongly convex, i.e., the function f(w) - (μ/2) ‖ w ‖2 is still convex, so the curvature of f is at least μ > 0 in every direction. Then F(η) is a contractive operator with respect to the same norm,  egin{equation} \Vert {\mathcal{F}^{(\eta)}({\mathbf w}) - \mathcal{F}^{(\eta)}({\mathbf w}')} \Vert \le (1 - \mu\eta) \Vert {{\mathbf w} - {\mathbf w}'} \Vert \quad 	ext{ for } 0 < \eta \le 1/L 	ext{,} \end{equation} for any w, w' ∈ Rd. In this case, the contraction Eq. (2) and Banach's fixed-point theorem give a unique fixed point ŵ (the minimizer of f) to which GD converges at a geometric rate. For linear regression, these properties are explicit: the gradient of the average squared error loss is an affine function of w, and the contraction factor of F(η) is governed by the eigenvalues of the matrix XᵀX. Here, X denotes the feature matrix, whose rows are the feature vectors of the data points in the training set (see linear regression). How fast GD converges depends on the curvature of f, as quantified by the constants L and μ above. Let ŵ be a minimizer and f⋆ = f(ŵ). For convex f with L-Lipschitz gradient and the constant step size η = 1/L,  egin{equation} f ig({\mathbf w}^{(T)} ig) - f^{\star} \le  rac{L \Vert {{\mathbf w}^{(0)} - \widehat{{\mathbf w}}} \Vert^{2}}{2 T} 	ext{,} \end{equation} so by the bound Eq. (3) the suboptimality after T steps falls in proportion to 1/T: halving the suboptimality requires doubling the number of iterations. If f is in addition μ-strongly convex, the bound improves to the geometric rate  egin{equation} f ig({\mathbf w}^{(T)} ig) - f^{\star} \le \left(1 - 	frac{\mu}{L}ight)^{T}  ig(f({\mathbf w}^{(0)}) - f^{\star} ig) 	ext{.} \end{equation} The geometric rate Eq. (4) is consistent with the contractive operator factor 1 - μη above. A geometric rate means that the suboptimality shrinks by at least the constant factor 1 - μ/L in every single iteration. Thus, halving the suboptimality now costs a fixed number of iterations, however small the current suboptimality already is. Momentum methods, discussed below, improve both bounds. The iteration also has a continuous-time counterpart. Consider shrinking the step size η in the GD step Eq. (1) toward zero. For η → 0, the iterate w(t) converges to w(t η), the value at time t η of the continuous-time trajectory w(τ) that satisfies the ordinary differential equation ẇ(τ) = -∇ f(w(τ)), known as gradient flow. In particular, GD is the explicit Euler discretization of this gradient flow with step η. Replacing the time derivative ẇ(τ) by the difference quotient (w(t+1) - w(t))/η recovers the update Eq. (1). Fig. 2 illustrates how, for a small step size, the GD iterates closely follow the gradient flow trajectory. Returning to the discrete iteration, in two common settings that motivate variants of GD, the assumptions behind these guarantees fail or the gradient becomes too costly. First, when f is non-smooth, its gradient may fail to exist and GD is replaced by subgradient descent, which steps along a subgradient in place of the gradient. A concrete case is the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator objective, whose penalty term α ‖ w ‖1 is non-smooth. Second, in empirical risk minimization-based methods, f is an average of m loss functions, one for each data point, so evaluating the full gradient sums m gradients and its cost grows in proportion to the training set size m. GD is thus replaced by stochastic gradient descent, which uses a gradient estimate from a random subset of the training set at each step. Momentum methods provide another generalization of plain GD: each update combines gradients from several past steps rather than the current one alone. The name stems from a physical analogy: the iterates trace a particle whose momentum accumulates the force exerted by the negative gradient of the objective function. One prototypical example of a momentum method is Polyak's heavy-ball method. It adds a fraction β ∈ [0, 1) of the previous increment, {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} = {\mathbf w}^{(t)} - \eta 
abla f({\mathbf w}^{(t)}) +  eta ig({\mathbf w}^{(t)} - {\mathbf w}^{(t-1)} ig) 	ext{, for } t=1,\ldots. For a strongly convex quadratic f, this iteration converges faster than plain GD. Fig. 3 compares plain GD with the heavy-ball method on a strongly convex quadratic function. A related momentum algorithm is Nesterov's accelerated variant of GD, which improves the bound Eq. (3) for convex f with L-Lipschitz gradient to f ig({\mathbf w}^{(T)} ig) - f^{\star} \le  rac{2 L \Vert {{\mathbf w}^{(0)} - \widehat{{\mathbf w}}} \Vert^{2}} {(T+1)^{2}} 	ext{.} In contrast to the bound for plain gradient descent, which falls in proportion to 1/T, this bound falls in proportion to 1/T2. For μ-strongly convex f, acceleration improves the contraction factor from 1 - μ/L to 1 - √(μ/L).

terms.name: generalization
terms.abstract: Generalization is the ability of a machine learning method to make accurate predictions on data points that have not been used during training. Many machine learning methods implement training via empirical risk minimization, i.e., learning a hypothesis ĥ that minimizes the empirical risk on the training set D(train). The learned ĥ is then used to compute predictions on new data points outside D(train). A probabilistic model for data generation quantifies the prediction errors beyond D(train) via the risk of ĥ, i.e., the expected loss incurred on a new randomly chosen data point. The difference between the risk and the empirical risk is the generalization gap. The stability of the machine learning method bounds the expected generalization gap without reference to the size of the hypothesis space. A complementary deterministic view characterizes generalization via the robustness of ĥ: its prediction changes by at most a bounded multiple of a perturbation of the features of a data point.
terms.description: A weather forecaster trained on past data is useful only if its predictions are accurate on data points that did not belong to the training set. Generalization refers to the ability of a learned hypothesis ĥ to make similarly accurate predictions on data points that have not been used during training. It is the central goal of machine learning: learning patterns in the features and labels of data points that extend beyond the training set. The canonical learning technique is empirical risk minimization: the machine learning system obtains ĥ ∈ H by minimizing the empirical risk on the training set D(train). A low empirical risk on D(train) does not guarantee accurate predictions on data points outside D(train). The same question arises for online learning and Bayesian inference, where the training set is replaced by the data points processed so far or by a prior. Studying generalization mathematically requires formalizing the notion of data points outside the training set. A widely used approach is to assume a probabilistic model for the generation of data points, such as the independent and identically distributed assumption. Here, data points are interpreted as independent RVs with an identical, fixed but unknown, probability distribution P. Fig. 1 sketches this setup: the shaded ellipse depicts the region of typical data points under P, and the two large filled circles are the data points of the training set that empirical risk minimization fits with the learned hypothesis ĥ, and the arrows are small perturbations of them. The risk of ĥ is the expected loss: \[ \bar{L} \big( \widehat{h} \big) = \mathbb{E} \left\{ L\left({\mathbf z},\widehat{h} \right) \right\}. \] The difference L̄ ( ĥ ) - L̂(ĥ|D(train)) is the generalization gap. For any fixed hypothesis h ∈ H, L̄ ( h ) is a deterministic number that depends only on h and P. In contrast, the empirical risk L̂(h|D(train)) is a random variable that depends on the training set D(train) of size m, which, in turn, is a realization of an independent and identically distributed sequence of RVs z(1), …, z(m) ~ P. Bounding the generalization gap therefore means controlling the probability of the (undesirable) event \mathcal{A}^{(h)} := \left\{ \mathcal{D}^{(\rm train)}: \big| \widehat{L}\big(h|\mathcal{D}^{(\rm train)}\big) - \bar{L} \big( h \big) \big| > \varepsilon \right\}, where ε > 0 is a user-specified tolerance for the generalization gap. Each h ∈ H defines a different event A(h) (see Fig. 2). Since the learned hypothesis ĥ depends on D(train), a bound on the probability of A(h) for one fixed h does not apply to it. It suffices that A(h) has low probability uniformly over H, the argument introduced by Vapnik and Chervonenkis (2015): outside the union of these events, every h ∈ H, and so also ĥ, has a generalization gap of at most ε. Fig. 2 draws these events for a feature space and a label space that are both the real line, as subsets of the sample space of all training sets of size m. Controlling every event A(h) uniformly over H is not the only probabilistic route. If the machine learning method is stable, i.e., replacing a single data point of the training set changes the loss of the learned hypothesis only slightly on average, then the expected generalization gap equals that average change, regardless of the size of the hypothesis space (see stability;). Probability theory is not the only route to generalization. A complementary deterministic approach uses robustness: a good hypothesis ĥ should change its prediction ĥ(x) by at most a bounded multiple of the perturbation of the feature vector x of a data point z, i.e., it should be Lipschitz. For example, an object detection system trained on smartphone photos should still detect the object if a single pixel is changed. Trained deep nets have been shown to lack this property. The system should also deliver the same result if the object in the image is slightly translated or deformed. The arrows in Fig. 1 indicate small perturbations of each data point in the training set of a machine learning method.

terms.name: Gaussian mixture model (GMM)
terms.abstract: A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) is a probabilistic model for the generation of data points with numeric feature vectors. Each data point is generated by first drawing a latent cluster index and then drawing the feature vector from the multivariate normal distribution of that cluster. The resulting marginal distribution is a weighted sum of multivariate normal distributions. The model parameters are chosen to maximize the likelihood function of a dataset. The resulting maximum likelihood optimization problem is an instance of empirical risk minimization using a specific choice for the loss function. This optimization problem is non-convex and typically solved using the expectation–maximization algorithm. This algorithm consists of a fixed-point iteration that never increases the empirical risk.
terms.description: A photograph of a mountain is cut into small square patches, and each patch is described by two numbers: how green and how blue it is on average (Fig. 1). Vegetation, mountain and haze, and bright sky form three clusters of such patches, which are data points characterized by a feature vector x ∈ Rd. A GMM is a probabilistic model for the generation of such data points. A GMM assumes that each data point is generated by first drawing a latent cluster index I ∈ 1, …, k according to cluster probabilities \mathbb{P}\left(I=c\right) = p_{c}, \qquad \sum_{c=1}^{k} p_{c}=1\text{.} Given the choice I=c, the feature vector x is drawn from a multivariate normal distribution P(c)= N(μ(c),C(c)), with mean μ(c) and covariance matrix C(c). The resulting marginal distribution of x is therefore a weighted sum of multivariate normal distributions (Fig. 1), i.e., \mathbb{P} =\sum_{c=1}^{k} p_{c} \mathcal{N}\left({\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)},\mathbf{C}^{(c)}\right)\text{.} A GMM is parameterized by the cluster-specific probability pc = P(I=c), mean μ(c), and covariance matrix C(c) for c=1, …, k. These model parameters can be learned from a dataset D = x(1), …, x(m) by maximum likelihood. The resulting optimization problem has no closed-form solution, and the standard method for solving it approximately is the expectation–maximization algorithm, which alternates between two steps. The E-step computes, for every data point x(r) and every cluster index c, the posterior distribution under the current model parameters, \begin{equation} u_{c}^{(r)} := \mathbb{P}\left(I = c \mid {\mathbf x}^{(r)}\right) = \frac{p_{c} \mathcal{N}\left({\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)},\mathbf{C}^{(c)}\right)({\mathbf x}^{(r)})} {\sum_{c'=1}^{k} p_{c'} \mathcal{N}\left({\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c')},\mathbf{C}^{(c')}\right)({\mathbf x}^{(r)})}\text{,} \end{equation} and the M-step re-fits the model parameters as averages weighted by these posterior distributions, \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} p_{c} &:= \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} u_{c}^{(r)}, \qquad {\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)} := \frac{\sum_{r=1}^{m} u_{c}^{(r)} {\mathbf x}^{(r)}} {\sum_{r=1}^{m} u_{c}^{(r)}}, \mathbf{C}^{(c)} &:= \frac{\sum_{r=1}^{m} u_{c}^{(r)} ({\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)}) ({\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)})^{\top}} {\sum_{r=1}^{m} u_{c}^{(r)}} \quad \text{for } c = 1, \ldots, k\text{.} \end{aligned} \end{equation} The M-step formulas Eq. (2) are not a closed-form solution of the maximum likelihood optimization problem, because the posterior distributions on their right-hand side depend on the model parameters through the E-step Eq. (1). The two steps are repeated until the model parameters stop changing. The maximum likelihood optimization problem for the model parameters of a GMM is an instance of empirical risk minimization with a particular choice for the loss function. Assume that every covariance matrix C(c) is invertible, so that the GMM has a probability density function on Rd. The loss incurred by a feature vector x is the negative logarithm of this probability density function at x, L\left({\mathbf x},\mathbb{P} \right) = - \ln \sum_{c=1}^{k} p_{c} \mathcal{N}\left({\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)},\mathbf{C}^{(c)}\right) ({\mathbf x}) \text{.} The empirical risk of a GMM is then obtained as the average loss over the entire dataset. Minimizing it maximizes the likelihood function, since the logarithm is increasing and the sign is flipped. Fitting a GMM is therefore empirical risk minimization over the hypothesis space of mixtures of k multivariate normal distributions. The loss function is a non-convex function of the model parameters. The expectation–maximization algorithm might therefore converge to a local minimum of the empirical risk, so it is typically run several times with different initializations, keeping the run with the smallest empirical risk. A common construction of the initial model parameters runs k-means first and starts from its cluster centroids. Whatever its initialization, the expectation–maximization algorithm is, like k-means, a fixed-point iteration. Collect the model parameters of a GMM in one vector w. One iteration, the E-step Eq. (1) followed by the M-step Eq. (2), applies an operator F to the current model parameters, so the method is the fixed-point iteration w(t+1) = F(w(t)) for t = 0,1,…. The fixed points of F are model parameters at which the gradient of the empirical risk vanishes, i.e., the stationary points of the empirical risk (see zero-gradient condition). Convergence follows from monotone descent rather than from a contractive operator property: applying F never increases the empirical risk, so the sequence of empirical risk values is non-increasing. It converges if the empirical risk is bounded below. This bound is not automatic for a GMM: a component whose mean coincides with one data point and whose variance shrinks to zero drives the empirical risk to -∞. The bound holds once the eigenvalues of every covariance matrix C(c) are at least some δ > 0, since then the probability density function of the GMM nowhere exceeds (2πδ)-d/2. Under the conditions of Wu (1983, Thm. 2), which imply this bound, the sequence of empirical risk values converges and every limit point of the iterates w(t) is a fixed point. On the patches of Fig. 1, the empirical risk never increased in any of the 300 iterations of expectation–maximization. Trained by expectation–maximization on the 972 patches of Fig. 1, a three-component GMM separates vegetation, mountain and haze, and bright sky. Every patch it assigns to the bluest component lies in the upper half of the photograph. The learned model parameters define a soft clustering: the posterior distribution P(I = c | x) is the probability that a data point belongs to cluster c, and it quantifies the degree of belonging to cluster c. In contrast, hard clustering methods assign each data point to exactly one cluster. Fig. 2 shows these degrees of belonging on the photograph itself. The expectation–maximization algorithm for learning the model parameters of a GMM reduces to Lloyd's algorithm for k-means under additional constraints. Fix every cluster probability at 1/k and every covariance matrix at σ2 I, a multiple of the identity matrix with one common σ2. The posterior distribution then depends on x only through its Euclidean distances to the means, and as σ2 shrinks towards 0 it concentrates on the closest one. In the limit (σ2 → 0), the E-step Eq. (1) becomes an assignment of every data point to its nearest mean, and the M-step Eq. (2) re-centers the means on the data points assigned to them. The two steps are then one iteration of Lloyd's algorithm for k-means. Fig. 3 shows the effect of the common σ2 on the degree of belonging to the vegetation cluster. With σ2 = 10-4, every patch obtains a degree of belonging of 0 or 1, and the grading coincides with the k-means assignment on more than 99% of the patches. With σ2 = 2 · 10-2, 63% of the patches obtain a degree of belonging between 0.2 and 0.8. On the patches of Fig. 1, with σ2 = 1 the three means collapse onto the average of all patches and every patch obtains the same degree of belonging 1/3. Learning the covariance matrices and the cluster probabilities instead of fixing them lets the grading adapt to the data, where k-means assigns each data point to one cluster.

terms.name: gradient
terms.abstract: The gradient of a real-valued function is a vector that determines the local linear approximation of the function. The entries of the gradient are the partial derivatives of the function. Their existence does not by itself make the function differentiable: the vector they form need not give a local linear approximation. For a convex function, the existence of all partial derivatives at a point already makes it differentiable there. Geometrically, a nonzero gradient is orthogonal to the level sets and points in the direction of steepest ascent. In machine learning, gradients of the empirical risk minimization objective function define the update of gradient descent methods and are computed for deep networks by backpropagation.
terms.description: A linear model for the maximum temperature at Krems an der Donau has two model parameters, and changing either of them changes the average squared error loss on the training set. Training a machine learning model adjusts its model parameters w to reduce a loss f(w), which requires knowing how f changes as w moves. The gradient of a real-valued function f: Rd → R: w ↦ f(w) answers this by determining a local linear approximation of f. Formally, the gradient of f at a point w' ∈ Rd is a vector g ∈ Rd such that \begin{equation} \lim_{{\mathbf w} \rightarrow {\mathbf w}'} \frac{f({\mathbf w}) - \big( f({\mathbf w}') + {\mathbf g}^{\top} ({\mathbf w} - {\mathbf w}') \big)}{\left\lVert {\mathbf w} - {\mathbf w}' \right\rVert_{2}} = 0 \text{.} \end{equation} If such a vector exists, it is unique, the function f is differentiable at w', and the vector is denoted by ∇ f(w') or ∇ f(w) |w'. The function f(w') + (∇ f(w'))ᵀ (w - w') is the local linear approximation of f at w' (see Fig. 1). The entries of the gradient are the partial derivatives of f, ∇ f(w) = ( ∂ f/∂ w1, …, ∂ f/∂ wd )ᵀ; the partial derivative ∂ f/∂ wj is the rate of change of f when only the j-th entry of w varies. The existence of all partial derivatives of f at a point does not guarantee that the gradient exists there. Additional assumptions on f restore the implication; convexity is one sufficient condition. If a convex function f: Rd → R has partial derivatives ∂ f / ∂ wj, for j = 1, …, d, at a point w', then f is differentiable at w', and the gradient ∇ f(w') is the vector of these partial derivatives. At every point where f is differentiable and ∇ f ≠ 0, the gradient is orthogonal to the level set of f through that point, the set w: f(w) = c of points where f takes a common value c. It also points in the direction of steepest ascent of f. The negative gradient -∇ f(w') points in the direction of steepest descent, and gradient descent repeatedly steps along it (see Fig. 2;). At a local minimum of a differentiable function f: Rd → R, there cannot be any direction of descent and consequently the gradient must vanish (see zero-gradient condition). Gradients are used in the training of machine learning models. They determine the update of model parameters that minimizes the incurred loss on a training set D(train) = (x(r), y(r)) r=1m, which is the goal of empirical risk minimization. For example, linear regression minimizes the objective function defined by \[ f({\mathbf w}) := \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big( y^{(r)} - {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \big)^{2} \text{.} \] This function is convex and differentiable, with gradient \begin{equation} \nabla f({\mathbf w}) = - \frac{2}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big( y^{(r)} - {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \big) {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \text{.} \end{equation} Setting the gradient Eq. (2) to zero gives the normal equations of linear regression. For a deep artificial neural network whose activation functions, loss, and every other operation it is composed of are differentiable, the empirical risk minimization objective function is also differentiable, by the chain rule. The gradient of this objective function can be computed by backpropagation. The definition carries over to a real-valued function f: H → R on a real Hilbert space H, a Hilbert space over R. In the defining limit Eq. (1), the inner product ⟨ g, w - w' ⟩ of H replaces the term gᵀ (w - w'). The norm of H replaces the Euclidean norm ‖ w - w' ‖2.

terms.name: graph clustering
terms.abstract: Graph clustering decomposes the nodes of a weighted graph, one node per data point, into clusters: subsets of nodes with a large total edge weight inside and a small total edge weight to the rest. Each edge weight expresses the similarity of two data points. The graph is either a similarity graph built from feature vectors, such as an k-nearest-neighbor graph, or given by the application, such as papers joined by citations or users joined by friendships. The cut of a cluster is the total edge weight of the edges leaving it, and the ratio cut of a clustering is the sum of the cuts of its clusters, each divided by the number of nodes in the cluster, which keeps a single node from being split off. Finding the partition with the smallest ratio cut is computationally hard, so spectral clustering approximates it through eigenvectors of the Laplacian matrix, flow-based clustering through network flows, and convex clustering through a penalty term weighted by the edge weights. Applications include image segmentation, with pixels as nodes, and the detection of communities in social networks.
terms.description: Consider every 18th day of 2024 at Krems an der Donau, 21 days in all, each a data point with a feature vector x ∈ R2 that holds the morning minimum and the maximum daytime temperature. Instead of measuring how far apart two days are, record which days are similar. Each day is a node of a graph, and two days are joined by an edge if one is among the six nearest neighbors of the other. The edge carries an edge weight between 0 and 1 that is close to 1 for days with almost the same temperatures (Fig. 1(a)). Graph clustering decomposes the nodes of such a graph into clusters: subsets of nodes with a large total edge weight inside and a small total edge weight to the rest of the graph. For the 21 days, the two clusters are 11 cold days and 10 warm days, joined by a single edge. The graph is built from feature vectors, as a similarity graph such as the k-nearest-neighbor graph with Gaussian edge weights, or it is given by the application: scientific papers joined by citations, users of a social network joined by friendships, or web pages joined by links. In the second case the data points need no feature vectors at all, which is the main reason for clustering a graph rather than a feature space. Formally, the data points are the nodes i = 1, …, m of a weighted graph G that is an undirected graph with the edge weights Ai,i' = Ai',i ≥ 0, where Ai,i' = 0 means that the nodes i and i' are not joined by an edge. The cut of a cluster C ⊆ 1, …, m is the total edge weight of the edges that leave it, \begin{equation} \operatorname{cut}(\mathcal{C}) := \sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}} \sum_{i' \notin \mathcal{C}} A_{i,i'} \text{.} \end{equation} The cut Eq. (1) of a single node is its node degree d(i) = Σi'=1m Ai,i'. For a vector s ∈ -1, 1m with si = 1 for i ∈ C and si = -1 otherwise, the cut is the quadratic form cut(C) = (1/4) sᵀ L(G) s of the Laplacian matrix L(G). A clustering into k clusters C(1), …, C(k) assigns each node to exactly one of them, and the sum of their cuts counts every edge between two clusters twice. Choosing the clusters to minimize this sum alone often splits off a single node. For the 21 days, the smallest cut over all 220 two-way partitions is 0.32, for the cold and the warm days, but the second smallest, 1.15, already splits off the single day 26 December, the day with the smallest node degree. The ratio cut divides the cut of each cluster by its number of nodes, \begin{equation} \sum_{c=1}^{k} \frac{\operatorname{cut}(\mathcal{C}^{(c)})} {|\mathcal{C}^{(c)}|} \text{.} \end{equation} A small cluster is charged a large share of its cut, so the ratio cut Eq. (2) favors clusters of similar size. The normalized cut divides by the total node degree of the cluster instead, so that a cluster is measured by its edge weights rather than by its number of nodes. For the 21 days, the smallest ratio cut over all two-way partitions is 0.061, again for the cold and the warm days. Splitting off 26 December has the ratio cut 1.21, 20 times as much. Ranked by the cut, this split was the second best partition; ranked by the ratio cut, it is the 54th. A random partition into 11 and 10 days cuts 43 of the 80 edges, with the cut 24.9 and the ratio cut 4.75. Over all 167960 partitions of these sizes, the ratio cut averages 4.67. Finding a partition with the smallest ratio cut or normalized cut is computationally hard. For 21 nodes every partition can be enumerated, for the 12288 patches of a photograph it cannot. Graph clustering methods differ in how they approximate a minimizer. Spectral clustering relaxes the constraint that each node is assigned to one cluster and solves the relaxed problem through eigenvectors of the Laplacian matrix. For the ratio cut Eq. (2) of a connected graph and k = 2, the relaxed minimizer is the Fiedler vector, the eigenvector of the second smallest eigenvalue, the algebraic connectivity. The nodes are then split by the signs of its entries or at the best of the m - 1 thresholds along its sorted entries. For the 21 days, whose graph is connected, the Fiedler vector is negative on the 11 cold days and positive on the 10 warm days, and the best of the 20 thresholds returns the exact minimizer of the ratio cut (Fig. 1(b)). Flow-based clustering builds a feature vector for each node from network flows between selected nodes and applies k-means to these feature vectors. Convex clustering uses both the graph and the feature vectors of the nodes. It gives each node its own cluster centroid and adds a penalty term, weighted by the edge weights, that pulls the cluster centroids of joined nodes together until they coincide. The nodes that share a cluster centroid form a cluster. Graph clustering is unsupervised learning: the nodes carry no labels, and the hypothesis learned is the assignment of each node to a cluster index. The cut Eq. (1) is a sum over the edges rather than over the data points. An edge costs its edge weight when its two nodes are assigned to different clusters and nothing otherwise, so the cut is the generalized total variation of the assignment for the discrepancy that is 1 for two different indices and 0 for equal ones. Without the denominator of the ratio cut Eq. (2), assigning all but one node to the same cluster would be the cheapest choice, in the way that a training error of zero is reached by a hypothesis that is useless elsewhere. A photograph is clustered into regions by graph clustering with the pixels as nodes and edge weights that are large for nearby pixels of similar color, which is the image segmentation method that introduced the normalized cut. In a social network, graph clustering with the friendships as edges finds communities, groups of users with many friendships inside and few to the rest.

terms.name: hard clustering
terms.abstract: Hard clustering is the task of decomposing a dataset into a few clusters such that every data point belongs to exactly one cluster, so the clusters form a partition of the dataset. Its output is a cluster assignment, an index in 1, …, k for every data point, which is a label-like quantity computed from the feature vectors alone and carries no meaning beyond the partition. Written as a one-hot vector, the assignment is a degree of belonging that is either 0 or 1, so hard clustering is the special case of soft clustering in which every vector of degrees of belonging is a vertex of the probability simplex. k-means delivers a hard clustering whose clusters are convex regions around cluster centroids, density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise one whose clusters are chains of densely surrounded data points, and spectral clustering one computed from eigenvectors of the Laplacian matrix of a similarity graph. A method that represents a cluster by a cluster centroid learns a hypothesis that assigns any feature vector to a cluster, and minimizing its clustering error is empirical risk minimization.
