A hard clustering is evaluated internally by the clustering error and externally against a reference partition, by the accuracy after the best renumbering of the clusters or by the Rand index, the fraction of pairs of data points that both partitions place together or apart.
terms.description: Consider the 366 days of 2024 at Krems an der Donau, each a data point with a feature vector x ∈ R2 that holds the morning minimum and the maximum daytime temperature of the day. A heating utility that plans its fuel purchases by weather regime needs every day in exactly one regime. Hard clustering is the clustering task that delivers this: it decomposes the dataset into k clusters such that every data point belongs to exactly one of them. With k = 2, k-means splits the days into 192 cold days and 174 warm days (Fig. 1(a)); each day is a cold day or a warm day, never both and never neither. Formally, a hard clustering of a dataset D = x(1), …, x(m) consists of k clusters C(1), …, C(k) ⊆ D that are disjoint and together cover the dataset, \begin{equation} \mathcal{C}^{(c)} \cap \mathcal{C}^{(c')} = \emptyset \text{ for } c \neq c' \quad \text{and} \quad \bigcup_{c=1}^{k} \mathcal{C}^{(c)} = \mathcal{D} \text{,} \end{equation} i.e., a partition of the dataset. The partition Eq. (1) is the same object as the cluster assignment ĉ(r) ∈ 1, …, k of each data point r = 1, …, m, since C(c) = x(r): ĉ(r) = c. The assignment is a label-like output. Like the label of a data point in classification, it takes one of finitely many values. Unlike a label, it is not given with the data but computed from the feature vectors alone, which makes hard clustering a form of unsupervised learning. The index c of a cluster carries no meaning beyond the partition: renumbering the clusters yields the same hard clustering. The assignment of data point r can also be written as a vector of degrees of belonging uc(r), one for each cluster, \begin{equation} u_{c}^{(r)} := \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \widehat{c}^{(r)} = c \text{,} 0 & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases} \qquad c = 1, \ldots, k \text{,} \end{equation} a one-hot vector with a single entry 1. A soft clustering method assigns to each data point a vector (u1(r), …, uk(r))ᵀ of nonnegative degrees of belonging that sum to one, i.e., a point of the probability simplex Δk-1; a Gaussian mixture model, for example, uses the posterior distribution of the cluster index. Hard clustering is the special case in which every such vector is a vertex of the probability simplex, so each degree of belonging Eq. (2) is 0 or 1. A soft clustering is turned into a hard clustering by assigning each data point to the cluster with the largest degree of belonging, and a Gaussian mixture model whose covariance matrices are all σ2 I delivers, as σ2 → 0, the hard clustering of k-means. Hard clustering methods differ in how they represent a cluster. k-means represents cluster c by a cluster centroid w(c) ∈ Rd and assigns each data point to the nearest one, ĉ(r) = argminc = 1, …, k ‖ x(r) - w(c) ‖2. The feature vectors assigned to w(c) form a convex region of the feature space bounded by hyperplanes, one for each other cluster centroid, namely the perpendicular bisector of the segment between the two cluster centroids. For the two cluster centroids at Krems, (1.5, 10.5) and (13.4, 26.1), this boundary is the dashed line of Fig. 1(a); the day nearest to it, March 28, lies 0.22 degrees from it. Density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise represents a cluster as a maximal set of data points connected through a chain of densely surrounded data points, so a cluster can have any shape and the number k is an output rather than an input. Data points that belong to no such chain are noise, and the clusters of density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise partition the dataset only after the noise points are removed or collected in a set of their own. Spectral clustering represents the data points as the nodes of a similarity graph, computes from k eigenvectors of its Laplacian matrix a new feature vector in Rk for each node, and runs k-means on these new feature vectors. The resulting clusters are convex regions in the new feature space but need not be convex in the original one. A hard clustering method that represents a cluster by a cluster centroid learns a hypothesis: the map h(x) = w(c⋆(x)) that sends any feature vector to its nearest cluster centroid, with c⋆(x) = argminc = 1, …, k ‖ x - w(c) ‖2. The partition Eq. (1) of the dataset is the restriction of this map to the dataset, and a data point outside the dataset, say a day of 2025, is assigned to the cluster of its nearest cluster centroid without recomputing the partition. Choosing the cluster centroids that minimize the clustering error, the average squared Euclidean distance between a data point and its cluster centroid, is empirical risk minimization over the hypothesis space of all such maps. The clustering error is therefore the training error of the learned hypothesis, and it is the internal measure of a hard clustering, computed from the dataset alone. It falls as k grows and vanishes when every data point is its own cluster, so it cannot choose k. An external measure compares the hard clustering with a reference partition of the same dataset, here the cold half-year from October to March (183 days) and the warm half-year from April to September (183 days). Since the cluster indices carry no meaning, the comparison must not depend on their numbering. One way is to renumber the clusters by the bijection onto the reference indices that maximizes the fraction of data points on which the two partitions agree. This fraction is the accuracy of the renumbered hard clustering, one minus its average 0/1 loss against the reference indices, and the table of counts behind it is a confusion matrix. At Krems, 172 of the 192 cold days fall into the cold half-year and 163 of the 174 warm days into the warm half-year, an accuracy of 91.5 percent. The disagreement is concentrated in four months (Fig. 1(b)): January, February, November, and December lie entirely in the cold cluster, May to August entirely in the warm one, and the days of March, April, September, and October are split. The other way counts pairs of data points. Let a be the number of pairs that both partitions place in one cluster and e the number that both place in different clusters. The Rand index is \begin{equation} \frac{a + e}{\binom{m}{2}} \text{,} \end{equation} the fraction of pairs on which the partitions agree. It is 1 for identical partitions and unchanged by renumbering, since it never reads an index. Of the 66795 pairs of days at Krems, 28154 are together and 28256 apart in both partitions, a Rand index Eq. (3) of 0.845. An adjusted Rand index subtracts the value expected for two independent random partitions with the same cluster sizes. A reference partition is a standard set by the application, not a property of the feature vectors. With k = 4 clusters against the four seasons, the accuracy after renumbering drops to 59.6 percent and the Rand index to 0.741. Spring and autumn days have the same temperatures: the cluster that holds most spring days consists of 55 percent spring days and 25 percent autumn days. In image segmentation, a hard clustering of the pixels of a photograph by color assigns every pixel to exactly one region, and its evaluation against a hand-drawn segmentation uses the same two measures.

terms.name: high-dimensional regime
terms.abstract: A machine learning method operates in the high-dimensional regime when the effective dimension of its hypothesis space exceeds the sample size m of the training set. For a linear model, the regime begins where the number d of features passes the number m of data points. The feature matrix then has rank at most m, so the least squares solution is not unique and every solution interpolates the training set. A training error of zero therefore carries no information about the risk, so the regime removes the usual evidence about generalization. Regularization and dimensionality reduction restore a usable method, the first by adding a penalty term to the training error and the second by shrinking the hypothesis space. High-dimensional statistics develops theory and methods for this regime, and its guarantees need a structural assumption such as sparsity.
terms.description: Consider a weather service at Krems an der Donau (Austria) that predicts the maximum daytime temperature of a day from the maxima of the previous d days. Each day is a data point with feature vector x ∈ Rd and label y ∈ R, and a linear model h(x) = wᵀ x is learned by least squares on a training set D(train) of m = 30 days of 2023. For d = 1, the training error is 12.4 and the validation error on the validation set D(val) of the 366 days of 2024 is 10.1 squared degrees. For d = 29, the two numbers are 1.7 and 100.4, and for d = 30 they are 0 and 13444. Once the number of features reaches the number of data points in D(train), the training error carries no information about the loss on days outside D(train). Fig. 1 draws both errors for every d from 1 to 60. A machine learning method operates in the high-dimensional regime when the effective dimension of its hypothesis space H exceeds the sample size m of the training set, \begin{equation} d_{\rm eff} \left( \mathcal{H} \right) > m \text{.} \end{equation} For the linear model above, the condition Eq. (1) reads d > m. Empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss delivers a solution of the least squares problem \begin{equation} \min_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big( y^{(r)} - {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \big)^{2} \text{.} \end{equation} Here, the feature matrix X ∈ Rm × d stacks the feature vectors of D(train) as its rows and the vector y ∈ Rm stacks their labels. The rank of X is at most m, so for d > m the nullspace of X holds a nonzero vector and the solution of the least squares problem Eq. (2) is not unique: its minimizers form an affine set of dimension at least d - m. The pseudoinverse picks the one of smallest Euclidean norm, ŵ = X+ y. Every minimizer drives the training error to zero, which is interpolation of D(train). The curse of dimensionality is a separate consequence of a large d: the data points spread thin over the feature space Rd however many of them there are, while the high-dimensional regime compares two counts. Generalization is the performance of a learned hypothesis on data points outside D(train), and the regime removes the evidence that a small training error usually provides about it. A hypothesis that interpolates D(train) has a training error of zero whichever labels the data points of D(train) carry, so a zero training error leaves the risk undetermined and overfitting cannot be diagnosed from D(train) alone. A large artificial neural network is trained in the same regime, with far more trainable model parameters than data points. A deep network reaches a training error of zero even on a training set whose labels have been replaced by random ones. Learning theory measures the size of H by its Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension and by its Rademacher complexity. The sample size that a generalization guarantee needs grows in proportion to the Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension. Two routes restore a usable method on the same features, and both are forms of regularization. Adding the penalty term α ‖ w ‖22 to the training error gives ridge regression. With α = 100, the validation error of the weather example stays between 10.2 and 22.9 squared degrees for every d from 1 to 60. Dimensionality reduction shrinks H instead: least squares on the first d' = 5 principal directions of the feature vectors of D(train), which is principal component analysis, keeps the validation error between 9.8 and 22.1. At d = m neither learned hypothesis interpolates D(train): the training error is 4.2 with the penalty term and 11.2 after the reduction. Fig. 2 draws the validation error of both against the validation error of least squares on all d features. High-dimensional statistics is the branch of mathematical statistics that develops theory and methods for this regime. Without a structural assumption on the model parameters, no method estimates them consistently once d exceeds m. One such assumption is sparsity, which says that few model parameters are nonzero. The least absolute shrinkage and selection operator exploits it with a penalty term built from the ℓ1-norm. The regime is common wherever features are cheap and data points are not: a gene-expression dataset with 2308 features and 63 data points needs regularization before any classifier can be learned on it.

terms.name: Hilbert space
terms.abstract: A Hilbert space is a complete inner product space: every Cauchy sequence of its elements has a limit in the space. Three examples in machine learning are: a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, a space of finite-variance RVs on a common probability space, and a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Linear regression uses a Euclidean space as its feature space and to parameterize its hypothesis space. Optimal linear and nonlinear estimation of a random variable are orthogonal projections in the Hilbert space of finite-variance RVs. A kernel method uses a reproducing kernel Hilbert space as its transformed feature space and as its hypothesis space.
terms.description: Consider gradient descent for linear regression, or any iterative training method whose hypothesis space is a metric space: it produces the sequence h(1), h(2), … of hypotheses. For the sequence to converge to an optimal hypothesis h⋆, the hypotheses must form a Cauchy sequence: for every distance ε > 0, however small, there is an index N such that the distance between h(r) and h(r') is below ε for all r, r' ≥ N. Being a Cauchy sequence is not sufficient on its own. If the underlying metric space is complete, then every Cauchy sequence in that space converges to a point in the space. An example of a complete metric space is a Euclidean space Rd of finite dimension d. A Hilbert space is a generalization of a Euclidean space to possibly infinite dimensions. In particular, a Hilbert space (H, ⟨ ·, · ⟩) is an inner product space that is complete, i.e., in which every Cauchy sequence of its elements has a limit that again belongs to H (see Fig. 1). The elements of H are called vectors, whether they are arrays of numbers, RVs, or functions: what makes them vectors is that they can be added and scaled (see vector space). The inner product induces a norm ‖ u ‖H := √(⟨ u, u ⟩) and, in turn, a metric d(u,v) := ‖ u - v ‖H (see inner product), so a Cauchy sequence of H is one whose vectors eventually lie within any prescribed norm distance of each other. Three examples of Hilbert spaces are used throughout machine learning: a Euclidean space Rd as feature space, a space of RVs with finite variance on a common probability space, and a reproducing kernel Hilbert space of functions. The first of them carries the standard inner product ⟨ u, v ⟩ = uᵀ v, and its completeness follows from that of the real numbers. Linear regression uses the Euclidean space Rd in two roles. The feature vectors x ∈ Rd of the data points it is applied to are vectors of this space, and so are the weights w ∈ Rd that parameterize its hypothesis space h(x) = ⟨ w, x ⟩ : w ∈ Rd. Gradient descent searching for those weights produces a sequence w(1), w(2), … of model parameters, the sequence depicted in Fig. 1. The model parameters are vectors in the second role, so the condition of the opening paragraph is met here: Rd is complete, and a Cauchy sequence of model parameters converges to model parameters. The second example is the set of all RVs x with finite variance, defined on a common probability space. Here, two RVs are identified whenever the expectation of their squared difference is zero, E (x - x')2 = 0, i.e., whenever x = x' with probability one. With this identification, the expectation ⟨ x, x' ⟩ := E x x' is an inner product, and the resulting space is complete. In the Hilbert space of finite-variance RVs on a common probability space, optimal linear estimation is an orthogonal projection (see Fig. 2). A linear estimator ŷ of a random variable y from an observed random variable x is an element of the subspace a x : a ∈ R spanned by x. The corresponding estimation error y - ŷ is measured by the induced norm √(⟨ y - ŷ, y - ŷ ⟩). The smallest error is obtained by the linear estimator whose error is orthogonal to x, \begin{align} 0 & = \langle y - \widehat{y}, x \rangle \nonumber & = \mathbb{E} \big\{ \big(y - \widehat{y} \big) x \big\} \text{.} \nonumber \end{align} When the RVs y,x are zero-mean, this orthogonality means that the error y - ŷ is uncorrelated with x. Optimal nonlinear estimation can also be represented as an orthogonal projection, but on a larger subspace. Projecting y onto the RVs that are functions of x, rather than onto the multiples a x alone, gives the conditional expectation E y | x: it has the smallest squared error among all estimators computed from x. The third example is a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. It is a Hilbert space H of functions h: X → R whose inner product reproduces point evaluations. In particular, each reproducing kernel Hilbert space is associated with a kernel k(·,·) such that k(x,·) ∈ H for every x ∈ X and \[ h({\mathbf x}) = \langle h, k\big({\mathbf x},\cdot\big) \rangle \quad \text{for every } h \in \mathcal{H} \text{.} \] Thus, each vector h ∈ H is itself a hypothesis map X → R, evaluated by taking an inner product with k(x,·). This construction of a hypothesis map generalizes the linear model, which uses the standard inner product of the Euclidean space. The map x ↦ k(x,·) is a feature transformation, carrying the feature vector of a data point into H. A kernel method uses a reproducing kernel Hilbert space in two roles. It is the transformed feature space, in which a data point is represented by k(x,·), and it is the hypothesis space from which a hypothesis is learned. The two roles are also those of Rd in linear regression, with one difference: there a vector parameterizes a hypothesis, here a vector is one. The three examples differ in what their vectors are, not in their geometry. Every Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis, and any two Hilbert spaces whose orthonormal bases have the same number of elements are copies of one another: mapping one basis onto the other extends to a linear map that preserves inner products and, in turn, distances. Such a linear map is therefore an isometry.

terms.name: hyperparameter
terms.abstract: A hyperparameter is any quantity that specifies the components of a machine learning method. Examples are the maximum degree in polynomial regression, the regularization strength in ridge regression, and the number of data points used to construct a training set. Hyperparameters can also determine the behavior of the optimization method used to solve empirical risk minimization, that is, to train a model; one example is the learning rate in gradient descent. A hyperparameter selects one machine learning method out of several alternatives and can therefore be chosen by model selection techniques, such as those based on the validation error.
terms.description: Predicting the maximum temperature of a day at Krems an der Donau from its minimum temperature calls for decisions before any training happens: which maps the method may return, how many data points to collect, and how to search those maps. Fig. 1 shows twelve days as data points, each with the minimum temperature as its feature x and the maximum temperature as its label y. Three straight lines depict hypotheses of the underlying hypothesis space, or model, of the machine learning method. A loss function is used to measure the prediction error incurred on a data point. A hyperparameter is any quantity that specifies one of these components of a machine learning method. The maximum degree in polynomial regression specifies the model, the regularization strength in ridge regression affects the loss function, and the number of data points gathered specifies the training set. The third decision of the opening, how to search the model, is specified by hyperparameters of the optimization method that solves empirical risk minimization. The learning rate of gradient descent, for example, bounds the distance between the iterate of gradient descent, minimizing the training error, and its starting point after a fixed number of gradient steps, and a larger learning rate raises that bound. Thus, the set of model parameters it can reach, and with them the effective hypothesis space, grows. Fig. 2 depicts this for five gradient steps on one training set, starting from the zero initialization w(0) = (0,0)ᵀ, at three values η1 < η2 < η3 of the learning rate. The effective hypothesis spaces H(η1) ⊂ H(η2) ⊂ H(η3) are nested, so the learning rate indexes a family of models ordered by size, as the maximum degree does in polynomial regression. Whichever component it specifies, a hyperparameter selects one machine learning method out of a family of alternatives, and that is what makes a single rule for choosing it possible. The usefulness of a specific hyperparameter value can be assessed by model selection techniques such as validation. As with learning the model parameters by empirical risk minimization on a training set, a hyperparameter is chosen by minimizing the validation error, with the validation error in place of the training error. The search often runs over a grid or a randomly drawn set of candidate values, keeping the one with the smallest validation error on the validation set. Fig. 3 shows this choice for the degree of a polynomial model learned by polynomial regression from 20 data points. The training error falls with every increase of the degree and would select the largest one. The validation error on 100 further data points is smallest at degree 3 and rises steeply beyond it, so validation selects degree 3.

terms.name: hypothesis space
terms.abstract: A hypothesis space H is a set of hypothesis maps h: X → Y from a feature space into a label space. Every machine learning method uses an underlying hypothesis space, which is a subset of the set YX of all possible maps from X into Y. Available computational resources limit the size of H, which in turn determines the method's computational cost and generalization gap. The hypothesis space typically carries geometric structure: real-valued hypotheses can be compared via the deviation in their predictions on a reference dataset, and a parametric model inherits a geometric structure from the underlying parameter space W.
terms.description: A weather service predicting tomorrow's maximum daytime temperature from today's morning temperature must commit to a set of candidate prediction maps: for example, all linear functions of the morning temperature. This set of candidates is the hypothesis space of the method; more generally, every machine learning method commits to a specific hypothesis space H, the set from which it learns a single hypothesis ĥ. Formally, H is a subset of the set YX of all possible maps from the feature space into the label space (see Fig. 1). Linear regression and other linear methods use the linear model as H, i.e., the set of all linear maps Rd → R. Another canonical example is the set of input--output maps realizable by an artificial neural network of fixed architecture, as the model parameters vary. The same H can be used by different machine learning algorithms, such as empirical risk minimization on a fixed training set, online learning on a stream of data points, or Bayesian inference that returns a posterior distribution over H rather than a single hypothesis. The choice of H is a central design decision for a machine learning method. From a machine learning engineering perspective, it is guided by two factors. The first is the available computational resources, such as memory, processing time, and communication bandwidth. The second factor is the number of available data points, which limits the maximum size of H that can be effectively trained without overfitting. In principle, H could be as large as YX itself. The size of H allows the anticipation of generalization before any training is carried out. A small H typically incurs a small generalization gap, while a large H is more prone to overfitting. For a finite H, the effective size is its cardinality. For an infinite H, an effective size can be quantified by the Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension or the Rademacher complexity. The word space (rather than set) reflects the fact that H typically carries some geometric structure. In general, H is not a vector space: the sum of two hypotheses in H need not belong to H. What is more, there are hypothesis spaces that are not equipped with an algebraic structure at all, i.e., there is no meaningful way to add two hypotheses in H or to multiply a hypothesis by a scalar. For real-valued hypotheses, two h, h' ∈ H can be compared by their average squared prediction deviation on a reference dataset D = x(1), …, x(m), \[ \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big(h({\mathbf x}^{(r)}) - h'({\mathbf x}^{(r)})\big)^{2} \text{.} \] Fig. 2 illustrates this comparison: the two hypotheses are evaluated at the feature values of the data points in D and the squared differences in their predictions are averaged. The square root of this average, dD(h,h'), is a pseudo-metric on H: it is the Euclidean norm of the difference of the two prediction vectors divided by √(m), so it is symmetric and satisfies the triangle inequality, and it vanishes for two distinct hypotheses that agree on D. This construction is not meaningful for hypotheses with a finite label space, as used in classification methods. Instead, two such hypotheses can be compared by their disagreement rate on D. A parametric model H = h(w): w ∈ W inherits a geometric structure from the underlying parameter space W ⊆ Rd. A norm on Rd induces the candidate distance d(h(w),h(w')) := ‖ w - w' ‖ on H. When the parameterization w ↦ h(w) is injective, distinct weight vectors give distinct hypotheses, and this candidate distance is a metric. The linear model H = h(w)(x) = wᵀ x: w ∈ Rd is a canonical example of an injective parameterization: distinct weight vectors w produce distinct linear maps, so ‖ w - w' ‖ is a metric on H. When the parameterization is not injective, two distinct weight vectors w ≠ w' can represent the same hypothesis h(w) = h(w'). The distance ‖ w - w' ‖ is then strictly positive even though the two hypotheses coincide, so it is only a pseudo-metric. Permuting the hidden units of an artificial neural network, for instance, changes w but leaves h(w) unchanged.

terms.name: hypothesis
terms.abstract: A hypothesis is a map h: X → Y from the feature space X to the label space Y. Given a data point with features x, the hypothesis returns a prediction h(x) for the label y. A machine learning method selects a single learned hypothesis ĥ from a restricted hypothesis space H ⊆ YX. This restriction reflects finite computational resources of a practical machine learning method. An empirical risk minimization-based method finds ĥ by a search that uses the structure of H, e.g., gradient descent on a parametric model.
terms.description: Predicting tomorrow's maximum daytime temperature from today's morning temperature is a typical machine learning task. A hypothesis is the map that performs this prediction. Formally, a hypothesis is a map (also called a function) h: X → Y from the feature space X to the label space Y. Given a data point with features x, the hypothesis h returns an estimate ŷ = h(x) of the true label y. The same structure, features in and prediction out, appears in a very different application: Fig. 1 shows a hypothesis that predicts a Freddie-likeness score from the samples of an audio recording, i.e., the measured amplitudes at successive time instants. A machine learning method aims to find (or learn) a hypothesis h such that y ≈ h(x) for any data point with features x and label y. Finite computational resources require restricting the search to a subset of \[ \mathcal{Y}^{\mathcal{X}} = \big\{ h: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y} \big\} \text{,} \] the set of all functions from X to Y. This subset is the hypothesis space H (also called the model) underlying the method. The output of a machine learning algorithm acting on a training set is a single learned hypothesis ĥ ∈ H obtained via empirical risk minimization, i.e., an element of H that minimizes the empirical risk on the training set. The search does not examine the hypotheses one by one. For a parametric model, whose hypotheses are indexed by a vector of weights, gradient descent moves through H by following the gradient of the empirical risk, which is possible only because H carries that structure. Different hypothesis spaces admit different representations of their hypothesis maps. Polynomial regression (with a single scalar feature x) represents each h ∈ H as an algebraic expression h(x) = Σj=0p wj xj, where p is the degree of the polynomial and the coefficients wj are the model parameters. A hypothesis space of computer programs represents h as executable source code, e.g., a Python function with a prescribed signature. A decision tree or an artificial neural network represents h as a signal-flow chart whose nodes apply simple operations (e.g., comparisons, weighted sums, nonlinear activations) and whose edges define the order in which these operations are composed. These representations differ in which functions they can express and in how efficiently the empirical risk minimization problem can be solved over the corresponding H. Fig. 2 shows the three representations side by side.

terms.name: independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.)
terms.abstract: A collection of RVs is independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) if all of them follow the same probability distribution and they are mutually independent. Two rolls of the same die are i.i.d.: both values have the same probability distribution, and the first says nothing about the second. The two requirements are separate, and each one can fail without the other. Mutual independence means that the probability of any combination of values is the product of one probability per random variable. This is stronger than independence of every pair. For jointly Gaussian RVs the two requirements hold exactly when all means are equal and the covariance matrix is a scaled identity matrix.
terms.description: Two rolls of the same die are independent and identically distributed: both values follow the same probability distribution, and the first says nothing about the second. A collection of RVs with these two properties is called i.i.d. Formally, consider RVs z(1), …, z(m), all defined on one common probability space (Ω, Σ, P) and taking values in a measurable space Z. They are i.i.d. if every z(r) follows the same probability distribution and the RVs are mutually independent. The common probability space is what makes mutual independence well defined: one outcome has to fix all m values at once (see random variable). The two requirements are separate, and each can fail without the other. Two sensors of different accuracy, read once each, deliver independent values that are not identically distributed. The temperature measured by one sensor at two consecutive times is identically distributed and dependent, since the second value almost repeats the first. Mutual independence is reflected by a factorization of the probability distribution: the probability of any combination of their values is the product of one probability per random variable. For any measurable sets A1, …, Am ⊆ Z, \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}\left( {\mathbf z}^{(1)} \in \mathcal{A}_{1}, \ldots, {\mathbf z}^{(m)} \in \mathcal{A}_{m}\right) = \prod_{r=1}^{m} \mathbb{P}\left( {\mathbf z}^{(r)} \in \mathcal{A}_{r}\right) \text{.} \end{equation} The product rule Eq. (1) has to hold for the whole collection, not only for pairs. Let b1 and b2 be independent RVs, each taking the values 0 and 1 with probability 1/2, and let b3 be their sum modulo two. All three take the values 0 and 1 with probability 1/2, so they are identically distributed, and any two of them are independent. The three together are not: P(b1 = 1, b2 = 1, b3 = 1) = 0, because 1 + 1 = 0 modulo two, while the product of the three single probabilities is 1/8. Pairwise independence is therefore weaker than mutual independence, and these three RVs are identically distributed and pairwise independent without being i.i.d. For jointly Gaussian RVs the two requirements take one compact form. Consider a random vector x = (x1, …, xd)ᵀ of jointly Gaussian RVs with mean vector μ and covariance matrix C. Its components are i.i.d. exactly when μ = (μ, …, μ)ᵀ and C = σ2 I is a scaled identity matrix. Indeed, for C = σ2 I the joint probability density function is a product of univariate Gaussian densities with means μj and the common variance σ2, so the components are independent, and they are identically distributed exactly when the means agree. Conversely, i.i.d. components have equal means, equal variances, and zero covariances. Every component then has the same variance σ2, whose square root σ is the standard deviation along each axis. The off-diagonal zeros make the components uncorrelated. For jointly Gaussian RVs this already implies mutual independence, so the three RVs b1, b2, b3 have no jointly Gaussian counterpart. The equal diagonal entries and the equal means make the components identically distributed. Fig. 1 shows realizations of such a random vector for d = 2.

terms.name: independent and identically distributed assumption (i.i.d. assumption)
terms.abstract: The independent and identically distributed assumption (i.i.d. assumption) is the probabilistic model that represents the generation of a sequence of data points by independent and identically distributed RVs. It consists of two separate requirements, joint independence and one common probability distribution. The assumption makes the average loss on a training set an unbiased estimate of the risk, which is what justifies empirical risk minimization and the use of a validation set to estimate the loss outside the training set. Each requirement can be tested. Independence can be tested through its consequence for predictability of individual data points. A common probability distribution can be tested by the largest gap between the empirical cdfs of two blocks of the sequence. The assumption fails under distribution shift, when the data points met after training follow a different probability distribution.
terms.description: A weather station at Krems an der Donau recorded the maximum air temperature of each day throughout 2024. Fig. 1 shows four of those months, each a dataset with one number per day. The numbers of one such month can be viewed as realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs. That interpretation is the i.i.d. assumption, and the figure shows evidence against it. The four months have different averages. Inside every month a warm day is often followed by a warm one, so which day is read decides what the neighboring values are. The i.i.d. assumption is the probabilistic model, standard in statistical learning theory, representing the generation of the data points z(1), …, z(m) ∈ Z of a dataset by independent and identically distributed RVs with one unknown probability distribution p(z). For any events A1, …, Am ⊆ Z, \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}\left( {\mathbf z}^{(1)} \in \mathcal{A}_{1}, \ldots, {\mathbf z}^{(m)} \in \mathcal{A}_{m}\right) = \prod_{r=1}^{m} \mathbb{P}\left( {\mathbf z}^{(r)} \in \mathcal{A}_{r}\right) \text{,} \end{equation} and each factor is computed from the same p(z). The assumption therefore consists of two separate requirements: the data points follow one common probability distribution, and they are jointly independent. Joint independence is stronger than independence of every pair, since the product rule Eq. (1) is required for all m events at once: there are collections in which every pair factorizes and the whole collection does not. The assumption names a quantity to aim at beyond the training set: the risk of a hypothesis, its expected loss E L(z,h ) on a data point drawn from p(z). Under the i.i.d. assumption the average loss on a training set is an unbiased estimate of it. Let σ2 be the variance of the loss of a fixed hypothesis on one data point. The average loss over m data points then has variance σ2/m, and for losses confined to an interval [a,b], Hoeffding's inequality bounds the probability that it deviates from the risk by more than ε by 2 exp ( -2 m ε2/(b-a)2 ). The bound is the argument for empirical risk minimization and for using a validation set to estimate the loss outside the training set. The assumption can fail: a distribution shift violates the identically distributed requirement across datasets, since the probability distribution that generated the training set differs from the one that generates the data points encountered after deployment. Verifying that a given dataset can be approximated by realizations of i.i.d. RVs has two parts, each a form of hypothesis testing. A test first examines whether the data points are realizations of independent RVs. A second test then examines whether those RVs share one probability distribution. One basic independence test uses the consequence that statistical independence has for the predictability of a data point from a few preceding ones. If z(1), …, z(d), z(d+1) are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs, then no hypothesis predicts z(d+1) from z(1), …, z(d). The hypothesis is learned from data points constructed out of the sequence: each is an overlapping block of d+1 consecutive values, whose first d values are its features and whose last value is its label. Learning by empirical risk minimization on part of the blocks and measuring the average loss on the rest gives the quantity to compare. If the values are realizations of independent RVs, that loss is similar to the loss of a hypothesis that uses no features at all, namely the best constant. Any hypothesis space serves: a linear model with d = 1 under the squared error loss, learned and judged on the same blocks, lowers the average loss below that of the best constant by the factor 1 - r2, where r is the autocorrelation at lag one, the Pearson correlation coefficient between consecutive values. The factor follows from least squares: the slope is r times the ratio of the standard deviations of label and feature, and the average squared residual is then 1 - r2 times the sample variance of the labels. A decision tree, in turn, registers dependence that no Pearson correlation coefficient can. Fig. 2 runs this on the Krems record. A decision tree of depth three with the preceding days as features reaches an average loss of 11.8 on days it was not fitted on, against the 84.6 of the best constant, so the preceding days carry information about the next one and the data points are not realizations of independent RVs. The check detects only the dependence that its hypothesis space and its label can express. A sequence can be dependent and still have a flat conditional expectation, and then no hypothesis space helps. For x(r) = ε(r) ε(r-1) with independent and identically distributed standard Gaussian RVs ε, decision trees of depth one through four all predict the next value worse than the best constant does, and monotonically worse the deeper the tree. Enlarging the hypothesis space lowers no loss when there is nothing in the conditional expectation to find, and worsens generalization: the larger hypothesis space only lowers the loss on the days the hypothesis was trained on. Predicting the squared value instead brings the loss below the constant's. Enlarging the hypothesis space therefore detects dependence only where it appears in the conditional expectation; changing what the hypothesis is asked to predict detects it elsewhere. Neither alone turns the check into a test of independence (see autocorrelation). The identically distributed requirement needs to be verified in turn. Cut the dataset into blocks of equal size and compare the empirical distributions of two blocks by the largest vertical gap between their cdfs. That gap is the two-sample Kolmogorov--Smirnov statistic. It is at most one, and it equals one exactly when every value of one block lies below every value of the other. The Krems record fails this requirement too, and by a wide margin. Fig. 3 applies the block comparison over periods of growing length. Within January the largest gap between the two 15-day blocks is 0.33; over January to June and over the whole year it is 1, so every value of one of the two blocks lies below every value of the other. For two blocks of n values each, i.i.d. RVs produce a gap above √(ln(2.17/α)/n) with probability at most α, by the two-sample form of the Dvoretzky--Kiefer--Wolfowitz inequality. The constant 2.17 is what two blocks of equal size n ≥ 4 require. The value 2, tight for the one-sample inequality, holds in the two-sample case only from n = 458 on. For n = 15 and α = 0.05 the threshold is 0.50, which the January gap of 0.33 does not reach. A gap below its threshold proves nothing beyond itself: the blocks then carry no evidence against a common probability distribution, while a dependence between consecutive values can still be present. Both parts of the assumption therefore need a check of their own. A cruder check compares monthly averages: January averages 5.95 degrees and July 28.99. Take the common probability distribution to be Gaussian, with its expectation and variance set to the sample mean 17.91 and the sample variance of the whole year, a standard deviation of 9.21 degrees. The difference between two monthly averages of 31 days each then has expectation zero and standard deviation 2.34 degrees, so the observed gap of 23.03 degrees lies 9.8 standard deviations from zero, which that probability distribution produces with probability below 10-21. Subtracting the seasonal average removes this violation, and the dependence survives it.

terms.name: inner product
terms.abstract: The inner product of two vectors in a vector space is a number that measures their similarity. Many machine learning applications represent a data point by a numeric array of features, such as the color intensities of an image, the amplitudes of a sensor signal, or the embeddings of the tokens used by LLMs. Each such array is a vector in some vector space. Many machine learning methods rely on measuring the similarity between the vectors that represent data points. Each neuron of an artificial neural network matches its input against a learned template, and the attention unit of a large language model compares the query vector of one token with the key vector of another. Both comparisons compute an inner product.
terms.description: The color intensities of the pixels of an image, the amplitudes of a sensor signal at regular intervals, and the embedding of a token in a large language model are numeric arrays, and data points are often characterized by features that form such an array. Such an array can be represented by a vector, i.e., an element of a vector space. Many machine learning methods compare two data points by measuring how similar the vectors that represent them are. One such measure of similarity is an inner product. Consider a vector space V over the field of real numbers R. An inner product in V is a function \[ \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle: \mathcal{V} \times \mathcal{V} \to \mathbb{R} \] that satisfies the following properties for all vectors u, v, w ∈ V and all scalars β ∈ R: \begin{itemize} \item Symmetry: ⟨ u, v ⟩ = ⟨ v, u ⟩; \item Linearity in the first argument: ⟨ β u + w, v ⟩ = β ⟨ u, v ⟩ + ⟨ w, v ⟩; \item Positive-definiteness: ⟨ u, u ⟩ ≥ 0, with equality if and only if u = 0. \end{itemize} Over the field of complex numbers, symmetry becomes conjugate symmetry, ⟨ u, v ⟩ = ⟨ v, u ⟩, and the inner product is conjugate-linear in the second argument; only real vector spaces are considered from here on. Two vectors u, v ∈ V are called orthogonal if their inner product is zero, ⟨ u, v ⟩ = 0. The pair (V, ⟨ ·, · ⟩) is called an inner product space. Each inner product induces a norm via ‖ u ‖ := √(⟨ u, u ⟩) for all u ∈ V, which in turn induces a metric via d(u,v) := ‖ u - v ‖ for all u, v ∈ V. For the Euclidean space V = Rd, the standard inner product, also called the dot product, is ⟨ x, x' ⟩ = xᵀ x' = Σj=1d xj x'j. Geometrically, the inner product determines orthogonal projections: the orthogonal projection of x' onto the direction of a nonzero vector x has the signed length ⟨ x, x' ⟩ / ‖ x ‖ (see Fig. 1). The inner product also defines the angle θ between two nonzero vectors x, x' ∈ V, via cos θ := ⟨ x, x' ⟩ / ( ‖ x ‖ ‖ x' ‖ ). The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality |⟨ x, x' ⟩| ≤ ‖ x ‖ ‖ x' ‖ ensures that this ratio lies in [-1, 1]. Here cos is the cosine function, which decreases strictly from cos 0 = 1 to cos π = -1, since its derivative -sin is negative on (0, π), and therefore takes each value of [-1,1] exactly once on the interval [0, π]. For the Euclidean plane R2, as illustrated by Fig. 1, the angle defined in this way agrees with the elementary geometric angle between two vectors. For two vectors with given norms, the sign and magnitude of their inner product are determined by the angle θ between them. The inner product is positive for θ < π/2, zero for θ = π/2, where the two vectors are orthogonal, and negative for θ > π/2. The angle drawn in Fig. 1 is smaller than π/2: the two vectors have a positive inner product, and the orthogonal projection therefore falls on the same side of the origin as x. Fig. 1 projects one vector onto the direction of another, that is, onto the line it spans. The same characterization holds for a whole subspace, and it is what turns approximation problems, with respect to the induced norm, into systems of linear equations. Consider a subspace U ⊆ V and a vector v ∈ V. In general, the vector of U closest to v with respect to some norm is called the projection of v onto U. If the norm is induced by some inner product, the projection becomes an orthogonal projection. A vector v̂ ∈ U minimizes ‖ v - u ‖ over all u ∈ U if and only if the approximation error v - v̂ is orthogonal to every vector in U, \begin{equation} \langle {\mathbf v} - \widehat{{\mathbf v}}, {\mathbf u} \rangle = 0 \quad \text{for all } {\mathbf u} \in \mathcal{U} \text{.} \end{equation} The reason is the Pythagorean identity \[ \Vert {{\mathbf v} - {\mathbf u}} \Vert^{2} = \Vert {{\mathbf v} - \widehat{{\mathbf v}}} \Vert^{2} + \Vert {\widehat{{\mathbf v}} - {\mathbf u}} \Vert^{2} \text{,} \] which holds for every u ∈ U whenever Eq. (1) does. The second term is non-negative, so no vector of U is closer to v than v̂ is: orthogonality of the error and being closest are the same condition. The orthogonality condition Eq. (1) is linear in v̂, so a minimizer can be computed by solving linear equations. Fig. 2 illustrates inner products between feature vectors in R2 that represent five European cities. Each city is characterized by its latitude and longitude as its two features, and drawn at the vector x1 u + x2 v for a fixed orthonormal pair u, v ∈ R2. The orthogonal projections of the other cities onto the direction of Helsinki rank them by their alignment with it. The characterization extends beyond subspaces. For a non-empty closed convex set C ⊆ Rd, a vector v̂ ∈ C is the projection of v onto C if and only if \begin{equation} \langle {\mathbf v} - \widehat{{\mathbf v}}, {\mathbf u} - \widehat{{\mathbf v}} \rangle \leq 0 \quad \text{for all } {\mathbf u} \in \mathcal{C} \text{.} \end{equation} Such a projection exists and is unique. One application of the subspace case Eq. (1) is a characterization of linear regression. The learned model parameters are those for which the prediction error is orthogonal to every column of the feature matrix (see normal equations). The resulting predictions are therefore the orthogonal projection of the label vector onto the column space of the feature matrix. The convex case Eq. (2) becomes relevant when linear regression is modified by adding a convex constraint on the model parameters. The Euclidean space Rd carries other inner products besides the standard one. For example, each symmetric and positive definite matrix A ∈ Rd × d, i.e., one with xᵀ A x > 0 for every nonzero x, induces an inner product ⟨ x, x' ⟩ := xᵀ A x'. Such a matrix weighs the coordinate directions against each other, and thereby fixes a different notion of similarity between data points. Take A = diag(4, 1/4), which counts the first feature sixteen times as heavily as the second, and the query x = (1, 1)ᵀ. Of the two candidates (0.9, 1.2)ᵀ and (1.3, 0.4)ᵀ, the standard inner product is larger for the first (2.1 against 1.7) and the weighted one larger for the second (5.3 against 3.9): the same query and the same candidates, but a different answer to which is more similar. Since an inner product also induces a norm and a metric, the choice of A fixes which data points count as nearest neighbors as well. An inner product also gives rise to the notion of an orthonormal basis. Consider a basis b(1), …, b(d) of a vector space V of dimension d. It is orthonormal if its elements are pairwise orthogonal and have unit norm, ⟨ b(j), b(j') ⟩ = 0 for j ≠ j' and ⟨ b(j), b(j) ⟩ = 1. The coordinates of a vector with respect to an orthonormal basis are delivered by inner products: u = Σj=1d βj b(j) with expansion coefficients βj = ⟨ u, b(j) ⟩. Conversely, an inner product can be defined by declaring a basis orthonormal. Take any basis b(1), …, b(d) of V. Then setting \[ \langle {\mathbf u}, {\mathbf v} \rangle := \sum_{j=1}^{d} \beta_{j} \beta'_{j} \quad \text{for } {\mathbf u} = \sum_{j=1}^{d} \beta_{j} {\mathbf b}^{(j)} \text{ and } {\mathbf v} = \sum_{j=1}^{d} \beta'_{j} {\mathbf b}^{(j)} \] yields the unique inner product for which this basis is orthonormal. The standard inner product of the Euclidean space arises in this way from the standard basis given by the columns of the identity matrix Id. Several machine learning constructions use the similarity measure of the opening paragraph. An embedding maps a text block to a vector in a vector space. The alignment of two text blocks is measured by an inner product of their corresponding embeddings. Each neuron of an artificial neural network matches its input vector against a vector of learned model parameters. Attention scores in a large language model are scaled inner products between query and key vectors. Many machine learning methods access the feature vectors of data points only through inner products between feature vectors. A linear model uses hypotheses h(x) = ⟨ w, x ⟩. Consider regularized empirical risk minimization over a training set D(train) = (x(r), y(r)) r=1m, with a loss that depends on w only through the predictions ⟨ w, x(r) ⟩ and a penalty that increases strictly with ‖ w ‖. Every minimizer is a linear combination of the feature vectors in the training set, ŵ = Σr=1m βr x(r). The expansion is the representer theorem, and the support-vector expansion of the support vector machine is a special case of it. The prediction for a new data point then reads \[ \widehat{h}({\mathbf x}) = \sum_{r=1}^{m} \beta_{r} \langle {\mathbf x}^{(r)}, {\mathbf x} \rangle \text{.} \] Training and prediction therefore use the feature vectors only through inner products. Within the training set these are ⟨ x(r), x(r') ⟩, and between the training set and the new data point they are ⟨ x(r), x ⟩. Kernel methods use a kernel k(x, x') to compute these inner products without ever forming feature vectors. Methods based on Euclidean distances access the feature vectors only through inner products as well, even when they are defined without reference to one. The squared Euclidean distance between two feature vectors is a sum of three inner products, ‖ x - x' ‖22 = ⟨ x, x ⟩ - 2 ⟨ x, x' ⟩ + ⟨ x', x' ⟩. A method that uses the feature vectors only through their Euclidean distances therefore also uses them only through inner products. k-nearest neighbors is one example: it ranks the data points in the training set by the distance of their feature vectors to the feature vector of the new data point. The same kernel substitution therefore applies to it: by the identity above, each Euclidean distance is computed from three kernel evaluations, and no feature vector is ever formed.

terms.name: interpretability
terms.abstract: The interpretability of a machine learning method is the extent to which a human user can comprehend the computational process it carries out. Interpretability is closely related to predictability: the user should be able to anticipate the predictions of the method on a test set. Interpretability differs from explainability, which concerns understanding specific predictions with the help of provided explanations.
terms.description: Consider a training set of monthly sales and a linear hypothesis learned from it. Computing next month's prediction from that hypothesis takes a slope, an intercept, and one multiplication, and a user can carry the computation out on paper. With d features, the fitted linear map has one weight per feature and the prediction takes d multiplications, still a computation the user can carry out. The same prediction delivered by a deep net arrives with no account a user could follow. Interpretability is what separates the two. A machine learning method is interpretable for a human user if they can comprehend the computational process of the method. The international terminology standard for artificial intelligence does not define interpretability. Its closest notion is predictability, the property of an artificial intelligence system that enables reliable assumptions by users about the predictions delivered by a machine learning method. Comprehension of a computation cannot be observed directly, so interpretability is judged through predictability: the user anticipates the predictions the method delivers, and the evaluations proposed in the literature measure how often those anticipations are right. Predictability is weaker than interpretability: a method whose computation the user can follow is predictable to that user, but a method whose predictions the user anticipates need not be one whose computation they could carry out. The terminology standard makes the same point: a user may rely on the predictions of an artificial intelligence system without being able to comprehend how the method produced them. Fig. 1 depicts a test of predictability. A training set is used by two different methods that learn hypotheses ĥ and ĥ'. The user anticipates the predictions on a test set, providing a pseudo-label for each of its data points, by visually extrapolating the linear trend of the training set. The predictions of ĥ agree with these anticipations: the method producing ĥ is predictable to the user. The predictions of ĥ' deviate from them: the method producing ĥ' fails the test of predictability and therefore cannot be one whose computation the user comprehends. The agreement alone does not establish interpretability, since the user anticipated the predictions of ĥ without carrying out its computation. The method producing ĥ is nevertheless also interpretable to a user familiar with the concept of a linear map: such a user could comprehend the computation of ĥ. Besides following the computation step by step, as for the linear map of the sales example, a user can comprehend a learned hypothesis through its decomposition into components that are themselves interpretable. The hypothesis ĥ in Fig. 1 decomposes into a slope and an intercept: the slope states how the prediction changes with the feature. A trained deep net lacks such a decomposition, since the activation of an individual neuron typically does not correspond to a human-interpretable concept. Mechanistic interpretability aims to recover interpretable components from a trained deep net by decomposition methods such as sparse coding of activations. The AI Risk Management Framework of the US National Institute of Standards and Technology distinguishes interpretability from explainability, the property pursued by explainable artificial intelligence. In contrast to interpretability, explainability requires that an explanation is provided along with each prediction. These explanations may take the form of saliency maps or reference examples from the training set. A challenge for explainable artificial intelligence methods is that a computed explanation can be unfaithful to the learned hypothesis and thereby mislead the user. An interpretable machine learning method avoids this: the account of its computation is the computation itself, so the account cannot be unfaithful to it.

terms.name: interpretable machine learning (interpretable ML)
terms.abstract: Interpretable machine learning (interpretable ML) refers to machine learning methods whose hypothesis space contains only hypotheses that a human user can comprehend directly, such as sparse linear models or shallow decision trees. Such methods let a user see how a prediction changes when the features of a data point change, and how the predictions change when a different training set is used. An interpretable hypothesis is its own explanation; post hoc explanations of the predictions of an opaque learned hypothesis can instead be unfaithful. Restricting the hypothesis space to interpretable hypotheses also acts as a form of regularization. A penalty term can pick a comprehensible hypothesis out of a hypothesis space that mostly holds others: least absolute shrinkage and selection operator sets some weights of a linear model to exactly zero, how many depending on its regularization parameter, leaving a hypothesis with few nonzero weights, and explainable empirical risk minimization penalizes deviations from the predictions one user supplies during training.
terms.description: A physician reads a rule that predicts a patient's risk from a handful of measurements and can check every step of it by hand. Interpretable ML refers to machine learning methods whose hypothesis space contains only such hypotheses, which a human user can comprehend directly (see interpretability). Such methods let a user follow both what a learned hypothesis does to its input and how training produced it. An interpretable machine learning method allows the user to understand how a prediction changes when the features of a data point change, and how the predictions change when a different training set is used. Thus, interpretable machine learning methods require suitable choices for the hypothesis space and the training algorithm. Examples of interpretable machine learning include empirical risk minimization with linear models that combine a small number of meaningful features, shallow decision trees whose predictions follow from a few explicit tests, GAMs, and lists of decision rules. Fig. 1 depicts a decision tree for medical triage in a hospital. This system involves two tests of vital signs, allowing the staff to trace every prediction by reading the tree. An interpretable hypothesis makes the effect of feature changes explicit. For a linear model h(w)(x) = wᵀx, changing the feature xj by an amount Δ changes the prediction by exactly wj Δ. Each weight states how strongly one feature affects the prediction. For the decision tree of Fig. 1, a prediction changes only when a feature crosses one of the explicit test thresholds. A patient at 38.5 ∘C with a heart rate of 110/min is routine; a rise to 38.9 ∘C leaves that prediction unchanged, while a rise to 39.5 ∘C turns it urgent. An interpretable machine learning method also makes the effect of training set changes traceable. This dependence is studied under stability, which formalizes a machine learning method as a map from a training set to a learned hypothesis. For linear regression, this map is available in closed form through the normal equations whenever the feature matrix has full column rank, so the user can compute how a perturbed label in the training set shifts the predictions (see linear regression). An interpretable hypothesis is its own explanation: no separate explanation is constructed for it. The explanation delivered with a prediction can then be a description of the learned hypothesis itself: the weights of a linear model that combines few features, or the flow chart of a shallow decision tree as in Fig. 1. A hypothesis space containing only such hypotheses is called intrinsically interpretable. This contrasts with explainable artificial intelligence, which constructs post hoc explanations for the predictions of a possibly opaque learned hypothesis. For high-stakes applications, such as the medical triage of Fig. 1, using an interpretable model can be preferable to explaining an opaque model, since post hoc explanations can be unfaithful to the hypothesis they explain. Restricting H to interpretable hypotheses is model pruning, one of the three routes that regularization distinguishes. The penalty-term route gives an interpretable learned hypothesis without restricting the hypothesis space beforehand. A penalty term added to the objective function of empirical risk minimization penalizes the hypotheses a user cannot follow, so training picks a comprehensible one out of a hypothesis space that mostly holds the others. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator does this for linear models, which are no more comprehensible than a deep net once they combine hundreds of features. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator uses the ℓ1-norm ‖ w ‖1 of the weights w as the penalty term, which sets some weights to exactly zero, how many depending on the regularization parameter α. The learned hypothesis is then a weighted sum of the remaining features, so a user can name the features the prediction uses and how much each one changes it. A method close to this route, but not interpretable machine learning, is explainable empirical risk minimization, which extends the idea to the training of an arbitrary model. Its penalty term is built from the predictions that one specific user supplies for the data points of the training set (see explainable empirical risk minimization). It therefore delivers explainability to that user rather than interpretability, and it leaves the hypothesis space as it is. The user predictions need not be elicited one data point at a time. They might be obtained as the predictions of a simpler proxy model that the user considers interpretable, so that the penalty term measures the deviation from that proxy. In Fig. 2, the user predictions are obtained from a simple linear model fitted to the training set.

terms.name: inverse
terms.abstract: An inverse of a function is a second function that undoes it. For f: U → V it is the function g: V → U with g(f(u)) = u and f(g(v)) = v, and it exists precisely when f is injective and every element of V has a nonempty preimage. The inverse of a linear map of Rn is again a linear map, represented by the inverse matrix A-1 with A A-1 = A-1 A = I, which exists exactly when the square matrix A is of full-rank, equivalently when its determinant is nonzero. Where no inverse exists, a left or right inverse or the Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse takes its place. In machine learning, inverses appear in the closed-form solution of linear regression, in the pair formed by the sigmoid function and the logit, which turns a score into a probability and back, and in drawing a realization through the inverse of a cumulative distribution function.
terms.description: A frost warning for Krems an der Donau delivers a real-valued score for the day, and the sigmoid function turns that score into the probability of frost: the score 0 becomes the probability 0.5, the score 2.2 becomes 0.9. Reading the score back off a reported probability undoes this step, and the function that does so is the logit ln( p / (1-p) ). The logit is the inverse of the sigmoid function. An inverse of a function f: U → V is a function g: V → U that undoes it in both directions: g(f(u)) = u for every u ∈ U, and f(g(v)) = v for every v ∈ V. Such a g exists precisely when f is injective and every v ∈ V has a nonempty preimage. It is then unique and written f-1. If only the first identity holds, g is a left inverse, and if only the second holds, a right inverse. Fig. 1 shows both cases for a function on a domain of four shapes. The best known instance is the inverse of a linear map. A square matrix A ∈ Rn × n represents a linear map of Rn into itself, and that map has an inverse exactly when A is of full-rank, meaning its columns are linearly independent. Such a matrix is said to be invertible. The inverse linear map is itself a linear map, and the matrix representing it is the inverse matrix A-1, which satisfies \[ {\mathbf A} {\mathbf A}^{-1} = {\mathbf A}^{-1} {\mathbf A} = \mathbf{I} \text{.} \] A square matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is nonzero. Fig. 2 shows the two linear maps acting on the standard basis of R2. For a matrix that is not square or not of full-rank, the one-sided inverses are what remains: a left inverse B satisfies B A = I, and a right inverse C satisfies A C = I. The Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse A+ selects one generalized inverse for every matrix. Inverses are used throughout machine learning. Solving a system of linear equations is one task, and ridge regression is another: its closed-form solution inverts the matrix Xᵀ X + α I, which is invertible for every positive regularization strength α. The sigmoid function and the logit of the opening paragraph are an invertible pair, which allows translating between the score of a linear classifier and a probability value. A feature transformation that is invertible loses no information, since the raw feature vector can be recovered from the transformed one. The inverse of a continuous cumulative distribution function allows generating realizations of a random variable with that cumulative distribution function from a realization of another, simpler random variable, one uniformly distributed on [0,1]. A counterfactual explanation for a learned hypothesis can be constructed from a right inverse of it, which returns, for a given prediction, one feature vector of its preimage. A learned hypothesis usually maps many feature vectors to the same prediction, so it has no inverse and no left inverse; a right inverse is what remains, and choosing which element of the preimage it returns is what makes one counterfactual more useful than another.

terms.name: kernel method
terms.abstract: A kernel method applies a linear method, such as a linear model or a linear classifier, to transformed feature vectors. The transformation is constructed from a kernel: each feature vector is mapped to a function with domain equal to the original feature space, and inner products between transformed feature vectors reduce to evaluations of a kernel. Kernel methods apply to any feature space on which a kernel is defined, including sets of text documents and graphs.
terms.description: Deciding whether an image shows a specific object, or which topic a text document belongs to, are tasks for kernel methods. A kernel method is a machine learning method that applies a linear method, such as a linear model for regression or a linear classifier for classification, to transformed feature vectors that are constructed from a kernel. Linear methods learn a hypothesis that combines the features of a data point linearly, e.g., h(x) = wᵀ x for the feature space X = Rd. Such a hypothesis predicts well only if the relation between the feature vectors and the labels of data points is approximately linear. Moreover, a linear method requires numeric feature vectors and is not directly applicable to data points from an arbitrary feature space X, such as text documents or graphs. Both limitations can be mitigated by a feature transformation φ: X → H from the original feature space X to a transformed feature space H, chosen as a Hilbert space. Fig. 1 shows a binary classification problem with the first limitation: no straight line separates the two classes in the original feature space, so no linear classifier has a decision boundary that classifies them correctly. A suitable feature transformation makes a dataset ``more linear'': the relation between the transformed feature vectors φ(x) and the labels is closer to linear in H than the relation between the original feature vectors x and the labels is in X. A useful feature transformation φ often delivers transformed feature vectors in a Hilbert space H of high (possibly infinite) dimension. Computing and storing the transformed feature vectors φ(x) explicitly can then be infeasible. However, linear methods access the feature vectors of data points only through inner products between pairs of feature vectors (see linear model). For example, the prediction delivered by a trained support vector machine is a weighted sum of inner products between the feature vector of a new data point and the feature vectors in the training set. To apply a linear method to the transformed feature vectors, it is therefore enough to know the inner products ⟨ φ(x), φ(x') ⟩ for every possible pair of feature vectors x, x' ∈ X. These inner products are the values of a single function of two arguments, the kernel defined by \[ k\big({\mathbf x},{\mathbf x}'\big) := \langle \phi({\mathbf x}), \phi({\mathbf x}') \rangle \text{, for } {\mathbf x}, {\mathbf x}' \in \mathcal{X} \text{.} \] The value k(x,x') quantifies the similarity of the feature vectors x and x'. As an inner product of transformed feature vectors, the kernel is symmetric, and every matrix of pairwise kernel values is positive semi-definite; these two properties characterize kernels. A linear method that is applied to the transformed feature vectors thus requires only the kernel k; the feature transformation φ itself is never evaluated. Kernel methods reverse this construction: they start from a kernel k: X × X → R and construct the feature transformation from it. The feature transformation sends a feature vector x ∈ X to the function k(x,·), i.e., the transformed feature vector z := φ(x) = k(x,·) is itself a function with domain X, for every x ∈ X. These functions belong to the reproducing kernel Hilbert space Hk associated with the kernel k. Take two original feature vectors x, x' ∈ X. The inner product between their transformed feature vectors is a single kernel evaluation, \[ \langle k\big({\mathbf x},\cdot\big), k\big({\mathbf x}',\cdot\big) \rangle = k\big({\mathbf x},{\mathbf x}'\big) \text{.} \] More generally, the inner product between the transformed feature vector k(x,·) and any function h ∈ Hk is a point evaluation, \[ \langle h, k\big({\mathbf x},\cdot\big) \rangle = h({\mathbf x}) \text{,} \] which is referred to as the reproducing property of the reproducing kernel Hilbert space Hk. This reproducing property contains ⟨ k(x,·), k(x',·) ⟩ = k(x,x') as a special case that is obtained for the choice h = k(x',·). So the conclusion of the forward construction holds here too: the (possibly infinite-dimensional) transformed feature vectors never need to be computed explicitly. Fig. 2 depicts the reproducing kernel Hilbert space Hk for a training set with two data points: a hypothesis h is a single vector in Hk, the two transformed feature vectors span a subspace, and h has an orthogonal projection onto it. The value ⟨ h, k(x,·) ⟩ = h(x) is a linear function of the transformed feature vector k(x,·) ∈ Hk, but the function x ↦ h(x) induced on the original feature space X is nonlinear in general. Linearity in the original feature vector x may not even be defined, since the feature space X need not be a vector space, e.g., when it consists of text documents or graphs. Kernel methods can be formulated as regularized empirical risk minimization over the reproducing kernel Hilbert space Hk, \[ \min_{h \in \mathcal{H}_{k}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\left(\big({\mathbf x}^{(r)}, y^{(r)}\big),h \right) + \alpha \left\lVert h \right\rVert_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}^{2} \text{,} \] over a training set with feature vectors x(r) and labels y(r), for r = 1, …, m. The regularization parameter α > 0 weights the penalty term ‖ h ‖Hk2. The loss function L((x(r), y(r)),h ) depends on h only through the prediction h(x(r)), i.e., it is a function of the prediction h(x(r)) and the label y(r) only. Since h ∈ Hk, the reproducing property delivers this prediction as an inner product, h(x(r)) = ⟨ h, k(x(r),·) ⟩. By the representer theorem, this optimization problem has a minimizer of the form ĥ = Σr=1m βr k(x(r),·) with expansion coefficients β1, …, βm ∈ R. Fig. 2 illustrates the underlying projection argument. Replacing a hypothesis h by its orthogonal projection h̃ onto the subspace spanned by k(x(1),·), …, k(x(m),·) leaves the predictions on the training set unchanged and never increases the penalty term. Some minimizer ĥ therefore lies in this subspace and has the above form. Training thus reduces to an optimization problem in these m coefficients. For a loss function that is convex in the prediction, it is a convex optimization problem: each prediction ĥ(x(r')) = Σr=1m βr k(x(r),x(r')) on the training set is linear in the coefficients, and the penalty term ‖ ĥ ‖Hk2 = Σr=1m Σr'=1m βr βr' k(x(r),x(r')), obtained from the reproducing property, is a quadratic form with the positive semi-definite matrix of pairwise kernel values and hence convex. The prediction ĥ(x) = Σr=1m βr k(x(r),x) requires only kernel evaluations. Examples of such kernel methods are the kernel support vector machine, obtained for the hinge loss, and kernel ridge regression, obtained for the squared error loss. For X = Rd, a widely used choice of the kernel k is the Gaussian kernel k(x,x') = exp(- ‖ x - x' ‖22 / (2 σ2) ) with bandwidth σ > 0. Kernels are also available for data points without numeric features, such as strings and graphs. Fig. 3 shows the nonlinear decision boundary ĥ(x) = 0 of a hypothesis ĥ learned by a Gaussian-kernel method with squared error loss from a training set of two concentric rings that no linear classifier separates. Here, kernel ridge regression fits the labels y(r) ∈ -1, +1 and the prediction is the sign of the fitted value, a construction referred to as regularized least-squares classification. Kernel methods impose the smoothness assumption through the reproducing kernel Hilbert space norm. That norm ‖ h ‖Hk quantifies the smoothness of a hypothesis h: it is large for a rapidly varying h and small for a smooth h. Moreover, different kernels impose different kinds of smoothness. The Gaussian kernel is infinitely differentiable, and so is every h(x) = ⟨ h, k(x,·) ⟩ in its reproducing kernel Hilbert space; the reproducing kernel Hilbert space norm penalizes derivatives of all orders and thereby high-frequency components. The Matérn kernels are a family of kernels indexed by a smoothness parameter ν > 0: their reproducing kernel Hilbert space coincides, with equivalent norms, with the Sobolev space of order determined by ν, whose functions have derivatives up to that order in the weak sense. The penalty term α ‖ h ‖Hk2 in the above regularized empirical risk minimization is the squared reproducing kernel Hilbert space norm. It therefore implements smoothness as quantified by ‖ h ‖Hk: among hypotheses with the same training error, the regularized empirical risk minimization objective function is smallest for the hypothesis with the smallest reproducing kernel Hilbert space norm. The choice of kernel determines not only training but also the predictions of the learned hypothesis: for localized kernels, such as the Gaussian kernel, the prediction ĥ(x) is dominated by the data points in the training set whose feature vectors are close to x. In this sense, kernel methods implement the smoothness assumption: data points with nearby feature vectors obtain similar predictions. The locality of the predictions also makes kernel methods a soft-weighted analogue of k-nearest neighbors: instead of averaging the labels of a fixed number of nearest data points, the prediction weights all data points in the training set by the kernel value k(x(r),x).

terms.name: kernel ridge regression
terms.abstract: Kernel ridge regression applies ridge regression to transformed feature vectors constructed from a kernel, and thereby learns a nonlinear hypothesis. It performs regularized empirical risk minimization over hypothesis maps that are elements of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. By the representer theorem, the learned hypothesis is a weighted sum of kernel evaluations with coefficients obtained in closed form by solving a single system of linear equations. The kernel is a hyperparameter that needs to be matched to the structure of the feature space: for the hours of a day, a kernel built from the shortest-path length on the cycle graph of the hours makes the hours 23 and 0 as similar as the hours 0 and 1. Like ridge regression, also kernel ridge regression equals empirical risk minimization on an augmented training set: the transformed feature vectors are perturbed by realizations of a zero-mean Gaussian process whose covariance function is the kernel scaled by the regularization parameter.
terms.description: Predicting the temperature at Krems an der Donau for a given hour of the day is a machine learning application. A data point is one hour of one day. Its feature x ∈ 0, …, 23 is the hour of the day, and its label y is the temperature measured in that hour. The feature space is X = 0, …, 23 and the label space is Y = R, so the application is a regression problem. It requires a hypothesis space of nonlinear hypothesis maps h(x), since the temperature rarely changes linearly with the hour of the day. Fig. 2 shows 24 of the data points of a training set of size m = 744 that represent the hourly temperature measurements of July 2024 at the GeoSphere weather station Krems an der Donau. The relation between feature and label is nonlinear: the temperature falls until the early morning, rises until the afternoon, and falls again. Kernel ridge regression extends ridge regression, which uses a linear model, by replacing the original feature x with a transformed feature vector φ(x). The feature transformation φ is constructed from a kernel k: X × X → R. The value k(x,x') measures the similarity between two data points with feature values x and x'. The kernel is a hyperparameter of kernel ridge regression that must be matched to the structure of the feature space. For the temperature example, the hours of a day are the nodes of a cycle graph (see Fig. 1), and the similarity of two feature values is determined by the length min|x - x'|, 24 - |x - x'| of the shortest path between the corresponding nodes, \begin{equation} k\big(x,x'\big) := \exp\big( - \min\{|x - x'|, 24 - |x - x'|\} / \sigma \big) \text{,} \end{equation} with a bandwidth σ > 0 measured in hours. The hours 23 and 0 are then as similar as the hours 0 and 1, which the absolute difference |x - x'| alone would not deliver. Since X has 24 elements, the function Eq. (1) is a kernel if and only if the 24 × 24 matrix of its values is positive semi-definite; for σ = 3, its smallest eigenvalue is 0.16. The kernel Eq.
