(1) uses the exponential of the shortest-path length and not its Gaussian exp( - min|x - x'|, 24 - |x - x'|2 / (2 σ2) ). The Gaussian of a distance is a kernel for every bandwidth only if the data points with that distance can be placed in a Euclidean space. The nodes of a cycle graph with the shortest-path length cannot: for σ = 3, the 24 × 24 matrix of Gaussian values already has a negative eigenvalue. With the kernel Eq. (1) for σ = 3 and α = 10-2, the hypothesis learned from the 744 data points follows the daily cycle (see Fig. 2), with a training mean squared error of 9.0, and its values at the hours 23 and 0 differ by 0.5 degrees. Ridge regression on the raw hour can only learn a linear hypothesis, with a training mean squared error of 18.6, whose values at the hours 23 and 0 differ by 5.2 degrees. Mathematically, kernel ridge regression learns a hypothesis from the reproducing kernel Hilbert space Hk of a kernel k: X × X → R by minimizing the penalized average squared error loss on a training set D(train) = ( x(r),y(r) ) r=1m with numeric labels y(r) ∈ R, \begin{equation} \widehat{h} = \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{h \in \mathcal{H}_{k}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big( y^{(r)} - h\big({\mathbf x}^{(r)}\big) \big)^{2} + \alpha \left\lVert h \right\rVert_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}^{2} \text{.} \end{equation} By the reproducing property of Hk (see reproducing kernel Hilbert space), every hypothesis h ∈ Hk satisfies h(x) = hφ(x)Hk, with the inner product ··Hk of Hk and the transformed feature vector φ(x) = k(x,·). The learned hypothesis ĥ is therefore linear in the transformed feature vector and typically nonlinear as a map on the original feature space. It is linear on X only if the feature transformation itself is linear, which is the case for a kernel of the form k(x,x') = xᵀ Q x' with a positive semi-definite matrix Q. Algorithm 1 states the method in full; the following paragraphs derive its steps. \begin{algorithm}[H] \caption{Kernel ridge regression } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex Input: training set D(train) = ( x(r),y(r) ) r=1m, kernel k, regularization parameter α > 0 \State compute the Gram matrix K ∈ Rm × m with entries Kr,r' = k(x(r),x(r')) \State solve the system of linear equations (K + α m I) β = y with the label vector y = (y(1), …, y(m))ᵀ for β̂ \Statex Output: the hypothesis ĥ(x) = Σr=1m β̂r k(x(r),x) \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} The penalty term in the kernel ridge regression problem Eq. (2) is the scaled squared reproducing kernel Hilbert space norm α ‖ h ‖Hk2 with a regularization parameter α > 0. The resulting method is an instance of regularized empirical risk minimization, as is ridge regression, whose penalty term is the scaled squared Euclidean norm α ‖ w ‖22 of the model parameters. The average squared error loss is a convex function of h, and the squared norm is strictly convex. The kernel ridge regression problem Eq. (2) therefore has a unique minimizer ĥ for any training set, as does ridge regression. By the representer theorem (see kernel method), the minimizer of the kernel ridge regression problem Eq. (2) has the form ĥ = Σr=1m βr k(x(r),·) with a coefficient vector β = (β1, …, βm)ᵀ. Inserting this form into the kernel ridge regression problem Eq. (2) yields the finite-dimensional optimization problem \[ \min_{\boldsymbol{\beta} \in \mathbb{R}^{m}} \frac{1}{m} \left\lVert {\mathbf y} - \mathbf{K} \boldsymbol{\beta} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} + \alpha \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top} \mathbf{K} \boldsymbol{\beta} \text{,} \] with the label vector y = (y(1), …, y(m))ᵀ and the Gram matrix K with entries Kr,r' = k(x(r),x(r')) (see kernel). By the zero-gradient condition, a coefficient vector solving this optimization problem satisfies the system of linear equations \[ \mathbf{K}\big( \big(\mathbf{K} + \alpha m \mathbf{I}\big) \boldsymbol{\beta} - {\mathbf y} \big) = \mathbf{0} \text{.} \] Since K is positive semi-definite and α > 0, the matrix K + α m I is invertible, and a minimizer is obtained in closed form as \begin{equation} \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \big( \mathbf{K} + \alpha m \mathbf{I} \big)^{-1} {\mathbf y} \text{.} \end{equation} The prediction for a data point with feature vector x is \begin{equation} \widehat{h}({\mathbf x}) = \sum_{r=1}^{m} \widehat{\beta}_{r} k\big({\mathbf x}^{(r)},{\mathbf x}\big) \text{.} \end{equation} Training is a one-shot computation: kernel ridge regression requires no iterative optimization method (and hence no fixed-point interpretation), only the unique solution of the m × m system of linear equations with the invertible matrix K + α m I, which is the closed form Eq. (3), followed by the prediction Eq. (4). For the linear kernel k(x,x') = xᵀ x' on X = Rd, kernel ridge regression produces the same predictions as ridge regression applied to the raw feature vectors. The Gram matrix is then K = X Xᵀ, with the feature matrix X = (x(1), …, x(m))ᵀ. Multiplying out both sides shows that (Xᵀ X + α m I) Xᵀ = Xᵀ (X Xᵀ + α m I), and hence Xᵀ (K + α m I)-1 = (Xᵀ X + α m I)-1 Xᵀ. The prediction ĥ(x) = xᵀ Xᵀ β̂ of kernel ridge regression therefore equals xᵀ (Xᵀ X + α m I)-1 Xᵀ y, the prediction of ridge regression. Like ridge regression, kernel ridge regression has an interpretation as a form of data augmentation. Training with noise added to the feature vectors is equivalent to adding a penalty term. Replacing each data point by a probability distribution centered at it is the vicinal form of empirical risk minimization: the average loss over the data points is replaced by the expected loss under these probability distributions, each describing the vicinity of one data point. Its effect on kernel methods is a regularization of the learned hypothesis. The following example makes the equivalence explicit for a linear kernel on the plane, so that the perturbed copies can be drawn. Consider data points with two features, the feature space X = R2, and the kernel \begin{equation} k\big({\mathbf x},{\mathbf x}'\big) := {\mathbf x}^{\top} {\mathbf C}^{-1} {\mathbf x}' \text{,} \end{equation} with a positive definite matrix C ∈ R2 × 2. This kernel is an inner product of R2 with a modified metric: the squared norm k(x,x) = xᵀ C-1 x scales the two features differently and couples them, and its unit ball is an ellipse instead of the circle of the Euclidean norm. The reproducing kernel Hilbert space Hk of this kernel is R2 with this inner product. The transformed feature vector k(x,·) is the linear function x' ↦ xᵀ C-1 x', every hypothesis in Hk is a linear model h(w)(x) = wᵀ x with model parameters w ∈ R2, and its reproducing kernel Hilbert space norm is ‖ h(w) ‖Hk2 = wᵀ C w. The kernel ridge regression problem Eq. (2) therefore reads \begin{equation} \widehat{{\mathbf w}} = \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathbb{R}^{2}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big( y^{(r)} - {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \big)^{2} + \alpha {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf C} {\mathbf w} \text{,} \end{equation} which is ridge regression with the penalty term α ‖ w ‖22 replaced by α wᵀ C w. Its unique minimizer is ŵ = ( Xᵀ X + α m C )-1 Xᵀ y with the feature matrix X = (x(1), …, x(m))ᵀ, and it coincides with C-1 Xᵀ β̂ for the coefficients Eq. (3) with the Gram matrix K = X C-1 Xᵀ. For C = I, the kernel Eq. (5) is the linear kernel and the penalized problem Eq. (6) is ridge regression itself. Adding the penalty term in the penalized problem Eq. (6) is equivalent to empirical risk minimization on an augmented training set, i.e., to computing the average squared error loss of h(w) on it. This augmented training set is obtained from the original training set. For each data point ( x(r),y(r) ), r = 1, …, m, the feature vector x(r) is replaced by realizations of infinitely many independent and identically distributed RVs x(r) + ε(r) with Gaussian RVs ε(r) ~ N(0,α C). The label y(r) is left unchanged. The penalty term is exactly the amount by which the average squared error loss of h(w) over the perturbed copies exceeds its squared error loss on the original data point. Since E ε(r) = 0, the increase is \[ {\mathbb{E}} \big\{ \big( {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\boldsymbol \varepsilon}^{(r)} \big)^{2} \big\} = {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbb{E}} \big\{ {\boldsymbol \varepsilon}^{(r)} \big({\boldsymbol \varepsilon}^{(r)}\big)^{\top} \big\} {\mathbf w} = \alpha {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf C} {\mathbf w} \text{.} \] The equivalence is exact for the linear model h(w), while for a nonlinear hypothesis it holds up to terms of higher order in the noise amplitude. As in ridge regression, this increase of the average loss under data augmentation is an estimate for the generalization gap. Accordingly, linear regression on a large augmented training set recovers the predictions of kernel ridge regression. The kernel determines the shape of these perturbations (see Fig. 3). The covariance matrix α C of ε(r) is the scaled inverse of the matrix in the kernel Eq. (5). The one-standard-deviation contour of the perturbed copies is therefore \[ \big({\mathbf x} - {\mathbf x}^{(r)}\big)^{\top} {\mathbf C}^{-1} \big({\mathbf x} - {\mathbf x}^{(r)}\big) = \alpha \text{.} \] This contour is the set of feature vectors x with k(x - x(r),x - x(r)) = α, i.e., the ball of radius √(α) around x(r) in the norm induced by the kernel. For C = I, this ball is a circle of radius √(α): the perturbations in the data augmentation interpretation of ridge regression have covariance matrix α I and no preferred direction. For a general C, it is an ellipse, so the ellipses drawn around the data points are the balls of radius √(α) of the norm induced by the kernel. The size of a perturbation is measured by its kernel norm, and the penalty term α wᵀ C w is the average squared error loss that perturbations of kernel norm √(α) cause. The ellipses also show the eigenvalue decomposition of the matrix C. Inserting the eigenvalue decomposition C = Σj=12 λj u(j) (u(j))ᵀ, with eigenvalues λ1 ≥ λ2 > 0 and orthonormal eigenvectors u(1), u(2), into the contour gives \[ \sum_{j=1}^{2} \frac{\big( \big(\mathbf{u}^{(j)}\big)^{\top} \big({\mathbf x} - {\mathbf x}^{(r)}\big) \big)^{2}}{\alpha \lambda_{j}} = 1 \text{.} \] The principal axes of every ellipse therefore point along the eigenvectors of C, and the semi-axes have lengths √(α λ1) and √(α λ2). The perturbations spread most along the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue, and the penalty term grows with the square of a displacement of w along u(j), in proportion to λj. For the kernel Eq. (5), the perturbation acts linearly on the transformed feature vectors, k(x(r) + ε(r),·) = k(x(r),·) + k(ε(r),·). The random function k(ε(r),·) is therefore a zero-mean Gaussian process whose covariance function is the kernel scaled by the regularization parameter, \begin{equation} {\mathbb{E}} \big\{ k\big({\boldsymbol \varepsilon}^{(r)},{\mathbf x}\big) k\big({\boldsymbol \varepsilon}^{(r)},{\mathbf x}'\big) \big\} = {\mathbf x}^{\top} {\mathbf C}^{-1} {\mathbb{E}} \big\{ {\boldsymbol \varepsilon}^{(r)} \big({\boldsymbol \varepsilon}^{(r)}\big)^{\top} \big\} {\mathbf C}^{-1} {\mathbf x}' = \alpha k\big({\mathbf x},{\mathbf x}'\big) \text{.} \end{equation} For a general kernel, the raw feature vectors cannot be perturbed in this way. The feature transformation φ is nonlinear, so noise added to x(r) does not add a zero-mean random function to φ(x(r)). On a finite feature space such as the hours of a day, there is no noise to add at all. The perturbation of the transformed feature vector itself remains defined: it replaces φ(x(r)) = k(x(r),·) by φ(x(r)) + g(r) with a zero-mean Gaussian process g(r) whose covariance function is α k. Since h(x) = hφ(x)Hk, the perturbation changes the prediction by hg(r)Hk. Expanding h and g(r) in the eigenfunctions of the kernel gives \begin{equation} {\mathbb{E}} \big\{ \langle h, g^{(r)} \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}^{2} \big\} = \alpha \left\lVert h \right\rVert_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}^{2} \text{,} \end{equation} so the penalty term is the expected increase of the squared error loss under this perturbation for every kernel. For a kernel with an infinite-dimensional reproducing kernel Hilbert space, the realizations of g(r) are not elements of Hk. The inner product in the expected increase Eq. (8) is then the limit of the partial sums of the expansion, which converges since ‖ h ‖Hk is finite. For the hours of a day, φ(x) is the column for hour x of the 24 × 24 matrix of kernel values, and g(r) is a Gaussian vector whose covariance matrix is α times that matrix. Up to the scaling by α in the covariance function Eq. (7), this is the Gaussian process with covariance function k and noise variance α m whose posterior mean kernel ridge regression computes: the prediction ĥ(x) coincides with that mean.

terms.name: k-fold cross-validation (k-fold CV)
terms.abstract: k-fold cross-validation (k-fold CV) divides a dataset into k folds of equal size and uses each fold once as the validation set while the other k-1 folds form the training set of a given machine learning method. The k resulting validation errors are averaged into a single number, an indicator of generalization beyond the training set. While a single validation step estimates the risk of a single hypothesis, k-fold CV estimates the risk of a machine learning method. Leave-one-out cross-validation is the extreme case of k-fold CV with one data point per fold.
terms.description: Fig. 1 depicts four data points, representing daily weather conditions at Krems an der Donau (Austria). Each data point is characterized by the minimum temperature of a day as the feature x and its maximum temperature as the label y. Three of the four data points are used as the training set for polynomial regression with degree three. The remaining data point serves as the validation set. A polynomial of degree three (a cubic) has four coefficients and the training set holds three data points. Thus, unless two data points have the same feature, polynomial regression delivers a hypothesis that passes exactly through those three data points and, in turn, the training error is zero. However, as depicted in Fig. 1, the learned hypothesis ĥ does not generalize well beyond the training set, i.e., polynomial regression with degree three is overfitting. The validation error on the held-back data point can reveal this overfitting, but a single split does so unreliably. Holding back the first data point gives a validation error of 1.37, which suggests a reliable hypothesis. Holding back the second, third, or fourth data point instead gives validation errors of 8.05, 7.02, and 72.42, as panels (b) to (d) of Fig. 1 illustrate. Their average 22.22 is the 4-fold CV estimate. Using different splits of a dataset into training set and validation set offers a more reliable assessment of a machine learning method. Consider a machine learning method A that maps a training set to a learned hypothesis ĥ = A(D(train)). k-fold CV estimates the expected loss (or risk) of the method A as follows. It divides a dataset D evenly into k subsets, the folds D(1), …, D(k) (Fig. 2). For each fold b = 1, …, k, one iteration trains the model on the union of all folds except D(b) and evaluates the resulting hypothesis on the held-out fold D(b). The k per-fold validation errors are then averaged to obtain the CV error ECV, the CV estimate of the expected loss. Algorithm 1 summarizes this procedure. \begin{algorithm}[H] \caption{k-fold CV } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex Input: machine learning method A, dataset D, number of folds k \State divide D evenly into the folds D(1), …, D(k) \For{b = 1, …, k} \State D(train) := D D(b), \quad D(val) := D(b) \State ĥ(b) := A(D(train)) \State Ev(b) := L̂(ĥ(b)|D(val)) \EndFor \Statex Output: CV error ECV = (1/k) Σb=1k Ev(b) \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} A single validation set assesses one hypothesis, e.g., the one that A delivers from a training set. In contrast, k-fold CV does not assess a single hypothesis. Instead, every iteration learns a potentially different hypothesis; panels (a) to (d) of Fig. 1 show four such hypotheses. Thus, the average validation error ECV measures the method A rather than one hypothesis. In Fig. 1, A is polynomial regression with degree three and ECV = 22.22. In particular, ECV measures the average risk of the hypotheses obtained from training sets holding the fraction (k-1)/k of the dataset. Compared to a single split into training set and validation set, k-fold CV uses each data point for both training and validation. In Fig. 2, for example, each data point has been used four times for training and once for validation after all five iterations. Like k-fold CV, the bootstrap estimates the risk of a method by averaging over several hypotheses, each learned from a different resample of the dataset; unlike the folds of k-fold CV, these resamples overlap. Important variants and special cases of k-fold CV include the following: \begin{itemize} \item Stratified k-fold cross-validation: It preserves the class proportions of the full dataset in every fold. Stratification matters for classification with imbalanced data: a plain random partition can leave a fold with almost no data points of the minority class. The validation error of that fold is then computed on a validation set whose class proportions differ from those of the full dataset, so it is an unreliable estimate of the risk. \item Leave-one-out cross-validation: It is the extreme case k = m, with m the number of data points in the dataset, where each fold contains a single data point. It trains on almost the full dataset in every iteration, at the cost of m training runs and a high variance of the estimate. \item Repeated k-fold CV: It averages the results of several runs with different random fold assignments. This reduces the variance contributed by the partitioning and is useful for small datasets, where a single partitioning strongly affects the estimate. \end{itemize} The k iterations cost k training runs, against the single run of one split, and the gain depends on k. In a separate experiment, 2000 datasets of fifteen data points are drawn from a linear model with additive Gaussian noise, and linear regression has an expected loss of 2.62 there. The bias of ECV against that loss falls from +0.48 at k = 2 to +0.01 at k = 15, and the standard deviation of ECV across the 2000 datasets from 1.87 to 1.01. The upward bias at k = 2 follows from what ECV measures there, hypotheses learned from half of each dataset. The folds also require the independent and identically distributed assumption. For consecutive data points of a time series, or for several data points recorded at one weather station, a random partition places correlated data points in both the training set and the held-out fold, so ECV understates the risk. Folds built from contiguous blocks, or from whole groups, keep correlated data points on one side of each split. A step that uses the full dataset before the split also makes ECV understate the risk. Hastie et al. (2009, Sect. 7.10.2) select the 100 features most correlated with the label over all 50 data points, and the ECV of the resulting one-nearest-neighbor hypothesis is 3% on average, while no hypothesis in that setting has a risk below 50%. Such a step belongs inside every iteration.

terms.name: k-means
terms.abstract: k-means is a hard clustering method for data points with numeric feature vectors. Each data point is assigned to exactly one of k clusters, each represented by a cluster centroid, namely the cluster whose cluster centroid is nearest in Euclidean distance. The cluster centroids are chosen to minimize the clustering error, the average squared Euclidean distance between a data point and its nearest cluster centroid. The resulting k-means optimization problem is an instance of empirical risk minimization using a specific choice for the loss function. This optimization problem is non-convex and NP-hard, and typically solved using Lloyd's algorithm. This algorithm consists of a fixed-point iteration that never increases the clustering error and reaches a fixed point after finitely many iterations. Replacing the squared Euclidean distance by the Euclidean distance itself gives k-medians, whose averaging step computes a geometric median and which is less sensitive to outliers.
terms.description: A photograph of a mountain is cut into small square patches, and each patch is described by two numbers: how green and how blue it is on average (Fig. 1). Vegetation, mountain and haze, and bright sky form three clusters of such patches, which are data points characterized by a feature vector x ∈ Rd. k-means is a hard clustering method for such data points. The idea of k-means is to assign each data point of a dataset D = x(1), …, x(m) to exactly one of k clusters indexed by c = 1, …, k. Each cluster is represented by a cluster centroid w(c) ∈ Rd, and a data point is assigned to the cluster whose cluster centroid is nearest in Euclidean distance. The quality of a given choice of cluster centroids, and of the resulting hard clustering, is measured by the clustering error: the average squared Euclidean distance between a data point and its nearest cluster centroid, \frac{1}{m}\sum_{r=1}^{m} \min_{c = 1, \ldots, k} \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(c)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2}\text{.} The k-means principle is to choose cluster centroids that minimize the clustering error, \min_{{{\mathbf w}}^{(1)}, \ldots, {{\mathbf w}}^{(k)}} \frac{1}{m}\sum_{r=1}^{m} \min_{c = 1, \ldots, k} \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(c)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2}\text{.} The inner minimization assigns each data point to its nearest cluster centroid, and the outer minimization moves the cluster centroids (Fig. 1). The k-means optimization problem has no closed-form solution, and solving it exactly is NP-hard. The standard method for solving it approximately is Lloyd's algorithm, which alternates between two steps. The assignment step assigns every data point to its nearest cluster centroid, \begin{equation} \widehat{c}^{(r)} := \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{c = 1, \ldots, k} \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(c)} \right\rVert_{2} \quad \text{for } r = 1, \ldots, m\text{,} \end{equation} and the averaging step moves each cluster centroid to the mean of the data points assigned to it, \begin{equation} {{\mathbf w}}^{(c)} := \frac{1}{\big|\{r: \widehat{c}^{(r)} = c\}\big|} \sum_{r: \widehat{c}^{(r)} = c} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \quad \text{for } c = 1, \ldots, k\text{.} \end{equation} The two steps are repeated until the assignment Eq. (1) stops changing. Algorithm 1 states the method in full. \begin{algorithm}[H] \caption{k-means, Lloyd's algorithm } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex Input: feature vectors x(1), …, x(m), cluster count k, initial cluster centroids w(1), …, w(k) \Repeat \State assignment: for each r = 1, …, m, assign x(r) to the cluster argminc = 1, …, k ‖ x(r) - w(c) ‖2, as in Eq. (1) \State averaging: for each c = 1, …, k, set w(c) to the mean of the feature vectors assigned to cluster c, as in Eq. (2) \Until{no assignment changes} \Statex Output: cluster centroids w(1), …, w(k) and the assignment they induce \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} Run on the 972 patches of Fig. 1 with k = 3, k-means separates vegetation, mountain and haze, and bright sky. Every patch it assigns to the bluest cluster centroid lies in the upper half of the photograph. The learned cluster centroids define a hard clustering: every data point belongs to exactly one cluster, the one with the nearest cluster centroid. Fig. 2 shows this assignment on the photograph itself. The k-means principle is an instance of empirical risk minimization with a particular choice for the hypothesis space and the loss function. The hypothesis space Hk consists of all maps h: Rd → Rd of the piecewise-constant form h({\mathbf x}) = {{\mathbf w}}^{( c^{\star}({\mathbf x}))}, \qquad c^{\star}({\mathbf x}) = \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{c = 1, \ldots, k} \left\lVert {\mathbf x} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(c)} \right\rVert_{2}\text{,} parameterized by the k cluster centroids w(1), …, w(k) ∈ Rd. Each such hypothesis maps every feature vector to its nearest cluster centroid. The region of feature space mapped to one cluster centroid is bounded by hyperplanes, one for each other cluster centroid (the dashed lines of Fig. 1). Thus, every cluster found by k-means is a convex region. The loss incurred by a feature vector x is the squared Euclidean distance to its nearest cluster centroid, L(x,h ) = ‖ x - h(x) ‖22. The clustering error is then obtained as the average loss, i.e., the empirical risk, over the entire dataset. Minimizing the clustering error is therefore empirical risk minimization over Hk. The clustering error is a non-convex function of the cluster centroids: with a single data point at x = 0 and two scalar cluster centroids w(1), w(2) ∈ R, it is min((w(1))2, (w(2))2), so both (1, 0) and (0, 1) are global optima with value 0, but their midpoint (0.5, 0.5) gives 0.25. The non-convexity leaves Lloyd's algorithm with more than one fixed point. Consider the four data points (± 5, ± 1)ᵀ and k = 2 (Fig. 3). Started from one cluster centroid on the left and one on the right, the assignment step groups the two left and the two right data points, and the averaging step returns the cluster centroids (-5, 0)ᵀ and (5, 0)ᵀ, with clustering error 1. Started from one cluster centroid above and one below, the two steps return (0, 1)ᵀ and (0, -1)ᵀ, with clustering error 25. Both pairs are fixed points: with the cluster centroids (± 5, 0)ᵀ every data point is nearer the cluster centroid on its own side, since 1 < √(101), and with (0, ± 1)ᵀ every data point is nearer the cluster centroid on its own level, since 5 < √(29). Neither start moves, and the second has 25 times the clustering error of the first. Since Lloyd's algorithm can stop at such a fixed point, a local minimum of the clustering error, it is typically run several times with different initializations, keeping the run with the smallest clustering error. A variant of k-means referred to as k-means++ uses a specific construction of the initial cluster centroids. Lloyd's algorithm is a fixed-point iteration. Collect the cluster centroids in one vector w := (w(1), …, w(k)). One iteration, the assignment step Eq. (1) followed by the averaging step Eq. (2), applies an operator F to the current cluster centroids, so the method is the fixed-point iteration w(t+1) = F(w(t)) for t = 0,1,…. The fixed points of F are cluster centroids that each coincide with the mean of the data points assigned to them. Convergence follows from monotone descent rather than from a contractive operator property: each of the two steps minimizes the clustering error over one set of variables with the other held fixed, so applying F never increases the clustering error. Non-increase alone does not exclude cycling through partitions of equal clustering error. If a data point changes its cluster centroid in the assignment step Eq. (1) only when another one is strictly closer, every change of the partition strictly lowers the clustering error, so no partition is visited twice. A finite dataset admits only finitely many partitions, so the partition stops changing after finitely many iterations, and the averaging step then leaves the cluster centroids unchanged: the iterates have reached a fixed point. On the patches of Fig. 1, Lloyd's algorithm reached a fixed point after 12 iterations, and the clustering error never increased along the way. Lloyd's algorithm for k-means is the limit of the expectation–maximization algorithm for a Gaussian mixture model under additional constraints. Fix every cluster probability of the Gaussian mixture model at 1/k and every covariance matrix at σ2 I, a multiple of the identity matrix with one common σ2. The posterior distribution of the cluster index then depends on x only through its Euclidean distances to the means, and as σ2 shrinks towards 0 it concentrates on the closest one. In the limit (σ2 → 0), the E-step of expectation–maximization becomes the assignment step Eq. (1) and the M-step becomes the averaging step Eq. (2) of Lloyd's algorithm. On the patches of Fig. 1 with σ2 = 10-4, the expectation–maximization algorithm assigns 99.4% of the patches like k-means. Leaving the covariance matrices and the cluster probabilities free is what lets a Gaussian mixture model provide a degree of belonging where k-means assigns each data point to one cluster. The loss function is what separates k-means from its generalizations, and it decides what the averaging step of Lloyd's algorithm computes. Replacing the squared Euclidean distance by the Euclidean distance itself, L(x,h ) = ‖ x - h(x) ‖2, gives the k-medians optimization problem. The assignment step Eq. (1) is unchanged, since the nearest cluster centroid is the same under both losses, but the averaging step Eq. (2) becomes the geometric median of the data points assigned to a cluster, which has no closed form and is computed by Weiszfeld's fixed-point iteration. The gain is robustness to outliers: adding 10 far-away patches to the vegetation cluster of Fig. 1 moves their mean by 0.044 but their geometric median by 0.004, while k-medians assigns 98.5% of the patches like k-means. The averaging step is not tied to the squared Euclidean distance alone: for any Bregman divergence L(x,h ) = xh(x)φ as loss, the mean of the assigned data points still minimizes their summed loss, so only the assignment step changes. The Euclidean distance is not a Bregman divergence, which is why it changes the averaging step. Restricting each cluster centroid to be one of the data points assigned to it gives k-medoids, which uses only the pairwise distances between data points and therefore applies to data points without numeric feature vectors. Returning to k-means itself, Fig. 4 shows the effect of the number k of clusters on the patches of Fig. 1. Each patch is painted with the average color of its cluster, which is image segmentation. With k = 2, the sky and the mountain are separated from the vegetation. With k = 3, the mountain and haze form their own cluster. With k = 4, the vegetation splits into the sunlit meadow and the dark foliage. The clustering error decreases with k, from 0.034 for k = 2 to 0.018 for k = 3 and 0.011 for k = 4, and it reaches 0 when every data point is its own cluster centroid.

terms.name: k-means++
terms.abstract: k-means++ is a randomized rule for the initial cluster centroids of Lloyd's algorithm: the first is a data point drawn uniformly at random, each further one a data point drawn with probability proportional to its squared Euclidean distance to the nearest cluster centroid already chosen. The initial cluster centroids are thereby spread across the dataset, so that Lloyd's algorithm rarely starts with several of them in the same cluster. The expected clustering error of the initial cluster centroids is at most 8 (ln k + 2) times the smallest clustering error attainable with k cluster centroids, for every dataset and before a single iteration of Lloyd's algorithm; uniform seeding has no such guarantee. Since Lloyd's algorithm never increases the clustering error, the bound also holds for its output. The seeding changes neither the fixed-point iteration of Lloyd's algorithm nor its fixed points; it selects the starting point and thereby which fixed point is reached. On the patches of a photograph with three clusters, Lloyd's algorithm reaches the best clustering found from 64% of the k-means++ seeds and from 48% of the uniform seeds, and it needs fewer iterations.
terms.description: Lloyd's algorithm for k-means needs k initial cluster centroids before its first iteration, and the clustering it delivers depends on them. Consider a photograph of the Oetscher massif cut into 972 square patches, each a data point with a feature vector x ∈ R2 that holds its average greenness and blueness. Vegetation, mountain and haze, and sky form three clusters of patches, and the best cluster centroids found for k = 3 have the clustering error 0.018. Started from three patches drawn uniformly at random, Lloyd's algorithm ends in 516 of 1000 runs at a different fixed point with clustering error 0.025: two cluster centroids share the vegetation, and the mountain patches are divided between the sky cluster centroid and one of the vegetation cluster centroids. k-means++ is a randomized rule for the initial cluster centroids that spreads them across the dataset. Started from its seeds, Lloyd's algorithm ends at the worse fixed point in 359 of 1000 runs. The clustering error is not a convex function of the cluster centroids. Lloyd's algorithm never increases it and stops at a fixed point, which can be a local minimum rather than a global one; which fixed point is reached depends on the initial cluster centroids. The usual remedy is to run Lloyd's algorithm from several initial choices and keep the run with the smallest clustering error, the simplest initial choice being k data points drawn uniformly at random. Uniform seeding tends to place several initial cluster centroids in the largest cluster: 566 of the 972 patches are vegetation, so all three uniform seeds are vegetation patches with probability 0.20. k-means++ draws the seeds one after the other and lets the data points far from the seeds chosen so far be the likely next ones (Algorithm 1). The first seed w(1) is a data point drawn uniformly at random from the dataset D = x(1), …, x(m). For c = 2, …, k, the seed w(c) is a data point drawn with probability proportional to its squared Euclidean distance to the nearest seed already chosen: it equals the data point x(r), for r = 1, …, m, with probability \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}\left({{\mathbf w}}^{(c)} = {\mathbf x}^{(r)}\right) = \frac{\min_{c' = 1, \ldots, c - 1} \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(c')} \right\rVert_{2}^{2}} {\sum_{r' = 1}^{m} \min_{c' = 1, \ldots, c - 1} \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r')} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(c')} \right\rVert_{2}^{2}} \text{.} \end{equation} A data point that is already a seed has probability 0 under the seeding rule Eq. (1), and a data point twice as far from the seeds as another is twice as likely to be drawn. Given a vegetation patch as the first seed, the second seed is a sky patch with probability 0.74 under the seeding rule Eq. (1) and 0.21 under uniform seeding, the share of sky patches (Fig. 2(a)). It is another vegetation patch with probability 0.06 against 0.58. The seeds are the input of Lloyd's algorithm, and the combination of the seeding with Lloyd's algorithm is what Arthur and Vassilvitskii (2007) named k-means++. Ostrovsky et al. (2006) proposed the same seeding independently. \begin{algorithm}[H] \caption{k-means++ seeding } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex Input: feature vectors x(1), …, x(m), cluster count k \State draw w(1) uniformly at random from x(1), …, x(m) \For{c = 2, …, k} \State draw w(c) from x(1), …, x(m) with the probabilities Eq. (1) \EndFor \Statex Output: initial cluster centroids w(1), …, w(k) for Lloyd's algorithm \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} Fig. 1 shows the effect of the seeds on four data points with feature vectors (-5, 1)ᵀ, (-5, -1)ᵀ, (5, 1)ᵀ, and (5, -1)ᵀ and k = 2. Two seeds on opposite sides lead Lloyd's algorithm to the left/right split with cluster centroids (± 5, 0)ᵀ and clustering error 1, the smallest possible. Two seeds on the same side assign each right-hand data point to the seed at the same height, so the first averaging step delivers the cluster centroids (0, ± 1)ᵀ. These are a fixed point of Lloyd's algorithm, and the top/bottom split they define has clustering error 25. Uniform seeding draws two seeds on the same side with probability 1/3, two of the six pairs. Under k-means++, the second seed is the other data point on the side of the first with probability 4/(4 + 100 + 104) = 1/52 by the seeding rule Eq. (1). The expected clustering error after Lloyd's algorithm is therefore 9 under uniform seeding and 1.46 under k-means++. The seeds alone come with a guarantee. Let E⋆ denote the smallest clustering error that any k cluster centroids achieve on the dataset. The seeds w(1), …, w(k) of Algorithm 1 are RVs, and their expected clustering error satisfies, for every dataset and before a single iteration of Lloyd's algorithm, \begin{equation} \mathbb{E} \Bigg\{ \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \min_{c = 1, \ldots, k} \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(c)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \Bigg\} \leq 8 (\ln k + 2) E^{\star} \text{.} \end{equation} Since Lloyd's algorithm never increases the clustering error, its output started from the seeds satisfies the bound Eq. (2) as well. The logarithm cannot be removed: there are datasets on which the expected clustering error of the seeds is at least a constant multiple of ln k times E⋆. Uniform seeding has no bound of this kind: on the four data points of Fig. 1, the expected clustering error of two uniform seeds is 18, against 2.92 for k-means++ and the bound 8 (ln 2 + 2) · 1 = 21.55 of the guarantee Eq. (2). Moving the two pairs apart, to (± 50, ± 1)ᵀ, keeps E⋆ = 1 but raises the uniform value to 1668, while the k-means++ value is 3.00. On the patches, the mean clustering error of 1000 seed sets is 0.038 for k-means++ and 0.086 for uniform seeding, 2.1 and 4.8 times the best value found; the worst k-means++ seed set has clustering error 0.149, the worst uniform seed set 0.551. The seeding changes nothing about Lloyd's algorithm itself. With the cluster centroids collected in one vector w = (w(1), …, w(k)), Lloyd's algorithm is the fixed-point iteration w(t+1) = F(w(t)) for t = 0, 1, …. The operator F applies one assignment step and one averaging step. Its fixed points are cluster centroids that each equal the mean of the data points assigned to them, and its convergence follows from the monotone decrease of the clustering error. k-means++ only chooses the starting point w(0), and with it the fixed point that is reached and the number of iterations to reach it: on the patches, Lloyd's algorithm needs 10.0 iterations on average from k-means++ seeds and 12.7 from uniform seeds. The seeding itself is not an iterative method but k draws, so no fixed-point view applies to it; its output is a random variable, and the guarantee Eq. (2) is a statement about its expectation. Nor does the seeding exclude the worse fixed point; it makes it rarer (Fig. 2(b)). On the patches, 35.9% of the runs from k-means++ seeds and 51.6% of the runs from uniform seeds end at the clustering error 0.025, so with five restarts, keeping the run with the smallest clustering error, all five miss the best clustering with probability 0.6% against 3.7%. In terms of empirical risk minimization, k-means minimizes the training error of a hypothesis that maps a feature vector to its nearest cluster centroid; the seeding changes neither the hypothesis space nor the loss function, only the optimization method and thereby the local minimum of the training error that it finds. Painting each patch of the photograph in the average color of its cluster is image segmentation, and the two fixed points give two different segmentations. The better one separates sky, mountain, and vegetation; the worse one paints the 204 sky patches and 91 mountain patches in one color and cuts the vegetation in two. k-means++ is the default initialization of k-means in scikit-learn.

terms.name: label
terms.abstract: A label is an attribute of a data point that represents a quantity of interest and that typically requires human expertise to determine. Predicting the label of a data point from its features is the goal of supervised learning. Determining the label of a data point is error-prone and often involves human annotation. The choice of label determines the learning task: whether the task is classification or regression depends on the label space together with the loss function. In self-supervised learning, the label is constructed from the features themselves, so that no manual annotation is required.
terms.description: For a data point that represents a patient, a feature could be the body weight, while the label could be the presence of a disease. A label of a data point z is one of its attributes that represents a higher-level fact, or quantity of interest, and that typically requires human expertise or domain knowledge to determine. Unlike a feature, which can be computed or measured easily, a label is usually harder to obtain. Whether a given attribute serves as a feature or a label is often a design choice that depends on the resources available in a given machine learning application. If an oncologist is readily available, a cancer prognosis can serve as a feature. On the other hand, if no oncologist is available, the cancer prognosis is a label that needs to be predicted from patient features. The notion of a label is made precise by introducing a labeling function h̄: Z → Y. The domain of this function is the data point space Z, the set of all possible data points that can occur in a given machine learning application. Its values lie in the label space Y, the set of all possible values the label of a data point can take on. The function assigns each data point z its label y = h̄(z). The labeling function h̄ acts on the data point z itself, that is, on the whole patient. A trained model (or learned hypothesis) ĥ instead acts on the feature vector x, a fixed list of recorded features such as the patient's body weight and age. The feature vector usually records only some attributes of a data point. The data point space Z contains patients, whereas the feature space X contains only their recorded feature vectors. Two patients with the same feature vector may therefore carry different labels, since they can differ in information that was never recorded as a feature. No hypothesis ĥ that depends on x alone can then deliver perfect predictions. In practice, the true label h̄(z) of a data point is rarely known exactly. Even with full access to the data point, its label must be determined by human judgment or measurement, which is imperfect. The available label is then a noisy version of h̄(z), as in the additive error model of Hastie et al. (2009, Sect. 2.6). For instance, an object category assigned by a human annotator or a diagnosis obtained from a clinician may be wrong, even though the annotator or clinician examines the data point directly. The discrepancy between such an observed label and the true label is called label noise and can degrade training and raise the risk of the learned hypothesis. This source of error differs from the incompleteness of the recorded features discussed above: here the data point is accessible, but its label is determined imperfectly. One way to reduce the effect of label noise is label smoothing, which slightly perturbs the labels of data points used for model training. It is a form of data augmentation that acts as regularization. Label noise also matters for regulation. The EU AI Act requires the training set of a high-risk artificial intelligence system to be, to the best extent possible, free of errors and the system to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy; erroneous labels are one such error. When labels are personal data, the general data protection regulation requires them to be accurate. Beyond how reliably a label is determined, which attribute is taken as the label, i.e., the choice of the labeling function h̄, determines the learning task. For the image of a cow herd in Fig. 1, the label could be a binary indicator of whether the image contains cows (binary classification). Other choices are the number of cows or the average green level (regression), and a masked center pixel predicted from the surrounding pixels (self-supervised learning). Whether a learning task is a classification problem or a regression problem depends not only on the label space Y but also on the loss function. For example, the label space Y = 0,1,2,3,… can be used for a classification method that uses the 0/1 loss as the loss function. The same label space can also be used for a regression method that uses the squared error loss as the loss function. In self-supervised learning, the label is constructed from the features themselves, so no manual annotation is required. A prominent example is large language model training: consider the sentence ``All human beings are born free and equal,'' tokenized as the sequence (``All'', ``human'', ``beings'', ``are'', ``born'', ``free'', ``and'', ``equal''). The label for the subsequence (``All'', ``human'', ``beings'') is the next token ``are,'' the label for (``All'', ``human'', ``beings'', ``are'') is ``born,'' and so on. Taking every prefix of the sequence in turn, a single sentence produces many labeled data points from plain text alone.

terms.name: linear discriminant analysis (LDA)
terms.abstract: Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) learns a linear feature transformation that replaces the feature vector of a data point by one feature, chosen so that the two label values of a binary classification problem are told apart as well as possible. The criterion is the Fisher criterion, the ratio of the between-class to the within-class scatter of the new feature. The direction attaining its maximum is obtained by solving one linear system, so LDA is a closed form rather than an iterative method. The two scatter matrices add up to the sample covariance matrix, the matrix whose quadratic form principal component analysis maximizes, so principal component analysis keeps the direction of largest total sample variance while LDA weighs the two parts against each other. A direction can carry nearly all of the sample variance and nearly none of the between-class part. With more than two label values, LDA delivers at most one direction fewer than there are values. The name also denotes the classifier that reaches the same direction from a multivariate normal distribution per label value with one shared covariance matrix.
terms.description: A weather station at Krems an der Donau (Austria) records the morning minimum and the maximum daytime temperature of each day, and a forecaster wants one number per day that tells the days with precipitation from the dry ones. The two temperatures move together: a cold day is cold in the morning and in the afternoon, a warm day is warm in both. That shared swing is the direction along which the days vary most, and it is the direction principal component analysis keeps. It is also close to useless for the question asked, because it says how warm a day was and not whether it rained. LDA produces one number per day as well, and it chooses the direction from the labels. LDA is a feature learning method for binary classification. Consider a training set D(train) = (x(1), y(1)), …, (x(m), y(m)) of sample size m, with feature vectors x(r) ∈ Rd and labels y(r) ∈ -1,+1. LDA learns a linear feature transformation \phi^{({\mathbf w})}: \mathbb{R}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}: {\mathbf x} \mapsto {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x} \text{,} which replaces the d raw features of a data point by the single new feature φ(w)(x). The labels enter through two matrices. Let μ(c) be the sample mean of the feature vectors carrying the label value c, and pc the fraction of the training set that carries it. The sample mean of all feature vectors is then μ = Σc ∈ -1,+1 pc μ(c). The two matrices are: \begin{equation} \mathbf{S} := \frac{1}{m} \sum_{c \in \{-1,+1\}} \sum_{r : y^{(r)} = c} \big( {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - \widehat{{\boldsymbol \mu}}^{(c)} \big) \big( {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - \widehat{{\boldsymbol \mu}}^{(c)} \big)^{\top} \text{,} \end{equation} \begin{equation} {\mathbf B} := \sum_{c \in \{-1,+1\}} p_{c} \big( \widehat{{\boldsymbol \mu}}^{(c)} - \widehat{\boldsymbol \mu} \big) \big( \widehat{{\boldsymbol \mu}}^{(c)} - \widehat{\boldsymbol \mu} \big)^{\top} \text{.} \end{equation} The within-class scatter matrix S averages the spread of the feature vectors around the sample mean of their own label value, and the between-class scatter matrix B measures how far the two sample means lie apart. Along a direction w, the new feature has within-class sample variance wᵀ S w and between-class sample variance wᵀ B w. The criterion LDA maximizes is the ratio of the two, the Fisher criterion, \begin{equation} \max_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d} : \Vert {{\mathbf w}} \Vert = 1} \frac{{\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf B} {\mathbf w}}{{\mathbf w}^{\top} \mathbf{S} {\mathbf w}} \text{.} \end{equation} A direction scores high when the two sample means are far apart on it and the days of one label value stay close together on it. The ratio of the two sample variances in the Fisher criterion Eq. (3) does not change when w is rescaled, so the constraint costs nothing and what is learned is a direction. For an invertible S, the maximizing direction is that of \begin{equation} \widehat{{\mathbf w}} = \mathbf{S}^{-1} \big( \widehat{{\boldsymbol \mu}}^{(+1)} - \widehat{{\boldsymbol \mu}}^{(-1)} \big) \end{equation}. The LDA direction Eq. (4) is computed in closed form, by solving one linear system: LDA is not an iterative method, so no operator has its output as a fixed point. The name also denotes a classifier, not only the feature transformation. Modeling each label value by a multivariate normal distribution with its own mean and one shared covariance matrix, and estimating these model parameters by maximum likelihood, gives a linear classifier whose decision boundary is a hyperplane with the normal vector Eq. (4). The direction is the same, and the probabilistic model supplies the threshold that the Fisher criterion leaves open. The difference from principal component analysis is one matrix. The within-class scatter matrix Eq. (1) and the between-class scatter matrix Eq. (2) add up to the sample covariance matrix, \begin{equation} \mathbf{S} + {\mathbf B} = \widehat{{\mathbf C}} \text{.} \end{equation} The labels have disappeared from the sum Eq. (5). Principal component analysis maximizes wᵀ Ĉ w over the directions of unit norm, which is the total sample variance of the new feature and says nothing about which part of the sum Eq. (5) it comes from. The Fisher criterion Eq. (3) weighs the two parts against each other instead. A direction can therefore carry nearly all of the total sample variance and nearly none of the between-class part, which is what the opening example describes. That example is measurable. The training set holds the 1461 days of 2020 to 2023 at Krems, each with the morning minimum and the maximum daytime temperature as its two features and the label +1 when precipitation was recorded. The eigenvector of Ĉ belonging to its largest eigenvalue carries 93 percent of the total sample variance and reaches a Fisher criterion of 0.00034, while the LDA direction Eq. (4) reaches 0.103, larger by a factor of 303. The two directions are 89 degrees apart, so what the labels depend on lies almost exactly along the direction principal component analysis ranks last (Fig. 1). The LDA direction weighs the two features with opposite signs, (0.817, -0.577), so its new feature is large on a day whose temperature changed little between morning and afternoon, which is what cloud cover does. The criterion Eq. (3) has one maximum over the directions of the plane and one minimum, and Fig. 2 shows where the two directions sit on it. Thresholding the single LDA feature at the value learned on the 1461 training days classifies 63.7 percent of the 366 days of 2024, kept aside as the test set, correctly. The single principal component analysis feature reaches 60.9 percent and always predicting the majority label value 60.7 percent. Two temperatures of one day say little about rain, and the little they say lies in the direction principal component analysis discards. Three limits come with the closed form Eq. (4). It needs an invertible S, which fails when the training set holds fewer data points than features. Shrinking S towards a multiple of the identity matrix, which is regularization by a penalty, is the usual repair. With more than two label values, the between-class scatter matrix is built from all the sample means and has rank at most one below their number, so LDA delivers at most that many directions, however large d is. And the single new feature is only as good as a linear combination can be: two labels separated by a curved decision boundary overlap on every direction. Where a linear combination is not enough, the answer is to run LDA on an enlarged feature vector that also holds the squares and the products of the raw features. A hyperplane in the feature space of the enlarged feature vector is a curved decision boundary in the feature space of the raw features, and a kernel method is the general form of the step. What LDA buys for the cost of solving one linear system is the factor of 303 in the Fisher criterion Eq. (3). Of the two single features at Krems, the one chosen from the labels gains 3.0 percentage points on predicting the majority label value and the principal component analysis feature gains 0.3.

terms.name: learning rate
terms.abstract: A learning rate is a hyperparameter of an iterative machine learning method that controls the extent of a single update of the current hypothesis. A prime example for a learning rate is the step size of gradient descent. A learning rate that is too small makes little progress within the available number of iterations, and one that is too large can result in divergent iterations. For a fixed number of iterations, the learning rate bounds the effective hypothesis space of a machine learning method, which makes it a means of regularization. The learning rate can be chosen by the validation error of the learned hypothesis.
terms.description: Learning a linear model by gradient descent on the average squared error loss over a training set, as in Fig. 1, is an iterative machine learning method for learning a useful hypothesis h ∈ H. Such a method repeats similar update steps that modify the current hypothesis to obtain an improved one. A learning rate is a parameter of such a method that controls the extent to which the current hypothesis can be modified during a single iteration. The main example of a learning rate η is the step size of gradient descent, \begin{equation} {\mathbf w}^{(t + 1)} = {\mathbf w}^{(t)} - \eta \nabla f({\mathbf w}^{(t)}) \text{.} \end{equation} Here, the objective function f(w) is the empirical risk incurred by a hypothesis h(w) on a training set, and each gradient step moves the model parameters against its gradient ∇ f(w(t)) by a distance proportional to η. Fig. 1 illustrates one gradient step Eq. (1) of gradient descent for a linear model, started from the same hypothesis with three choices of the learning rate. The learning rates are given as multiples of 1/L, with L the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian of f. For the squared error loss, a gradient step lowers f for every learning rate below 2/L; the largest learning rate of Fig. 1 lies above that threshold, and its step raises f. Each iteration of a machine learning method should make large progress towards a useful hypothesis, so the learning rate should not be too small. The step with η = 2.5/L in Fig. 1 shows the other failure: a too large step size of gradient descent makes the gradient steps overshoot a minimum of the objective function. Fig. 2 illustrates both cases. Consider an iterative machine learning method that learns a hypothesis from some underlying hypothesis space H by running a fixed number T of iterations. Varying the learning rate implements regularization by pruning the effective H. For example, each gradient step above Eq. (1) moves the model parameters by η ‖ ∇ f(w(t)) ‖. By the triangle inequality, \begin{equation} \Vert {{\mathbf w}^{(T)} - {\mathbf w}^{(0)}} \Vert \leq \eta \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \Vert {\nabla f({\mathbf w}^{(t)})} \Vert \text{.} \end{equation} Together with T, the learning rate thus determines the region of the parameter space that the method can reach, and thereby the effective hypothesis space: the hypotheses h(w) whose model parameters w lie in that region. Fig. 3 draws the balls around w(0) with the radius Eq. (2) for T = 10 gradient steps of gradient descent solving the empirical risk minimization problem of linear regression, and three learning rates. Reducing the learning rate shrinks the effective hypothesis space that can be reached by the gradient steps. Choosing the learning rate too small or too large can then result in underfitting or overfitting. As a hyperparameter, the learning rate can be chosen by validation: the hypotheses learned with different learning rates are compared by their validation error on a validation set.

terms.name: linear classifier
terms.abstract: A linear classifier is a classifier whose decision regions are separated by hyperplanes. Each linear classifier is obtained by comparing the value of a linear hypothesis map against a threshold. For binary classification, the sign of the value can be used to determine the predicted label, and the absolute value divided by the Euclidean norm of the weight vector is the distance of the data point from the decision boundary. The model parameters of a linear classifier are the weight vector of the underlying hypothesis map and the offset. They are learned by empirical risk minimization with different loss functions: logistic regression uses the logistic loss and the support vector machine the hinge loss. For multi-class classification, a linear classifier is characterized by several linear model hypothesis maps, one per label value, and the resulting decision regions are intersections of halfspaces.
terms.description: An aerial photograph of a wine-growing region is divided into small areas, and each area is to be classified as vineyard or not. Each area is a data point characterized by two features obtained from the photograph (Fig. 1). The label of each area indicates whether the area belongs to a vineyard (y = 1) or not (y = -1). The labeled areas form the training set. A linear classifier separates the two classes by a straight line, its decision boundary, which is fixed by a normal vector, and it classifies a new area by its signed distance from that line. A linear classifier is a classifier whose decision regions are separated by hyperplanes in Rd. For binary classification, with label space Y = -1, +1, each linear classifier can be written as the thresholding rule ŷ = sign(h(x)) with the hypothesis \[ h({\mathbf x}) = {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x} + b \text{.} \] The hypothesis map is parameterized by the weight vector w ∈ Rd 0 and the offset b ∈ R, which is also called the threshold or the bias. A data point with feature vector x is classified as ŷ = 1 if h(x) ≥ 0 and as ŷ = -1 otherwise. The resulting decision boundary is the hyperplane \[ \{ {\mathbf x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}: {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x} + b = 0 \} \text{,} \] with normal vector w. This boundary separates two halfspaces, which are the decision regions R1 = x: h(x) ≥ 0 and R-1 = x: h(x) < 0. The feature vectors on the decision boundary, with h(x) = 0, are assigned to R1 by convention. Consider a feature vector x and any vector x' on the decision boundary, h(x') = 0. Subtracting wᵀ x' + b = 0 from h(x) gives \[ h({\mathbf x}) = {\mathbf w}^{\top} \big( {\mathbf x} - {\mathbf x}' \big) \text{.} \] The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality bounds the right-hand side in magnitude by ‖ w ‖2 ‖ x - x' ‖2. Every vector of the decision boundary is therefore at distance at least |h(x)| / ‖ w ‖2 from x. That distance is attained by the orthogonal projection \[ {\mathbf x}' = {\mathbf x} - \frac{h({\mathbf x})} {\left\lVert {\mathbf w} \right\rVert_{2}^{2}} {\mathbf w} \text{.} \] The distance of x from the decision boundary is thus |h(x)| / ‖ w ‖2. Fig. 1 illustrates the distance to the decision boundary for one data point. The value |h(x)| is a measure of the noise tolerance at the feature vector x. Perturbing x by a vector δ changes the hypothesis value by wᵀ δ, which the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality bounds in magnitude by ‖ w ‖2 ‖ δ ‖2. The sign of h(x), and with it the prediction, is therefore unchanged by every perturbation with ‖ δ ‖2 < |h(x)| / ‖ w ‖2. Multiplying h(x) by the label y gives the margin. A positive margin means that the data point is correctly classified, a negative margin that it is misclassified, and a zero margin that it lies on the decision boundary, where the rule above assigns ŷ = 1. The model parameters (w, b) are learned from a training set D(train) = (x(r), y(r)) r = 1m by empirical risk minimization. Using the 0/1 loss results in an objective function that is piecewise constant, and minimizing it is computationally hard in general. Practical methods replace the 0/1 loss by a convex loss of the margin: logistic regression uses the logistic loss and the support vector machine uses the hinge loss. For a linearly separable training set, the support vector machine with a sufficiently small regularization parameter α, the factor that scales its penalty term, learns the linear classifier whose smallest margin is largest. Both learn the model parameters of a linear classifier by minimizing a convex objective function: gradient descent minimizes the smooth objective function of logistic regression, and subgradient descent the non-smooth objective function of the support vector machine. The squared error loss is a function of the margin as well, since (y - h(x))2 = (1 - y h(x))2 for y ∈ -1, +1, so linear regression, ridge regression, and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator applied to the labels ± 1 also learn linear classifiers. For multi-class problems, with label space Y = 1, …, K and K > 2, a linear classifier uses one linear model hypothesis gc(x) = ( w(c) )ᵀ x + b(c) per label value c ∈ Y and predicts the value with the largest score, ŷ = argmaxc ∈ Y gc(x). The decision region Rc is then an intersection of K - 1 halfspaces and is therefore a convex set. The border between two decision regions Rc and Rc' lies in the hyperplane on which the two scores agree. The resulting partition of the feature space is shown in Fig. 2 for a linear classifier with K = 3 classes. A linear classifier can be generalized to allow for non-linear decision boundaries by using a feature transformation. Applying a feature transformation φ: Rd → Rd' first and a linear classifier to φ(x) afterwards gives a decision boundary that is a hyperplane in Rd' but non-linear in the original feature space. A kernel method constructs such a feature transformation from a kernel, and a deep net uses its first layers as a trainable feature transformation.

terms.name: linear regression
terms.abstract: Linear regression is a regression method that learns a linear hypothesis map for predicting the numeric label of a data point from its features. Its least squares variant chooses a map that minimizes the average squared error loss on a training set. Linear regression is an instance of empirical risk minimization that is obtained by using the linear model and the squared error loss. The optimal model parameters are determined by the normal equations. This system can be solved in closed form or iteratively, for example, by gradient descent. Adding a penalty term to the average squared error loss yields regularized variants such as ridge regression and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator.
terms.description: Linear regression can be used to predict tomorrow's temperature from weather measurements recorded over the last five days, using them as features and tomorrow's temperature as the label. Linear regression methods use a linear model: they learn a linear hypothesis map that delivers a prediction of the numeric label of a data point. The prediction is based solely on the features of the data point, which are fed as input to the learned hypothesis map. Formally, linear regression learns a linear hypothesis map h(w)(x) = wᵀx to predict the numeric label y ∈ R of a data point from its feature vector x = (x1, …, xd)ᵀ ∈ Rd. Here, d denotes the number of features of a data point. The model parameters w are learned from a training set D(train) = ( x(r),y(r) ) r=1m of data points. Appending a constant feature to x lets one entry of w act as an intercept, so wᵀx represents an affine function of the original measurements. Below, x denotes whichever feature vector is fed to the linear hypothesis map, original or augmented, unless stated otherwise. The least squares variant of linear regression measures the quality of a linear hypothesis map by its average loss, the squared error loss, on the training set. As an instance of empirical risk minimization, it learns the model parameters w by solving the optimization problem \[ \min_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big( y^{(r)} - {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \big)^{2} \text{.} \] Fig. 1 illustrates this linear regression problem for a training set with a constant scalar feature x(r)=1 for r=1,…,m. The optimization problem can be written more compactly using the feature matrix X and the label vector y, \[ {\mathbf X} = \big({\mathbf x}^{(1)}, \ldots, {\mathbf x}^{(m)}\big)^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d} \text{,} \qquad {\mathbf y} = \big( y^{(1)}, \ldots, y^{(m)} \big)^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{m} \text{.} \] In terms of X and y, the optimization problem reads \begin{equation} \min_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}} \underbrace{\frac{1}{m} \left\lVert {\mathbf y} - {\mathbf X} {\mathbf w} \right\rVert_{2}^{2}}_{f({\mathbf w})} \text{.} \end{equation} The average squared error loss f(w) is a convex and differentiable function of w. By the zero-gradient condition, a vector ŵ solves the optimization problem Eq. (1) if and only if it satisfies the system of linear equations \begin{equation} {\mathbf X}^{\top}{\mathbf X} \widehat{{\mathbf w}} = {\mathbf X}^{\top} {\mathbf y} \text{.} \end{equation} The normal equations Eq. (2) always have a solution because Xᵀy lies in the column space of Xᵀ, which coincides with the column space of XᵀX. However, the solution of the normal equations Eq. (2) is unique only if the feature matrix X has full column rank. Full column rank requires at least as many data points as features, m ≥ d. When this holds, and the columns of X are linearly independent, the matrix XᵀX is invertible and the normal equations Eq. (2) have the unique closed-form solution \begin{equation} \widehat{{\mathbf w}} = \big({\mathbf X}^{\top}{\mathbf X}\big)^{-1} {\mathbf X}^{\top} {\mathbf y} \text{.} \end{equation} If instead m < d (more features than data points), X cannot have full column rank, XᵀX is singular, the closed form Eq. (3) does not apply, and the optimization problem has infinitely many solutions. All of them incur the same minimal average squared error loss on the training set, but their predictions for data points outside the training set can differ arbitrarily. Choosing among them is therefore a matter of generalization (see overfitting). A unique solution can be selected, for example, by picking the minimum-norm solution X+ y given by the pseudoinverse X+. A common remedy is regularization: adding a penalty term to the average squared error loss. The penalty term can be interpreted as an estimate of how much higher the loss is on data points outside the training set than on it. Different penalty terms yield regularized variants of linear regression. Ridge regression uses the penalty term α ‖ w ‖22 and the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator uses α ‖ w ‖1. The hyperparameter α > 0 sets the weight of the penalty term. Linear regression also has a statistical interpretation. Consider a probabilistic model with a joint probability distribution P(x, y) over the features and the label. Under the squared error loss, the Bayes estimator (i.e., the hypothesis with minimum risk) is the conditional expectation Ey | x. In this statistical interpretation, x denotes the original feature vector. Let the features and the label be jointly Gaussian RVs with zero mean and invertible covariance matrix C(x) = Ex xᵀ. This Bayes estimator is then \[ h^{*}({\mathbf x}) = \big({\mathbf w}^{\star}\big)^{\top}{\mathbf x} \text{, with } {\mathbf w}^{\star} = \big(\mathbf{C}^{({\mathbf x})}\big)^{-1} \mathbf{c}^{({\mathbf x},y)} \text{.} \] Here, c(x,y) = Ex y is the covariance between the features x and the label y. This Bayes estimator is linear in x. Without the zero-mean assumption, it is an affine function of x, which a constant feature absorbs as before. Least-squares linear regression is the empirical risk minimization counterpart of this predictor. It replaces C(x) and c(x,y) with the sample-based estimates (1/m)XᵀX and (1/m)Xᵀy. For invertible XᵀX, this recovers the unique solution ŵ = (XᵀX)-1Xᵀy of the normal equations Eq. (2). Instead of solving the normal equations Eq. (2) directly (via the inverse or pseudoinverse), machine learning methods often solve it by an iterative optimization method, as implemented in widely used machine learning software libraries such as scikit-learn and PyTorch. Starting from initial model parameters w(0), such a method repeatedly applies an update operator F, \[ {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} = \mathcal{F}\big({\mathbf w}^{(t)}\big) \text{, for } t = 0,1,\ldots \text{.} \] The operator F is designed such that the sequence of model parameters w(t) converges to a solution of the normal equations Eq. (2). One such iterative optimization method is gradient descent, which uses the gradient descent step operator \[ \mathcal{F}^{(\eta)}({\mathbf w}) = {\mathbf w} - \eta \nabla f({\mathbf w}) \text{.} \] Here, η > 0 is a step size that must be chosen small enough to ensure convergence. The superscript in F(η) makes the dependence of the operator on η explicit. Inserting the average training error into the general form of the gradient descent step yields the explicit update \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{F}^{(\eta)}({\mathbf w}) &= {\mathbf w} + \frac{2\eta}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big( y^{(r)} - {\mathbf w}^{\top}{\mathbf x}^{(r)} \big) {\mathbf x}^{(r)} &= \Big(\mathbf{I} - \frac{2\eta}{m}{\mathbf X}^{\top}{\mathbf X}\Big){\mathbf w} + \frac{2\eta}{m}{\mathbf X}^{\top}{\mathbf y} \text{.} \end{aligned} \] The fixed points of F(η) are exactly the solutions of the normal equations Eq. (2), since F(η)(ŵ) = ŵ holds if and only if XᵀXŵ = Xᵀy. The update operator is affine, \mathcal{F}^{(\eta)}({\mathbf w}) = {\mathbf M} {\mathbf w} + {\mathbf b} \text{,} with linear part M = I - (2η/m)XᵀX and offset b = (2η/m) Xᵀy. When X has full column rank, so that XᵀX is positive definite, F(η) is a contractive operator with respect to the Euclidean norm for every step size 0 < η < m/λmax. Here, λmax is the largest eigenvalue of XᵀX. The eigenvalues of the linear part M are 1 - (2η/m) λj, with the positive eigenvalues λj of XᵀX. They lie strictly between -1 and 1 exactly for such step sizes. The more general case of any smooth, strongly convex objective function and step sizes η ≤ m/(λmin + λmax) is covered by Nesterov (2004, Thm. 2.1.15), with the smallest eigenvalue λmin of XᵀX. The fixed-point iteration converges to the unique solution ŵ. Moreover, the convergence speed of gradient descent is governed by the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue of XᵀX, that is, by its condition number κ (XᵀX) = λmax/λmin. The gradient descent step above uses the entire training set to compute the gradient. When the data points instead arrive sequentially at time instants t=1,2,…, or the training set is too large to fit in memory, the model parameters can be learned by online gradient descent. At each time step t, it applies a single gradient descent step. That step uses only the arriving data point ( x(t),y(t) ), \[ {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} = {\mathbf w}^{(t)} + 2\eta \big( y^{(t)} - \big({\mathbf w}^{(t)}\big)^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(t)} \big) {\mathbf x}^{(t)} \text{.} \] This is the gradient descent step on the loss function (y(t) - wᵀx(t))2 of the arriving data point alone, rather than on the average squared error loss f(w). It is the least mean squares update. It avoids storing the entire training set, and its per-iteration complexity is independent of the training set size m. The optimality condition Eq. (2) allows one to study the stability of linear regression. Ideally, the learned model parameters are insensitive to limited perturbations of the training set. A perturbed training set yields a feature matrix X̃ = X + Δ X and a label vector ỹ = y + Δ y, with perturbation matrix Δ X and vector Δ y. Substituting them into the normal equations gives the perturbed normal equations \begin{equation} \widetilde{{\mathbf X}}^{\top} \widetilde{{\mathbf X}} \widetilde{{\mathbf w}} = \widetilde{{\mathbf X}}^{\top} \widetilde{{\mathbf y}} \text{.} \end{equation} Matrix perturbation theory quantifies how much w̃ deviates from a solution ŵ of the clean normal equations Eq. (2). For a label-only perturbation, which replaces a single label of the training set with an outlier or another corrupted value, Δ X = 0, and the perturbed and clean normal equations share the coefficient matrix XᵀX. Assume X has full column rank, so XᵀX is invertible and the solution is unique. Subtracting the clean normal equations Eq. (2) from the perturbed normal equations Eq. (4) yields \[ \widetilde{{\mathbf w}} - \widehat{{\mathbf w}} = \big({\mathbf X}^{\top}{\mathbf X}\big)^{-1} {\mathbf X}^{\top} \Delta {\mathbf y} = {{\mathbf X}}^{+} \Delta {\mathbf y} \text{,} \] with the pseudoinverse X+. The effect of perturbing the training set is thereby quantified, \[ \left\lVert \widetilde{{\mathbf w}} - \widehat{{\mathbf w}} \right\rVert_{2} \leq \left\lVert {{\mathbf X}}^{+} \right\rVert_{2} \left\lVert \Delta {\mathbf y} \right\rVert_{2} \text{.} \] When X has full column rank, the pseudoinverse has the norm ‖ X+ ‖2 = 1/√(λmin(XᵀX)) = √(κ (XᵀX))/‖ X ‖2, where κ (XᵀX) = λmax/λmin is the condition number of XᵀX (see pseudoinverse). In the setting of Fig. 1, X = 1 (the all-ones vector), so X+ Δ y = (1/m) Σr=1m Δ y(r). Fig. 2 illustrates such a label-only perturbation of the training set from Fig. 1: a single label perturbation shifts ŵ by one third of it, as Fig. 2 shows. The effect of perturbations can also be studied on the level of a specific optimization method. For example, the update of online gradient descent becomes \[ \begin{aligned} {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} &= {\mathbf w}^{(t)} + 2\eta \big( \widetilde{y}^{(t)} - \big({\mathbf w}^{(t)}\big)^{\top} \widetilde{{\mathbf x}}^{(t)} \big) \widetilde{{\mathbf x}}^{(t)} &= {\mathbf w}^{(t)} + 2\eta \big( y^{(t)} - \big({\mathbf w}^{(t)}\big)^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(t)} \big) {\mathbf x}^{(t)} + {\boldsymbol \varepsilon}^{(t)} \text{.} \end{aligned} \] Here, ε(t) is a perturbation term that depends on the data point perturbation ( Δ x(t),Δ y(t) ) and the current model parameters w(t). A bounded perturbation term moves each iterate by a bounded amount. The perturbed online gradient descent update has no fixed point in general, since a single perturbed data point leaves w̃ unchanged only if w̃ interpolates it. The gradient descent step operator F(η) computed on the perturbed training set instead has as its fixed points exactly the solutions of the perturbed normal equations Eq. (4), by the same computation as for the clean training set. Among them is the perturbed solution w̃, whose displacement from ŵ was computed above.

terms.name: large language model (LLM)
terms.abstract: A large language model (LLM) is an artificial neural network, typically with billions of model parameters, that implements a hypothesis map from a prompt to a response. The training of an LLM often proceeds in stages: pretraining uses self-supervised learning, splitting raw text into overlapping fragments that yield data points without manual annotation, and fine-tuning uses a small dataset of manually curated prompt--response pairs. LLM agents extend LLMs beyond text: a program interprets the response, for example as code to run or as a tool to execute, and can append the result to the next prompt, so the LLM chooses actions that the surrounding program carries out.
terms.description: Consider a chat-based artificial intelligence system such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, or Mistral: a user types a question, the prompt, and receives a reply, the response. The system that produces the reply is an LLM: an artificial neural network, typically a transformer with billions of model parameters, trained to produce output text given input text. Each data point of this learning task is a pair of texts, and the trained LLM implements a hypothesis map from the prompt to the response (Fig. 1). A prompt and a response are sequences of tokens, so the feature space and the label space of this learning task are sets of token sequences. In contrast, a text classifier that maps a document to one of a fixed set of labels is not an LLM: it returns a label, not text. Most LLMs implement ĥ autoregressively: the response is generated one token at a time, each drawn from a probability distribution over the vocabulary that the network computes from the prompt and all tokens generated so far. Alternative constructions exist: masked probabilistic models predict removed tokens and serve text analysis rather than generation, and diffusion language models generate many tokens in parallel. The training of an LLM consists of several stages. One stage typically uses self-supervised learning: a given text is split into overlapping fragments, and each fragment amounts to a data point whose label is one of its tokens and whose features are the remaining tokens. Training sets built from text fragments require no manual annotation; a next-token fragment construction is used by Brown et al. (2020) and a masked-token one by Devlin et al. (2019). Pretraining then minimizes the average loss over the fragments, i.e., it is empirical risk minimization, the aim being a small expected loss on text fragments outside the training set. Another stage is fine-tuning, which uses a small dataset of manually curated prompt--response pairs. The pretrained model parameters are what fine-tuning adapts to each task; an LLM whose model parameters are reused across many learning tasks in this way is a foundation model. LLM inference, i.e., computing the response for a given prompt, is computationally much cheaper than its training. Still, the inference itself is computationally costly and is often implemented using cloud computing services. An LLM can also run locally: open-weight LLMs, whose model parameters are published, can be compressed by quantization. Quantization stores each model parameter in a few bits instead of a 16-bit floating-point number. An LLM with billions of model parameters then runs on a laptop or phone (see edge computing). The output of an LLM by itself is nothing but a sequence of letters that constitute the response. An LLM (or coding) agent interprets the response of an LLM as instructions for computations to be executed. For example, the prompt can instruct the LLM to produce a response that is valid source code in a programming language such as Python, as in the spelled-out data point of Fig. 1. The delivered source code can then be executed, and the result can be appended to the next prompt. The response can likewise be read as a call to an external tool, so that the LLM generates the text that specifies the actions the surrounding program carries out.

terms.name: logistic loss
terms.abstract: The logistic loss is a convex and smooth surrogate for the 0/1 loss in binary classification. Like the hinge loss, it depends on a data point only through its margin, the product of its label and the hypothesis value.
