Unlike the hinge loss it is differentiable everywhere, which suits it to gradient-based optimization methods such as gradient descent. Running empirical risk minimization with a linear model and the logistic loss gives logistic regression. The logistic loss is the negative logarithm of the conditional probability distribution of the label given the feature vector, so minimizing it is maximum likelihood estimation of the model parameters. A probabilistic model in which the features are jointly Gaussian RVs given the label induces exactly that conditional probability distribution, and it is not the only one that does.
terms.description: A spam filter is a binary classification method that learns a hypothesis that maps the features of an email to either spam or no spam. The performance of such a spam filter can be measured by counting the fraction of emails that are misclassified. This fraction is the average 0/1 loss. However, this average loss is flat almost everywhere as a function of the model parameters, so it gives gradient descent no direction to move in. Its shape is the step drawn in Fig. 1: flat on either side of the decision boundary and with no slope anywhere to follow. Practical classification methods therefore use a convex and smooth surrogate for the 0/1 loss with a nonzero slope everywhere. One such surrogate is the logistic loss, defined next. Consider a binary classification problem with feature space X and a real-valued hypothesis h: X → R. The two classes are encoded below by the label y ∈ -1, +1. The logistic loss incurred by h on a data point (x, y) is \begin{equation} L\left(({\mathbf x}, y),h \right) := \ln\big(1 + \exp(-y \cdot h({\mathbf x}))\big) \text{.} \end{equation} Like the hinge loss, the logistic loss Eq. (1) depends on the data point only via the margin y · h(x). Normalizing the logistic loss by ln 2 makes it a convex upper bound on the 0/1 loss, with equality at margin 0 (see Fig. 1). The rescaling is what makes it a bound: at margin 0 the logistic loss itself is ln 2 ≈ 0.69, below the value 1 of the 0/1 loss there. Scaling a surrogate so that it passes through 1 at margin 0 is the usual convention when such loss functions are compared. Unlike the hinge loss, the logistic loss is everywhere differentiable. It is therefore well suited for gradient-based optimization methods such as gradient descent. Empirical risk minimization with a linear model and the logistic loss yields logistic regression. The logistic loss arises naturally from a simple probabilistic model in which the data points are independent and identically distributed RVs with a common joint probability distribution P(x, y) of feature vector and label. Conditioned on the label y, the feature vector x is a Gaussian random variable with mean vector μ(-1) for y = -1 and μ(+1) for y = +1. The conditional covariance matrix is the same for both, and fixed to I. Under that probabilistic model, the posterior probability of y = +1 is the sigmoid function σ(h(x)) with σ(z) = 1/(1 + e-z). The identity holds for the affine hypothesis h(x) = wᵀ x + b with the model parameters \[ {\mathbf w} = {\boldsymbol \mu}^{(+1)} - {\boldsymbol \mu}^{(-1)} \text{,} \quad b = - \tfrac{1}{2} \big( \left\lVert {\boldsymbol \mu}^{(+1)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} - \left\lVert {\boldsymbol \mu}^{(-1)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \big) + \ln \frac{\mathbb{P}\left(y = +1\right)} {\mathbb{P}\left(y = -1\right)} \text{.} \] It is the shared covariance matrix that makes h affine: the terms quadratic in x are the same under both labels and cancel in the ratio, leaving only the inner product with w. When the two labels are equally likely the logarithm vanishes and b is the midpoint term alone. The probability of y = -1 is then σ(-h(x)), because the sigmoid function satisfies σ(-z) = 1 - σ(z). The logistic loss is thus the negative logarithm of the conditional probability of the label given the feature vector, and minimizing the average logistic loss is maximum likelihood estimation of the weight vector w and the offset b of h under that conditional probability distribution. The Gaussian probabilistic model is not the only one that induces this conditional probability distribution. If, given the label, the feature vector has a density of the form h(x) exp( (w(y))ᵀ t(x) - A(w(y)) ), a member of an exponential family whose natural parameter w(y) depends on the label while the base measure h and the sufficient statistic t(x) do not, then the logarithm of the posterior odds of y = +1 is affine in t(x), and the posterior is again the sigmoid function of an affine function. Its weight vector is the difference of the two natural parameters, w = w(+1) - w(-1), which for the Gaussian model above, where t(x) = x and the natural parameter is the mean vector, is the identity w = μ(+1) - μ(-1) displayed there. Conditionally independent binary features, the model behind naive Bayes, are another case. A binary classification problem whose label space is some other pair a, b is covered by an encoding e: a, b → -1, +1 with e(a) = -1 and e(b) = +1. The logistic loss Eq. (1) is then evaluated at the encoded label, \[ L\left(({\mathbf x}, y),h \right) = \ln\big(1 + \exp(-e(y) \cdot h({\mathbf x}))\big) \text{.} \] The label spaces 0, 1 and no spam, spam are both handled this way. Take the label space 0, 1, with e(0) = -1 and e(1) = +1. The loss can then be written out as \[ - y \ln \sigma\big(h({\mathbf x})\big) - (1 - y) \ln \big(1 - \sigma(h({\mathbf x}))\big) \text{,} \] which is the binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss: the cross-entropy between the label and the predicted probability σ(h(x)), with the label 1 leaving the second summand zero and the label 0 the first. Summed over a training set it is the cross-entropy error function of logistic regression. Written that way the loss no longer needs the label to be one of two values. Let ỹ be a soft label, a number between 0 and 1 giving the probability that the data point belongs to the class encoded by 1. Putting ỹ in place of y gives the cross-entropy loss \[ - \tilde{y} \ln \sigma\big(h({\mathbf x})\big) - (1 - \tilde{y}) \ln \big(1 - \sigma(h({\mathbf x}))\big) \text{,} \] which reduces to the previous display at ỹ ∈ 0, 1 and carries over to more than two classes through the softmax function. The value of the logistic loss is harder to interpret than the 0/1 loss, because it depends on the size of the margin and not only on its sign. Each hypothesis compared below is a linear classifier h(x) = wᵀ x + b. Take the three data points of Fig. 2, two of them with label +1 at (1,1) and (2,3) and one with label -1 at (3,1), and the linear classifier ĥ(1)(x) = -0.1 x1 + 0.05 x2 + 0.15. Its margins are 0.1 on each of the three, so it classifies all three correctly and incurs an average logistic loss of about 0.64. Multiplying its model parameters by 50 gives 50 ĥ(1), which leaves the decision boundary exactly where it was and so changes no prediction, yet the average logistic loss falls below 0.01. Two hypotheses far apart in logistic loss can therefore make exactly the same decisions. The logistic loss and the 0/1 loss can also rank two hypotheses in opposite orders. A second linear classifier ĥ(2) has a decision boundary parallel to the first but shifted, which leaves the data point at (3,1) on the wrong side. Its margins are 5, 5, and -0.5, an accuracy of 2/3 against 1 for ĥ(1), and it still attains the smaller average logistic loss, about 0.33 against 0.64. Its two large margins cost almost nothing, so even the single negative margin, which costs about 1, totals less than the three small margins of ĥ(1). Choosing between the two by logistic loss alone selects the less accurate one. Only one reading of the number is safe, the upper bound above: a small logistic loss forces a small 0/1 loss.

terms.name: logistic regression
terms.abstract: Logistic regression learns a linear hypothesis map for binary classification, that is, for data points whose label takes one of two values, y ∈ -1, 1. The predicted label is the sign of the hypothesis value, and its absolute value measures the confidence in the classification. The parameters are learned by empirical risk minimization with the average logistic loss on the training set. Minimizing the average logistic loss is equivalent to maximum likelihood estimation under a simple probabilistic model, under which the sigmoid function of the hypothesis value is the probability of the label 1. When a data point carries this probability as a soft label instead of a class, the logistic loss is replaced by the cross-entropy between soft label and prediction, equivalently their Kullback–Leibler divergence. The resulting objective function is convex and smooth, so variants of gradient descent can be used to minimize it.
terms.description: Consider predicting whether it freezes tomorrow from recent temperature measurements. Records from a weather station turn this question into data: each day is a data point with two numeric features, the maximum temperature of the day and that of the preceding day, collected in the feature vector x = (x1, x2)ᵀ ∈ R2. The label y ∈ -1, 1 is y = 1 if the minimum temperature of the following day stays at or above 0∘C and y = -1 otherwise. Fig. 1 shows such data points. Logistic regression learns, for such a binary classification task, a linear hypothesis map h(x) = wᵀ x + b with weight vector w and offset b. Despite its name, the method solves a classification problem: the regression refers to fitting the real-valued map h, not to a numeric label. The set of feature vectors with h(x) = 0 is the decision boundary between the two classes, and w is its normal vector. The prediction, i.e., the classification, is obtained from the sign of h(x), which makes the learned h a linear classifier whose decision boundary is the hyperplane wᵀ x + b = 0 with normal vector w. The absolute value |h(x)| is used as a measure of the confidence in the classification: it grows with the distance of x from the decision boundary, and a value close to zero indicates low confidence. The parameters w and b of logistic regression are learned via empirical risk minimization. The loss it minimizes is the logistic loss. On a data point (x, y), a hypothesis h incurs \[ L\left(({\mathbf x}, y),h \right) = \ln\big(1 + \exp(-y h({\mathbf x}))\big) \text{.} \] Fig. 2 shows this loss for a data point with y = 1 as a function of h(x). A correct classification with high confidence incurs a small loss. A wrong classification incurs a loss whose size grows with the confidence in the wrong classification. Averaging this loss over the training set D(train) = (x(r), y(r))r=1m of m data points, empirical risk minimization delivers \[ \begin{aligned} (\widehat{{\mathbf w}}, \widehat{b}) &\in \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}, b \in \mathbb{R}} f({\mathbf w}, b), \quad\text{with} f({\mathbf w}, b) &:= \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \ln\Big(1 + \exp\big(-y^{(r)} ({\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} + b)\big)\Big) \text{.} \end{aligned} \] The logistic loss is the negative log-likelihood of the label under a simple probabilistic model for the classification task. In this probabilistic model, given the label y, the feature vector x is a Gaussian random variable whose mean μ(y) depends on the label while its covariance matrix C does not; the two means μ(-1), μ(+1) ∈ Rd are the parameters of the model. When both labels are equally probable a priori, the linear classifier with the smallest risk under this model, the Bayes classifier, assigns x to the label whose mean is nearer, with distances measured by C-1, and its decision boundary is the hyperplane through the midpoint of the two means. Its weight vector is w = C-1(μ(+1) - μ(-1)). Its offset is b = -12 (μ(+1) + μ(-1))ᵀ w, which places the decision boundary at the midpoint, plus the logarithm of the ratio of the two prior probabilities when they differ. Multiplying w and b by the same positive number leaves the decision boundary where it is, but only this pair reproduces the posterior probability below. Under the model, the posterior probability of y = 1 is the sigmoid function σ(wᵀ x + b) with σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e-z). Logistic regression estimates w and b directly, by maximizing the conditional likelihood function of the labels given the feature vectors. This leaves the distribution of the feature vectors unspecified and is a different estimator from maximum likelihood for the means and the covariance matrix of the Gaussian model. Maximizing the conditional likelihood function coincides with minimizing the average logistic loss f. The probabilistic model makes the confidence reading of |h(x)| above precise: σ(h(x)) is the probability that the label of a data point with feature vector x is y = 1, and σ(-h(x)) = 1 - σ(h(x)) the probability of y = -1. A forecast h(x) = 2 thus says that 88 percent of the days with these temperatures are followed by a frost-free day, and a forecast of 0 that half of them are. Whether these numbers can be trusted is the question of calibration. In most applications a data point carries only its label, the class that occurred. The logistic loss is the loss for this case. It is the cross-entropy between the probability mass function concentrated on the observed label and the predicted probability mass function (σ(h(x)), 1 - σ(h(x))). Some data points carry more than a class: a soft label ỹ ∈ [0, 1], the probability of y = 1 itself. It may be the frequency of frost among the recorded days with the same temperatures, the share of several annotators who chose the class, or the output of a larger classifier, as in knowledge distillation. For such a data point the logistic loss is replaced by the cross-entropy between the soft label and the prediction, \[ L\left(({\mathbf x}, \tilde{y}),h \right) = - \tilde{y} \ln \sigma(h({\mathbf x})) - (1 - \tilde{y}) \ln \big(1 - \sigma(h({\mathbf x}))\big) \text{,} \] which for ỹ ∈ 0, 1 is the logistic loss again. Learning then minimizes the average of this loss over the training set, as before. This cross-entropy equals the Kullback–Leibler divergence from the predicted probability mass function to the soft label probability mass function (ỹ, 1 - ỹ) plus the entropy of the soft label probability mass function. Indeed, with q := σ(h(x)), \[ - \tilde{y} \ln q - (1 - \tilde{y}) \ln (1 - q) = \tilde{y} \ln \frac{\tilde{y}}{q} + (1 - \tilde{y}) \ln \frac{1 - \tilde{y}}{1 - q} - \tilde{y} \ln \tilde{y} - (1 - \tilde{y}) \ln (1 - \tilde{y}) \text{,} \] where the first two summands are the Kullback–Leibler divergence and the last two the entropy, which does not depend on h. Minimizing either therefore learns the same h, and the loss on a data point is smallest exactly when q = ỹ, when the confidence of the prediction matches the probability of the class. A hard label can never be matched this way, since σ never reaches 0 or 1. The logistic loss therefore keeps decreasing as |h(x)| grows on a correctly classified data point. With hard or soft labels, the parameters are found by minimizing the average loss f. Unlike linear regression with the squared error loss, the minimization admits no closed-form solution. As in linear regression, however, the objective function f is convex and smooth, so gradient descent applies. The parameters are collected as the pair (w, b), and the gradient descent step reads \[ ({\mathbf w}, b)^{(t+1)} = T\big(({\mathbf w}, b)^{(t)}\big) \text{, with } T({\mathbf w}, b) := ({\mathbf w}, b) - \eta \nabla f({\mathbf w}, b) \text{, for } t = 0,1,\ldots \text{,} \] with learning rate η. The gradient ∇ f of the average logistic loss has the weight part \[ \nabla_{{\mathbf w}} f = -\frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} y^{(r)} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \sigma\big(-y^{(r)} ({\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} + b)\big) \text{,} \] and analogously for b. The pair (w, b) is a fixed point of the operator T precisely when ∇ f(w, b) = 0, which by convexity of f is exactly when (w, b) is a minimizer. The gradient ∇ f is Lipschitz continuous, because the derivative σ'(z) = σ(z)(1 - σ(z)) ≤ 1/4 of the sigmoid function is bounded: the Hessian of f is (1)/(m) Σr=1m s(r) x̃(r) (x̃(r))ᵀ with x̃(r) := (x(r), 1) and s(r) := σ(h(x(r))) σ(-h(x(r))) ∈ (0, 1/4], so a constant is L = (1)/(4 m) Σr=1m ‖ x̃(r) ‖22. For a constant learning rate η < 2/L, every gradient descent step decreases f. For the standard choice η = 1/L and a minimizer (ŵ, b̂) of f, the gap f((w, b)(t)) - min f after t ≥ 1 steps is at most 2 L ‖ (w, b)(0) - (ŵ, b̂) ‖22 / t, whose iteration count starts at 1 where the one above starts at 0. The iterates (w, b)(t) themselves need not converge: on a linearly separable training set the minimum is not attained, and the norm of the iterates grows without bound while the training error tends to zero. Adding the penalty term α ‖ w ‖22, with a positive α, to f removes this singularity. The penalized objective function is strictly convex in (w, b): its second derivative along a direction (u, c) ≠ (0, 0) is \[ \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} s^{(r)} \big({\mathbf u}^{\top}{\mathbf x}^{(r)} + c\big)^{2} + 2\alpha \left\Vert {{\mathbf u}} \right\Vert^{2}_{2} \text{,} \] with the positive s(r) from above, and this vanishes only for u = 0 and c = 0. When both labels occur in the training set, the penalized objective function also grows without bound along every unbounded sequence of pairs (w, b), so it has a unique minimizer. Its gradient is Lipschitz continuous with constant L + 2α. For a learning rate η < 2/(L + 2α) the values of the gradient descent iterates again converge to the minimum, the iterates stay bounded, and they approach the unique minimizer. In practice, plain gradient descent is seldom used to minimize f: the smooth convex objective function is minimized faster by Newton's method, equivalently iteratively reweighted least squares, by the quasi-Newton solver L-BFGS, and by coordinate descent. What these solvers minimize is the average logistic loss, but that is not the only loss with which a linear classifier can be learned. In principle, the squared error loss serves too: with the label values encoded as the real numbers +1 and -1, the squared error (y - (wᵀx + b))2 is well defined. Minimizing the squared error loss, however, has a flaw: it penalizes a prediction wᵀx + b that is large, positive, and correct, while the logistic loss keeps decreasing as this margin grows (Fig. 3). The hinge loss of the support vector machine shares this behavior on a correctly classified data point but stays flat once the margin exceeds one. For more than two label values, logistic regression extends in two ways. A simple reduction trains one binary classification logistic regression per label, each separating that label from the rest, and predicts with the most confident of them; this is one-vs-rest classification. An alternative replaces the sigmoid function by the softmax function, which models the probabilities of all labels jointly as one probability mass function that sums to one; learning its parameters by maximum likelihood yields multinomial logistic regression.

terms.name: loss
terms.abstract: The loss incurred by a hypothesis on a single data point is a scalar that quantifies the error of the hypothesis when evaluated on that data point. The ultimate goal of machine learning methods is to train a model such that the learned hypothesis delivers predictions with minimum loss. A key characteristic of machine learning applications and methods is the accessibility of loss values. In supervised learning, the loss can be evaluated for every hypothesis. In reinforcement learning, the loss is observed only for the action actually taken.
terms.description: In temperature forecasting, the quality of a predicted temperature is naturally measured by how far it deviates from the temperature actually measured the next day. The loss formalizes this idea. The loss incurred by a hypothesis h ∈ H on a single data point is a scalar that quantifies the error of h when evaluated on that data point. A smaller loss value indicates a smaller error. In supervised learning, this error is the discrepancy between the prediction h(x) delivered for the features x and the label y of that data point. Some losses (e.g., the squared error loss) take a continuum of values, while others (e.g., the 0/1 loss) are binary, indicating only whether the prediction matches the label. For the temperature forecast, the loss on a given day can be the squared difference between the predicted temperature (the prediction) and the measured one (the label); see Fig. 1. Loss values are typically nonnegative: many losses are built from a norm or metric and are therefore bounded below by zero. Nonnegativity is not required, however: the logarithmic loss (negative log-likelihood) underlying maximum likelihood methods can take negative values, since a probability density function can exceed one. The loss is also not specific to supervised learning. In unsupervised learning there is no label: a clustering loss measures how far a data point lies from its assigned cluster centroid, and the loss of an autoencoder is the reconstruction error between a data point and its reconstruction. Machine learning methods use observed loss values to construct an objective function for model training. The average loss across a training set of data points is the empirical risk that empirical risk minimization minimizes. Machine learning applications can be categorized by how the loss values are accessible. In supervised learning, the loss can, in principle, be evaluated for every hypothesis in the hypothesis space, since the true label of each training data point is observed. In reinforcement learning, the situation differs. At each time step, the machine learning method (implemented by an agent) selects an action via the currently used hypothesis. The agent then observes the loss incurred by the action actually taken. The loss that would have been incurred by the other actions is not revealed. This limited accessibility of loss values is known as bandit (or partial) feedback. For example, a route-planning system learns the actual travel time only for the route the driver took, not for any alternative route. Similarly, a self-driving car selects a steering direction, and the incurred loss can be measured from onboard sensors such as collision detectors and lane-departure warnings, but only for the trajectory actually driven.

terms.name: matrix
terms.abstract: A matrix is a two-dimensional array of numbers, arranged in rows and columns. The entry Ar,j of a matrix A ∈ Rm × d sits in row r and column j. A prominent example in machine learning is the feature matrix of a dataset, obtained by stacking the feature vectors of m data points row-wise. A matrix represents several distinct mathematical objects. One is a system of linear equations, such as the normal equations of linear regression. Another is a linear map between two vector spaces, after fixing a basis for each. A third is a tabular dataset with one row per data point and one column per feature.
terms.description: Consider a spreadsheet of daily weather records at one station: each row holds a single day, each column one measurement such as temperature or humidity. Such a tabular dataset holds m data points, each described by the same number d of numerical features. The features of the r-th data point are collected in its feature vector x(r) = (x(r)1, …, x(r)d)ᵀ ∈ Rd, one entry per column of the spreadsheet. Stacking these m feature vectors row-wise, so that the r-th row is (x(r))ᵀ, produces an m × d rectangular array of numbers. Its entry in row r and column j is the j-th feature of the r-th data point. This two-dimensional numeric array is referred to as the feature matrix X of the dataset; Fig. 1 carries out the construction on three days of the weather example. More generally, a matrix of size m × d is a two-dimensional array of numbers denoted by {\mathbf A} = \begin{pmatrix} A_{1,1} & A_{1,2} & \dots & A_{1,d} A_{2,1} & A_{2,2} & \dots & A_{2,d} \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots A_{m,1} & A_{m,2} & \dots & A_{m,d} \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}\text{.} Here, Ar,j denotes the matrix entry in the r-th row and the j-th column. A digital image is a matrix of exactly this kind. Recording how green each pixel is turns a 16 × 16 image into a 16 × 16 matrix G whose two indices are pixel positions (Fig. 2). Matrices represent several distinct mathematical objects, including the following: \begin{itemize} \item Systems of linear equations: A matrix collects the coefficients of a system of linear equations, \begin{pmatrix} A_{1,1} & A_{1,2} A_{2,1} & A_{2,2} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x_1 x_2 \end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix} b_1 b_2 \end{pmatrix} \text{, written compactly as } {\mathbf A} {\mathbf x} = {\mathbf b} \text{.} Here, x is the vector of unknowns and b the right-hand side. One important example is the normal equations XᵀX w = Xᵀy, whose solutions are the model parameters that minimize the training error in linear regression, as the derivation following Fig. 3 shows. \item Linear maps: Consider two vector spaces U and V, of dimension d and m, respectively. Fixing a basis u(1), …, u(d) for U and a basis v(1), …, v(m) for V, each matrix A ∈ Rm × d defines a linear map f(A): U → V (see Fig. 3) via f^{({\mathbf A})}\big({\mathbf u}^{(j)}\big) = \sum_{r=1}^{m} A_{r,j} {\mathbf v}^{(r)}\text{.} Taking U = Rd and V = Rm with the standard bases, the image of a vector x under f(A) is the matrix-vector product f(A)(x) = Ax. \item Datasets: As in the opening example, a matrix can represent a dataset with each row holding a single data point and each column a specific feature or label. \end{itemize} Written with the feature matrix, the training error that empirical risk minimization-based linear regression minimizes becomes a succinct algebraic expression. Collecting the labels of the training set in y ∈ Rm, the training error of the hypothesis h(w)(x) := wᵀx is (1/m) \left\lVert {\mathbf X} {\mathbf w} - {\mathbf y} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{,} with gradient (2/m) Xᵀ(X w - y). Each gradient descent step is therefore one multiplication by X followed by one by Xᵀ, and equating the gradient to zero leads back to the normal equations from the first example above. Matrices appear across machine learning beyond the feature matrix. The Jacobian matrix and the Hessian collect the first- and second-order partial derivatives of a multivariate function and are the input of gradient-based training. The covariance matrix records the pairwise covariances of a probability distribution over features. Principal component analysis, singular value decomposition, and a random projection factor or compress the feature matrix to lower its dimension. A kernel method replaces explicit feature vectors by a matrix of pairwise inner products, and a tabular Markov decision process stores its transition probabilities as a matrix. A graph is represented by matrices as well: its adjacency matrix lists which nodes are joined and with what edge weight. The Laplacian matrix assembled from those weights is the matrix whose eigenvectors graph clustering uses to split the nodes into clusters.

terms.name: maximum likelihood
terms.abstract: Maximum likelihood chooses the model parameters of a probabilistic model under which an observed dataset has the largest probability density (or probability mass), that is, the model parameters that maximize the likelihood function. The dataset is modeled as realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs with a common probability density function from a family indexed by the model parameters. Taking the negative logarithm turns the product of pdfs into an average of losses, so maximum likelihood is empirical risk minimization with the negative log-likelihood as loss function; linear regression with Gaussian noise, logistic regression, and the Gaussian mixture model are maximum likelihood under specific probabilistic models. For a normal distribution the estimates are the sample mean and the mean squared deviation; where no closed form exists, gradient descent or the expectation–maximization algorithm computes the estimate as a fixed-point iteration. Under regularity conditions the estimate converges to the true model parameters as the dataset grows and is asymptotically normal with the variance of the Cramér--Rao bound. With a large hypothesis space the estimate overfits, and adding a penalty term to the negative log-likelihood, which is maximum a posteriori estimation, or shrinking the hypothesis space regularizes it.
terms.description: Consider the 366 daily maximum temperatures recorded in 2024 at the weather station Krems an der Donau. Fig. 1(a) shows their histogram. A probabilistic model for these numbers treats each of them as the realization of a random variable whose probability density function belongs to a family indexed by a few model parameters, such as the normal distributions indexed by mean and variance. Maximum likelihood chooses the model parameters under which the recorded year is most probable: among all normal distributions, it picks the one whose probability density function, evaluated at the 366 observed temperatures and multiplied out, is largest. For the days at Krems, this is the normal distribution with mean 17.9∘C and standard deviation 9.2∘C, drawn in Fig. 1(a). Formally, consider a dataset D = z(1), …, z(m) whose data points are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs with a common probability density function (or probability mass function) p(z;w)(·) that depends on the model parameters w ∈ W. The likelihood function of w is the joint probability density function of the dataset, viewed as a function of w with the dataset fixed, \begin{equation} L^{(\mathcal{D})}({\mathbf w}) := \prod_{r=1}^{m} p^{({\mathbf z};{\mathbf w})}\left({\mathbf z}^{(r)}\right) \text{.} \end{equation} The maximum likelihood estimate is a maximizer of the likelihood function Eq. (1). Since the logarithm is increasing, it is also a minimizer of the negative log-likelihood per data point, \begin{equation} \widehat{{\mathbf w}} \in \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathcal{W}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big( - \ln p^{({\mathbf z};{\mathbf w})}\left({\mathbf z}^{(r)}\right) \big) \text{,} \end{equation} in which the product has become a sum. The probability density function is taken with respect to a base measure that does not depend on w; changing it multiplies the likelihood function by a factor independent of w, so the estimate is unchanged. The negative log-likelihood per data point in the estimate Eq. (2) is an average loss. Each value w of the model parameters defines a hypothesis h(w), the probability density function p(z;w)(·), and the loss it incurs on a data point z is L(z,h(w) ) := - ln p(z;w)(z). A data point at which the probability density function is small costs much, one at which it is large costs little. Maximum likelihood is therefore empirical risk minimization over the hypothesis space H = h(w): w ∈ W with the negative log-likelihood as loss function, and the minimum in the estimate Eq. (2) is the training error of the learned hypothesis ĥ = h(ŵ). Several machine learning methods are maximum likelihood under a specific probabilistic model. Linear regression with Gaussian noise of a fixed variance is maximum likelihood with the squared error loss. Logistic regression is maximum likelihood with the logistic loss, the negative log-likelihood of the label under a probabilistic model in which the sigmoid function of a linear function is the probability of the label. Learning a Gaussian mixture model is maximum likelihood with the clustering error of a soft clustering, the negative logarithm of the mixture probability density function. Consider the normal distribution N(μ,σ2) for scalar data points x(1), …, x(m) ∈ R, so that the model parameters are w = (μ, σ2). The negative log-likelihood per data point in the estimate Eq. (2) is then \begin{equation} \frac{1}{2} \ln \big( 2 \pi \sigma^{2} \big) + \frac{1}{2 \sigma^{2} m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big( x^{(r)} - \mu \big)^{2} \text{.} \end{equation} For a fixed σ2, the Gaussian negative log-likelihood Eq. (3) is an increasing affine function of the average squared error, so the mean with the largest likelihood function is the mean with the smallest average squared error. The zero-gradient condition for the Gaussian negative log-likelihood Eq. (3) delivers the closed form \begin{equation} \widehat{\mu} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} x^{(r)} \text{,} \qquad \widehat{\sigma}^{2} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big( x^{(r)} - \widehat{\mu} \big)^{2} \text{,} \end{equation} the sample mean and the mean squared deviation from it. For the days at Krems, μ̂ = 17.9∘C and σ̂2 = 84.6 squared degrees, and no pair of model parameters on a fine grid around them has a larger likelihood function. Fig. 1(b) shows the average log-likelihood as a function of μ with σ2 fixed at σ̂2: a downward parabola with its vertex at the sample mean. The variance estimate in the closed form Eq. (4) is biased. Its expectation is (m - 1) σ2 / m, so it underestimates the variance by the factor (m - 1) / m, which is 0.997 for the 366 days. The closed form is computed in one step, so there is no iteration to read as a fixed-point iteration. For a Gaussian mixture model, for logistic regression, and for most probabilistic models with more than a few model parameters, the zero-gradient condition has no closed-form solution, and the estimate Eq. (2) is computed by an iterative method. Gradient descent on the average negative log-likelihood is a fixed-point iteration w(t+1) = F (w(t)) for t = 0, 1, …, whose fixed points are the points where the gradient of the negative log-likelihood vanishes. For probabilistic models with an unobserved attribute, such as the cluster index of a Gaussian mixture model, the expectation–maximization algorithm is the standard fixed-point iteration: one iteration never decreases the likelihood function, and its fixed points are again points with vanishing gradient. The negative log-likelihood of a Gaussian mixture model is not convex, so either method can stop at a local minimum. How close is ŵ to the model parameters w⋆ of the probability distribution that generated the dataset? This is the generalization question for maximum likelihood, posed under the independent and identically distributed assumption. The expectation of the loss L(z,h(w) ) under p(z;w⋆)(·) is the risk of h(w). It exceeds the risk of h(w⋆) by the Kullback–Leibler divergence from p(z;w⋆)(·) to p(z;w)(·), which is nonnegative. The true model parameters therefore minimize the risk, and maximum likelihood minimizes its empirical counterpart. Consider a single model parameter w ∈ W ⊆ R with a true value w⋆ in the interior of W. Assume that the probability density function is smooth in w, that distinct values of w give distinct probability distributions, and that the support of the probability density function does not depend on w. Then the zero-gradient condition of the log-likelihood has, with probability tending to one as m → ∞, a root ŵ that converges in probability to w⋆. Maximum likelihood is consistent. Any such consistent sequence of roots is asymptotically normal: with the Fisher information I(w) := E ( (∂)/(∂ w) ln p(z;w)(z) )2 of one data point, \begin{equation} \sqrt{m} \big( \widehat{w} - w^{\star} \big) \to \mathcal{N}\left(0,1 / I(w^{\star})\right) \quad \text{in distribution as } m \to \infty \text{,} \end{equation}. The information inequality, also known as the Cramér--Rao bound, states that no unbiased estimator of w that is computed from m data points and satisfies mild regularity conditions has a variance below 1 / (m I(w)). The asymptotic normality Eq. (5) says that the variance of ŵ approaches this bound, which is why maximum likelihood is called asymptotically efficient. For the mean of a normal distribution with known variance σ2, the Fisher information is I(μ) = 1 / σ2, and the sample mean attains the bound exactly: its variance is σ2 / m. For the days at Krems, the standard deviation of μ̂ is therefore σ̂ / √(366) = 0.48∘C. The second derivative of the parabola in Fig. 1(b) is -1 / σ̂2, the Fisher information with a minus sign. The 365 days of 2023 give a second parabola in the same panel, with its vertex at the 2023 mean of 17.4∘C, half a degree from the 2024 estimate. Maximum likelihood chooses the model parameters that are best for the training set, and with a large hypothesis space this is overfitting. Enlarging the hypothesis space for the days at Krems shows the effect. With twelve means, one per calendar month, and one common variance, the average log-likelihood rises from -3.64 to -2.84 on the 366 days of 2024. It also rises, from -3.63 to -3.12, on the 365 days of 2023, which did not enter the estimate: the seasons are real, so the larger hypothesis space helps on new data too. With one mean per calendar day, maximum likelihood places every mean on its observation, and the variance estimate is zero. The likelihood function of 2024 then exceeds every bound as σ → 0, while the average log-likelihood of 2023 under the same model parameters falls below every bound: -22 at σ = 1∘C and -2083 at σ = 0.1∘C. The same singularity is present in a Gaussian mixture model with a component whose mean coincides with one data point and whose variance shrinks to zero. Both remedies are forms of regularization. One shrinks the hypothesis space: fewer means, or a lower bound on the variance. The other adds a penalty term to the negative log-likelihood. This is maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation, \begin{equation} \widehat{{\mathbf w}} \in \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathcal{W}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big( - \ln p^{({\mathbf z};{\mathbf w})}\left({\mathbf z}^{(r)}\right) \big) - \frac{1}{m} \ln p^{({\mathbf w})}\left({\mathbf w}\right) \text{,} \end{equation} in which the penalty term is the negative logarithm of a prior distribution with probability density function p(w)(·) over the model parameters. A minimizer of the penalized negative log-likelihood Eq. (6) maximizes the posterior distribution of w given the dataset. A Gaussian prior distribution on the weight vector of linear regression gives ridge regression. A Gaussian prior distribution N(μ0,τ2) on the mean of a normal distribution with known σ2 moves the estimate from the sample mean μ̂ toward μ0, to (m τ2 μ̂ + σ2 μ0) / (m τ2 + σ2). The penalty term in the MAP estimate Eq. (6) is divided by m, so it vanishes as the dataset grows, and the MAP estimate approaches the maximum likelihood estimate.

terms.name: mean
terms.abstract: The mean of a random vector x is its expectation, the Lebesgue integral of x with respect to its probability distribution. The term also refers to the sample mean, i.e., the average of the data points in a dataset. The two usages are consistent: the sample mean is the mean of the random vector obtained by drawing a data point uniformly from the dataset. Both usages share a further characterization: for a random vector with a finite second moment, the mean is the unique solution of a risk minimization problem under the squared error loss. For the random vector from a dataset, this optimization problem reduces to empirical risk minimization in the simplest regression setting: predicting a numeric label without features, for which the learned hypothesis is the sample mean of the labels.
terms.description: A weather station records the daily maximum temperature for a year. Adding the 365 numbers and dividing by 365 returns a single value that summarizes the whole record. The value is the mean of the recorded numbers, and the same word names the corresponding quantity for a probability distribution. The mean of a random vector x, which takes on values in a Euclidean space Rd, is its expectation Ex. It is the Lebesgue integral of x with respect to its probability distribution P (e.g., see Billingsley (1986, Thm. 16.12, Eq. (21.17)) or Rudin (1987)), i.e., \[ \mathbb{E}\{{\mathbf x}\} = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}} {\mathbf x} \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}({\mathbf x}) \text{.} \] Here, P is the probability distribution that x induces on Rd, so the integral runs over the values x takes rather than over the underlying sample space. No probability density function need exist for the mean to be defined; when one does, denoted by p, it is ∫Rd x p(x) dx. The average of the opening paragraph is the sample mean of a finite dataset of sample size m, D = x(1), …, x(m) ∈ Rd. These two usages are consistent. A dataset defines a discrete random variable x̃(D)=x(I) on the sample space 1, …, m. Here, the index I is chosen uniformly at random, i.e., P(I=r)=1/m for all r=1,…,m. The mean of x̃(D) is precisely the sample mean \[ ({1}/{m}) \sum_{r=1}^{m} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \text{.} \] The probability distribution of x̃(D), which places mass 1/m on each data point, is the empirical distribution of the dataset. Fig. 1 shows both readings for a real-valued random variable and a dataset of seven numbers, with the empirical distribution drawn as its cumulative distribution function. The two readings are further connected by a shared characterization. Consider any random vector with a finite second moment, i.e., E ‖ x ‖22 < ∞. Its mean is the unique solution of the following risk minimization problem: \[ \mathbb{E}\{{\mathbf x}\} = \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{{\mathbf c} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}} \mathbb{E} \big\{\left\lVert {\mathbf x} - {\mathbf c} \right\rVert_{2}^{2}\big \} \text{.} \] The objective function of this problem is a strictly convex function of the optimization variable c ∈ Rd. For the discrete random variable that a dataset defines, the risk is the average squared error over the dataset, so this risk-minimization characterization applies directly to the simplest machine learning problem, predicting a numeric label without any features. Consider a training set D(train) = y(1), …, y(m) that consists of labels y(r) ∈ R only. A hypothesis is then a single number h ∈ R that serves as the prediction for every data point. Empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss searches over candidate hypotheses h' ∈ R and learns \[ \widehat{h} = \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{h' \in \mathbb{R}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big(y^{(r)} - h'\big)^{2} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} y^{(r)} \text{,} \] i.e., the learned hypothesis is the sample mean of the labels (see Fig. 2). This setting coincides with linear regression for data points that carry the constant scalar feature x = 1. Squaring the deviations also makes the mean sensitive to outliers. Moving one of m data points by an amount δ shifts the sample mean by δ / m, so a single corrupted data point can move the mean arbitrarily far. The trimmed mean that discards a fraction γ at each end stays bounded however far at most γ m data points are moved, since the moved data points end up among the discarded ones. The median stays bounded however far fewer than half of the m data points are moved, since the unmoved data points are then a majority and the two middle values of the sorted list lie between the smallest and the largest of them. Both are therefore preferred when features or labels may be unreliable (pythondemos/mean.py).

terms.name: membership inference attack
terms.abstract: A membership inference attack aims at determining whether a particular data point was used to train a machine learning model. The basic idea is that a learned hypothesis delivers more accurate predictions for data points that are similar to those used for training. An adversary queries the learned hypothesis and compares the loss of its prediction against a threshold. Mitigation strategies include regularization, which makes a machine learning method generalize beyond the training set: the learned hypothesis then behaves similarly for data points in the training set and for those outside it, which makes it harder for an adversary to guess the data points of the training set.
terms.description: A volunteer observer at Krems an der Donau reports the minimum and the maximum temperature for selected days. Each day is one data point z = ( x,y ), whose feature x is that day's minimum temperature and whose label y is that day's maximum temperature, and the reported days form the training set D(train). A company learns a hypothesis ĥ from D(train) to predict the maximum temperature of a day from its minimum. The company publishes ĥ, so anyone can query it at any minimum temperature. The GeoSphere weather station at Krems publishes the minimum and the maximum temperature of every day. Anyone with both can try to determine whether the report of a specific day was used for training. Since the reports come from one person, a yes tells that the observer was around Krems an der Donau on that day. Whether the observer was at Krems on a specific day is personal data, even though a temperature is not. This scenario is an example of a membership inference attack: a privacy attack where an adversary tries to determine whether a particular data point was used to train a machine learning model. For a specific day, the adversary reads that day's x and y from the station's record, computes the prediction ĥ(x), and compares it against y. A loss (y - ĥ(x))2 below a threshold indicates that the report of that day was used for training. Fig. 1 carries this attack out on the 31 days of October 2024 at Krems. One threshold labels all 31 days correctly: the loss is zero on every day the observer reported and never below 0.23 ∘C2 on any other day. The days it declares reported form two blocks of consecutive days, 7 to 13 and 20 to 26 October, which is when the observer was there. The hypothesis behind the figure is obtained by linear regression on the features x'j = cos((j-1) π u) for j = 1, …, d, with u the minimum temperature x rescaled to [0,1] over the month; for d = 14, one feature per reported day, least squares reproduces every reported day exactly. The number d sets the effective dimension of the underlying hypothesis space and so how far the machine learning method can overfit. Fig. 2 plots how much the attack gains from that. Fix a threshold τ on the loss. Of the 14 days the observer reported, the fraction incurring a loss of at most τ is the detection rate. Of the 17 days of the month the observer did not report, the fraction incurring a loss of at most τ is the false-alarm rate. The advantage of the attack is the largest value of the detection rate minus the false-alarm rate over all thresholds. An adversary that answers yes on every day, or no on every day, leaves the two rates equal and the advantage zero, which is why the advantage measures what the attack gains over guessing, and a threshold that separates the two groups makes it one. The threshold is chosen with the answer already known, so the advantage is the most any threshold could achieve rather than what an adversary would obtain. With two features, it is 0.10, and it reaches one once d reaches the number of reported days. The attack succeeds only to the extent that the learned hypothesis incurs a smaller loss inside the training set than outside it, which is what the generalization gap measures. Under a probabilistic model for how the data points and their membership of the training set arise, the success of such an attack is tied to that gap. The quantity is the same difference as above, with the two rates replaced by probabilities under that model. For a loss bounded by a constant B, an adversary that answers yes with a probability decreasing in the loss has a difference that grows in proportion to the expected generalization gap. Regularization controls that gap: for a convex loss that is Lipschitz with constant L, adding the penalty term α ‖ w ‖22 bounds the expected generalization gap by 2L2/(α m). Fig. 3 repeats the attack against the same features learned with that penalty term, and the picture no longer tells the two groups apart. Regularization therefore serves two purposes, accurate predictions outside the training set and a defence against a membership inference attack. For the observer at Krems, that is the difference between a published hypothesis that reveals nothing about them and one that reveals the days they were in town.

terms.name: machine learning pipeline (ML pipeline)
terms.abstract: A machine learning pipeline (ML pipeline) is the composition of the functions by which a machine learning system turns raw data into predictions. Its stages typically are data preprocessing, feature learning or hand-designed feature extraction, model training, and inference on new data points. Each stage is a function whose output is the input of the next, so the whole pipeline is one map from raw data to predictions and is applied identically during training and in deployment. Fitting stages such as feature scaling inside the pipeline, on the training set only, prevents data leakage from the validation set or test set.
terms.description: The weather station Krems an der Donau reports eight measurements of each day to the GeoSphere Austria data hub. Turning that stream into a forecast of tomorrow's minimum temperature takes four steps: cleaning the records, extracting features, training a model, and computing the prediction. The sequence of such steps is an ML pipeline: a composition (i.e., concatenation) of several functions within a machine learning system. The individual functions include data preprocessing, feature learning or hand-designed feature extraction, model training, and inference on new data points. By combining them, a machine learning system turns raw data into predictions (Fig. 1). Written as math, a pipeline of three stages is the concatenation \begin{equation} h = h^{(3)} \circ h^{(2)} \circ h^{(1)} \text{,} \end{equation} with h(1) the feature map, h(2) the hypothesis applied to the resulting features, and h(3) the post-processing of its output. Of the four steps above, cleaning and feature extraction form h(1), the trained hypothesis is h(2) (training is how it is chosen, not a factor of h), and the post-processing of the prediction is h(3). Each factor is chosen from a hypothesis space of its own, h(j) ∈ H(j) for j = 1, 2, 3. The concatenations Eq. (1) are themselves a hypothesis space, \[ \mathcal{H} = \bigl\{ h^{(3)} \circ h^{(2)} \circ h^{(1)} : h^{(j)} \in \mathcal{H}^{(j)}, j = 1, 2, 3 \bigr\} \text{,} \] so training the pipeline is empirical risk minimization over H rather than over any one stage. Each stage is a function whose output is the input of the next, so the pipeline is one map from raw data to predictions, applied identically during training and in deployment. Stages with their own parameters, such as feature scaling, are fitted on the training set only. Fitting them on all available data leaks information from the validation set or the test set into the learned hypothesis, so that the validation error or the error on the test set underestimates the risk (see data leakage). Software libraries therefore bundle the stages into one object that is trained as a whole on the training set. The pipeline is the computational part of a machine learning system, which additionally comprises data storage, deployment, and monitoring.

terms.name: model
terms.abstract: In machine learning, the word model is used in different ways. Formally, a model is a hypothesis space H: the set of candidate hypothesis maps from which a machine learning method picks (or learns) one. In applied machine learning literature and in software libraries, the word model also refers to the trained predictor, i.e., to the learned hypothesis returned by a machine learning algorithm; the EU AI Act uses this sense in the compound term general-purpose AI model. A different type of mathematical model is a probabilistic model, which specifies a family of probability distributions that characterize a data generation process.
terms.description: Consider the problem of predicting tomorrow's maximum daytime temperature from today's morning temperature. Machine learning methods learn a hypothesis map ĥ that maps today's morning temperature, the feature, to an accurate prediction of tomorrow's maximum temperature, the label. This learned hypothesis is chosen from a (typically large) set of candidate hypothesis maps, i.e., a hypothesis space H. The hypothesis space underlying a machine learning method is its model: the set of candidate hypothesis maps, chosen in advance, from which the method picks one. For example, linear regression and logistic regression use the linear model as their hypothesis space. A decision tree method uses a hypothesis space that consists of hypothesis maps generated by a flow chart. Large language model systems use a hypothesis space consisting of non-linear maps represented by an artificial neural network. Model training refers to the process of finding a hypothesis in the hypothesis space that yields accurate predictions. A trained (or fitted) model is a learned hypothesis ĥ = A(D(train)), the output of the map A by which the machine learning method turns a training set D(train) into a hypothesis. In applied machine learning literature and in software libraries, the word model typically refers to a trained model, i.e., to a specific hypothesis map ĥ. The EU AI Act uses the word model in the same sense (i.e., a learned hypothesis) in the compound term general-purpose AI model. A different type of mathematical model is a probabilistic model, which specifies a family of probability distributions. Each such probability distribution defines a data generator: data points are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs with the given probability distribution. Fig. 1 illustrates these three uses of the word model: the hypothesis space, the trained model, and the probabilistic model.

terms.name: model selection
terms.abstract: Model selection chooses among several alternative machine learning methods by comparing their validation errors. Each machine learning method learns a hypothesis via a training method such as empirical risk minimization. A basic design choice of a machine learning method is the underlying hypothesis space, or model. The effective hypothesis space of a machine learning method can also depend on hyperparameters of the optimization algorithms used to solve empirical risk minimization. The training error of a machine learning method cannot be the criterion for model selection, as it always chooses the largest of nested hypothesis spaces. The validation error can be obtained from the average loss on a single validation set, or via k-fold cross-validation. The selected hypothesis must be assessed on data points that have been used neither for learning any individual hypothesis nor for choosing among them using a validation set.
terms.description: Fig. 1 depicts data points collected by a weather station at Krems an der Donau (Austria). Each data point represents a day, with the minimum daytime temperature as feature x and the maximum daytime temperature as label y. The figure also shows two hypothesis maps, each learned by a machine learning method via empirical risk minimization from a training set D(train) that consists of six data points. One is a linear hypothesis ĥ(1), learned over a linear model. The other is a degree-five polynomial ĥ(2), learned over the larger hypothesis space of polynomial regression. The polynomial ĥ(2) delivers perfect predictions on every data point of D(train), so its training error, the average squared error loss over D(train), is zero. In contrast, the linear hypothesis ĥ(1) results in a training error of 0.47. The training error therefore ranks the polynomial first, and following that ranking would pick the candidate that predicts worst on a data point outside D(train). Model selection ranks the two instead by the validation error Ev which is computed on a validation set D(val) that is disjoint from the training set D(train). On the fourteen validation data points shown in Fig. 1, the average squared error loss is 2065 for the polynomial and 7.06 for the linear hypothesis, so model selection picks the linear hypothesis ĥ(1). The validation error of the selected hypothesis is biased downward, since the selection favored the candidate with the smallest one. In the setting of Fig. 1, consider twelve new days generated like the data points of that figure, six of them used for selecting among six candidate degrees and six for evaluating the selected candidate. Over 2000 random draws of these twelve days, the smallest average squared error loss on the six days used for selecting is 4.70 on average, while the average squared error loss of the selected candidate on the six other days is 9.61. A test set D(test), disjoint from both D(train) and D(val), is therefore set aside before model selection. Its average loss estimates the risk of the selected hypothesis. The six data points of the test set in Fig. 1 are used for this purpose, and the average squared error loss on them is the estimate its caption reports. Model selection chooses among several alternative machine learning methods by comparing their validation errors. Consider C candidates ĥ(c), c = 1, …, C, obtained from empirical risk minimization with a different effective hypothesis space, or model, H(c). The effective hypothesis space can also depend on hyperparameters of the optimization algorithm used to solve empirical risk minimization. Examples of such hyperparameters include the learning rate of a gradient-based method, the strength α of a regularization penalty term, and the depth of a decision tree. The training error of the learned hypotheses ĥ(c) is not useful as a criterion for choosing between them. As a case in point, for nested candidates H(1) ⊆ ⊆ H(C), it always chooses the largest hypothesis space: each hypothesis space contains the previous one, so the smallest training error over H(c+1) is at most the smallest training error over H(c). This holds even when the largest hypothesis space results in overfitting, as the degree-five polynomial of Fig. 1 does. Fig. 2 shows this for the polynomial hypothesis spaces H(c) of degree c = 0, …, 5 on the training set and validation set of Fig. 1: the training error falls with the degree, while the validation error has its minimum at degree one. Model selection therefore follows model training, e.g., via empirical risk minimization, and model validation, e.g., via k-fold cross-validation. Algorithm 1 summarizes a complete machine learning workflow, consisting of model training, model validation, and model selection. \begin{algorithm}[H] \caption{Model selection } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex Input: training set D(train), validation set D(val), a loss function L for training and a loss function Lv for validation, candidate hypothesis spaces H(c) with their hyperparameter settings, for c = 1, …, C \For{c = 1, …, C} \State learn a hypothesis via empirical risk minimization, \[ \widehat{h}^{(c)} = \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{h \in \mathcal{H}^{(c)}} \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}^{(\rm train)}|} \sum_{{\mathbf z} \in \mathcal{D}^{(\rm train)}} L\left({\mathbf z},h \right) \] \State compute the validation error Ev(ĥ(c)) via the average Lv of ĥ(c) on D(val) \EndFor \State c⋆ := argminc = 1, …, C Ev(ĥ(c)), a tie going to the smaller hypothesis space \Statex Output: the selected hypothesis ĥ(c⋆) \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} The two loss functions used in Algorithm 1 for training and validation can be different: empirical risk minimization needs one that its optimization method can handle, while validation can use the loss function that is relevant for the application, such as the 0/1 loss. When the training set is too small to spare a validation set, steps 2 and 3 of Algorithm 1 can be replaced by k-fold cross-validation. The final hypothesis ĥ(c⋆) delivered by Algorithm 1 must be evaluated on a test set. A test set consists of data points used neither to learn any individual ĥ(c) nor to choose between them. Under an independent and identically distributed assumption for the data generation, the average loss on D(test) is an unbiased estimator of the risk of ĥ(c⋆). The data points of D(test) are independent of how ĥ(c⋆) was obtained, so each loss has the risk as its expectation, and so has their average. If D(train) and D(val) are modeled as RVs, so is ĥ(c⋆), and with it the risk being estimated: the expectation is then conditional on ĥ(c⋆), over D(test) alone.

terms.name: mean squared error (MSE)
terms.abstract: The mean squared error (MSE) of a hypothesis is the average of its squared error loss, the squared difference between the label of a data point and the prediction for it. The average is either an expectation under a probabilistic model for the data, the independent and identically distributed assumption, which makes the MSE the risk under the squared error loss, or the average over the data points of a dataset, which makes it the empirical risk, the training error or the validation error. The two readings coincide for the empirical distribution of the dataset, which assigns the same probability to each of its data points. When the independent and identically distributed assumption holds, the average over a dataset estimates the expectation and improves with the sample size. The root MSE, its square root, is measured in the unit of the label.
terms.description: Consider a hypothesis h that predicts the maximum daytime temperature of a day at Krems an der Donau (Austria) from its morning minimum. A weather service that uses it reports one number for how far the predictions are off on average, and the MSE is that number: the average of the squared error loss, the squared difference between the label of a data point and the prediction for it. The word average has two readings here, and the MSE is defined in both. The first reading needs a probabilistic model for how the data come about. The independent and identically distributed assumption is the simplest one: it treats the daily weather measurements as realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs, so that each day, a data point with feature vector x and label y, is an independent draw from one probability distribution P that does not change from day to day. Under this model, the MSE of h is the expectation of its squared error loss, \begin{equation} \bar{L} \big( h \big) := \mathbb{E} \big\{ \big(y - h({\mathbf x})\big)^{2} \big\} \text{,} \end{equation} which is the risk of h under the squared error loss. The expectation Eq. (1) is taken over the probability distribution P of the data point, which the independent and identically distributed assumption postulates but does not specify: in a machine learning application, P is unknown. What can be computed is the MSE on a dataset D = (x(1), y(1)), …, (x(m), y(m)) of sample size m, the average of the squared error loss over its data points, \begin{equation} \widehat{L}\big(h|\mathcal{D}\big) := \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big(y^{(r)} - h({\mathbf x}^{(r)})\big)^{2} \text{,} \end{equation} which is the empirical risk of h on D under the squared error loss. It is the training error when D is the training set and the validation error when D is the validation set. For a linear model learned by least squares on the 365 days of 2023 at Krems, the MSE Eq. (2) is 21.1 on those days and 19.2 on the 366 days of 2024, in squared degrees. Its square root, the root MSE of 4.4 degrees, has the unit of the label. The two definitions are one definition applied to two probability distributions. The empirical distribution P(D) of the dataset D assigns the probability 1/m to each of its data points. The expectation of the squared error loss under P(D) is therefore a sum of m terms with weight 1/m each, \begin{equation} \mathbb{E}_{({\mathbf x}, y) \sim \mathbb{P}^{(\mathcal{D})}} \big\{ \big(y - h({\mathbf x})\big)^{2} \big\} = \widehat{L}\big(h|\mathcal{D}\big) \text{.} \end{equation} By the identity Eq. (3), the average Eq. (2) is the expectation Eq. (1) with the empirical distribution of D in place of P. Every statement about the MSE as an expectation then holds for the average with P(D) in that role, such as its split into the variance of the label around its conditional mean and the squared deviation of h from that mean. Fig. 1(a) draws the empirical distribution of the squared errors of the 366 days of 2024. Its mean is the MSE 19.2, while its median is 9.1 and two thirds of the days have a loss below the MSE: a few far-off days weigh heavily in a squared average. Conversely, when the data points of D are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs with probability distribution P, the average Eq. (2) is an estimate of the expectation Eq. (1) that improves with the sample size m by the law of large numbers. Fig. 1(b) shows this for the days of 2024 in a random order: over the first 30 days, the average lies between 12.6 and 26.7 in nine of ten orders, over the first 180 days between 17.0 and 21.3. How far the training error can lie from the risk is the subject of generalization. Squaring the deviation is what makes a far-off day weigh heavily, and that is the MSE's main limitation. A single mismeasured label enters the average in proportion to the square of its deviation, so it can dominate the number reported for a whole year. The mean absolute error, the average of the absolute error loss instead of the squared error loss, weighs each day in proportion to its deviation alone. The difference shows in what each average asks a constant prediction to be: the MSE is smallest at the mean of the labels, the mean absolute error at their median. On the 366 days of 2024 at Krems, these are 17.91 and 17.60 degrees. A decimal point in the wrong place moves one of those 366 labels by 5, 10, 20, or 50 degrees. The mean then moves by 0.014, 0.027, 0.055, and 0.137 degrees, the error divided by the sample size. The median moves by at most 0.1 degrees, the step to the neighboring label, however large the error becomes. The MSE is therefore the wrong summary for a record with outliers or a long-tailed error distribution, and the mean absolute error or a least absolute deviation regression is the usual answer. What the MSE buys in return is the mean it points at: it is differentiable everywhere, which is what lets least squares have a closed form. See also: squared error loss, risk, empirical risk, training error, validation error, empirical distribution, expectation, probabilistic model, independent and identically distributed assumption, law of large numbers, generalization, mean absolute error, absolute error loss, outlier, linear regression, loss.

terms.name: multivariate normal distribution
terms.abstract: The multivariate normal distribution is the probability distribution of a Gaussian random vector in Rd, determined by a mean vector and a covariance matrix. Its probability density function is proportional to the exponential of a negative quadratic form in the inverse of the covariance matrix, so its level sets are ellipsoids centered at the mean vector with axes along the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix and half-axes proportional to the square roots of its eigenvalues. The family is closed under affine maps and under conditioning, and among all random vectors with a given covariance matrix the Gaussian one has the largest differential entropy. The maximum likelihood estimates of the two parameters from a dataset are the sample mean and the sample covariance matrix, in closed form. When the covariance matrix is singular, no probability density function exists and the random vector is confined to an affine subspace. In machine learning, the multivariate normal distribution is the component of a Gaussian mixture model, the probabilistic model for the noise behind the squared error loss, and the class-conditional probability distribution behind linear discriminant analysis.
terms.description: Consider the 366 days of 2024 at Krems an der Donau, each a data point with a feature vector x ∈ R2 that holds the morning minimum and the maximum daytime temperature of the day. A warm morning usually comes with a warm afternoon, so the days form an elongated cloud around their mean vector (Fig. 1(a)). The multivariate normal distribution is a probabilistic model for such feature vectors that describes this picture with two parameters. A mean vector μ ∈ Rd locates the center of the cloud, and a covariance matrix C ∈ Rd × d fixes its spread along every direction. The multivariate normal distribution is denoted by N(μ,C), and a random vector with this probability distribution is a Gaussian random vector. For an invertible covariance matrix C, which is then positive definite, the multivariate normal distribution has the probability density function \begin{equation} \mathcal{N}\left({\mathbf x} ; {\boldsymbol \mu}, {\mathbf C}\right) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2} \sqrt{\det({\mathbf C})}} \exp\Big( -\frac{1}{2} ({\mathbf x} - {\boldsymbol \mu})^{\top} {\mathbf C}^{-1} ({\mathbf x} - {\boldsymbol \mu}) \Big) \quad \text{for } {\mathbf x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d} \text{.} \end{equation} The exponent is a quadratic form in the inverse C-1, the precision matrix. The probability density function Eq. (1) is largest at μ and falls off with the value of this quadratic form; the factor in front of the exponential, which contains the determinant of C, makes it integrate to one. A random vector with the probability density function Eq. (1) has mean vector μ and covariance matrix C, which is what the two symbols are named for. For d = 1, the probability density function Eq. (1) is the probability density function of a Gaussian random variable with mean μ and variance σ2. A level set of the probability density function Eq. (1) is the set of feature vectors at which the quadratic form takes a given value c2, for some positive number c, \begin{equation} \big\{ {\mathbf x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}: ({\mathbf x} - {\boldsymbol \mu})^{\top} {\mathbf C}^{-1} ({\mathbf x} - {\boldsymbol \mu}) = c^{2} \big\} \text{.} \end{equation} The covariance matrix is a symmetric matrix and admits a spectral decomposition C = V Λ Vᵀ, with orthonormal eigenvectors as the columns of V and the eigenvalues λ1 ≥ … ≥ λd > 0 on the diagonal of Λ. The level set Eq. (2) is then an ellipsoid centered at μ, whose axes point along the eigenvectors and whose half-axis along the jth eigenvector has length c √(λj). On it, the probability density function equals exp(-c2/2) times its value at μ. Fig. 1(a) shows the level sets at c = 1 and c = 2 for the days at Krems. The eigenvalues are 130.9 and 7.9 squared degrees Celsius, so the level set at c = 2 has half-axes of 22.9 and 5.6 degrees Celsius. Its major axis points along the eigenvector (0.61, 0.79)ᵀ, the direction in which minimum and maximum rise together. The probability that a Gaussian random vector lies inside the level set Eq. (2) depends on c and d only: the quadratic form of a Gaussian random vector has a chi-squared distribution with d degrees of freedom. For d = 2, this probability is 1 - exp(-c2/2), that is, 39.3 percent at c = 1, 86.5 percent at c = 2, and 98.9 percent at c = 3. Fig. 1(b) compares these values with the fraction of the days at Krems inside each level set: 32.2, 89.6, and 100 percent. The days are spread along the major axis more evenly than a Gaussian random vector would be, since the seasons move a day along this axis. Only 59.8 percent of them lie within one standard deviation of the mean along it, against 68.3 percent for a Gaussian random vector, and no day lies beyond c = 2.6. A Gaussian mixture model with two components, one for the cold and one for the warm days, describes such a cloud better than a single multivariate normal distribution. Every Gaussian random vector is an affine function of a standard normal random vector z ∈ Rℓ, whose entries are independent and identically distributed standard Gaussian RVs: x = A z + μ with a matrix A ∈ Rd × ℓ, and then C = A Aᵀ. This construction also covers a singular covariance matrix, for which the probability density function Eq. (1) is undefined. The random vector is then confined to an affine subspace, the column space of A shifted by μ, which has volume zero in Rd, so no probability density function on Rd exists. A singular covariance matrix arises whenever one feature is an affine function of the others. Appending the daily temperature range, the maximum minus the minimum, as a third feature of a day at Krems yields a covariance matrix of rank two, and the three-dimensional feature vectors lie on a plane. Two properties make the multivariate normal distribution the default probabilistic model for numeric feature vectors. First, the family is closed under affine maps: for every matrix B ∈ Rq × d and every vector c ∈ Rq, \begin{equation} {\mathbf x} \sim \mathcal{N}\left({\boldsymbol \mu},{\mathbf C}\right) \quad \text{implies} \quad {\mathbf B} {\mathbf x} + {\mathbf c} \sim \mathcal{N}\left({\mathbf B} {\boldsymbol \mu} + {\mathbf c},{\mathbf B} {\mathbf C} {\mathbf B}^{\top}\right) \text{.} \end{equation} Choosing B to select some entries of x shows that every marginal distribution of a multivariate normal distribution is again a multivariate normal distribution. For the days at Krems, the daily temperature range is the affine map Eq. (3) with B = (-1, 1) and c = 0; under the probabilistic model, it has mean 10.7 and variance B C Bᵀ = 19.7 squared degrees Celsius. The family is also closed under conditioning. Given the values of some entries of x, the conditional probability distribution of the remaining entries is a multivariate normal distribution. Its mean is an affine function of the given values, and its covariance matrix does not depend on them. Consider d = 2, and write C1,1, C1,2, and C2,2 for the entries of the covariance matrix and μ1 and μ2 for the entries of the mean vector. The conditional probability distribution of x2, given x1, is then \begin{equation} \mathcal{N}\left(\mu_{2} + \frac{C_{1,2}}{C_{1,1}} (x_{1} - \mu_{1}),C_{2,2} - \frac{C_{1,2}^{2}}{C_{1,1}}\right) \text{.} \end{equation} The conditional mean in the conditional probability distribution Eq. (4) is the prediction of the maximum temperature from the minimum with the smallest risk under the squared error loss, and it is linear in x1 (see linear regression). For the days at Krems, it is the line learned by least squares, with slope 1.10, and the conditional standard deviation is 4.4 degrees Celsius. Second, among all random vectors with the covariance matrix C, the Gaussian random vector has the largest differential entropy. When only the mean vector and the covariance matrix are known, the multivariate normal distribution is therefore the least restrictive probabilistic model. The parameters μ and C are learned from a dataset D = x(1), …, x(m) by maximum likelihood. Under the independent and identically distributed assumption, the data points are realizations of independent and identically distributed random vectors x(r) ~ N(μ,C). The loss incurred by a data point is the negative logarithm of the probability density function Eq. (1) at its feature vector, and the average of this loss over D is the empirical risk of the pair (μ, C). Minimizing it is empirical risk minimization over the hypothesis space of all pdfs Eq. (1). The minimizer is available in closed form, so no iterative algorithm is needed: \begin{equation} \widehat{\boldsymbol \mu} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \quad \text{and} \quad \widehat{{\mathbf C}} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big( {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - \widehat{\boldsymbol \mu} \big) \big( {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - \widehat{\boldsymbol \mu} \big)^{\top} \text{.} \end{equation} The estimates Eq. (5) are the sample mean and the sample covariance matrix of D with the divisor m; under the independent and identically distributed assumption, the sample covariance matrix is smaller than C on average by the factor (m - 1)/m. For the days at Krems, the estimates Eq. (5) are μ = (7.2, 17.9)ᵀ and a sample covariance matrix with variances 54.2 and 84.6 and covariance 59.6, all in squared degrees Celsius; the correlation coefficient of minimum and maximum temperature is 0.88. The sample covariance matrix has rank at most m - 1, so with fewer than d + 1 data points it is singular and the probability density function Eq. (1) with these estimates is undefined. A common remedy replaces Ĉ by a weighted average of it and a positive multiple of the identity matrix. This shrinks the hypothesis space to covariance matrices whose eigenvalues are bounded away from zero, one of the routes that regularization distinguishes. The multivariate normal distribution is used throughout machine learning. A Gaussian mixture model draws the feature vector of a data point from one of k multivariate normal distributions, so each cluster of a soft clustering is a mean vector with a covariance matrix, drawn as an ellipse. In regression, the label of a data point is modeled as the value of a hypothesis plus a Gaussian random variable with mean zero. Maximum likelihood estimation of the hypothesis is then empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss, so linear regression by least squares assumes this probabilistic model for the label. In classification, modeling the feature vector of each class by a multivariate normal distribution and comparing the logarithms of the pdfs Eq. (1) yields a classifier with the smallest risk under that probabilistic model. With one covariance matrix shared by all classes, the quadratic terms cancel and the decision boundary is a hyperplane, which is linear discriminant analysis. With a covariance matrix per class, the decision boundary is a quadratic surface.

terms.name: norm
terms.abstract: A norm on a vector space is a function that assigns each vector a nonnegative number, its length. A norm is definite and homogeneous, and it satisfies the triangle inequality. Every norm defines a metric via the norm of the difference of two vectors, and every inner product induces a norm, but not every norm is induced by one. The ℓp-norms on Rd include the ℓ1-norm, the Euclidean norm, and the ℓ∞-norm; among them only the Euclidean norm is induced by an inner product. In machine learning, norms are used to construct loss functions and regularizers.
terms.description: The hourly temperature recordings of one day at a weather station form the feature vector x ∈ Rd of that day, with one entry per hour. Many machine learning methods use a measure for the size of such a vector or for the distance between two of them. A norm provides both: it assigns each vector a length, and the length of the difference of two vectors is their distance. Formally, a norm ‖ · ‖ on a vector space V over the field R is a function ‖ · ‖: V → R+ that satisfies the conditions below. These conditions hold for all vectors u, v ∈ V and all scalars β ∈ R, with |β| the absolute value of β: \begin{itemize} \item Definiteness: ‖ u ‖ = 0 u = 0; \item Homogeneity: ‖ β u ‖ = |β| · ‖ u ‖; \item Triangle inequality: ‖ u + v ‖ ≤ ‖ u ‖ + ‖ v ‖. \end{itemize} The same conditions define a norm on a vector space over the field of complex numbers C, with β ∈ C and |β| its modulus. A function that satisfies homogeneity and the triangle inequality but assigns the value zero to some nonzero vector is a seminorm, not a norm: on R2, the map u = (u1, u2)ᵀ ↦ |u1|, which keeps only the first entry, is a seminorm that is zero on (0,1)ᵀ. Every norm defines a metric by d(u,v) := ‖ u - v ‖, making ( V,d(·,·) ) a metric space. Some norms are induced by an inner product ⟨ ·, · ⟩, a function of two vectors that is symmetric, linear in each argument, and positive-definite (on Rd, ⟨ u, v ⟩ = uᵀ v).
