On an inner product space, ‖ u ‖ := √(⟨ u, u ⟩) is a norm, and the norm of a Hilbert space is of this form. An induced norm satisfies the parallelogram identity ‖ u + v ‖2 + ‖ u - v ‖2 = 2 ‖ u ‖2 + 2 ‖ v ‖2, obtained by expanding ⟨ u ± v, u ± v ⟩. For the vector space V = Rd of feature vectors x = (x1, …, xd)ᵀ and a number p ≥ 1, the ℓp-norm of x is defined as ‖ x ‖p = ( Σj=1d |xj|p )1/p. It satisfies the triangle inequality by Minkowski's inequality and is therefore a norm. Its instances include the ℓ1-norm ‖ x ‖1 = Σj=1d |xj| and the ℓ2-norm ‖ x ‖2 = ( Σj=1d xj2 )1/2 (the Euclidean norm); the limit p → ∞ yields the ℓ∞-norm ‖ x ‖∞ = maxj = 1, …, d |xj|. The ℓ2-norm is induced by the inner product uᵀ v, and it is the only ℓp-norm induced by an inner product. For u = (1, 0)ᵀ and v = (0, 1)ᵀ in R2, both u + v and u - v have ℓp-norm 21/p, so the left-hand side of the parallelogram identity is 2 · 22/p while the right-hand side is 4, and the two agree only for p = 2. The left-hand side equals 8 for the ℓ1-norm and 2 for the ℓ∞-norm. The three norms differ in which vectors they count as having unit length. The unit sphere S(1) := u ∈ R2: ‖ u ‖ = 1 of a norm on R2 contains those vectors, and Fig. 1 shows it for the ℓ1-, the ℓ2-, and the ℓ∞-norm. Machine learning methods use norms to construct loss functions and regularizers. In linear regression, the label vector y ∈ Rm stacks the labels of a training set of size m and the feature matrix X ∈ Rm × d stacks its feature vectors. The average squared error loss of a linear hypothesis with model parameters w is then the scaled squared Euclidean norm (1/m) ‖ y - X w ‖22 of the residual y - X w. Ridge regression adds the penalty term α ‖ w ‖22 to this training error, with a hyperparameter α > 0, while the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator adds α ‖ w ‖1. The choice of the norm determines the learned hypothesis by empirical risk minimization. Consider the two optimization problems \[ \min_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}} \left\lVert {\mathbf y} - {\mathbf X} {\mathbf w} \right\rVert_{2} \quad \text{ and } \quad \min_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}} \left\lVert {\mathbf y} - {\mathbf X} {\mathbf w} \right\rVert_{1} \text{,} \] which differ only in the norm of the residual. Squaring the ℓ2-norm does not change the set of minimizers, so minimizing the ℓ2-norm of the residual is equivalent to minimizing the average squared error loss. The distinction between induced and other norms matters here. An induced norm defines angles and orthogonal projections, and the squared ℓ2-norm of the residual is a quadratic function of w, so the least squares problem has a closed-form solution, obtained from the normal equations. The ℓ2-norm is therefore the norm of the loss function of linear regression. Minimizing the ℓ1-norm of the residual is a linear program, which has no closed-form solution and is solved iteratively, as is the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator problem with its ℓ1-norm penalty. Fig. 2 shows a training set of four data points, one of which is an outlier, and two linear hypotheses h(x) = w x learned from it. Minimizing the squared ℓ2-norm of the residual gives the slope ŵ = 46/30. This solution is moved toward the outlier because squaring makes the largest residual the main part of the training error. Minimizing the ℓ1-norm yields ŵ = 1, which predicts the three remaining data points exactly and leaves a single large residual at the outlier. The hypothesis learned with the ℓ1-norm is robust to the outlier in the sense that one unusual data point barely moves it, while the one learned by minimizing the squared ℓ2-norm is not (see robustness). Both slopes are learned from the training set; which of the two hypotheses has the smaller risk on data points outside it depends on whether outliers are present there as well.

terms.name: online learning
terms.abstract: Online learning refers to machine learning methods that continuously update the model parameters as new data points arrive over time. This contrasts with offline methods such as linear regression, which solve empirical risk minimization once over a fixed training set. The updates are based on some form of feedback: examples are an entire loss function determined by the new data point, or a reward signal. Online gradient descent uses an entire loss function as feedback; bandit and reinforcement learning methods replace the unavailable gradient by an estimate from the feedback. The figure of merit is the regret: the accumulated loss minus that of fixed model parameters chosen in hindsight. A method is successful if its regret per round vanishes as the number of rounds grows.
terms.description: A weather station reports one temperature reading per hour, and a forecast for the next hour must be issued before that reading arrives. An offline method such as linear regression first collects readings into a training set and trains a model on it once. It then forecasts with the learned model parameters, which stay fixed from then on: while it collects, it issues no forecast, and after it has trained, it no longer learns. An online learning method instead adapts its model parameters every time a new reading arrives; Fig. 1 shows both on three days of readings. Online learning proceeds in rounds: in each round, a machine learning method commits to model parameters, receives a feedback signal from its environment, and updates. The updates are based on some form of feedback. For the weather station, the feedback is the new data point itself. Any new temperature reading allows to compute the squared error loss against the current model parameters, and the loss can be evaluated for any possible choice of the model parameters. The feedback is therefore an entire loss function w ↦ L(z(t),w ). Online gradient descent is the online learning method for feedback by an entire loss function: it updates the model parameters by a gradient step on that loss function. Some online learning applications provide only a single loss or reward value as feedback, called bandit feedback in contrast to full information (Fig. 2). For example, a clinic that gives one of several treatments observes the outcome of that treatment alone, which is a multiarmed bandit. A thermostat whose heating decision changes the temperature it faces in the next hour receives a reward together with a new state, which is reinforcement learning. Consider model parameters w from a convex closed set W ⊆ Rd, the parameter space, and rounds at consecutive time instants t = 1, 2, …. At time t, the environment fixes a function f(t): W → R, and the current model parameters w(t) incur the loss f(t)(w(t)). Only then is a feedback signal r(t) about f(t) revealed. The feedback signal is written r(t), in the reward notation of reinforcement learning, although with full information it is a data point and with bandit feedback a loss value. Three kinds of feedback occur. With full information, the data point z(t) is revealed, and it determines f(t)(w) = L(z(t),w ) for every w ∈ W. On the temperature stream, the data point z(t) = (x(t), y(t)) has as features, collected in the feature vector x(t), the readings of the previous hours, and as label the reading of hour t. Its loss function f(t) is the squared error loss of the forecast h(w)(x(t)). With bandit feedback, only the value f(t)(w(t)) is revealed. In a multiarmed bandit with A actions, the model parameters w(t) ∈ ΔA-1 form the probability mass function from which the action a(t) is drawn. The environment fixes a loss vector ℓ(t) ∈ [0,1]A, whose entry ℓ(t)a is the loss of action a in round t, so the expected loss of the draw is f(t)(w) = ⟨ ℓ(t), w ⟩. The clinic observes the single entry ℓ(t)a(t), the loss of the action drawn, and no other entry. With reinforcement learning feedback, the immediate reward r(s(t), a(t)) of the action taken and the next state s(t+1) of a Markov decision process are revealed. The loss f(t)(w) is the negative expected reward of the policy with model parameters w in the state s(t). That state depends on the actions of the earlier rounds, so the environment's losses depend on the method's own past. The method then updates the model parameters using the feedback, \begin{equation} {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} := \mathcal{F}^{(t)}\big({\mathbf w}^{(t)}, r^{(t)}\big) \text{,} \end{equation} with an update operator F(t) specific to the method, the counterpart of the operator F of a fixed-point iteration (Fig. 3). The time index is also the iteration index: one update for any newly arriving data point. This contrasts with batch learning, which solves empirical risk minimization once over a fixed training set and then uses the learned hypothesis. The update Eq. (1) at time t applies an operator that depends on the feedback signal r(t). By contrast, gradient descent applies a fixed gradient step operator in every time step. An online learning method is therefore not a fixed-point iteration of one fixed operator. Instead, it concatenates operators that vary over the time steps. Unlike stochastic gradient descent, which uses one data point per step to approximate the gradient of one fixed objective function, an online learning method faces a different loss function in every round. With full information, online gradient descent uses the gradient g(t) := ∇ f(t)(w(t)) in a projected gradient step. Online mirror descent replaces the Euclidean distance of the projection by a Bregman divergence, e.g., the Kullback–Leibler divergence on the probability simplex, which gives the Hedge update of the probability mass function over the actions. Follow-The-Regularized-Leader commits, in every round, to a minimizer of the accumulated loss of all rounds so far plus a regularizer. With bandit feedback, the gradient of f(t) is not available, since only one entry of ℓ(t) is observed. Exp3 forms an unbiased estimate of ℓ(t) by dividing the observed entry by the probability of the drawn action, and applies the online mirror descent update to the estimate. With reinforcement learning feedback, Q-learning changes one entry of a table of action values, the entry of the state visited and the action taken. The entry moves by a fixed fraction of the difference between its target, the reward received plus the discounted largest value of the next state, and its current value. The update is a stochastic step of the Bellman operator, a contraction with factor γ in the supremum norm: taking the largest value over the actions cannot increase the largest difference between two value estimates, and the discount factor scales that difference by γ. Q-learning, unlike online gradient descent, does have a fixed point interpretation. Policy gradient methods instead estimate the gradient of the expected reward from the rewards collected along the visited states. The figure of merit of an online learning method is not the decrease of an objective function along the iterates, which measures the progress of gradient descent: online learning has no fixed objective function. The loss function f(t) of round t is evaluated once, around w(t), and the next round brings a different loss function. Instead, an online learning method is evaluated by its regret. The regret is the excessive accumulated loss compared to that of a fixed choice w ∈ W of the model parameters. This fixed choice w is kept for all rounds t = 1, …, T and can be chosen after all losses are known. After T rounds, the regret relative to w ∈ W is \[ \mathrm{Regret}_{T}({\mathbf w}) := \sum_{t=1}^{T} f^{(t)}({\mathbf w}^{(t)}) - \sum_{t=1}^{T} f^{(t)}({\mathbf w}) \text{.} \] In a multiarmed bandit, the fixed w of interest is the probability mass function concentrated on one action. The regret is then measured against the best single action in hindsight; in reinforcement learning, against the best fixed policy. No assumption is made on how the losses are generated: the regret is defined for every sequence f(1), f(2), …, even one chosen by an opponent who has seen w(t). An online learning method is successful if its regret per round, RegretT(w)/T, vanishes as T grows for every w ∈ W. Regret bounds. The rate at which the regret per round vanishes depends on the feedback. With full information and convex losses whose gradients have norm at most G on a parameter space of diameter D, online gradient descent with the learning rate η(t) = D/(G√(t)) has RegretT(w) ≤ 32 DG√(T). When the number of rounds T is known in advance, the constant learning rate η = D/(G√(T)) has RegretT(w) ≤ DG√(T) by the same argument. No online algorithm can guarantee a regret below a constant times DG√(T) for every sequence: for each algorithm there is a sequence of losses on which its regret is at least that. With bandit feedback over A actions and losses in [0,1], the expected regret of Exp3 is at most 2√((e-1) T A ln A): observing one entry of ℓ(t) instead of all of them costs the factor √(A). With reinforcement learning feedback in a Markov decision process with S states and A actions, the UCRL2 method has, with probability at least 1 - δ for any δ ∈ (0, 1) and any T > 1, regret at most a constant times S √(A T ln(T/δ)), the constant depending on how many steps it takes to reach any state from any other. In each case the regret per round vanishes as T grows. Fig. 4 shows the regret per round of online gradient descent and of follow-the-leader, the Follow-The-Regularized-Leader method without its regularizer, which commits in every round to a minimizer of the accumulated loss so far, on a year of hourly temperature readings. For linear regression with the squared error loss, that minimizer is computed by the recursive least-squares update, which carries the least-squares solution from time t - 1 to time t in closed form by the Sherman--Morrison formula for the inverse of a matrix after a rank-one change. Online gradient descent is run afresh for every number of rounds T shown, with the constant learning rate η = D/(G√(T)) on a parameter space of diameter D = 4 and with G the largest gradient norm encountered, so the bound DG/√(T) on its regret per round holds at every T shown. Fig. 5 turns the same stream into a multiarmed bandit. The actions are five fixed forecasters, each a rule that needs no training. They forecast the previous reading, the reading of the same hour one day earlier, the mean of the three previous readings, the linear extrapolation of the two previous readings, and the mean of all readings of the year so far. The loss of an hour is the scaled absolute error of the forecaster used, and the regret is measured against the best single forecaster in hindsight. With full information, all five errors are observed after each hour and Hedge updates the probability mass function; with bandit feedback, only the error of the forecaster used is observed and Exp3 updates the probability mass function from its estimate of the loss vector. The regret of Hedge after T rounds is at most √(2 T ln A) for losses in [0,1], a weakening of the bound ln A / η + η T / 8 of Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi (2006, Thm. 2.2) at the learning rate η = √(2 ln A / T); for Exp3, the bound on the expected regret stated for bandit feedback applies with A = 5. Both regrets per round vanish, and the regret of Exp3 stays larger than that of Hedge, the increase in regret caused by bandit feedback.

terms.name: outlier
terms.abstract: An outlier is a data point that deviates so far from the rest of a dataset that it is suspected of having come about in a different way. Being an outlier is a judgment made against a stated probabilistic model or dataset and not a property a data point carries on its own: a day is typical for the year and extreme for its month, and two features can deviate jointly while neither deviates alone. Two sources have to be told apart, a probability distribution with a heavy tail and a mistaken or coded reading, because only the second calls for a repair of the data. With more than two features, dimensionality reduction to two learned features makes the deviating data points visible in a scatterplot, which is why it is a common first step. How much an outlier changes the learned hypothesis depends on the loss function: the squared error loss weighs a residual by its square and is far more sensitive to a mismeasured label than the absolute error loss. Least absolute deviation regression, Huber regression, and robust principal component analysis are built on that difference, and a contamination model states how outliers enter the sample.
terms.description: A weather station at Krems an der Donau (Austria) recorded 81.7 millimeters of rain on 14 September 2024, more than forty times the average daily amount of 1.9 millimeters over that year. The same archive writes a day with no precipitation not as 0 but as -1 millimeters, a code that 199 of the 366 days carry. The two numbers are the largest and the smallest value of their column, and only one of them marks a day worth a second look. An outlier is a data point that deviates so far from the rest of a dataset that it is suspected of having come about in a different way. What counts as far is set by a stated notion of ordinary behavior, so being an outlier is a judgment made against a probabilistic model or a dataset and never a property the data point carries on its own. Changing the probabilistic model changes the answer while the data stay as they are. Consider the screen that calls a day unusual when its maximum daytime temperature lies more than two standard deviations from the mean. Under a probabilistic model in which that temperature is a Gaussian random variable with mean 17.9 and standard deviation 9.2 degrees, estimated from all 366 days of 2024, the screen flags three days. With the mean and the standard deviation estimated from the day's calendar month alone, it flags ten days, and only 31 December under both. On 17 May the maximum reached 16.6 degrees, which lies 0.14 standard deviations below the mean of the year and 2.60 below the mean of May: typical for the year, extreme for its month. The coldest maximum of 2024, the -3.6 degrees of 9 January, runs the other way, 2.34 standard deviations below the mean of the year and 1.94 below the mean of January, an ordinary cold winter day. Fig. 1 draws both screens over the year. A deviation can also sit in the relation between two features rather than in either one. Each day is a data point with the feature vector x = (x1, x2)ᵀ holding its morning minimum and its maximum daytime temperature. Over 2024, the two have correlation 0.88, so a probabilistic model that gives x a multivariate normal distribution with mean μ and covariance matrix C expects them to rise and fall together. It scores a day by the squared Mahalanobis distance \begin{equation} \big({\mathbf x} - {\boldsymbol \mu}\big)^{\top} {\mathbf C}^{-1} \big({\mathbf x} - {\boldsymbol \mu}\big) \text{,} \end{equation} of which the probability density function of the multivariate normal distribution is a decreasing function, so a large squared distance is a small likelihood function. The largest value of the squared Mahalanobis distance Eq. (1) over 2024, 6.7, belongs to 29 March: a morning minimum of 0.5 and a maximum of 21.2 degrees, 0.91 and 0.36 standard deviations from the respective means. Neither feature is remarkable on its own, and jointly they are the daily range of 20.7 degrees that is the fourth largest of the year. The weather station records eight measurements on each day, and eight numbers are more than a scatterplot can show. Dimensionality reduction to two features is therefore a common first step in finding outliers, because two numbers per data point are what a scatterplot does show. Principal component analysis learns a linear map from the eight standardized measurements of a day to d' = 2 features, which keep 63.6 percent of their variance; the first is a temperature direction and the second a wetness direction. In those two features, the deviating days are visible without any screen at all, as Fig. 2 shows. Evaluating the squared Mahalanobis distance Eq. (1) in those two features rather than in the two temperatures puts 14 September at 50.7, against 22.9 for the second farthest day and below 8.3 for each of the remaining 363 days. The code -1 of the opening is of a different kind. The archive writes a day with no precipitation as -1 millimeters and a day with less than 0.1 millimeters as 0, so -1 is not an amount at all. A plausibility screen that rejects a negative rainfall flags 199 of the 366 days, 54 percent of the year, and not one of those days is unusual; read as an amount, the code lowers the annual total from 712.0 to 513.0 millimeters. The deviation is from the assumption about the coding of the tabular data, not from the process that produced the data, and the repair is to recode the column rather than to drop the days. The two kinds have to be told apart before anything is removed, since an outlier arises either from a probability distribution with a heavy tail or from a mistaken reading, and a coding convention is neither. Removal is not the only response. How much an outlier changes the learned hypothesis depends on the loss function: the squared error loss weighs a residual by its square and the absolute error loss weighs it linearly, which makes least squares far more sensitive to a grossly mismeasured label than empirical risk minimization with the absolute error loss. On the Krems record, least squares over the linear model learns a hypothesis that predicts the maximum daytime temperature of a day from its morning minimum. The maximum of 21 January 2024 is 3.5 degrees. A misplaced decimal point that records it as 35 moves the predictions of that hypothesis by up to 0.56 degrees and leaves the one learned with the absolute error loss where it was. Raising the same label to 1000 moves the least squares predictions by 17.7 degrees, and the other hypothesis still does not move at all. How far a single replaced data point can move the learned hypothesis is a question about the stability of the method. Least absolute deviation regression, Huber regression with the Huber loss, and robust principal component analysis for a feature matrix are built on this difference, and a contamination model states how outliers enter the sample and what can then be guaranteed.

terms.name: overfitting
terms.abstract: Overfitting is the failure mode of a machine learning method that fits its training set too closely: the learned hypothesis incurs a small empirical risk on the training set but a large risk, i.e., the expected loss on data points drawn from the underlying probability distribution. Consequently, the learned hypothesis has a large generalization gap. Validation detects overfitting by comparing the training error with the validation error obtained on a validation set. Overfitting typically arises when the hypothesis space is too large for the number of data points in the training set; the Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension and the Rademacher complexity measure that size. Regularization counteracts overfitting by pruning the model, adding a penalty term to the empirical risk, or augmenting the training set.
terms.description: An image classifier that memorizes every photograph in its training set but misclassifies images outside its training set is overfitting. In general, consider a machine learning method that uses empirical risk minimization to learn a hypothesis ĥ ∈ H with minimum empirical risk L̂(ĥ|D(train)) on a given training set D(train). The method overfits D(train) if the empirical risk L̂(ĥ|D(train)) is small while the risk L̄ ( ĥ ), i.e., the expected loss on data points drawn, independently of D(train), from the underlying probability distribution, is large. Consequently, an overfitting machine learning method learns a hypothesis with a large generalization gap. A large generalization gap alone does not imply overfitting. Consider a linear model fitted to a small training set whose labels are noisy and depend nonlinearly on the features. It can incur a large training error and a still larger risk, so the generalization gap is large while the training error is not small. That example is underfitting, the opposite failure: a hypothesis space holding no hypothesis that represents the relation between the features and the label of a data point leaves both quantities large. Fig. 1 shows why a small training error is on its own no evidence against overfitting. Three data points lie on a straight line. None of the three curves is drawn by hand: each is a hypothesis ĥ delivered by empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss on those same three data points. What separates them is the hypothesis space that empirical risk minimization searched, and the three are nested, H(1) ⊂ H(2) ⊂ H(3): H(1) is the constants h(x) = b, H(2) the linear model, whose hypotheses are h(x) = w x + b, and H(3) all continuous functions on R. On H(1), empirical risk minimization has a unique solution: the constant whose value is the average of the three labels. That constant meets the middle data point and misses the other two, and no member of H(1) does better. The hypothesis space is too small here, and the method underfits. On H(2), the solution is unique as well and attains a training error of zero; the hypothesis space matches the relation between feature and label, and the method neither underfits nor overfits. On H(3), every continuous function through the three data points attains a training error of zero, and there are infinitely many of them: empirical risk minimization has infinitely many solutions there, and Fig. 1 draws one of them. The training error cannot separate that curve from the solution on H(2), the linear hypothesis that passes through the three data points, and it cannot choose among the solutions on H(3) either. The two hypotheses agree on the training set but differ at feature values between those of the training data points, and the risk differs between them, since data points drawn from the probability distribution also fall in that region. The hypothesis space is too large here, and the method overfits. Validation detects overfitting, because the generalization gap that defines it can be estimated: a machine learning method that overfits delivers a small training error but a large validation error on a validation set held out from training. Fig. 2 illustrates overfitting for polynomial regression. Each data point carries a single feature x and a noisy label y, drawn from a probability distribution described in the caption. Polynomials of degree p = 0, …, 9 are fitted, using empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss, to training sets of m = 5, 10, and 20 data points; each panel of Fig. 2 shows the training error and the validation error for one size. The training error decreases with increasing degree in every panel: the polynomial of degree 9 has 10 model parameters and interpolates the m = 10 data points; for m = 5, every degree from 4 on interpolates; for m = 20, no degree shown interpolates. The validation error is obtained on a shared validation set of 100 data points. It is in contrast smallest at a moderate degree and grows by several orders of magnitude for larger degrees. The high-degree polynomials overfit the training set, and the gap between validation error and training error estimates their large generalization gap. Comparing the three training set sizes shows that the smaller the training set, the lower the degree at which the validation error departs from the training error. For m = 5, the validation error jumps by nearly three orders of magnitude already at degree 4. Degree 4 is the lowest degree whose 5 model parameters suffice to interpolate the training set. For m = 20, the validation error varies by less than one order of magnitude across all degrees shown. Overfitting typically occurs when the hypothesis space H is too large relative to the number of data points in the training set (as for H(3) in Fig. 1). The Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension of H and its Rademacher complexity measure the size of H without counting model parameters. Counting model parameters is the obvious way to measure that size, but not always the right one: the hypotheses h(w)(x) = 0.5 sin( w x ) carry a single model parameter yet form a hypothesis space with infinite Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension. The count is exactly right, in contrast, for the classifiers h(x) = sign( w0 + w1 x + … + wp xp ) obtained by thresholding the polynomials of maximum degree p in a single feature. Their hypothesis space has Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension p + 1, the number of model parameters and one more than the maximum degree. The feature map x ↦ (x, x2, …, xp) turns these classifiers into linear classifiers on Rp, whose hypothesis space has Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension p + 1. Conversely, any p + 1 data points with distinct features are shattered. The classifiers realize every possible assignment of binary labels to these data points, since a polynomial of degree at most p interpolates arbitrary labels on them. These thresholded classifiers concern a different case than Fig. 2, which fits polynomials of the same degrees to a regression task. Both measures enter the upper bounds on the generalization gap, which grow with them and shrink with the number of data points in the training set. Regularization counteracts overfitting in three elementary forms: pruning the model, adding a penalty term to the empirical risk, or augmenting the training set via data augmentation.

terms.name: principal component analysis (PCA)
terms.abstract: Principal component analysis (PCA) is the linear case of feature learning: it maps the feature vector of a data point to a vector of fewer entries by a linear map, chosen so that a second linear map rebuilds the original as well as possible. The criterion is the reconstruction error on a dataset whose labels, if it has any, are not used, since what has to be reproduced is the data point itself, which makes PCA an instance of empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss. The linear map that minimizes this error is given by the eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix belonging to its largest eigenvalues, so PCA is computed by an eigenvalue decomposition. The error left is the sum of the eigenvalues that are dropped, which gives the error of every choice of the number of retained directions in advance. Each eigenvalue is the variance along its eigenvector, so the first direction is the one of largest variance. An autoencoder keeps the same criterion with ANNs in place of the two linear maps.
terms.description: A weather station at Krems an der Donau records eight numbers for each day of 2024: the lowest, highest and mean air temperature, precipitation, sunshine duration, humidity, air pressure and wind speed. Eight numbers per day are more than a scatterplot can show, and one of them, the mean temperature, is the midpoint of two others to within the precision of the archive. PCA replaces the eight by fewer, chosen so that a second linear map rebuilds the originals from the few with the smallest average squared error. PCA is the linear case of feature learning, and its criterion is the reconstruction error. The encoder is a linear map {\mathbf \Phi}^{({\mathbf W})}: \mathbb{R}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{d'}: {\mathbf x} \mapsto {\mathbf W} {\mathbf x} \text{,} given by a matrix W ∈ Rd' × d with d' < d, and the decoder is a linear map R ∈ Rd × d' that rebuilds the raw feature vector from the code, the lower-dimensional representation z = W x of the data point. The usefulness of a specific W is the minimum reconstruction error it leaves on a dataset D = x(1), …, x(m) of feature vectors x(r) ∈ Rd with sample mean zero, the decoder being learned alongside the encoder: \begin{equation} \min_{{\mathbf R} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d'}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {\mathbf R} {\mathbf W} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{.} \end{equation} Minimizing over R and W jointly yields the same pair; the inner minimum is taken first so that the reconstruction error becomes a loss function of W alone. No labels appear in the reconstruction error Eq. (1): the decoder has to reproduce the data point itself. PCA is therefore an instance of empirical risk minimization whose loss function is the squared error loss L(x,W ) = ‖ x - R̂ W x ‖22, for the decoder R̂ that attains the minimum. The eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix solve the reconstruction problem Eq. (1). The feature vectors are centered, i.e., their sample mean is zero, which is what makes the following matrix the sample covariance matrix: \widehat{\mathbf{Q}} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \big( {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \big)^{\top} \text{,} and it is positive semi-definite, since uᵀ Q̂ u = (1)/(m) Σr=1m ( uᵀ x(r) )2 ≥ 0 for every u ∈ Rd. A symmetric matrix has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, and a positive semi-definite one has nonnegative eigenvalues, so the eigenvalue decomposition of Q̂ is a spectral decomposition, Q̂ = Σj=1d λj u(j) ( u(j) )ᵀ with eigenvalues λ1 ≥ ≥ λd ≥ 0 and eigenvectors u(1), …, u(d) forming an orthonormal basis of Rd. Restricting the decoder R to orthonormal columns loses no generality, since the products R W range over the matrices of rank at most d' either way. For such an R the encoder attaining the minimum is the transpose W = Rᵀ: the best code holds the inner products Rᵀ x of x with the orthonormal columns of R. The reconstruction R Rᵀ x is therefore the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace they span. That projection is orthogonal to the error it leaves, and \left\lVert {\mathbf x} - {\mathbf R} {\mathbf R}^{\top} {\mathbf x} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} = \left\lVert {\mathbf x} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} - \left\lVert {\mathbf R}^{\top} {\mathbf x} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{.} Averaging over all data points in D turns the reconstruction error Eq. (1) into tr (Q̂) - tr (Rᵀ Q̂ R). The first trace does not depend on R, so minimizing the error is maximizing the second over matrices with orthonormal columns. That maximum is Σj=1d' λj, attained by the eigenvectors belonging to the d' largest eigenvalues. A matrix W = ( u(1), …, u(d') )ᵀ whose rows are those eigenvectors therefore minimizes the criterion Eq. (1), paired with the decoder R̂ = Wᵀ. The minimum reconstruction error is Σj=d'+1d λj, the eigenvalues left out, so the spectrum of Q̂ gives the reconstruction error of every code length in advance. Algorithm 1 states the computation in full. \begin{algorithm}[H] \caption{Principal component analysis } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex Input: feature vectors x(1), …, x(m) ∈ Rd, number d' ≤ d of retained features \State center the feature vectors: subtract their sample mean from each of them \State form the sample covariance matrix Q̂ of the centered feature vectors \State compute the eigenvalue decomposition of Q̂, giving eigenvalues λ1 ≥ … ≥ λd and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors u(1), …, u(d) \State stack the eigenvectors belonging to the d' largest eigenvalues as the rows of W = ( u(1), …, u(d') )ᵀ \Statex Output: the encoder W and the decoder R̂ = Wᵀ; the code of a feature vector is W x and its reconstruction Wᵀ W x \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} The eigenvectors u(1), …, u(d) of Q̂ are the principal directions of the dataset, ordered by decreasing eigenvalue. Stacking the centered feature vectors row-wise into the feature matrix X ∈ Rm × d writes the sample covariance matrix as Q̂ = (1/m) Xᵀ X, so they are equally the eigenvectors of Xᵀ X. The first d' of them span the subspace that PCA keeps, and each feature vector is replaced by its orthogonal projection onto it. That projection is the approximation whose squared error loss the reconstruction error Eq. (1) measures. The inner products of x with the first d' principal directions are its coordinates in that subspace, and they are the new features PCA delivers. The eigenvalues of Q̂ are the variances of the data along its eigenvectors, so u(1) is the direction of largest variance. Fig. 1 shows the two directions for the days at Krems taken with two features, the lowest and the highest temperature of the day (both centered). Their eigenvalues are 130.9 and 7.9 squared degrees, whose square roots are the standard deviations along them. On all eight measurements, each scaled to unit sample variance because temperatures, precipitation and pressure are measured in different units, the two largest eigenvalues carry 64% of the total variance. A code of two numbers leaves a reconstruction error of 2.91, exactly the sum of the six dropped eigenvalues. Fig. 2 plots the error left by every code length. The code length d' is a hyperparameter. Each number added to the code removes exactly the next eigenvalue from the error, and the ones removed first are the largest (see Fig. 2). No choice is optimal on the criterion itself, which falls to zero at d' = d, where nothing is compressed. What picks d' is the use the code is put to: a scatterplot needs two, a later learning task can be given the validation error of each length to choose from, and a storage budget fixes it outright. In particular, on the same eight measurements the smallest eigenvalue reveals as much as the largest. It is 6.5 · 10-6 against 3.62 for the largest, and its eigenvector loads on the three temperatures alone: the mean temperature of a day is the midpoint of its lowest and its highest, to within the 0.05 degrees the archive records. A direction of almost no variance is a dependency among the features, and PCA finds it without a test for it. Finding such dependencies is what makes PCA a dimensionality reduction method rather than only a feature learning one: the features it drops are the ones the others already determine. These numbers are averages over the dataset the eigenvectors were computed from. Whether the subspace also rebuilds data points outside it is the question of generalization. The answer depends on how well Q̂ estimates the covariance matrix of data points outside the dataset. The same criterion compresses images. Cutting a photograph into patches of 64 × 64 pixels makes each patch a data point with 12288 features, three color values per pixel, and PCA replaces those by a code of d' numbers (see Fig. 3). At d' = 5 the mountain and the meadow are already in place while the patch boundaries still show; at 15 the reconstruction is close to the original. Three variants of PCA change one thing each. Probabilistic principal component analysis keeps the subspace but replaces the criterion by a probabilistic model. The code is a Gaussian random variable, and the data point is its linear image plus isotropic Gaussian noise. Maximum likelihood, computed by expectation–maximization, recovers the PCA subspace as the noise variance tends to zero. Sparse principal component analysis keeps the criterion but adds a penalty on the entries (loadings) of an eigenvector. Each direction then involves few features and can be interpreted as a named combination of them. On the eight measurements, four loadings, the three temperatures and the sunshine duration, keep 81% of the variance of u(1). Robust principal component analysis replaces the squared error loss, which a single grossly corrupted entry can dominate, by a decomposition of the data matrix into a part of low rank plus a part with few nonzero entries. A small number of faulty measurements then falls into the second part instead of tilting the directions. An autoencoder keeps the reconstruction error Eq. (1) as its criterion and replaces the two linear maps by ANNs, which is the nonlinear counterpart of PCA. With a linear decoder and the squared error loss it reconstructs into the same subspace as PCA.

terms.name: policy (reinforcement learning)
terms.abstract: A policy in reinforcement learning is a function that maps the current state to an action. Sometimes a policy is stochastic and defined by a conditional probability distribution over the actions given the state. The policy of a reinforcement learning method can be viewed as the hypothesis of a machine learning method. It takes the features that characterize the current state of the agent as input and outputs a prediction of the best action to take. Instead of an average loss on a training set, reinforcement learning methods use the rewards observed after taking actions to guide the learning of a policy.
terms.description: A self-driving car observes its position and heading, chooses a steering direction, and is told how well it follows the road; Fig. 1 shows three time instants of it. In reinforcement learning, such an agent interacts with an environment: at each time instant t = 1, 2, …, the agent observes the state st of the environment, takes an action at, and receives the next state st+1 together with a reward rt+1. This interaction is modeled as a Markov decision process. For the car, the state is the position and heading of the car, the action is the steering direction, and the reward tells how well the car follows the road. In its simplest form, a policy is a function that specifies which action at to take in this Markov decision process when the current state is st. A policy differs from a plan, a fixed sequence of actions: a policy reacts to the state observed. A policy of this kind is deterministic. It is a special case of a stochastic policy, which defines a conditional probability distribution P(a | s) over the actions given the state, a probability distribution from which the action is drawn. A policy can be viewed as a hypothesis map h(x) that predicts the best action to take. The feature vector x fed into the hypothesis is either the state itself, when the state is fully observed, or some indirect measurements of it, when the state is only partially observed. What sets supervised learning apart from reinforcement learning is how the usefulness of a hypothesis is assessed. Instead of computing the average loss on a dataset of labeled data points, reinforcement learning methods use the expected return obtained when the policy is applied to a Markov decision process. The return at time instant t is the discounted sum of the rewards received afterwards, \[ G_{t} := \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^{k} r_{t+k+1} \text{,} \] with a discount factor γ ∈ [0,1]. The sum has a finite value when γ < 1 and the rewards are bounded. The case γ = 1 is used only for episodes that terminate after finitely many time instants, so that the sum has finitely many nonzero terms. The expected return, as a function of the starting state, is the value function of the policy. It can be estimated by executing the policy: the agent starts from the state several times, follows the policy for a number of time instants, records the rewards, and averages the observed returns.

terms.name: probabilistic principal component analysis (probabilistic PCA)
terms.abstract: Probabilistic principal component analysis (probabilistic PCA) is a probabilistic model for the feature vectors of a dataset: a low-dimensional Gaussian random vector, the code, is mapped into the feature space by a matrix, and isotropic Gaussian noise is added. The probability distribution of the feature vector is then a multivariate normal distribution whose covariance matrix is a matrix of rank d' plus a multiple of the identity matrix, so the model gives a probability density function value to every point of the feature space. That value is what principal component analysis does not deliver: a data point outside the training set can be ranked by how probable it is, and features missing from a feature vector are filled in by an expectation. The maximum likelihood estimate of the model parameters has a closed form in the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix: the columns of the matrix span the subspace that principal component analysis keeps, and the noise variance is the average of the discarded eigenvalues. The expectation–maximization algorithm computes the same estimate as a fixed-point iteration, without an eigenvalue decomposition. The posterior mean of the code pulls the principal component analysis coordinates toward the origin, and becomes the orthogonal projection on the subspace as the noise variance tends to zero, which recovers principal component analysis. The isotropic noise is the model's main restriction: it makes the learned subspace depend on the units of the features, and factor analysis gives each measurement its own noise variance instead.
terms.description: A weather station at Krems an der Donau (Austria) records eight numbers for each day of 2024: the lowest, highest, and mean air temperature, precipitation, sunshine duration, humidity, air pressure, and wind speed. Principal component analysis replaces the eight by two, few enough for a scatterplot, and says nothing about how probable a day is: 14 September 2024, which brought 81.7 mm of rain, is placed in the plane like any other day. Probabilistic PCA keeps the subspace that principal component analysis delivers and adds a probability distribution over the eight numbers, given by a probability density function on the feature space. The rainy day then carries a density value far below that of every other day of the year. Probabilistic PCA is a latent variable probabilistic model. Each data point of a dataset carries a feature vector x(r) ∈ Rd, for r = 1, …, m, with d = 8 and m = 366 for the days of 2024. The model builds it from a low-dimensional vector z(r) ∈ Rd', the code, whose length d' < d is a hyperparameter: \begin{equation} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} = {\mathbf W} {\mathbf z}^{(r)} + {\boldsymbol \mu} + {\boldsymbol \varepsilon}^{(r)} \text{, for } r = 1, \ldots, m \text{.} \end{equation} Here, W ∈ Rd × d' is a matrix and μ ∈ Rd a mean vector. The codes and the noise vectors of the model Eq. (1) are realizations of independent random vectors, z(r) ~ N(0,I) and ε(r) ~ N(0,σ2 I), with the identity matrix I and a noise variance σ2 > 0. The noise is isotropic: it has the same variance in every direction and no covariance between features. The matrix W maps a code to a feature vector, the role the decoder plays in principal component analysis, and the model parameters are W, μ, and σ2. Integrating the code out of the model Eq. (1) leaves a multivariate normal distribution for the feature vector itself, \begin{equation} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \sim \mathcal{N}\left({\boldsymbol \mu},{\mathbf C}\right) \text{, where } {\mathbf C} = {\mathbf W} {\mathbf W}^{\top} + \sigma^{2} \mathbf{I} \text{.} \end{equation} The covariance matrix C of the multivariate normal distribution Eq. (2) is a matrix of rank at most d' plus a multiple of the identity matrix. That is the one restriction separating probabilistic PCA from an unconstrained multivariate normal distribution: the variance along each of the d' retained directions is modeled on its own, while every direction orthogonal to all of them is given the same variance σ2. Because the model Eq. (1) states how a data point comes about, it is a generative model: drawing a code and adding noise produces a new day. Fig. 1 draws the probability distribution Eq. (2) learned from the days at Krems taken with two features, the lowest and the highest temperature of the day, as a level curve one standard deviation out from the mean vector. For a code of one number, the subspace that principal component analysis keeps is a straight line, and the probability distribution fills out an ellipse around it. What the probability distribution Eq. (2) delivers and principal component analysis does not is a number for every point of the feature space. A day that did not belong to the training set receives a density value, so days can be ranked by how probable the model finds them. With the model parameters learned from the 365 days of 2023 and d' = 3, the least probable day of 2024 at Krems is 14 September, where the logarithm of the probability density function Eq. (2) is -440.8, against -8.5 for the median day and -105.6 for the next lowest (Fig. 2). Its 81.7 mm of rain are 20.4 sample standard deviations above the 2023 average of 1.5 mm. Ranking data points by their density value is one route to anomaly detection, and it is closed to principal component analysis, which returns coordinates and no probability. The model parameters are learned by maximum likelihood, and the estimate has a closed form. The eigenvalues of the sample covariance matrix Ĉ of the training set, ordered as λ1 ≥ ≥ λd ≥ 0, come with orthonormal eigenvectors u(1), …, u(d). The estimate of the mean vector is the sample mean μ, the estimate of the noise variance is \begin{equation} \widehat{\sigma}^{2} = \frac{1}{d - d'} \sum_{j = d'+1}^{d} \lambda_{j} \text{,} \end{equation} and the estimate Ŵ has the columns √(λj - σ̂2) u(j), for j = 1, …, d'. The average Eq. (3) of the discarded eigenvalues is the variance the retained directions leave unexplained, spread evenly over the d - d' directions that carry it. The columns of Ŵ span the subspace that principal component analysis keeps, the one spanned by the first d' eigenvectors of Ĉ. Rotating those columns among themselves leaves the covariance matrix C unchanged, so maximum likelihood determines the subspace and not the individual columns. The expectation–maximization algorithm reaches the same estimate without an eigenvalue decomposition of Ĉ, which is the cheaper route when d is large and few directions are wanted. Collecting the model parameters W and σ2 in w, one iteration is a fixed-point iteration {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} = T \big( {\mathbf w}^{(t)} \big) \text{,} whose operator T re-estimates W from Ĉ and the posterior distribution of the codes, then sets σ2 to the variance the new W leaves unexplained. No iteration decreases the likelihood function, and the fixed points of T are the stationary points of that likelihood function. The closed-form estimate is the one among them at which the likelihood function attains its maximum; the stationary points built from eigenvectors other than the leading d' are saddle points. In the vocabulary of empirical risk minimization, probabilistic PCA changes two of the three parts of principal component analysis and keeps the third. The hypothesis space gains one number. Principal component analysis searches over the products of an encoder and a decoder, which are the matrices of rank at most d'. Probabilistic PCA searches over the multivariate normal distributions Eq. (2), whose covariance matrices are such a matrix plus σ2 I. The columns of W need not be orthonormal: those of Ŵ have squared lengths λj - σ̂2, for j = 1, …, d', so they fix the variance along each retained direction and not only the subspace. The loss function is the negative logarithm of the probability density function of the probability distribution P Eq. (2), in place of the squared error loss of principal component analysis, L\left({\mathbf x},\mathbb{P} \right) = - \ln \mathcal{N}\left({\mathbf x} ; {\boldsymbol \mu}, {\mathbf C}\right) \text{,} so minimizing the empirical risk is maximum likelihood. The third part is unchanged: the eigenvalue decomposition of Ĉ that solves principal component analysis delivers this minimum in closed form as well, and the expectation–maximization algorithm is the route that avoids it. The two loss functions meet as the noise variance tends to zero: 2 σ2 times the empirical risk tends to the minimum reconstruction error Σj = d' + 1d λj of principal component analysis. That sum is 1.636 for the eight standardized measurements of the 365 days of 2023 with d' = 3. Multiplied by 2 σ2, the empirical risk reaches 0.979 of it at σ2 = 10-2, 0.998 at 10-4, and 1.000 at 10-6. A data point is placed in the subspace through the posterior distribution of its code. The posterior mean of the code is \begin{equation} \mathbb{E} \big\{ {\mathbf z} \mid {\mathbf x} \big\} = \big( \widehat{{\mathbf W}}^{\top} \widehat{{\mathbf W}} + \widehat{\sigma}^{2} \mathbf{I} \big)^{-1} \widehat{{\mathbf W}}^{\top} \big( {\mathbf x} - \widehat{\boldsymbol \mu} \big) \text{,} \end{equation} whose j-th entry, for the closed-form estimate, is the j-th principal component analysis coordinate ⟨ u(j), x - μ ⟩ multiplied by √(λj - σ̂2) / λj, for j = 1, …, d'. That factor is below one for the three retained directions at Krems, where it is 0.50, 0.71, and 0.78. As σ̂2 tends to zero the factor tends to 1 / √(λj), here 0.53, 0.80, and 0.91. The limit of the posterior mean Eq. (4) is therefore the principal component analysis coordinate divided by √(λj), which both sources call an orthogonal projection into the space of the code. Measured against that limit, the code at σ̂2 > 0 is pulled toward the origin by the factor √(1 - σ̂2 / λj), here 0.95, 0.89, and 0.85. In the feature space, what matches principal component analysis is the reconstruction Ŵ E z | x + μ: at σ̂2 = 10-12 it agrees to 3 · 10-12 with the orthogonal projection of the feature vector on the subspace spanned by the first d' eigenvectors. At σ̂2 = 0.33 it is not that orthogonal projection, departing from it by 0.153 per entry in root mean square, and the reconstruction with the smallest squared error applies Ŵ ( Ŵᵀ Ŵ )-1 ( Ŵᵀ Ŵ + σ̂2 I ) to the posterior mean instead. At that limit the covariance matrix C is singular and the probability density function ceases to exist, so the limit that recovers principal component analysis is the one that gives up the probability distribution. A probability distribution over the feature space also handles missing data. Conditioned on the entries of a feature vector that were recorded, the probability distribution Eq. (2) is again Gaussian in the entries that were not, and its expectation is the filled-in value. Deleting the highest temperature of each of the 366 days of 2024 and filling it in this way, from the model parameters learned on 2023, leaves a mean squared error whose square root is 2.28 degrees, against 9.21 degrees for filling in the 2023 average instead. The projection that principal component analysis applies needs every entry of the feature vector and offers no such rule, while the same conditional reading lets the model parameters be learned from feature vectors with entries missing. The model makes two assumptions, and the days at Krems show what each one costs. The noise is isotropic, so every direction orthogonal to the retained subspace is given the same variance σ̂2 = 0.33 for the eight standardized measurements with d' = 3. The mean air temperature of a day is the average of its lowest and its highest to within 0.05 degrees on every day of 2023. The sample standard deviation of the days along the last eigenvector of Ĉ is therefore 0.0027, where the model expects σ̂ = 0.57. The isotropic noise also makes the learned subspace depend on the units of the measurements: multiplying the precipitation reading by ten turns it by 51 degrees, the largest angle between the subspace before and after the rescaling. That is why the eight measurements are standardized before the model parameters are learned. Factor analysis differs from probabilistic PCA only in giving the noise a covariance matrix that is a diagonal matrix, one variance per measurement, and a rescaling of one measurement leaves it unchanged. With its model parameters learned from the same 365 days of 2023, it raises the median logarithm of the probability density function over the 366 days of 2024 from -8.5 to -3.2, and what it gives up is the closed form. The second assumption is the Gaussian shape of the probability density function Eq. (2), on which the ranking of days by density value depends. If the days of 2024 were realizations of i.i.d. random vectors with the learned multivariate normal distribution, the quadratic form in the exponent of that probability density function would be a realization of a chi-squared random variable with eight degrees of freedom. Its 99th percentile is 20.1, which 3.7 of the 366 days would exceed on average. Twenty-six do, as do 16 of the 365 days of 2023 the model parameters were learned from. For 14 September 2024, the quadratic form is 870.6, which the same chi-squared random variable exceeds with probability 1.2 · 10-182, and that day occurred. The density value therefore ranks days, and it does not say how often a day of that kind occurs. Where one multivariate normal distribution is too simple, the standard extension is a mixture of probabilistic PCA models, a Gaussian mixture model whose component covariance matrices are each of the form W Wᵀ + σ2 I. What the two assumptions buy in return is a probability distribution over the whole feature space in closed form: it gives a density value to a day outside the training set and a filled-in value to a feature that was not recorded.

terms.name: pretraining
terms.abstract: Pretraining is the training of a model on a large, generic dataset to produce model parameters that are reused as the starting point for a later learning task. The loss minimized is typically self-supervised, so no manual annotation labour is needed. For a large language model, pretraining minimizes the average next-token prediction loss over a large text corpus. While transfer learning is the reuse of what was learned on one learning task for another, pretraining is the stage that produces what is reused, with a proxy task chosen for that purpose. The reuse takes several forms, by fine-tuning all model parameters from the pretrained ones, or by training only a subset of them on top of a pretrained feature transformation.
terms.description: Before a deep net is trained to detect tumors in a few hundred annotated scans, it is trained on millions of ordinary photographs that have nothing to do with tumors. That first step is pretraining: the training of a model on a large, generic dataset to produce model parameters that are reused as the starting point for a later learning task. The loss minimized during pretraining is typically self-supervised (see self-supervised learning): the label of a data point is constructed from the raw data itself, so no manual annotation labour is needed. For a large language model, pretraining minimizes the average next-token prediction loss over a large text corpus. The model parameters learned during pretraining are then adapted separately for each task-specific dataset by fine-tuning (Fig. 1). In the tumor example, the task-specific data points are the annotated scans, while the generic dataset is ImageNet, a corpus of more than three million labeled images at its release, so that pretraining is supervised, the exception to the self-supervised rule. The reuse takes a second form besides fine-tuning: a pretrained feature transformation φ X → Rd is concatenated with a task-specific model. In a deep net, the first layers are the pretrained φ and the final layers are trained separately for each learning task (Fig. 2). The same φ serves every learning task, so generic features are learned once, and each later learning task starts from an informative initialization instead of from scratch. A worked example. A piece of an aerial photograph of the Wachau, 2.4 km by 1.2 km, is cut into 4608 patches of 25 m. A parcel register labels a patch as vineyard when more than half of its pixels lie on vineyard parcels, which is the case for a third of them. The western half is the training set, the eastern half the test set. At this resolution the rows of vines are visible stripes, while the mean color of a patch tells little: vineyards, meadows and gardens are all green (Fig. 3). Pretraining uses the photograph alone, never the labels. The central 8 × 8 pixel block of a western patch is blanked. A convolutional neural network of two convolutional layers, each with eight 3 × 3 filters and a rectified linear unit, is followed by a linear readout at the blanked block. It is trained to predict the mean color of the blanked pixels from their surroundings. On the eastern patches the trained network predicts the blanked color with a squared error of 0.0008, a quarter of the error of the mean color of the rest of the patch (Fig. 4, top). A second pretext task trains the same network to tell whether a patch was rotated by 0, 90, 180 or 270 degrees. The direction of the rows and of the shadows answers that question. The network recognizes the rotation of 37 percent of the eastern patches, against 25 by chance. The two convolutional layers are then frozen: they are the feature transformation φ, and their output on the original patch, averaged over a 4 × 4 grid, gives 128 features. Logistic regression on these features is a linear classifier of vineyard against no vineyard. It is trained on as few as 8 and at most 128 labeled data points of the western half, and its accuracy is measured on the eastern half (Fig. 4, bottom). Labels are scarce on purpose: this is the regime in which pretraining decides the outcome. With so few labels a linear classifier on the pixels themselves is prone to overfitting: its Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension is the number of features plus one, and the number of labels that generalization requires grows in proportion to it. It has 768 features, the patch pooled to 16 × 16 pixels in three colors, and at most 128 patches to learn them from, and its accuracy stays below the majority baseline of 0.69 until 128 labels are available, where it reaches 0.72. The mean color of a patch stays at that baseline too, 0.67 with 128 labels. The control that every pretraining claim needs is the same two layers with their random initial weights, never trained: they reach 0.76 with 128 labels, since random convolutional filters with pooling already respond to texture. The color-pretrained layers exceed that control from 32 labels on, and the rotation-pretrained layers exceed it at every number of labels, reaching 0.82 with 128. Two conclusions follow. Pretraining helps when the labeled dataset is too small to learn what the pretext task already taught the layers. The pretext task matters too. A task that needs the direction of the stripes yields features that a classifier of vineyards needs, while predicting a color from its surroundings is largely solved by averaging. The numbers are computed by pythondemos/pretraining.py.

terms.name: probability distribution
terms.abstract: A probability distribution of a random variable is the probability measure that the random variable induces on the set of its values: it assigns a probability to every measurable set of values. A machine learning method reads in a dataset and delivers an output, such as a learned hypothesis or the prediction for a given data point, and should work well for any dataset that could arise in the machine learning application at hand. The independent and identically distributed assumption models such a dataset as realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs with a common probability distribution, which is postulated from domain knowledge or estimated from a dataset. The probability distribution of a binary random variable is fully specified by a single probability, that of a discrete random variable by a probability mass function, and that of a real-valued random variable with a probability density function by that probability density function.
terms.description: Consider a machine learning method that takes as input a dataset D = z(1), …, z(m), each data point a numeric feature paired with a numeric label, and delivers an output, such as a learned hypothesis ĥ or the prediction for a given data point. Feeding a different dataset into the same method can deliver a different output. In general, the method should work well for any dataset that could arise in the machine learning application at hand. The independent and identically distributed assumption models such a dataset as independent and identically distributed RVs z(1), …, z(m) ~ P with a common probability distribution P (see Fig. 1). The outputs obtained from different such datasets are themselves realizations of a random variable, whose probability distribution depends on P and on the method. How much the outputs spread, i.e., how much they differ from one another, is therefore determined by P and the method. Formally, a random variable is a measurable function z: Ω → Z from a probability space (Ω, Σ, P) to a measurable space Z, the set of values that z can take. The probability distribution of z is the probability measure P(z) that z induces on Z. This probability measure assigns to every measurable subset B ⊆ Z the probability \[ \mathbb{P}^{({\mathbf z})}(\mathcal{B}) := \mathbb{P}\left({\mathbf z} \in \mathcal{B}\right) = \mathbb{P}\big( \{ \omega \in \Omega: {\mathbf z}(\omega) \in \mathcal{B} \} \big) \text{,} \] the probability of the event that z takes a value in B (see Fig. 2;;; ). That event is the preimage z-1(B) = ω ∈ Ω: z(ω) ∈ B, the set of outcomes ω of the sample space Ω that z sends into B. Measurability of z guarantees that z-1(B) belongs to the σ-algebra Σ, so that P assigns z-1(B) a probability. The superscript of P(z) names the random variable whose distribution is meant, as in P(x,y) for a data point with features x and label y. When only one random variable is in play, the superscript is dropped, and z ~ P states that P is the probability distribution of z. Under the independent and identically distributed assumption, the probability distribution P of the data points determines how likely each dataset is: a dataset of realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs is likely when its data points lie where P assigns large probability. This distribution is generally unknown; only the dataset is observed. In practice, P is postulated based on domain knowledge or estimated from a dataset, e.g., by its empirical distribution or histogram, or by maximum likelihood within a parametric family. A parametric family is a set of probability distributions indexed by a few numbers, such as the normal distributions indexed by mean and variance. A probability mass function or a probability density function is a compact way of specifying a probability distribution. The probability distribution of a binary random variable y ∈ 0,1 is fully specified by the single probability P(y = 0), since P(y=1) = 1-P(y=0); more generally, the probability distribution of a discrete random variable is specified by its probability mass function. The probability distribution of a real-valued random variable x ∈ R that has a probability density function p(x)(·) is specified by that probability density function. The probability of a value in an interval [a,b] is the integral \[ \mathbb{P}\left( x \in [a,b] \right) = \int_{a}^{b} p^{(x)}\left(x\right) \mathrm{d}x \text{,} \] which is approximately p(x)(a) |b-a| for a short interval [a,b]. Because the probability density function gives the probability of a short interval around each value, it can be drawn. For data points z = (x, y) with a single numeric feature x and a numeric label y, a probability distribution can be visualized in the plane R2. Fig. 3 shows one as a grayscale over the feature--label plane: the darker a region, the larger its probability density function, i.e., the more likely a data point drawn from P falls in it. The depicted probability density function is a weighted sum of two Gaussian pdfs, i.e., a Gaussian mixture model. Paralleling Fig. 1, three datasets D(1), D(2), D(3), each consisting of m = 20 realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs with this distribution, are shown together with the three hypotheses ĥ(1), ĥ(2), ĥ(3) learned from them by the same polynomial regression method. As shown in Fig. 3, the three learned hypotheses differ most where the probability density function is small. The example also illustrates what empirical risk minimization can determine from a dataset. Empirical risk minimization chooses the hypothesis by its average loss over the dataset. It therefore gives little weight to a region in which the dataset contains few or no data points. Consequently, empirical risk minimization does not distinguish between hypotheses that differ only there and have nearly the same training error.

terms.name: projection
terms.abstract: The projection of a vector onto a closed non-empty subset of a Euclidean space is a point in the subset that is closest to the vector in the Euclidean norm. If the subset is convex, this closest point is unique and the solution of a convex optimization problem. If the subset is a subspace, the projection is a linear map, namely the orthogonal projection onto the subspace. Every projection is idempotent, and a linear map of a Hilbert space into itself is an orthogonal projection if and only if the map is idempotent and self-adjoint. In machine learning, projections enforce constraints on model parameters during training: projected gradient descent alternates gradient steps with projections onto the constraint set, e.g., the ℓ1-ball in an equivalent formulation of the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator.
terms.description: The least absolute shrinkage and selection operator learns a linear model whose model parameters w must keep an ℓ1-norm below a prescribed bound, and a gradient step can move w outside this set. The result must then be replaced by a closest admissible vector, and training any machine learning model under a constraint set faces the same replacement at every step. The projection formalizes this replacement. Consider a non-empty closed set W ⊆ Rd in the d-dimensional Euclidean space. The projection PW( w) of a vector w ∈ Rd onto W is \[ P_{\mathcal{W}}\big( {\mathbf w}\big) = \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{{\mathbf w}' \in \mathcal{W}} \left\lVert {\mathbf w} - {\mathbf w}' \right\rVert_{2}\text{,} \] a vector in W closest to w in the Euclidean norm. The minimum exists for every non-empty closed set W, but several closest vectors can exist. For the two-point set W = (-1,0)ᵀ, (1,0)ᵀ, both elements are closest to (0,0.7)ᵀ, and likewise to every other point on the vertical axis, which consists of exactly the points equidistant from the two elements. If W is closed and convex, the closest point in the Euclidean norm is unique. The construction extends beyond the Euclidean space: a non-empty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space contains, for each point of the space, a unique closest point. If W is a subspace, that is, a subset that contains all sums and scalar multiples of its elements (such as a line through the origin), the map w ↦ PW( w) is a linear map: it is the orthogonal projection onto W. Every projection is idempotent: the vector PW( w) lies in W, so its closest point in W is itself and PW( PW( w)) = PW( w). A linear map P of a Hilbert space into itself is the orthogonal projection onto the range of P if and only if P is idempotent and self-adjoint, i.e., ⟨ Pu, v ⟩ = ⟨ u, Pv ⟩ for all u, v. For a matrix P ∈ Rd × d acting on the Euclidean space, idempotence is the condition P2 = P and self-adjointness the condition Pᵀ = P. Idempotence alone is not sufficient for a linear map to be an orthogonal projection: an idempotent linear map that is not self-adjoint is an oblique projection. For example, the matrix P = pmatrix 1 & 1 0 & 0 pmatrix on R2 satisfies P2 = P but Pᵀ ≠ P. Its range is the horizontal axis, and it maps w = (0,1)ᵀ to P w = (1,0)ᵀ, while the point of the axis closest to w is the origin (0,0)ᵀ. In machine learning, projections enforce constraints on model parameters during training. Linear regression with the constraint ‖ w ‖1 ≤ τ, for a prescribed constant τ > 0, is an equivalent formulation of the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator, for a value of its penalty hyperparameter that depends on τ and on the training set. This constrained problem can be solved by projected gradient descent. Each iteration takes a gradient step on the training error and then projects the result onto the ℓ1-ball W = w' ∈ Rd: ‖ w' ‖1 ≤ τ. The projection step is what enforces the constraint: without it, basic gradient descent on the training error can produce iterates with ‖ w ‖1 > τ, and the result solves the unconstrained problem instead of the constrained one. Since W is not a subspace (scaling the vector (τ,0)ᵀ ∈ W by 2 yields a vector outside the ball), this projection is not a linear map but amounts to solving a convex optimization problem (see Fig. 1). Such a projection is distinct from the proximal operator: the proximal operator minimizes, over all of Rd, the sum of a convex function f(w') and half the squared Euclidean distance to w, while the projection minimizes the distance alone, over the given set W.

terms.name: random experiment
terms.abstract: A random experiment is a physical or computational data-generating process that produces an outcome ω from a known set of possibilities, the sample space of the experiment. Probability theory represents the process by a probability space (Ω, Σ, P), where the σ-algebra Σ collects the measurable events and the probability measure P(·) assigns each event a probability. This representation is a probabilistic model of the process, not a property of it. A measurement of the outcome is represented by a random variable, a measurable function x: Ω → X, and the measured value x(ω) is a realization. Repeating the experiment m times is itself a random experiment on the product sample space, and the measurements of the runs are modeled as independent and identically distributed RVs. In machine learning, the construction of a training set, the draw of a subset of it by stochastic gradient descent, and the noise added for differential privacy are random experiments.
terms.description: The weather station Krems an der Donau (Austria) records the minimum and the maximum temperature of every day (Fig. 1). On any given day neither temperature is known in advance, but the range they can take is. A process of that kind is a random experiment: it produces an outcome ω from a set Ω of possibilities, the sample space of the experiment. The outcome is uncertain, and the experiment can be repeated under identical conditions. Here one day is one run: the outcome ω is the weather of that day, and the two recorded temperatures are measurements of it. Probability theory represents a random experiment by a probability space (Ω, Σ, P). The sample space Ω collects the possible outcomes ω ∈ Ω. The σ-algebra Σ collects the events, those subsets A ⊆ Ω to which a probability is assigned. The probability measure P(·) assigns to each event A ∈ Σ a number P(A) ∈ [0,1] such that P(Ω) = 1 and the probability of a countable union of pairwise disjoint events is the sum of their probabilities. The triple (Ω, Σ, P) is a probabilistic model of the process, not a property of it. There are principled methods for choosing a useful probabilistic model (Ω, Σ, P) based on the observed data. Rolling a die is a random experiment small enough to write the triple out. Its sample space is Ω = 1, …, 6. Its σ-algebra Σ is the collection of all subsets of Ω: that the roll is even is the event A = 2,4,6. The uniform probability measure, P(A) = |A| / 6, is the model of a fair die, under which P(2,4,6) = 1/2. Whether a given die is fair is a question about the process rather than about the model, answered by the relative frequencies of its outcomes in many rolls. The observed data are measurements of the outcome of the experiment. In particular, each measurement is a measurable function x: Ω → X of the outcome. Such a measurable function is a random variable, and the value x(ω) it takes for the actual outcome ω is a realization of it. The temperature at 13:00 is a random variable on the weather of a day, and the number read on one day is a realization. The probability measure on Ω induces the probability distribution of the random variable, P(x)(B) = P(x ∈ B) for every measurable set B ⊆ X. Fig. 2 shows the process beside its mathematical representation: the experiment, its outcome and the measured value above, the probability space and the random variable that represent them below. Repeating a random experiment (Ω, Σ, P) a fixed number m of times, under identical conditions, defines a new random experiment (Ω, Σ, P)(m) whose outcomes are sequences (ω(1), …, ω(m)) of outcomes of the original one (Fig. 3). Its sample space is the product Ω(m) = Ω × × Ω, and its probability measure is the product P(m) = P × × P. The measurements x(1), …, x(m) of the runs are then independent and identically distributed RVs. In machine learning these measurements are the data points z(1), …, z(m) of a training set. While the outcome of a single experiment is uncertain, the long-run behavior of repeated experiments becomes predictable: the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem make this precise. The notion of a repeated experiment is an idealization that might result in a poor probabilistic model for a physical or computational data-generating process. Successive rolls of a die can typically be considered a repeated experiment. In contrast, the daily weather observations shown in Fig. 1 are not well represented as the result of a repeated experiment: a warm day tends to follow a warm day, so the daily readings are related rather than independent. The autocorrelation of such a record measures that relation. Random experiments arise in machine learning in three places: \begin{itemize} \item Data collection: the data points z(1), …, z(m) of a training set are modeled as RVs, i.e., as functions of the outcome ω ∈ Ω of a random experiment, and the independent and identically distributed assumption models their collection as the repetition of one experiment. Empirical risk minimization minimizes the average loss over those m data points; because they are independent and identically distributed RVs with probability distribution P(z), that average estimates the risk of a hypothesis, an expectation under P(z), which is what makes the risk a meaningful target for empirical risk minimization. \item Stochastic algorithms: stochastic gradient descent runs a random experiment at each iteration, the draw of a subset of the training set; the bootstrap draws resamples of the training set. \item Privacy protection methods run a random experiment to perturb the outputs of a machine learning method, which is what differential privacy requires. \end{itemize}

terms.name: random forest
terms.abstract: A random forest is the instance of bagging whose base learners learn decision trees. Each decision tree is trained on randomly selected data points of the training set, and each base learner also uses only a randomly selected subset of the features. The predictions of the base learners are aggregated by a majority vote in classification or by averaging in regression. The random selection of data points and of features aims at a decorrelation, so that aggregating reduces the variance of the returned prediction. Aggregation leaves the bias unchanged, and adding base learners does not cause overfitting. A random forest also yields a feature importance score per feature: the fraction of the overall splits that use that feature.
terms.description: A bank must decide, for each loan application, whether the applicant is creditworthy. A random forest answers with the majority vote of many different decision trees. A random forest is the instance of bagging whose base learners learn decision trees. As in bagging, each decision tree is trained on randomly selected data points of the training set. Besides the random selection of data points, each base learner also uses only a randomly selected subset of the features of the original data points. The predictions of the base learners are aggregated by a majority vote in classification or by averaging in regression (Fig. 2).
