The scatterplot of Fig. 1 shows a regression example: each data point is one of the 366 days of 2020 at the weather station Krems an der Donau, its feature the minimum and its label the maximum air temperature of the day. Three decision trees, each trained on its own random selection of the days, yield three different piecewise constant hypotheses; the random forest delivers their average. This construction works because averaging many high-variance predictions yields one of lower variance, provided the errors of the individual predictions are weakly correlated. A deep decision tree is well suited as a base learner here: it can fit the training set closely (small bias), but its prediction varies strongly with the training set (large variance). Averaging reduces this variance and leaves the bias unchanged, since the trees are identically distributed. Adding trees does not cause overfitting: as their number grows, the averaged prediction converges to its expectation over the random selections, and only this limit can overfit. Consider M identically distributed predictions, each with variance σ2 and with pairwise correlation ρ. The averaged prediction has variance \rho \sigma^{2} + \frac{1-\rho}{M} \sigma^{2} \text{,} which decreases with the number M of trees toward the lower bound ρ σ2 set by the correlation. The random selections are drawn independently of each other once the training set is fixed, which is what makes the predictions identically distributed. They are not independent when the underlying dataset is itself a random variable: every decision tree is grown from the same training set, and that shared dependence results in a nonzero correlation ρ in general. The random selection of data points and the random selection of features both aim at a decorrelation of the predictions that the base learners deliver for a feature vector x. While withholding features lowers the correlation ρ between the base learners, it raises the variance σ2 of each of them. The number of features offered to each base learner is therefore worth tuning: too many and the decision trees agree, too few and each of them predicts poorly. A random forest also yields a feature importance score for each feature: the fraction of the overall splits that use that feature. For the bank, these scores name the attributes of an application that its forest tests most often. Fig. 3 computes these scores for a forest grown on four features of a day at Krems an der Donau.

terms.name: random projection
terms.abstract: A random projection replaces the feature vector x ∈ Rd of a data point by A x ∈ Rd', with d' < d and a wide matrix A whose entries are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs. No data enter A, which separates a random projection from principal component analysis and from an autoencoder, whose maps for dimensionality reduction are learned from a training set. When the entries have mean zero and variance 1/d', the expectation of the squared length of A x equals the squared length of x, so squared Euclidean distances between data points survive on average. The Johnson--Lindenstrauss lemma turns this into a guarantee for a whole finite dataset: a target dimension of at least 4 ln m / (ε2/2 - ε3/3) keeps every pairwise squared Euclidean distance within the factor 1 ± ε. That requirement involves the sample size m and the tolerance ε and not the ambient dimension d, so the saving grows with the length of the original feature vector. The entries may be normal RVs or take the values ± 1/√(d') with probability one half each. A random projection costs one matrix multiplication per data point and no pass over the data.
terms.description: A weather archive at Krems an der Donau (Austria) keeps, for each day, the daily maximum air temperature of the preceding ten years. Such a day is a data point whose feature vector x ∈ Rd holds d = 3650 numbers, and a search for the days most similar to a given one compares these feature vectors by their Euclidean distance. A random projection shortens every record before the search: it replaces x by A x ∈ Rd', where d' < d and A ∈ Rd' × d is a wide matrix whose entries are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs. No data enter A, and that is what separates a random projection from principal component analysis and from an autoencoder, whose maps for dimensionality reduction are learned from a training set. The word projection is traditional here: the matrix A maps into Rd', so it is not a projection of Rd onto one of its subsets. The probability distribution of these RVs has mean zero and variance 1/d'. Consider a fixed u ∈ Rd. Each entry of A u is then a random variable with mean zero and variance ‖ u ‖22/d'. Adding the variances of the d' entries gives the expectation of the squared length of A u, \begin{equation} \mathbb{E} \big\{ \left\lVert {\mathbf A} {\mathbf u} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \big\} = \left\lVert {\mathbf u} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{.} \end{equation} Read with u = x(r) - x(r'), the identity Eq. (1) says that the squared Euclidean distance between two data points survives the projection on average. One draw of A is another matter. For two of the Krems days and d' = 16, the squared Euclidean distance after the projection ranged from 0.22 to 2.68 times the one before it over 4000 draws. That spread narrows as d' grows, and the Johnson--Lindenstrauss lemma, proved by Johnson and Lindenstrauss (1984), turns the narrowing into a guarantee that covers every pair of a finite dataset at once. Consider a dataset D = x(1), …, x(m) of sample size m and a tolerance ε with 0 < ε < 1. Whenever the target dimension satisfies \begin{equation} d' \ge \frac{4 \ln m} {\varepsilon^{2}/2 - \varepsilon^{3}/3} \text{,} \end{equation} there is a map Φ Rd → Rd' with \begin{equation} (1 - \varepsilon) \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {\mathbf x}^{(r')} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \le \left\lVert {\mathbf \Phi} \big( {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \big) - {\mathbf \Phi} \big( {\mathbf x}^{(r')} \big) \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \le (1 + \varepsilon) \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {\mathbf x}^{(r')} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{,} \end{equation} for every r, r' ∈ 1, …, m, and a random projection delivers such a map with positive probability, which repeated draws raise as high as wanted. The requirement Eq. (2) involves the sample size m and the tolerance ε, and not the ambient dimension d. Its denominator is largest at ε = 1, where it equals 1/6, so no tolerance below one is granted before d' ≥ 24 ln m, which is 134 for m = 256 days. The sample size enters through its logarithm: at ε = 1/2, a hundredfold larger dataset raises the requirement from 266 to 487. Fig. 1 holds the two-sided bound Eq. (3) against what one draw of A does to the 32640 pairwise squared Euclidean distances of 256 such days. Two probability distributions for the entries of A are in common use. Normal RVs with mean zero and variance 1/d' give the guarantee in the form stated above. Entries equal to 1/√(d') or -1/√(d'), each with probability one half, meet the same requirement Eq. (2), and the products in A x then reduce to additions and subtractions of the features. Either way the cost is d d' multiplications per data point, paid once: there is no iteration and no training. For the Krems archive and d' = 256, the ten-year record of a day shrinks from 3650 numbers to 256, a factor of 14.3. In a typical draw of A, no pair of the 32640 squared Euclidean distances changes by more than 36 percent and half of them change by less than 6 percent, against the 51 percent the requirement Eq. (2) grants at that target dimension. A method that reads the data points only through their pairwise Euclidean distances, such as k-nearest neighbors, therefore works on nearly the dataset it would have worked on before. When both the map and the reconstruction are linear, principal component analysis is the choice with the smallest average squared error over the training set, and a random projection is not. When the step back to Rd may be nonlinear, the ranking can turn around: feature vectors with few nonzero features are recovered better from a random projection than from principal component analysis.

terms.name: regularization
terms.abstract: Regularization refers to modifications to a machine learning method that improve its generalization. Three routes are distinguished by which component of the method is modified: pruning the hypothesis space, adding a penalty term to the loss function, and augmenting the training set with perturbed copies of its data points. The three routes often yield the same learned hypothesis. For example, augmenting the training set of linear regression with Gaussian feature perturbations is equivalent to adding the ridge regression penalty term to the training error.
terms.description: Training a large deep net (such as a large language model) on a fixed training set via plain empirical risk minimization typically leads to overfitting: the learned hypothesis ĥ performs well on the training set but poorly outside it. Regularization refers to modifications to a machine learning method to ensure the learned hypothesis performs nearly as well on data points outside the training set as on those in it. For empirical risk minimization-based methods, regularization can be done in three ways: \begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*)] \item {Model pruning:} shrink the hypothesis space H (the set of candidate hypotheses h) to a smaller H'. For a parametric model, the shrinkage can be implemented via constraints on the model parameters (e.g., w1 ∈ [0.4,0.6] on the weight of feature x1 in linear regression). \item {Loss penalization:} add a penalty term to the training error of empirical risk minimization. For the squared error loss, the penalty term is an estimate of how much the risk exceeds the average loss on the training set; for other losses it controls the generalization gap without estimating it (see support vector machine). \item {Data augmentation:} enlarge the training set D(train) with perturbed copies of its data points (e.g., adding the realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs to the feature vector of each data point). \end{enumerate} Fig. 1 illustrates the three routes. These routes can yield the same learned hypothesis. As an example, consider data augmentation for linear regression that adds zero-mean perturbations with covariance matrix σ2 I to the feature vector of each data point. Asymptotically in the number of perturbations, the resulting learned hypothesis coincides with the one obtained from ridge regression. Ridge regression adds the penalty term σ2 ‖ w ‖22 to the training error of linear regression. According to Lagrangian duality, adding this penalty term is equivalent to shrinking the hypothesis space to the set of hypotheses with ‖ w ‖22 ≤ C for some constant C. The above regularization techniques are not limited to empirical risk minimization-based methods but can also be applied to other types of machine learning algorithms. For example, in online learning, the Follow-The-Leader method can be regularized by adding a regularizer to the per-round objective function of Follow-The-Leader. The resulting Follow-The-Regularized-Leader method achieves lower regret than plain Follow-The-Leader. Another instance of regularization is the use of a prior distribution over H in Bayesian inference. The prior distribution acts as a regularizer: the negative logarithm of the prior distribution is a penalty term, so the maximum a posteriori estimate of the model parameters of linear regression under a Gaussian prior distribution is the ridge regression solution.

terms.name: reinforcement learning (RL)
terms.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is the task of learning to act optimally within some environment. The actions are taken by an agent based on observations about the environment. The standard mathematical model of the interaction between agent and environment is a Markov decision process. An MDP includes a transition function, the conditional probability distribution of the next state given the current state and action. Another component of an MDP is a reward function that maps each pair of state and action to a reward value, which can be interpreted as a negative loss value. RL differs from supervised learning in the construction of the loss function: at each time step, the reward is observed only for the action taken, and it depends on previous actions, which forces a trade-off between exploring new actions and exploiting the ones found best.
terms.description: Consider a robot on the 4 × 4 gridworld of Fig. 1: a grid of cells, the cell in row r and column c written ⟨ r, c ⟩, with a wall at ⟨ 2, 2 ⟩ and a goal at ⟨ 3, 3 ⟩. At each time step, the robot moves up, down, left or right. A move into the wall or the boundary leaves it in place. Every move yields a reward of -1, while the move that enters the goal yields a reward of +1 and results in a stand still. RL is the task of learning, from such interaction, to choose actions that eventually reach the goal. The learner is not told which action is correct but must discover the actions that yield the most reward by trying them, and an action affects not only the immediate reward but also the next state and, through it, all later rewards. These two properties, trial-and-error search and delayed reward, distinguish RL from other forms of learning. The standard mathematical model of an RL application is a Markov decision process: a state space S, an action space A, the conditional probability distribution of the next state and reward given the current state and action, and a discount factor γ ∈ [0, 1]. The conditional probability distribution of the next state alone is the transition function. An agent interacts with its environment in time steps t = 1, 2, …: it observes the state st, chooses an action at, and receives the reward rt+1 and the next state st+1. The actions are chosen by a policy π, which for a stochastic policy is a conditional probability distribution P(a | s) over the actions given the state. The quantity to be maximized is the return, the discounted sum of the rewards to come, Gt = Σk=0∞ γk rt+k+1, where the discount factor γ weighs later rewards less. The state-value function of a policy, \[ v_{\pi}(s) := \mathbb{E}_{\pi} \big\{ G_{t} \mid s_{t} = s \big\} \text{,} \] is the expected return from a state when the actions are chosen by π. An optimal policy π* is one whose state-value function is at least that of every other policy at every state. In the gridworld with γ = 1, a shortest route of d moves earns -1 for each of its first d - 1 moves and +1 for the last, so vπ*(s) = -(d-1) + 1 = 2 - d. As a special case of machine learning, RL also trains a model on data: a policy is the hypothesis of RL. The two properties named above set it apart from supervised learning. The first, trial-and-error search, is the construction of the loss function. A supervised learning method holds the label of each data point and can evaluate the loss of every candidate hypothesis and its predictions. An RL method can evaluate the loss, the negative reward, only for the action it took, since the rewards of the actions not taken are not observed. The second, delayed reward, is that the loss at time step t depends on the previous actions. RL is not unsupervised learning either: it maximizes a reward signal instead of finding structure in unlabeled data points. Within RL itself, methods differ in the amount of information about the environment required upfront, from a known Markov decision process to nothing beyond the observed rewards. If the Markov decision process is known, methods such as value iteration and policy iteration compute an optimal policy before the agent executes it. A policy is greedy with respect to a value function v if it maximizes, at every state s ∈ S, the expected immediate reward plus the discounted value of the next state. It therefore chooses an action in argmaxa ∈ A E rt+1 + γ v(st+1) | st = s, at = a. Value iteration and policy iteration use two facts. The state-value function of a policy is the fixed point of its Bellman operator, which iterative policy evaluation reaches from any starting value function. And the policy that is greedy with respect to vπ is at least as good as π. When the Markov decision process is not known, an RL method has to learn from the interaction itself, and every reward it observes is that of an action it has taken. This forces a trade-off between exploration, trying actions whose reward is unknown, and exploitation, choosing the actions found best so far. Q-learning learns the action-value function qπ*(s, a), the expected return of taking a in s and following π* afterwards, from the rewards of the actions it tries, updating after each time step. Other methods learn the policy directly, or estimate a model of the environment and plan with it. Two special cases of the Markov decision process remove the delayed reward and leave only the trade-off between exploration and exploitation. The first has a single state: the transition function yields that state whatever the action, so the return is a sum of rewards that each depend on the current action alone. The single-state case is the multiarmed bandit. An ad server that shows one of ten banners and observes the clicks of the banner shown, but not of the nine it withheld, faces this case. The upper confidence bound method handles it by adding to the sample mean of each action a confidence term that shrinks with the number of times the action was chosen. The second case keeps several states but draws st from a fixed probability distribution that does not depend on the actions taken. The action at time t then changes the reward rt+1 and nothing else, and the state is called the context. The second case is the contextual bandit. The learning task is to learn a hypothesis that maps a context to an action, which has the form of a supervised learning problem, except that the loss is still observed only for the action taken. News recommendation is an instance: the context is the visitor profile, the action is the article placed on the front page, and the reward is the click. RL is often a form of online learning: the agent learns while it acts, and the data points it learns from arrive one per time step and depend on its current policy. Offline RL instead learns a policy from a fixed dataset of recorded interactions, without acting in the environment during training. The exploration is then fixed by whoever collected the dataset.

terms.name: reward
terms.abstract: A reward is an observed quantity that allows a machine learning method to estimate the loss incurred by the prediction of a hypothesis. One example of such a quantity is the label of a data point itself. Many machine learning applications, however, do not allow the label to be observed, but only a noisy estimate of it; some allow only the prediction error of one specific prediction to be observed. Reinforcement learning methods learn a sequence of hypothesis maps from the rewards obtained by their predictions. For example, a self-driving vehicle predicts, at each time instant, a steering direction, and observes as a reward whether that direction keeps the vehicle on its lane, with a low reward for a direction that carries it off the road.
terms.description: A self-driving car has to choose a steering direction at each time instant, and the optimal direction is never observed; what is observed is whether the chosen direction keeps the car on its lane (Fig. 1). The ultimate goal of machine learning is to learn a hypothesis that predicts the label of a data point well from its features, and choosing among different hypothesis maps requires a measure of the prediction error that a hypothesis incurs. Such a measure is the loss, which can be defined, for example, by comparing the prediction h(x) with the actual label value y. For the car, a data point is the current time instant and its label is the optimal steering direction, which cannot be accessed at all. A reward is an observed quantity from which a machine learning method estimates the loss incurred by the prediction of a hypothesis. One example of such a quantity is the label of a data point itself. Many machine learning applications, however, do not allow the label to be observed, but only a noisy estimate of it. Some allow only the prediction error of one specific prediction to be observed. The self-driving car of Fig. 1 is of the last kind: the reward is whether the steering direction h(x) predicted at a time instant keeps the car on its lane, and a low reward is assigned to a direction that carries the car over a contour of the road. A reward replaces the label of supervised learning: it does not reveal the correct prediction, only how good the chosen prediction, the action, was, and it may arrive delayed, several time steps after the action that caused it, or corrupted by noise. Reinforcement learning methods learn a sequence of hypothesis maps from the rewards obtained by their predictions: the negative reward is the loss of the action taken, and the actions chosen are those that maximize the cumulative reward, the return. In the self-driving car of Fig. 1, the state st is the position and orientation of the car on the road at time instant t, and the action at is the steering direction predicted there. Fig. 2 shows how states, actions and rewards follow one another over two time steps.

terms.name: ridge regression
terms.abstract: Ridge regression learns a linear hypothesis map by minimizing the average squared error loss on a training set plus a penalty term proportional to the squared Euclidean norm of the model parameters. The penalty term enforces regularization: it prevents overfitting when the number of features exceeds the number of data points, or when features are nearly collinear. In contrast to least absolute shrinkage and selection operator, ridge regression uses an objective function with a unique minimizer, given in closed form by one system of linear equations, for any training set. In the basis of the singular vectors of the feature matrix, ridge regression shrinks each component of the linear regression solution by a factor between 0 and 1 that is small for a small singular value, which bounds the noise amplification of linear regression. The penalty term represents the increase of the average squared error loss under data augmentation with random feature perturbations. Ridge regression on transformed feature vectors constructed from a kernel is kernel ridge regression.
terms.description: Predicting the maximum temperature of tomorrow at Krems an der Donau from the 24 hourly temperatures of today is a machine learning application. A data point is one day, its feature vector x ∈ R24 lists the hourly temperatures of the day, and its label y is the maximum temperature of the next day. A training set of m = 20 days of July 2024 has fewer data points than features, d = 24, and the features are nearly collinear: the temperatures at 13:00 and at 14:00 have correlation 0.93. Linear regression then learns a linear model that reproduces the 20 training labels exactly and predicts the maximum temperatures of August 2024, the test set, with a mean squared error of 141. Ridge regression learns a linear model from the same training set with a training mean squared error of 5.4 and a mean squared error of 8.3 on the test set (see Fig. 1). Ridge regression learns the model parameters w of a linear hypothesis map h(w)(x) = wᵀx, as does linear regression. It minimizes the penalized average squared error loss on a training set D(train) = ( x(r),y(r) ) r=1m, \begin{equation} \widehat{{\mathbf w}}^{(\alpha)} = \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big( y^{(r)} - {\mathbf w}^{\top}{\mathbf x}^{(r)} \big)^{2} + \alpha \left\lVert {\mathbf w} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{.} \end{equation} The optimization problem can be written more compactly using the feature matrix X and the label vector y, \[ {\mathbf X} = \big({\mathbf x}^{(1)}, \ldots, {\mathbf x}^{(m)}\big)^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d} \text{,} \qquad {\mathbf y} = \big( y^{(1)}, \ldots, y^{(m)} \big)^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{m} \text{.} \] In terms of X and y, the ridge regression problem Eq. (1) reads \[ \widehat{{\mathbf w}}^{(\alpha)} = \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}} \frac{1}{m} \left\lVert {\mathbf y} - {\mathbf X} {\mathbf w} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} + \alpha \left\lVert {\mathbf w} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{.} \] Ridge regression is obtained from linear regression by adding a penalty term to the average squared error loss. The penalty term is the scaled squared Euclidean norm α ‖ w ‖22 with a regularization parameter α > 0. The resulting method is an instance of regularized empirical risk minimization. The purpose of the penalty term is regularization. It prevents overfitting in the high-dimensional regime, where the number of features d exceeds the number of data points m in the training set, as it does for the 20 days with 24 hourly temperatures each. An alternative method for regularization is least absolute shrinkage and selection operator, which differs from ridge regression in the construction of the penalty term: least absolute shrinkage and selection operator uses the ℓ1-norm ‖ w ‖1 instead of the squared Euclidean norm ‖ w ‖22. In contrast to least absolute shrinkage and selection operator, whose objective can have several minimizers, the ridge regression objective function has, for any feature matrix X and label vector y, the unique minimizer \begin{equation} \widehat{{\mathbf w}}^{(\alpha)} = \big( {\mathbf X}^{\top}{\mathbf X} + \alpha m \mathbf{I} \big)^{-1} {\mathbf X}^{\top}{\mathbf y} \text{.} \end{equation} The normal equations of plain linear regression, by comparison, can have infinitely many solutions, as they do for the 20 days of July: every one of them reproduces the training labels. Training is a one-shot computation: ridge regression requires no iterative optimization method, and hence no fixed-point interpretation, only the solution of the d × d system of linear equations ( XᵀX + α m I ) w = Xᵀy with an invertible matrix, the zero-gradient condition of the penalized objective function. For many features, gradient descent on the penalized objective function is the alternative, and the penalty term adds α m to every eigenvalue of XᵀX, which lowers the condition number that sets the convergence rate of gradient descent. The singular value decomposition of the feature matrix shows why the linear regression solution amplifies the noise in the labels and how the penalty term bounds the amplification. Write X = V Λ Uᵀ with singular values λ1 ≥ … ≥ λp > 0, where p is the rank of X, with left singular vectors v(j) and right singular vectors u(j). The solution of linear regression with the smallest Euclidean norm is \[ \widehat{{\mathbf w}} = \sum_{j=1}^{p} \frac{({\mathbf v}^{(j)})^{\top}{\mathbf y}}{\lambda_{j}} {\mathbf u}^{(j)} \text{.} \] Two properties of this solution cause its large test error. A component of y along v(j) is divided by λj, so a small singular value amplifies the noise in y by the factor 1/λj. Small singular values arise from nearly collinear features: the singular values of the 20 days of hourly temperatures run from 504 down to 0.21. And a direction u(j) with j > p, which exists whenever d > m, leaves X w unchanged, so the training set does not determine the component of w along it. Inserting the singular value decomposition into the closed form Eq. (2) gives \[ \widehat{{\mathbf w}}^{(\alpha)} = \sum_{j=1}^{p} \frac{\lambda_{j}^{2}}{\lambda_{j}^{2} + \alpha m} \cdot \frac{({\mathbf v}^{(j)})^{\top}{\mathbf y}}{\lambda_{j}} {\mathbf u}^{(j)} \text{.} \] Ridge regression multiplies each component of ŵ in the basis of the right singular vectors by the shrinkage factor λj2 / (λj2 + α m), which lies strictly between 0 and 1. For λj2 ≫ α m the factor is close to 1 and the component is kept. For λj2 ≪ α m the component is shrunk toward 0. The product of the factor and 1/λj is λj / (λj2 + α m), which never exceeds 1/(2√(α m)), so the noise amplification is bounded: for the 20 days and α = 1, the bound is 0.11, where 1/λj reaches 4.9. The undetermined components with j > p are set to 0, which is why the minimizer is unique for any feature matrix. Fig. 1 shows the effect on the learned model parameters: those of linear regression swing between -4.1 and 4.9 from one hour to the next, those of ridge regression stay within ± 0.4. The penalty term α ‖ w ‖22 has an interpretation as a form of data augmentation. In particular, adding the penalty term to the average squared error loss of the hypothesis h(w) is equivalent to computing its average squared error loss on an augmented training set (see Fig. 2). This augmented training set is obtained from the original training set. For each data point ( x(r),y(r) ), r=1,…,m, the feature vector x(r) is replaced by realizations of infinitely many independent and identically distributed RVs x(r) + ε(r) with Gaussian RVs ε(r) ~ N(0,α I), i.e., each feature is perturbed independently with variance α. The label y(r) is left unchanged. The penalty term α ‖ w ‖22 is exactly the amount by which the average squared error loss of h(w) over the infinitely many perturbed copies of a data point exceeds its squared error loss on the original data point. Since E ε(r) = 0, the increase is \[ {\mathbb{E}} \big\{ \big( {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\boldsymbol \varepsilon}^{(r)} \big)^{2} \big\} = {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbb{E}} \big\{ {\boldsymbol \varepsilon}^{(r)} \big({\boldsymbol \varepsilon}^{(r)}\big)^{\top} \big\} {\mathbf w} = \alpha \left\lVert {\mathbf w} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{.} \] This increase of the average loss under data augmentation is an estimate for the generalization gap. Ridge regression applied to transformed feature vectors constructed from a kernel is kernel ridge regression, which learns a nonlinear hypothesis in closed form; the perturbation then acts on the transformed feature vectors.

terms.name: robust principal component analysis (robust PCA)
terms.abstract: Robust principal component analysis (robust PCA) decomposes a feature matrix into a low-rank matrix, whose rows lie in a subspace of small dimension, and a sparse matrix that carries a few corrupted feature values. Unlike principal component analysis, it does not compute the low-rank matrix from the recorded values, so a large fault lands in the sparse matrix instead of turning the subspace. One approach states robust PCA as a convex optimization problem, referred to as principal component pursuit. Convex optimization methods solve it, among them the alternating direction method of multipliers. The resulting method delivers estimates for the principal directions that span the subspace, and for the corrupted entries in the features of each data point.
terms.description: The weather station Krems an der Donau records the air temperature every hour, so ten days of 2024 give ten rows of 24 values (Fig. 1). Stacking the 24 values of one day gives the feature vector x ∈ Rd, with d = 24, of the corresponding data point. Stacking the m = 10 feature vectors row-wise gives the m × d feature matrix X. Each feature vector is centered by subtracting the average of the m feature vectors, so that this average is the zero vector. Principal component analysis uses the feature matrix to learn a given number d' of orthonormal vectors u(1), …, u(d'), the principal directions of X. They span a d'-dimensional subspace U of Rd such that each feature vector x(r), for r = 1, …, m, can be well approximated by its projection \mathbf{P} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} = \sum_{j=1}^{d'} \langle \mathbf{u}^{(j)}, {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \rangle \mathbf{u}^{(j)} \text{.} Here, P ∈ Rd × d denotes the orthogonal projection matrix on the subspace U. It is given explicitly by P=Σj=1d' u(j) ( u(j) )ᵀ and provides a fully equivalent representation of the subspace U spanned by the principal directions. The projection matrix P delivered by principal component analysis decomposes each feature vector as x(r) = P x(r) + e(r), with the approximation error e(r). These decompositions (one for each r=1,…,m) can be expressed more compactly in terms of the feature matrix as \begin{equation} {\mathbf X} = {\mathbf L} + \mathbf{E} \text{, where } {\mathbf L} = {\mathbf X} \mathbf{P} \text{ and } \mathbf{E} = {\mathbf X} - {\mathbf L} \text{.} \end{equation} The rank of L is at most d', since every row of L lies in the subspace U. The error matrix E carries the e(r) as its rows, so ‖ E ‖F2 = Σr=1m ‖ e(r) ‖22. Principal component analysis chooses P to make this quantity as small as possible. In this reading, principal component analysis splits the feature matrix into a low-rank part L and a small remainder E. The decomposition Eq. (1) suggests using a representation of the component P x(r) as new features. One such representation is the vector z(r) = ( ⟨ u(1), x(r) ⟩, …, ⟨ u(d'), x(r) ⟩ )ᵀ whose entries are the inner products between x(r) and the principal directions of the feature matrix X. For d' = 2 the new features z1, z2 can be used as coordinates in a scatterplot, as panel (a) of Fig. 2 shows. Sometimes a feature value is faulty, for example because a temperature sensor fails. The red square in Fig. 1 marks such a failure: the noon reading of day five is increased by 22 degrees, which gives the perturbed feature vector x̃(5) and, in turn, the perturbed feature matrix X̃. Panel (b) of Fig. 2 shows the scatterplot that principal component analysis delivers from X̃. The new features z(5)1, z(5)2 obtained for x̃(5) are far from those of the other days, and the second learned principal direction turns toward the axis of the perturbed feature. Thus, an isolated but large fault can substantially distort the coordinates of every data point. The decomposition Eq. (1) explains why. Applied to X̃, it has the low-rank part L = X̃ P, which is computed from the recorded values, and a remainder E that principal component analysis keeps small in the Frobenius norm. The 22 degrees can therefore not be left in E. Most of them have to appear in L, and the only way a matrix of rank at most d' can carry a large value at a single entry is for the subspace U to turn toward the faulty feature. Robust principal component analysis drops the constraint L = X P and adds a third summand for the faulty entries, \begin{equation} {\mathbf X} = {\mathbf L} + \mathbf{S} + \mathbf{E} \text{.} \end{equation} The low-rank matrix L is now an unknown in its own right, constrained only by rank(L) ≤ d'. The sparse matrix S carries the faulty feature values and is zero in every other entry. The remainder E stays small, as in the principal component analysis decomposition Eq. (1). Row r of the decomposition Eq. (2) splits the feature vector x(r) into these three parts. The subspace and the principal directions are computed from L afterwards. The rows of L span a subspace of dimension at most d', and the principal directions u(1), …, u(d') are the leading right singular vectors of L, delivered by its singular value decomposition. The projection matrix P follows from them, and L = L P holds because every row of L already lies in the subspace that P projects on. Robust principal component analysis therefore delivers the same objects as principal component analysis, but from a matrix L that is free of the faulty feature values, since S carries them. The goal of making E small while S carries only a few non-zero entries can be stated as an optimization problem \begin{equation} \min_{{\mathbf L}, \mathbf{S} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}} \left\lVert {\mathbf X} - {\mathbf L} - \mathbf{S} \right\rVert_{F} \quad \text{ subject to } \mathop{\mathrm{rank}}({\mathbf L}) \leq d', \left\lVert \mathbf{S} \right\rVert_{0} \leq s \text{.} \end{equation} The optimization variables are the two matrices L and S, and the objective function is the Frobenius norm of the remainder E = X - L - S. The pseudo-norm ‖ S ‖0 denotes the number of non-zero entries of S, and s is a given bound on the number of faulty feature values. The optimization problem Eq. (3) is non-convex, since neither the rank nor the number of non-zero entries is a convex function. Principal component pursuit replaces it with the convex optimization problem \begin{equation} \min_{{\mathbf L}, \mathbf{S} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}} \left\lVert {\mathbf L} \right\rVert_{*} + \alpha \left\lVert \mathbf{S} \right\rVert_{1} \quad \text{ subject to } {\mathbf X} = {\mathbf L} + \mathbf{S} \text{,} \end{equation} with a regularization parameter α > 0. Here, ‖ L ‖* is the sum of the singular values of L, and ‖ S ‖1 the sum of the absolute values of the entries of S. These two norms are convex, as every norm is, and take the place of the rank of L and of the number of non-zero entries of S. A large regularization parameter α makes every non-zero entry of S expensive, so the solution keeps S sparser and leaves more of X to L. The rank of L, and with it the dimension d' of the subspace, then comes out larger, while a small α has the opposite effect. Principal component analysis is an instance of empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss. Principal component pursuit Eq. (4) changes its hypothesis space, its criterion, and its optimization method. The hypothesis space is larger: a candidate of principal component analysis is one projection matrix P, which already fixes L = X P, whereas a candidate of robust principal component analysis is a pair (L, S), so the sparse matrix is a second unknown. The squared error loss is gone, because the constraint X = L + S leaves no remainder to measure. What principal component pursuit minimizes is therefore not a loss function. It is a convex relaxation of the rank and sparsity constraints of the non-convex optimization problem Eq. (3), and that relaxation is what makes the optimization problem tractable. The optimization method changes with the criterion: one singular value decomposition of the feature matrix suffices for principal component analysis, since its leading right singular vectors are the principal directions, whereas Algorithm 1 computes one singular value decomposition per iteration. Robust principal component analysis methods differ in the optimization method used to solve principal component pursuit Eq. (4). Algorithm 1 summarizes one such method, obtained by applying the alternating direction method of multipliers. Panel (c) of Fig. 2 shows the scatterplot that principal component analysis delivers from the low-rank matrix L that Algorithm 1 recovers from the perturbed feature matrix X̃. The ten days are back at the coordinates of panel (a). The non-zero entries of S point at the faulty readings themselves, which is why robust principal component analysis is also used for anomaly detection. Algorithm 1 is a fixed-point iteration \big({\mathbf L}^{(t+1)}, \mathbf{S}^{(t+1)}, {\mathbf W}^{(t+1)}\big) = T\big({\mathbf L}^{(t)}, \mathbf{S}^{(t)}, {\mathbf W}^{(t)}\big) \text{,} whose operator T chains two proximal operators with the update of the matrix W. Shrinking the singular values of B by 1/ρ is the proximal operator of the nuclear norm, which is why that step needs the singular value decomposition. Shrinking every entry of C by α/ρ is the proximal operator of ‖ · ‖1, the one that solvers for the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator also use and the one step where α enters the iteration. At a fixed point of T the three updates leave the iterate unchanged. A fixed point is reached precisely when X = L + S holds, (L, S) solves principal component pursuit Eq. (4), and ρ W is a Lagrange multiplier of the constraint. The optimization problem Eq. (4) is convex, so the iteration converges for every ρ > 0: the residual X - L - S tends to zero and the objective function to its minimum. For the averages of the iterates over the first T iterations, this convergence holds with an explicit bound. \begin{algorithm}[H] \caption{Principal component pursuit by alternating direction method of multipliers } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex Input: feature matrix X ∈ Rm × d, regularization parameter α>0, penalty parameter ρ>0, tolerance ε(tol)>0 \State L(0):=0, S(0):=0, W(0):=0, t:=0 \Repeat \State B := X-S(t)+W(t) \State compute the singular value decomposition B = V Λ Uᵀ, whose singular values are the diagonal entries Λj,j = λj ≥ 0, for j = 1, …, minm,d \State L(t+1) := V Λ Uᵀ, where Λ ∈ Rm × d has the diagonal entries maxλj - 1/ρ, 0 and is zero off the diagonal \State C := X-L(t+1)+W(t) \State S(t+1)r,j := sign(Cr,j) max|Cr,j| - α/ρ, 0, for r = 1,…,m and j = 1,…,d \State W(t+1):=W(t)+ X-L(t+1)-S(t+1) \State t:=t+1 \Until{‖ X-L(t) -S(t) ‖F ≤ε(tol)‖ X ‖F} \Statex Output: low-rank matrix L(t) and sparse matrix S(t) \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}

terms.name: random variable (RV)
terms.abstract: A random variable (RV) is a measurable function that maps each outcome of a random experiment to an element of a measurable space. Important types of RVs include binary RVs, discrete RVs, real-valued RVs, random vectors, and random matrices. The analysis of machine learning methods often relies on probabilistic models that represent data sources as RVs. The most widely used probabilistic model assumes that data points are independent and identically distributed RVs with a common probability distribution, which is unknown in general.
terms.description: The weather on a given day in the Austrian city Krems an der Donau is the outcome of a random experiment. Each possible outcome ω is characterized by a maximum daytime temperature, the temperature at 13:00, and recording this temperature assigns a real number x(ω) to the outcome. This assignment is an RV x. The temperatures recorded on consecutive days are realizations of this RV (see Fig. 1). More generally, an RV maps the outcomes of a random experiment to elements of a measurable space. Mathematically, an RV is a measurable function x: Ω → X whose domain is the sample space Ω of a probability space and whose co-domain is a measurable space X. Measurability refers to the σ-algebras of the two spaces: the preimage x-1(B) of every measurable set B ⊆ X must belong to the σ-algebra of the probability space, so that the probability of x taking a value in B is defined. The value x(ω) ∈ X that x assigns to an outcome ω ∈ Ω is the image of ω under x (see Fig. 2). Different types of RVs include \begin{itemize} \item {binary RVs}, which map each outcome to an element of a binary set (e.g., -1,1 or cat, no cat); \item {discrete RVs}, which take on values in a countable set (which can be finite or countably infinite; e.g., the number of heads in ten coin flips, with values in 0,1,…,10); \item {real-valued RVs}, which take on values in the real numbers R (e.g., the maximum daytime temperature in Krems); \item {random vectors}, which map outcomes to the Euclidean space Rd (e.g., the red-green-blue (RGB) values of a pixel, which form a vector in R3); \item {random matrices}, which map outcomes to a space of matrices Rm × d (e.g., the data matrix of a dataset). \end{itemize} The sample space and the RVs on it are a modeling choice, not fixed by the data. The daily Krems temperatures admit two standard constructions (Fig. 3). In the first, each day r has its own probability space with sample space Ω(r), and the temperature of that day is an RV x(r): Ω(r) → R; the recorded value is one realization x(r)(ω(r)). In the second, one probability space with sample space Ω represents all days at once: a single outcome ω ∈ Ω fixes the temperatures of all days, and each day is an RV x(r): Ω → R on this common space. The independent and identically distributed assumption is a statement about the second construction: the x(r) share one probability distribution and are independent, a property defined for RVs on one common probability space. The common-space construction is the one used for learning from data, because a single probability distribution then governs an entire dataset. In machine learning, RVs represent data sources, so that the behavior of learning methods can be analyzed. For example, the generation of a training set or validation set is represented by independent and identically distributed RVs sharing one underlying probability distribution in the common-space construction. This probability distribution is either postulated or estimated from actual datasets, for example via maximum likelihood. Ideally, a machine learning method should work well on datasets that arise as realizations of high probability. Good performance on those datasets is the generalization goal that empirical risk minimization pursues, minimizing the average loss on the training set as a proxy for the expected loss of the learned hypothesis on a new data point drawn from the common probability distribution.

terms.name: sample size
terms.abstract: The sample size is the number m of data points in a sample. It is the basic measure of how much a sample carries, but not a universal one: listing a data point twice raises the count and adds nothing, correlated data points make the count overstate what a sample carries, and it says nothing about how well the data points cover the feature space. Many machine learning methods model the data points as realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs and judge a hypothesis by its expected loss, the risk; since the probability distribution is unknown, the risk is estimated by the average loss on the sample, for training by empirical risk minimization and for validation. How close that average is to the risk depends on the sample size. A concentration inequality such as Hoeffding's inequality bounds the deviation of the average from the risk and turns a required accuracy ε and confidence 1 - δ into a sample size of order ln(1/δ) / ε2 for validation; for training, the sample size must also be compared with the size of the model. For data points recorded in sequence, autocorrelation lowers the effective sample size. The same reasoning gives the sample size for a statistical test, such as whether two features are correlated: the sample size needed to detect a correlation grows as the inverse square of that correlation.
terms.description: A frost warning for Krems an der Donau predicts, from the minimum and the maximum temperature of a day, whether the next day brings frost. A hypothesis h for this task is judged by its expected loss, the risk L̄ ( h ) = E L(z,h ), where the expectation is over a data point z drawn from the probability distribution P(z) of the days. Many machine learning methods use the independent and identically distributed assumption: the data points are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs z(1), …, z(m) ~ P(z). In practice, P(z) is unknown, and a method observes only these m data points, a sample. Their number m is the sample size. With the probability distribution unknown, the risk is estimated by the average loss on the sample, \begin{equation} \widehat{L}\big(h|\mathcal{D}\big) := \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\left({\mathbf z}^{(r)},h \right) \text{,} \end{equation} which is the empirical risk. Empirical risk minimization minimizes this average over the hypotheses of a model on a training set, and validation compares the learned hypotheses by the same average on a validation set. Both uses require the average to be close to the risk, and how close it is depends on the sample size: by the law of large numbers, the average Eq. (1) converges to L̄ ( h ) as m grows. Fig. 1 shows this for the frost warning: the sample average of the 0/1 loss of one fixed hypothesis, computed on samples of m = 10 to 1585 days, scatters around the risk 0.118 with a spread that falls like 1/√(m). The spread is the standard deviation of the average over repeated samples, and Hoeffding's inequality, stated below, turns it into a deviation that holds with a prescribed probability. The sample must be large enough, and one approach to deciding how large uses a concentration inequality, which bounds the probability that the average deviates from the risk by more than a given amount. For a loss function with values in [0, 1], such as the 0/1 loss, Hoeffding's inequality gives, for every ε > 0, \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}\left( \big| \widehat{L}\big(h|\mathcal{D}\big) - \bar{L} \big( h \big) \big| > \epsilon \right) \leq 2 \exp\big( -2 m \epsilon^{2} \big) \text{,} \end{equation} see Hoeffding (1963) and Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David (2014, Lemma 4.5). The bound holds for a hypothesis chosen before the sample is drawn, which is the situation of validation: the hypothesis was learned on the training set, and the validation set is a fresh sample. Setting the right-hand side to a tolerated failure probability δ and solving for m turns a required accuracy ε and confidence 1 - δ into a sample size: \begin{equation} m \geq \frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2 \epsilon^{2}} \text{,} \end{equation} and this many data points make the validation error lie within ε of the risk with probability at least 1 - δ. For the frost warning, ε = 0.05 and δ = 0.05 give m ≥ 738 days; at that sample size all of 2000 drawn samples (pythondemos/samplesize.py) lie within 0.05 of the risk. The bound is loose, since it holds for every probability distribution and every loss function in [0, 1]; the sample size Eq. (3) is therefore enough, but not always needed. Its shape is what carries over: halving ε quadruples the sample size, while the sample size grows only logarithmically in 1/δ. For training, the same question has a second answer. The hypothesis is then chosen by looking at the sample, so the bound Eq. (2) for a fixed hypothesis no longer applies to the learned one. The sample size then has to be compared with the size of the model. For a model of Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension d, a sample size proportional to d / ε2 makes the training error of every hypothesis in the model lie within ε of its risk at once. A sample that is small against the effective dimension of the model is the typical cause of overfitting, and the learning curve shows the validation error of the learned hypothesis as a function of the sample size. Sample size enters a third task, hypothesis testing: are two features of a data point correlated? For the days of 2024 at Krems, is the minimum temperature of a day correlated with its diurnal range, the maximum minus the minimum? Over the whole year, the Pearson correlation coefficient of the two features is ρ = 0.16. A test is given a sample of m days and computes the sample correlation r, a function of sample means. Under the hypothesis that the two features are independent, r scatters around 0 with a standard deviation close to 1/√(m). For features that are Gaussian RVs, the variance of r is exactly 1/(m-1). For independent features with finite variances of any other probability distribution, √(m) r converges to a standard Gaussian random variable by the central limit theorem applied to the products of the standardized features, whose variance is one under independence. For features that are Gaussian RVs, Fisher's transformation artanh(r) is approximately a Gaussian random variable with mean artanh(ρ) and standard deviation 1/√(m - 3). The test rejects ``uncorrelated'' when |artanh(r)| √(m - 3) exceeds the quantile z1-α/2 of the standard Gaussian random variable, which bounds the probability of a false rejection by the significance level α. A correlation ρ is then detected with probability at least 1 - β, the power of the test, once \begin{equation} m \geq 3 + \bigg( \frac{z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta}} {\operatorname{artanh}(\rho)} \bigg)^{2} \text{.} \end{equation} For ρ = 0.16, α = 0.05 (z0.975 = 1.96) and a power of 0.8 (z0.8 = 0.84), the sample size Eq. (4) is 304 days. Fig. 2 shows the power of the test against the sample size: 0.84 at m = 304, and 0.10 for a sample of 30 days. The shape is that of Eq. (3) again: halving the correlation to be detected quadruples the sample size, so a weak correlation needs a large sample before ``uncorrelated'' can be rejected. The count m is not by itself a measure of how much a sample carries. If it were, information could be created by copying: listing every day of a sample twice gives a sample of sample size 2m that says exactly what the original says. Its empirical distribution is unchanged, since each day now holds two entries of probability 1/(2m). So is the average loss Eq. (1) of every hypothesis, and so is the spread of that average over repeated samples. Only 2m days drawn afresh reduce that spread, by the factor √(2). Read with 2m in place of m, the bound Eq. (2) would promise a deviation smaller by that same factor. That promise does not follow, since a copy of a day is not independent of the day it copies, while Hoeffding's inequality holds for realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs. The sample size counts the entries of a list, and how much they carry depends on how the list was generated. Dependence is rarely as extreme as an outright copy. The sample sizes above assume independent and identically distributed RVs, and data points recorded in sequence, such as consecutive days, often show autocorrelation: a frost day is more likely after a frost day, and so is a wrong prediction. Dependent data points carry less information than independent ones. For a stationary sequence with autocorrelation ρℓ at lag ℓ, the variance of the average of m consecutive values is that of m independent values multiplied by \begin{equation} 1 + 2 \sum_{\ell=1}^{m-1} \Big( 1 - \frac{\ell}{m} \Big) \rho_{\ell} \text{,} \end{equation} see Brockwell and Davis (1991, Thm. 7.1.1). The average is therefore as accurate as that of m divided by Eq. (5) independent values, the effective sample size. For the 0/1 loss of the frost warning, the sample autocorrelation of consecutive days is 0.24 at lag 1 and stays positive for a week, and the factor Eq. (5) is 4.2 for m = 30. The average over 30 consecutive days therefore scatters as much as that over 7 days drawn at random. A sample of consecutive data points must then be larger than Eq. (3) or Eq. (4) say, by the factor Eq. (5), or be drawn at random from the whole record, as the days of Fig. 1 are. Dependence aside, the count says nothing about where the data points lie. Two samples of the same size can cover the feature space differently: one spread over the whole range of the features, the other crowded in a part of it. For a method whose prediction at a feature vector depends on the data points near it, the largest distance from a point of the feature space region of interest to the nearest data point governs the prediction error there, however large m is (see covering). A weather record of summer days alone, however long, leaves the winter part of the feature space empty, and no sample size compensates for it.

terms.name: scatterplot
terms.abstract: A scatterplot draws a dataset with two numeric features as one marker per data point, placed in the plane at the horizontal and vertical position given by the two feature values. It is how a dataset of two features is inspected by eye before and after a feature transformation, since clusters, outliers, and a trend along a line are visible in the picture and not in the table of numbers. Where the vertical axis carries the label of a data point, a hypothesis is a curve in the same plane, so the markers and the map that predicts their height are seen at once. A scatterplot of a split dataset draws the training set as filled circles, the validation set as open triangles, and the test set as open squares, so the three roles are told apart without color. Markers that nearly coincide hide each other, so a legible scatterplot carries at most about twenty of them, chosen by a stated rule, while every number quoted beside it is computed from the whole dataset. A dataset with more than two features is inspected by a matrix of scatterplots, one panel for every pair of features, or by a dimensionality reduction to two features.
terms.description: Consider the 366 days of 2024 at Krems an der Donau (Austria), each recorded by a morning minimum and a maximum daytime temperature. A table of 366 rows of two numbers hides what one marker per day in the plane shows at a glance, at the horizontal position of the minimum and the vertical position of the maximum. That picture is a scatterplot: the drawing of a dataset D = x(1), …, x(m) whose data points carry two numeric features, x(r) = (x(r)1, x(r)2)ᵀ ∈ R2, with the rth marker placed at (x(r)1, x(r)2) for r = 1, …, m. Nothing but the two numbers of a data point decides where its marker goes, so the picture holds the same information as the dataset. A single feature is pictured by a histogram instead, which keeps the values and discards the pairing. In a machine learning application, one of the two numbers is often the label and the other the feature. The vertical axis then carries the label y, and a hypothesis h is drawn in the same plane as the curve through the points (x, h(x)), so that the markers and the map that predicts their height are seen at once. A scatterplot of a split dataset carries the role of each data point in its marker shape and needs no color: the training set D(train) is drawn as filled circles, the validation set D(val) as open triangles, and the test set D(test) as open squares. Fig. 1(a) draws the days at Krems this way, with the hypothesis ĥ learned by least squares on the 220 training set days, and Fig. 1(b) draws the same days after a feature transformation. Four properties of a dataset are visible in the picture and not in the table of numbers. The markers of Fig. 1(a) lie along a rising line, a sample correlation coefficient of 0.88 over all 366 days. A marker far from the others is an outlier: over all 366 days the largest deviation from the learned line is 10.8 degrees, on 7 April 2024, whose maximum of 28.5 degrees followed a minimum of 7.1. Markers that fall into separated groups show the clusters of a dataset before any clustering method is run, and a region of the plane left empty shows where a hypothesis will be used without evidence. A feature transformation changes the picture, and the two pictures beside each other say what it did. Fig. 1(b) replaces the two recorded temperatures by the daily mean (x1 + x2)/2 and the daily range x2 - x1, an invertible linear map. The elongated cloud becomes a cloud with no line through it: over all 366 days the sample correlation coefficient falls from 0.88 to 0.43, and the daily mean alone carries 76.6 percent of the sum of the two sample variances, against 39.0 percent for the morning minimum. Keeping one of two features is the smallest dimensionality reduction, and a scatterplot is how its cost is judged by eye. Markers that nearly coincide hide each other, so a scatterplot stays legible only while it carries few of them. Of the 366 days at Krems, 176 lie within half a degree of another day and overlap at any legible marker size. A scatterplot therefore draws about twenty data points at most, chosen by a stated rule, while every number quoted beside it is computed from the whole dataset. The 21 days of Fig. 1 are chosen this way, and no two of them lie within half a degree of each other; their sample correlation coefficient is 0.94, close to the 0.88 of all 366 days. A dataset with more than two features has no single scatterplot. One answer is a matrix of them, one panel for every pair of features, and another is a dimensionality reduction to two features, such as principal component analysis, after which the picture shows what survived the reduction. Neither answer is free. A matrix of panels grows with the square of the number of features, and it asks the reader to hold one panel against another. A reduction to two features draws the new features and not the recorded ones. What the scatterplot buys for that price is what a table of numbers withholds: a dataset a reader takes in at a glance. The device has outlived every change in how data are stored, and the first known scatterplot is Herschel's 1833 plot of the position angle against the separation of double stars.

terms.name: self-supervised learning
terms.abstract: Self-supervised learning constructs the labels of a training set from the data points themselves. Some features of a data point are withheld and used as its label while the rest remain features, so what results is an ordinary supervised learning problem, solved by empirical risk minimization on data that no annotator has touched. In natural language processing the withheld feature is the next token, which is how a large language model is trained. In computer vision it is a set of pixels, deleted from an image and predicted from the patches left visible.
terms.description: An open image database returns thousands of photographs for a keyword such as cat, and a web crawl yields billions of sentences. Neither comes with a label saying what should be predicted. A prediction task can be made from any one of them: hide the last word of a sentence, and the words before it become a question whose answer is already known. Self-supervised learning constructs labels this way, from the data point itself. In general, some of the features of a data point are withheld and used as the label; the remaining ones stay as the features. The result is an ordinary supervised learning problem, solved by empirical risk minimization, and its training set needs nothing beyond the raw data. A single unlabeled collection yields as many training sets as there are ways of hiding part of a data point (see Fig. 1). The term goes back to de Sa (1993), who uses it for a classifier whose label for one sensory modality is derived from a co-occurring input in another. The withheld feature can be a token. In natural language processing a data point is a stretch of text, its features are the n tokens v(1), …, v(n) of a context window of length n, and its label is the token v(n+1) that follows. Every position in every document is one labeled data point, so a corpus of m tokens gives on the order of m of them. Predicting the next token is the training task of a large language model such as GPT-3, an autoregressive language model, i.e., one trained to predict the next token. Masking a token in the middle and predicting it from both sides withholds a different feature of the same data point. Similarly, in computer vision the withheld features are pixels: an image is split into patches, most of them are deleted, and the method predicts the missing pixel values from those that remain. He et al. (2022, Sect. 1 and Fig. 2) delete 75% of the patches and still recover recognizable content. A deep net solving either task computes a composition ĥ = s ∘ φ. The feature transformation φ X → Rd, with X the set of raw inputs (texts or images), sends a data point to a vector of activations, and the map s predicts the withheld feature from that vector. That feature can be predicted only from what φ has kept: a next token cannot be recovered from a vector that has discarded the context, nor a deleted patch from one that has dropped its surroundings. Training the composition therefore constrains φ to keep that information, even though φ appears nowhere in the loss. The constraint does not determine φ uniquely: for any invertible map g of Rd onto itself, the composition (s ∘ g-1) ∘ (g ∘ φ) equals s ∘ φ and so has the same loss. He et al. (2022, Sect. 3) name the two halves: their encoder is φ and receives only the patches left visible, while their decoder is s and rebuilds the pixels from its output. What restricts φ there is the deletion of most of the input, not a narrow layer as in an autoencoder. In both domains it is φ that is carried over. The map s is dropped, and a small replacement for it is fitted on the output of φ using the few labels the later task does have (see transfer learning, foundation model). Self-supervised learning is therefore one answer to the same shortage that motivates semi-supervised learning: there, unlabeled data points assist a label-scarce problem directly; here, they are turned into a labeled problem of their own first. Unsupervised learning is the third answer, and it gives up the label entirely: it finds structure among the feature vectors instead of predicting a withheld one.

terms.name: sensitive attribute
terms.abstract: A sensitive attribute of a data point is an attribute, such as gender or ethnic origin, that must not influence the prediction a machine learning system delivers for that data point, whether or not it belongs to the feature vector. The word carries two senses that are kept apart: a regulatory one, in which data protection law fixes which categories of personal data are special, and a machine learning one, in which the application names the attribute s that a fairness criterion compares predictions across. Dropping s from the feature vector does not remove it from the data, because the remaining features can be dependent on it. Learned features, such as those principal component analysis delivers, are no exception: the criterion that learns them never mentions s, and they can be predictive of it all the same. How much of s they carry is measured by the recovery accuracy, the accuracy with which a linear classifier predicts s from them on data points it was not learned from. For the weather at Krems an der Donau (Austria), two learned features recover the half of the year a day belongs to with a recovery accuracy of 0.94, against a majority-class rate of 0.51. Projection of the learned features onto the orthogonal complement of the direction the linear classifier uses lowers that accuracy without bringing it to the majority-class rate, so a sensitive attribute is easier to measure than to remove.
terms.description: Consider a bank that decides on loan applications from the income, the occupation, and the address of an applicant. A supervisor asks whether the decisions depend on the gender of the applicant. The bank answers that the gender was never recorded as a feature: the feature vector x that the learned hypothesis ĥ reads holds those three numbers and nothing else. That answer settles nothing. The occupation and the address of an applicant can be predictive of the gender, and a prediction computed from x then depends on the gender all the same. A sensitive attribute of a data point is an attribute that must not influence the prediction delivered for that data point, whether or not it belongs to the feature vector. A data point then carries three parts: the feature vector x ∈ X, the label y, and the sensitive attribute s, which typically takes few values. The gender of a loan applicant is written s ∈ 0, 1 below. Which attribute counts as sensitive is settled in two different ways, and the two senses are kept apart. In the regulatory sense, the answer is given by law. The general data protection regulation prohibits, with exceptions, the processing of personal data revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, or trade union membership, and of genetic data, biometric data used to identify a person, health data, and data concerning sex life or sexual orientation. The EU AI Act adopts that list under the name special categories of personal data. In the machine learning sense, the application decides, and its choice need not belong to that list: the gender of the loan applicant is a sensitive attribute of the example above and is not a special category under the GDPR. A fairness criterion compares the predictions of ĥ across the values of s, while privacy protection asks instead that the output of the machine learning system not allow inference of s, an inference measured by privacy leakage. The obvious mitigation is the one the bank applied: leave s out of the feature vector. It removes s from the feature vector and not from the data. The data point is modeled as a realization of RVs, with the feature vector and the sensitive attribute drawn jointly. The attribute is still present whenever the two are dependent, \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}\left(s = 1 \mid {\mathbf x} \in \mathcal{A}\right) \neq \mathbb{P}\left(s = 1\right) \text{ for some } \mathcal{A} \subseteq \mathcal{X} \text{.} \end{equation} A feature for which the dependence Eq. (1) holds is a proxy for s. Such redundant encodings are what lets a decision rule that ignores s discriminate all the same. Feature learning does not undo the dependence Eq. (1). It replaces the raw features by learned ones, z = Φ(x) ∈ Rd', delivered by a feature transformation Φ that is itself learned from a dataset. Principal component analysis learns a linear Φ whose rows are the d' eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix with the largest eigenvalues, a criterion in which s never appears. The learned features can be predictive of s nonetheless, and how much of it they carry is a number that can be measured. A linear classifier ĥ(s) that predicts s from z is learned by least squares on a training set D(train), and its recovery accuracy is its accuracy on a test set D(test) of data points outside D(train), \begin{equation} \operatorname{acc}\big(\widehat{h}^{(s)} \mid \mathcal{D}^{(\rm test)}\big) := 1 - \frac{1}{\big|\mathcal{D}^{(\rm test)}\big|} \sum_{({\mathbf z}, s) \in \mathcal{D}^{(\rm test)}} L^{(0/1)}\left(({\mathbf z}, s),\widehat{h}^{(s)} \right) \text{,} \end{equation} with the 0/1 loss, which is 1 for a wrong prediction and 0 otherwise. The recovery accuracy Eq. (2) is read against the majority-class rate, the accuracy of predicting the more frequent value of s for every data point. The features that principal component analysis learns from the weather at Krems an der Donau (Austria) show what this measurement reports. Each day from January 6 to December 31 of 2024 is a data point, and its raw features are the eight daily measurements of each of the five previous days, forty numbers. Its attribute s says whether the day lies in the cold half of the year, October through March; 178 of the 361 days do, so the majority-class rate is 0.51. The half-year is not among the forty raw features. Each raw feature is scaled to zero sample mean and unit sample variance first, because temperatures, precipitation, and pressure carry different units. Two learned features recover it with a recovery accuracy Eq. (2) of 0.94, averaged over twenty random splits of the days into two halves, D(train) and D(test), and a single learned feature already gives 0.94. The decision boundary of one such linear classifier is a line in the plane of the two learned features (Fig. 1(a)). Dropping every temperature measurement from the raw features, the obvious proxy for the season, leaves twenty-five numbers per day. The recovery accuracy is then 0.82 with two learned features and 0.89 with five. The two curves of Fig. 1(b) compare the two sets of raw features for d' = 1, …, 10. The half-year of a day is not a sensitive attribute. It stands in for one here, and the computation does not depend on what the attribute means. A sensitive attribute is easier to measure than to remove. The linear classifier ĥ(s) uses a single direction of the learned feature space, the one given by its learned model parameters ŵ. The projection of the learned features onto the orthogonal complement of that direction, the nullspace of the linear map z ↦ ŵᵀ z, removes it and no more. For ten learned features of the days at Krems, a linear classifier learned afresh on the projected features still reaches 0.84 on one of the twenty splits, against 0.93 before the projection, so the other directions carry the attribute too. Learning a feature transformation under a penalty term for the recovery of s attacks the same problem where the features are learned. Every one of these steps needs s to be recorded, which is why the EU AI Act lets a provider of a high-risk artificial intelligence system process special categories of personal data when that is strictly necessary for detecting and correcting bias, under safeguards.

terms.name: sigmoid function
terms.abstract: The sigmoid function maps the real line into the open interval (0, 1). It translates the real-valued score of a binary classifier into an estimate for the probability of a specific label value. It is smooth and strictly increasing, with a derivative that approaches zero as the magnitude of the argument grows. Machine learning uses it in two roles: as an activation function inside a neuron, and as part of the log-likelihood function for learning the model parameters of a probabilistic model.
terms.description: A frost warning for Krems an der Donau has to say how likely frost is, not only whether it is expected. Fig. 1 shows minimum daytime temperatures measured at that station. A classifier that warns of frost reads the lowest temperature of a day, its feature vector x with this single feature, and delivers a real-valued score h(x). The classification is a threshold: a frost warning for the next day is issued if and only if h(x) > 0, and the magnitude |h(x)| measures the confidence in that warning. In practice it is often more useful to state a probability. The sigmoid function translates the score h(x) into a number between 0 and 1 that can be read as the probability of frost, as Fig. 1 shows for its last day. The sigmoid function maps the real line into the open interval (0, 1). It is the function σ: R → (0,1) given by \[ \sigma(z) := \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} \text{.} \] It rises from σ(z) → 0 as z → -∞ to σ(z) → 1 as z → +∞, and passes through σ(0) = 1/2 (see Fig. 2). It is also called the logistic function. For two classes with scores z and 0, the softmax function returns the pair (σ(z), 1 - σ(z)), so the sigmoid function is the softmax function for two classes: it delivers the probability of one class, and the other class has the complementary probability. The sigmoid function is smooth and strictly increasing, and it satisfies the symmetry σ(-z) = 1 - σ(z). Its derivative is available in closed form, and in terms of the function itself, \[ \sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)\big(1 - \sigma(z)\big) \text{.} \] These properties make the sigmoid function a popular choice for the activation function of an artificial neural network. One drawback of that choice is that the derivative decreases quickly as the argument grows in magnitude, which slows the progress of gradient-based learning methods, the vanishing gradient problem. The vanishing gradient problem is why sigmoidal activation functions are rarely used in the hidden layers of feedforward deep nets, where other activation functions such as the rectified linear unit are preferred. A probabilistic model for a binary label uses the sigmoid function to turn a score into a probability. Let the label y be either 1 or -1, and let the score be wᵀ x with model parameters w. The model reads \[ \mathbb{P}\left(y = 1 \mid {\mathbf x}\right) = \sigma\big({\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x}\big) \text{,} \qquad \mathbb{P}\left(y = -1 \mid {\mathbf x}\right) = \sigma\big(-{\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x}\big) \text{,} \] where the second follows from the symmetry σ(-z) = 1 - σ(z). Both cases are the single expression σ(y wᵀ x), which is where the sigmoid function enters the log-likelihood. For a training set D(train) = ( x(r),y(r) ) r=1m of labeled data points, the log-likelihood of the model parameters is \[ \sum_{r=1}^{m} \ln \sigma\big( y^{(r)} {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \big) \text{.} \] Maximizing it over w is maximum likelihood estimation, and it is logistic regression. Each summand is the negative of a logistic loss, so maximizing the log-likelihood and minimizing the average logistic loss are the same computation. For example, consider the classifier map h learned by logistic regression from the days of 2024 at Krems. Where its score is zero the sigmoid returns 1/2, so the warning is issued exactly where the probability passes one half. A score of 2.120 becomes a probability of 0.89 for frost tomorrow, and a score of -2.637 becomes 0.07.

terms.name: Sobolev space
terms.abstract: A Sobolev space is a set of functions whose derivatives, taken in a generalized sense, have bounded size. Machine learning methods whose hypothesis space is a ball in a Sobolev space with a bound on the gradient enforce a well-defined quantitative notion of robustness. Any hypothesis map in such a ball can be locally approximated by a linear map with bounded slope. A small change of the features of a data point therefore changes the prediction by at most a proportional amount. The generalized derivative is needed because hypothesis maps such as those of a deep net with rectified linear unit activation functions have kinks. A decision tree, whose hypothesis map jumps, belongs to no Sobolev space and admits no such guarantee. Linear regression whose hypothesis space is a ball in a Sobolev space, rather than the linear maps, is nonparametric regression. Sobolev norms also serve as regularizers, and they describe the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of a Matérn kernel.
terms.description: A weather service forecasts the maximum temperature of a day from its minimum temperature. Fig. 1(a) shows 20 of the 366 days of 2024 at the station Krems an der Donau of GeoSphere Austria as the data points of a scatterplot, with the minimum temperature of a day as its feature and the maximum temperature as its label. The panel also shows three hypotheses learned from these data points: the non-linear map of a deep net with rectified linear unit activation functions, the step function of a depth-2 decision tree, and the curve of linear regression with a Sobolev penalty term. A trustworthy forecaster must not change its prediction, the forecast, abruptly: a thermometer error of half a degree in the minimum temperature must not move the forecast by several degrees. Sobolev spaces make this requirement precise. They consist of the functions whose derivatives have bounded size. A bound on the derivative is a bound on how fast the forecast can change. The derivative is understood in a generalized sense, since the deep net of Fig. 1(a) has kinks and no classical derivative exists there. The generalized derivative starts from integration instead of differentiation. On the real line, a function with f(x) = f(a) + ∫ax g(t) dt is the integral of its slope g, and g is called a weak derivative of f. On an open set Ω ⊆ Rd, consider an infinitely differentiable test function that vanishes outside a bounded subset of Ω. A function gj is a weak partial derivative of f if, for every such , \[ \int_{\Omega} f({\mathbf x}) \frac{\partial \varphi({\mathbf x})}{\partial x_{j}} \mathrm{d}{\mathbf x} = - \int_{\Omega} g_{j}({\mathbf x}) \varphi({\mathbf x}) \mathrm{d}{\mathbf x} \text{.} \] This is integration by parts with all derivatives moved onto . It holds when f is the integral of gj along the jth coordinate, and it does not require a derivative of f at any particular point. The slope of the deep net, the step function of Fig. 1(b), satisfies it for every test function tried (pythondemos/sobolevspace.py). For p ∈ [1,∞], the Sobolev space W1,p(Ω) consists of the functions whose weak derivatives exist and have finite Lp norm ‖ · ‖p. The case p = 2 gives the Hilbert space H1(Ω), and the spaces Wk,p(Ω) require weak derivatives up to order k. The case that matters most for machine learning is W1,∞, the functions with a bounded weak gradient. On a convex set Ω, a function f belongs to it with ess supx ∈ Ω ‖ ∇ f(x) ‖2 ≤ L precisely when it is Lipschitz continuous with constant L.
