Perturbing a feature vector by δ then changes f by at most L ‖ δ ‖2: convexity keeps the segment from x to x + δ inside Ω, and integrating the gradient along it bounds the change by L ‖ δ ‖2. Conversely, the gradient of a Lipschitz continuous f exists almost everywhere, and where it exists its length is the slope of f in its own direction, at most L. The deep net of Fig. 1 has L = 2.44, so an error of 0.5 ∘C in the minimum temperature moves its forecast by at most 1.22 ∘C; the largest change among 20000 random perturbations of that size was 1.21 ∘C. The guarantee comes from the bound, not from the space: W1,∞ contains functions with every value of L. A machine learning method whose hypothesis space is the ball of functions with slope at most L learns a robust hypothesis by construction, whatever the training set. The choice p = ∞ is what makes the bound hold at every feature vector; H1 bounds the slope only on average. The bound concerns perturbations of the features only; robustness against perturbations of the training set is a property of the training map (see stability). The bound also says that near almost every feature vector the hypothesis agrees with a linear map whose slope is at most L (Rademacher's theorem, ). This linear map is the explanation that gradient-based explainable artificial intelligence delivers and that local interpretable model-agnostic explanations fits from perturbed data points. For the forecast, it reads: one additional degree in the minimum adds s(x) degrees to the forecast, with the slope s(x) of Fig. 1(b) between 0 and 2.44. Since the deep net is piecewise linear, the approximation is exact whenever no kink lies between x and x + δ for a perturbation δ of the minimum temperature, which is the case for most pairs with |δ| ≤ 0.1 ∘C. For the deep net, the weak gradient is bounded by the product of the spectral norms of its weight matrices, i.e., of their largest singular values, here 46.0 against the true 2.44: valid but loose. For a classifier that takes the sign of such an f, the bound certifies that no perturbation of Euclidean norm below |f(x)|/L changes the prediction, since |f(x + δ) - f(x)| ≤ L ‖ δ ‖2 < |f(x)| leaves the sign of f unchanged. The decision tree of Fig. 1(a) has no such bound: at its root threshold of 5.5 ∘C, a change of 2 · 10-9 ∘C in the minimum temperature moves the forecast by 7.81 ∘C. A jump has no weak derivative that is a function, so no Sobolev space contains the tree. Sobolev spaces also serve as hypothesis spaces in their own right. Plain linear regression minimizes the average squared error loss over the linear maps. Replacing the linear maps by a ball in H1, or equivalently adding the squared H1 seminorm ∫Ω ‖ ∇ f(x) ‖22 dx as a penalty term, a norm that ignores constant shifts of f (see regularization), gives nonparametric regression. The dotted curve of Fig. 1(a) minimizes the training error plus ten times that seminorm; it reaches a training error of 18.03, below the 18.66 of the deep net, with slope at most 3.05 (pythondemos/sobolevspace.py). A computer cannot search all of H1, and it need not. For a scalar feature, where Ω is an interval of the real line, a minimizer of the training error plus the seminorm is piecewise linear with kinks at the m data points, since between two data points the straight line has the smallest seminorm for given end values (a consequence of the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality). The search therefore runs over m numbers, the values at the kinks; this is kernel ridge regression with the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of H1. For a piecewise linear function the seminorm is a sum of squared slopes, one per segment and weighted by its length, so the normal equations of the penalized problem form one linear system. The seminorm expresses the smoothness assumption. Its counterpart for a function on the nodes of a graph replaces the gradient by differences across edges, the form used by generalized total variation and generalized total variation minimization; penalizing the gradient in L1 instead gives total variation regularization, which allows jumps. The reproducing kernel Hilbert space of a Matérn kernel is a Sobolev space Ws,2(Ω) whose order s is set by the smoothness parameter of the kernel. A kernel method with that kernel is therefore again nonparametric regression over a Sobolev ball, the setting of Wainwright (2019, Ch. 13) above. Finally, a bound L is also of regulatory interest. Article 15 of the EU AI Act requires a high-risk artificial intelligence system to be robust and to have its accuracy metrics declared in the instructions for use. A Lipschitz constant is such a metric: it states, as a single number, how much a perturbation of a feature vector can change the prediction.

terms.name: soft clustering
terms.abstract: Soft clustering assigns each data point to every cluster with a degree of belonging, a number between zero and one, so that the degrees of belonging of one data point form a vector in the probability simplex. Hard clustering is the special case in which this vector is a vertex of the simplex, with one entry equal to one and the others equal to zero. For numeric feature vectors, the principled choice of the degrees of belonging is the posterior distribution of the cluster index under a Gaussian mixture model whose model parameters are learned by the expectation–maximization algorithm. With equal cluster probabilities and covariance matrices σ2 I, the degrees of belonging tend to the vertices as σ2 shrinks, and the expectation–maximization algorithm becomes Lloyd's algorithm for k-means. Fuzzy c-means delivers degrees of belonging without a probabilistic model by minimizing a weighted clustering error over the simplex, and it also reduces to k-means as its fuzzifier tends to one. Assigning each data point to the cluster with the largest degree of belonging turns a soft clustering into a hard clustering, and one minus that largest degree of belonging measures how far the assignment is from certain.
terms.description: Consider the 366 days of 2024 at Krems an der Donau, each a data point with a feature vector x ∈ R2 that holds the morning minimum and the maximum daytime temperature of the day. k-means with k = 2 clusters assigns every day to the nearer of two cluster centroids, (1.5, 10.5) for 192 cold days and (13.4, 26.1) for 174 warm days. A day in April whose temperatures lie halfway between the two cluster centroids becomes a cold day or a warm day all the same, and nothing records that it was a borderline case. Soft clustering keeps that information: it assigns each data point to every cluster with a degree of belonging uc(r), a number between 0 and 1 for data point r = 1, …, m and cluster c = 1, …, k. The degrees of belonging of one data point form the vector \begin{equation} {\mathbf u}^{(r)} := \big(u_{1}^{(r)}, \ldots, u_{k}^{(r)}\big)^{\top} \in \Delta^{k-1}, \quad \text{i.e., } u_{c}^{(r)} \geq 0 \text{ and } \sum_{c=1}^{k} u_{c}^{(r)} = 1 \text{,} \end{equation} a point of the probability simplex Δk-1. A hard clustering is the special case in which every vector Eq. (1) is a vertex of the simplex: one entry is 1 and the other k-1 entries are 0. A soft clustering method learns a hypothesis h: X → Δk-1 that maps a feature vector to a degree of belonging vector, so it can be evaluated for a day that did not belong to the dataset. A hard clustering method learns a map into the k vertices only. For data points with numeric feature vectors, the principled choice of the degrees of belonging is a probabilistic model, the Gaussian mixture model. It generates a data point by drawing a cluster index I with probabilities p1, …, pk and then the feature vector from the multivariate normal distribution of that cluster, with mean μ(c) and covariance matrix C(c). The degree of belonging of data point x(r) to cluster c is the posterior distribution of its cluster index, \begin{equation} u_{c}^{(r)} := \mathbb{P}\left(I = c \mid {\mathbf x}^{(r)}\right) = \frac{p_{c} \mathcal{N}\left({\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)},\mathbf{C}^{(c)}\right) ({\mathbf x}^{(r)})} {\sum_{c'=1}^{k} p_{c'} \mathcal{N}\left({\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c')},\mathbf{C}^{(c')}\right) ({\mathbf x}^{(r)})} \text{,} \end{equation} which Bishop (2006, Sect. 9.2) calls the responsibility of cluster c for the data point. The model parameters are learned by maximum likelihood with the expectation–maximization algorithm, whose E-step computes the degrees of belonging Eq. (2) and whose M-step recomputes the model parameters as averages weighted by them. Maximum likelihood is empirical risk minimization with the negative logarithm of the probability density function as the loss, so the learned model parameters minimize a clustering error, and the expectation–maximization algorithm is a fixed-point iteration that never increases it. On the days at Krems, the expectation–maximization algorithm started from the k-means cluster centroids stops after 273 iterations with cluster probabilities 0.63 and 0.37 and means (3.1, 12.4) and (14.2, 27.5). For 58 of the 366 days, no degree of belonging reaches 0.8; 23 of them are in May, and none is in January, February, November, or December. A soft clustering is turned into a hard clustering by assigning each data point to the cluster with the largest degree of belonging, and 1 - maxc = 1, …, k uc(r) measures how far that assignment is from certain. For the days at Krems, this assignment agrees with k-means on 335 of the 366 days. Fig. 1(a) shows why the two disagree: the curve on which the two degrees of belonging Eq. (2) are equal is not the decision boundary of k-means, the perpendicular bisector of the two cluster centroids. It bends around the warm cluster, because the warm days scatter less than the cold ones and the covariance matrix of the warm cluster is smaller. Hard clustering is a limit of the Gaussian mixture model. Fix every cluster probability at 1/k and every covariance matrix at σ2 I, a multiple of the identity matrix with one common σ2; this shrinks the hypothesis space, which is model pruning, one of the three routes that regularization distinguishes. The degree of belonging Eq. (2) then depends on the feature vector only through its squared Euclidean distances to the means, \begin{equation} u_{c}^{(r)} = \frac{\exp\big(- \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} / (2\sigma^{2})\big)} {\sum_{c'=1}^{k} \exp\big(- \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {\boldsymbol \mu}^{(c')} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} / (2\sigma^{2})\big)} \text{,} \end{equation} the softmax function of the negative squared Euclidean distances divided by 2σ2. As σ2 shrinks towards 0, the degree of belonging Eq. (3) of the nearest mean tends to 1 and all others to 0, so the vector Eq. (1) tends to the vertex of the nearest-cluster centroid assignment, and the expectation–maximization algorithm becomes Lloyd's algorithm for k-means. With the means at the k-means cluster centroids of the days at Krems, 26 days have a degree of belonging between 0.2 and 0.8 for σ2 = 25, three days for σ2 = 4, and none for σ2 = 1, while for every σ2 the largest degree of belonging names the nearest cluster centroid. Fig. 1(b) draws the degree of belonging to the cold cluster along the line through the two cluster centroids, parametrized by s with s = 0 at the cold and s = 1 at the warm cluster centroid. Along this line, k-means jumps from 1 to 0 at s = 1/2, the Gaussian mixture model crosses 1/2 later and gradually, and the constrained Gaussian mixture model with σ2 = 4 is close to the jump. Fuzzy c-means delivers degrees of belonging without a probabilistic model. It minimizes a weighted clustering error, \begin{equation} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \sum_{c=1}^{k} \big(u_{c}^{(r)}\big)^{\varphi} \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(c)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{,} \end{equation} jointly over the cluster centroids w(1), …, w(k) ∈ Rd and the degrees of belonging, each vector Eq. (1) constrained to the probability simplex, with a fuzzifier > 1. For fixed cluster centroids, the minimizing degrees of belonging are proportional to ‖ x(r) - w(c) ‖2-2/(- 1), normalized to sum to one; for fixed degrees of belonging, the minimizing cluster centroid w(c) is the average of the feature vectors weighted by (uc(r)). Alternating the two updates is a fixed-point iteration: each update minimizes the objective Eq. (4) exactly in one block of variables with the other fixed, so no iteration increases the objective, and a fixed point is a pair of cluster centroids and degrees of belonging at which neither update changes anything. As tends to 1, the degrees of belonging tend to the vertices of the simplex and the objective Eq. (4) to the clustering error of k-means. With = 1.05 on the days at Krems, the cluster centroids lie within 0.05 of those of k-means and the objective is 42.0, the clustering error of k-means. For 358 of the 366 days, the largest degree of belonging exceeds 0.99. With = 2, 66 days have no degree of belonging of 0.8 or more, and with = 10 every degree of belonging lies between 0.26 and 0.74. The degrees of belonging of fuzzy c-means decay like the reciprocal of a squared Euclidean distance, so far away from every cluster centroid they approach 1/k. At the ends of the line in Fig. 1(b), the degree of belonging to the cold cluster is 0.91 at s = -1/2 and 0.09 at s = 3/2, where the Gaussian mixture model gives 1 and 0 to within 0.02. In image segmentation by clustering the patches of a photograph by their colors, a patch on the horizon between a mountain and the sky is partly both, and its degree of belonging vector records both shares while a hard clustering must choose one. A soft clustering of the days at Krems records the transitional days of spring and autumn, which a hard clustering into a cold and a warm regime hides.

terms.name: spectral clustering
terms.abstract: Spectral clustering is a graph clustering method that computes the clusters of a dataset from the eigenvectors of the Laplacian matrix of a graph whose nodes are the data points and whose edge weights express their similarity. The Laplacian matrix is positive semi-definite, and the multiplicity of its eigenvalue 0 equals the number of connected components of the graph, with their indicator vectors as eigenvectors. For k clusters, the entries of the k eigenvectors with the smallest eigenvalues form a new feature vector for each node, and k-means on these feature vectors delivers the clusters. For two clusters, the method thresholds the Fiedler vector. Spectral clustering is a relaxation of the ratio cut, which divides the total weight of the edges between the clusters by their sizes, and the second-smallest eigenvalue is a lower bound on the ratio cut of every bipartition. Unlike k-means on the raw feature vectors, spectral clustering finds clusters that are connected in the graph but not convex in the feature space. The number of clusters and the construction of the graph are its hyperparameters.
terms.description: Each day of 2024 at the weather station Krems an der Donau is a data point with a feature vector x ∈ R2 that holds the morning minimum and the maximum daytime temperature of the day. Connecting each day with its ten nearest days, measured by the Euclidean distance between their feature vectors, turns the 366 days into the nodes i = 1, …, n of an k-nearest-neighbor graph G with n = 366 nodes and 2209 edges (Fig. 2(a)). A cluster of this graph is a set of days that are joined by many edges among themselves and by few edges to the remaining days. Spectral clustering is a graph clustering method that finds such clusters from the eigenvectors of the Laplacian matrix of the graph. Consider a similarity graph of the dataset: a weighted graph G with nodes i = 1, …, n, one node per data point, and edge weights Ai,i' = Ai',i ≥ 0 that express the similarity between the data points i and i'; a missing edge has weight 0. The edge weights form the adjacency matrix A(G) ∈ Rn × n, and the node degree d(i) = Σi'=1n Ai,i' of node i is the sum of its edge weights. The Laplacian matrix of G is \begin{equation} {\mathbf L}^{(\mathcal{G})} := \mathbf{D} - {\mathbf A}^{(\mathcal{G})} \quad \text{with } \mathbf{D} := \operatorname{diag}\big\{d^{(1)}, \ldots, d^{(n)}\big\} \text{.} \end{equation} For every vector u ∈ Rn with entries ui, the Laplacian matrix Eq. (1) satisfies \begin{equation} {\mathbf u}^{\top} {\mathbf L}^{(\mathcal{G})} {\mathbf u} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{i'=1}^{n} A_{i,i'} \big( u_{i} - u_{i'} \big)^{2} \text{,} \end{equation} a weighted sum of squared differences across the edges. The quadratic form Eq. (2) is never negative, so L(G) is a symmetric matrix that is positive semi-definite. It has an eigenvalue decomposition L(G) = V Λ Vᵀ with an orthogonal matrix V = ( v(1), …, v(n) ) of eigenvectors and with eigenvalues 0 = λ1 ≤ λ2 ≤ … ≤ λn. The constant vector is an eigenvector for the eigenvalue 0, since every row of L(G) sums to zero. More generally, the multiplicity of the eigenvalue 0 is the number of connected components of G, and the indicator vectors of the components span its eigenvectors. The reason is the quadratic form Eq. (2): L(G) u = 0 forces ui = ui' across every edge, so u is constant on each component. Fig. 1 shows an undirected graph with two components; its two eigenvectors for the eigenvalue 0 place the nodes of each component on a single point of a scatterplot. A graph whose clusters are joined by few edges of small weight is a perturbation of a graph with several components. The eigenvectors of its smallest eigenvalues are then a perturbation of the indicator vectors. Spectral clustering with k clusters therefore uses these eigenvectors as new features: node i is represented by the feature vector \begin{equation} \widetilde{{\mathbf x}}^{(i)} := \big( v^{(1)}_{i}, \ldots, v^{(k)}_{i} \big)^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{k} \text{,} \end{equation} which holds the ith entries of the k eigenvectors with the smallest eigenvalues. k-means is then applied to the feature vectors x̃(1), …, x̃(n). Algorithm 1 states the method in full. \begin{algorithm}[H] \caption{Spectral clustering } \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex Input: weighted graph G with nodes i = 1, …, n and edge weights Ai,i', cluster count k \State compute the Laplacian matrix Eq. (1) of G \State compute eigenvectors v(1), …, v(k) of L(G) for its k smallest eigenvalues \State form the feature vectors Eq. (3) for i = 1, …, n \State run k-means with k clusters on x̃(1), …, x̃(n) \Statex Output: the cluster of each node i, i.e., of each data point \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} For k = 2 the first eigenvector is constant, so the new feature of node i is its entry v(2)i in the Fiedler vector, the eigenvector of the algebraic connectivity λ2. The Fiedler vector is orthogonal to the constant vector, so it has entries of both signs, and k-means on its entries amounts to a threshold. On the days at Krems, the graph is connected with λ2 = 0.044 and λ3 = 0.179, and the Fiedler vector has 190 negative and 176 positive entries (Fig. 2(b)). k-means on these entries delivers 192 cold days and 174 warm days. Every day of January, February, November, and December is a cold day, and every day from May to August is a warm day. Each of the two clusters is connected in the graph, and the two are joined by 25 of the 2209 edges. k-means on the raw feature vectors x(i), whose clusters are always convex regions of the feature space, delivers almost the same hard clustering: the two methods disagree on two days of October only. The methods differ once the clusters are not convex. Data points on two concentric rings are joined by the edges of an k-nearest-neighbor graph along each ring; spectral clustering returns the rings, while k-means on the raw feature vectors cuts through them. Spectral clustering approximately solves a graph partitioning problem. For a subset C ⊆ V of the nodes, the cut cut(C) := Σi ∈ C Σi' ∉ C Ai,i' is the total weight of the edges leaving C. The subset with the smallest cut is often a single node, so the ratio cut divides the cut by the sizes of both parts, \begin{equation} \operatorname{RatioCut}(\mathcal{C}) := \operatorname{cut}(\mathcal{C}) \bigg( \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|} + \frac{1}{|\mathcal{V} \setminus \mathcal{C}|} \bigg) \text{.} \end{equation} Minimizing the ratio cut Eq. (4) over all subsets C is NP-hard. The vector u with entries ui = √(|V C| / |C|) for i ∈ C and ui = -√(|C| / |V C|) otherwise satisfies uᵀ L(G) u = n RatioCut(C) by the quadratic form Eq. (2), as well as uᵀ 1 = 0 and ‖ u ‖22 = n. Dropping the requirement that u takes only these two values leaves the relaxed problem \begin{equation} \min_{{\mathbf u} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}} {\mathbf u}^{\top} {\mathbf L}^{(\mathcal{G})} {\mathbf u} \quad \text{subject to } {\mathbf u}^{\top} \mathbf{1} = 0 \text{ and } \left\lVert {\mathbf u} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} = n \text{,} \end{equation} and the relaxed problem Eq. (5) has the minimum n λ2, attained at √(n) v(2) by the Rayleigh--Ritz theorem. Thresholding the Fiedler vector turns this minimizer back into a subset, and every subset has a ratio cut of at least λ2. On the days at Krems, the spectral bipartition has a ratio cut of 0.274, the bipartition of k-means on the raw feature vectors one of 0.383 (it cuts 35 edges), and a random bipartition one of 12.5, against λ2 = 0.044. For general k, the same relaxation of the ratio cut leads to the first k eigenvectors and the feature vector Eq. (3). Replacing |C| by the sum of the node degrees in C gives the normalized cut, whose relaxation leads to the eigenvectors of the normalized Laplacian matrix D-1 L(G). A variant uses the eigenvectors of D-1/2 L(G) D-1/2 and scales each feature vector Eq. (3) to unit norm. Spectral clustering is not a fixed-point iteration: the eigenvalue decomposition is computed once, and iterations occur only in the k-means step. That step is empirical risk minimization with the clustering error measured in the feature vectors Eq. (3) rather than in the raw ones. The learned hypothesis assigns a cluster to each node of the given graph only; a new data point needs a new node, a new Laplacian matrix, and a new eigenvalue decomposition. The hyperparameters are the number k of clusters and the construction of the graph: how many neighbors the k-nearest-neighbor graph connects, or the bandwidth of a Gaussian kernel that turns distances into edge weights. A gap in the spectrum, as between λ2 = 0.044 and λ3 = 0.179 at Krems, is the usual informal guide to k; with k = 3, the days at Krems split into 107 cold, 170 mild, and 89 warm days, each cluster connected in the graph. Spectral clustering is used for image segmentation, where the nodes are pixels or patches and the edge weights decrease with the difference in color and in position, and for community detection in social networks, where the edges are given and no feature vector is needed.

terms.name: squared error loss
terms.abstract: The squared error loss of a hypothesis on a data point with a numeric label is the square of the difference between the label and the prediction that the hypothesis delivers for the features of the data point. Its average over a training set is the training error, also called the mean squared error (MSE), and minimizing that average over a linear model is least squares, whose solution the normal equations give in closed form. Up to an increasing affine transformation, the squared error loss is the negative log-likelihood function of the label under Gaussian noise around the prediction, so least squares is maximum likelihood estimation. The hypothesis with the smallest risk under the squared error loss is the conditional expectation of the label given the features, and the risk of any other hypothesis exceeds it by the expected squared difference from that conditional expectation. The squared error loss is convex and differentiable in the prediction with a slope proportional to the error, so a single outlier moves the learned hypothesis in proportion to its error, while the absolute error loss and the Huber loss bound that displacement.
terms.description: A weather service predicts the maximum daytime temperature at Krems an der Donau from the morning minimum of the same day. Each day is a data point with the feature x, the morning minimum, and the label y ∈ R, the maximum. A hypothesis h delivers the prediction ŷ = h(x), and the maximum measured in the afternoon says by how many degrees that prediction was off. For a data point with feature vector x ∈ X and numeric label y ∈ R, consider a hypothesis h: X → R. The squared error loss it incurs is the square of the difference between the label and its prediction, \begin{equation} L\left(\left( {\mathbf x},y \right),h \right) := \big(y - h({\mathbf x})\big)^{2} \text{.} \end{equation} On 8 December 2024 the morning minimum at Krems was 3.0 degrees and the maximum 4.6 degrees. The linear hypothesis ĥ(x) = 9.62 + 1.01 x learned below predicts 12.66 degrees for that morning, so its squared error loss Eq. (1) on that day is (4.6 - 12.66)2 ≈ 65.0 squared degrees. The squared error loss is measured in the squared unit of the label, vanishes exactly when the prediction is correct, and is the same for a prediction too high as for one too low by the same amount. As a function of the prediction ŷ, the squared error loss Eq. (1) is a parabola with its minimum at ŷ = y, as Fig. 1 shows. It is convex and differentiable, with derivative -2(y - ŷ): its slope grows in proportion to the error. For a linear model h(x) = wᵀ x, the squared error loss is a convex and differentiable function of the model parameters w as well, which is what makes gradient descent applicable. The absolute error loss |y - ŷ| is convex too but non-smooth at ŷ = y, and its slope is ± 1 whatever the size of the error. The Huber loss with threshold δ > 0 is quadratic for a small error and linear for a large one. In terms of the error e := y - h(x), it is \begin{equation} \begin{cases} e^{2} & \text{for } |e| \leq \delta \text{,} 2 \delta |e| - \delta^{2} & \text{otherwise} \text{,} \end{cases} \end{equation} so it agrees with the squared error loss for an error up to δ and its slope is capped at 2 δ beyond. The average of the squared error loss over a training set D(train) = ( x(r),y(r) ) r=1m, \begin{equation} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \big(y^{(r)} - h({\mathbf x}^{(r)})\big)^{2} \text{,} \end{equation} is the training error of h, also called its mean squared error, and empirical risk minimization selects from a model the hypothesis with the smallest training error. With a linear model, empirical risk minimization under the squared error loss is linear regression by least squares. The training error Eq. (3) then reads (1/m) ‖ y - X w ‖22, with the feature matrix X ∈ Rm × d whose rows are the feature vectors and the label vector y ∈ Rm. Its gradient vanishes exactly at the solutions of the normal equations Xᵀ X w = Xᵀ y, and when X has full column rank the unique solution is \begin{equation} \widehat{{\mathbf w}} = \big({\mathbf X}^{\top} {\mathbf X}\big)^{-1} {\mathbf X}^{\top} {\mathbf y} \text{.} \end{equation} The closed form Eq. (4) needs no iteration, so there is no update whose fixed point the solution would be. When Xᵀ X is too large to invert, gradient descent on the training error Eq. (3) is used instead, and its fixed points are again the solutions of the normal equations (see linear regression). Take as training set every 18th day of 2024 at Krems, 21 days, with the constant feature 1 appended to the morning minimum so that ŵ holds an intercept and a slope. The closed form Eq. (4) gives the line ĥ(x) = 9.62 + 1.01 x of Fig. 2(a), with training error 12.75 squared degrees, or 3.57 degrees after taking the root. The best constant prediction under the squared error loss is the sample mean of the labels, 17.14 degrees, and its training error is their sample variance, 62.05: the average squared error of a constant c is that variance plus (c - 17.14)2. Under the absolute error loss the best constant is the median of the labels instead, 15.80 degrees. The squared error loss is the loss behind maximum likelihood estimation when the label is modeled as the prediction plus Gaussian noise. Let y = h(x) + ε with a Gaussian random variable ε of mean zero and variance σ2, so that y given x has the probability density function N(h(x),σ2). The negative logarithm of that probability density function at the observed label is \begin{equation} - \ln \mathcal{N}\left(h({\mathbf x}),\sigma^{2}\right) (y) = \frac{1}{2 \sigma^{2}} \big(y - h({\mathbf x})\big)^{2} + \frac{1}{2} \ln \big(2 \pi \sigma^{2}\big) \text{,} \end{equation} an increasing affine function of the squared error loss Eq. (1). For data points that are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs, the negative log-likelihood function of the training set is the sum of the terms Eq. (5) over its data points, which is m / (2 σ2) times the training error Eq. (3) plus a constant. The maximum likelihood estimate of w is therefore the least squares solution Eq. (4), whatever σ2 is, and the maximum likelihood estimate of σ2 is the training error itself, 12.75 for the 21 days. The logistic loss is the negative log-likelihood function for a binary label, and Laplacian instead of Gaussian noise gives the absolute error loss. The risk of a hypothesis is its expected loss under a probabilistic model with a joint probability distribution P(x, y) of the feature vector and the label. Under the squared error loss, the risk is minimized by the conditional expectation h*(x) = Ey | x, the Bayes estimator for this loss. The risk of any hypothesis h splits into two parts, \begin{equation} \mathbb{E}\big\{\big(y - h({\mathbf x})\big)^{2}\big\} = \mathbb{E}\big\{\big(h^{*}({\mathbf x}) - h({\mathbf x})\big)^{2}\big\} + \mathbb{E}\big\{\big(y - h^{*}({\mathbf x})\big)^{2}\big\} \text{,} \end{equation} the expected squared difference between h and the conditional expectation, and the expected conditional variance of the label, which no hypothesis can reduce. For a hypothesis learned from a random training set, the first part of the decomposition Eq. (6) splits further into the squared bias and the variance of the learned prediction, the decomposition behind the bias--variance trade-off. Under the absolute error loss the Bayes estimator is the conditional median. The two constant predictions above are the training set versions of these two facts, with the average over the 21 days in place of the expectation. The growing slope of the parabola has a cost. A data point whose label is far from the prediction enters the gradient of the training error Eq. (3) in proportion to its error, so an outlier pulls the learned hypothesis toward itself without bound. For least squares the pull is explicit. Adding Δ to the label of the rth training day changes the solution Eq. (4) by (Xᵀ X)-1 x(r) Δ. The prediction for that day changes by ℓr Δ, where ℓr = (x(r))ᵀ (Xᵀ X)-1 x(r) is the leverage of the day. Among the 21 days, the one with the warmest morning, 17 July 2024 with minimum 19.5 and maximum 27.8 degrees, has leverage 0.192. Each degree added to its label moves the least squares line at that morning by 0.192 degrees, which is 5.76 degrees for Δ = 30, and the slope of the line rises from 1.01 to 1.37 (Fig. 2(b), solid curve). Under the absolute error loss, whose empirical risk minimization solution is least absolute deviation regression, the line moves by at most 1.75 degrees, and not at all once Δ exceeds 3 (dashed curve). The slope of the absolute error loss is ± 1, so once the corrupted day is above the line, its term in the optimality condition no longer depends on the size of its error. The Huber loss with δ = 3 moves its line by 1.93 degrees and not at all beyond Δ = 6 (dotted curve), since its slope is capped. This bounded pull is what robustness to outliers means for a loss. The absolute error loss is non-smooth, and the Huber loss adds the threshold δ as a hyperparameter; the squared error loss has neither drawback, and no such bound. When the label is a vector, the squared error loss is the squared Euclidean norm of the difference between label and prediction. The clustering error of k-means, which compares a data point with the cluster centroid that stands in for it, and the reconstruction error of principal component analysis and of an autoencoder are of this form, with the feature vector itself in the place of the label.

terms.name: stochastic gradient descent (SGD)
terms.abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is a variant of gradient descent in which the gradient of the objective function is replaced by a computationally cheaper stochastic approximation. Its main application in machine learning is empirical risk minimization on a training set that is large or distributed: the gradient of the empirical risk averages over the entire training set. SGD approximates it by averaging over a randomly drawn batch of data points. The batch size trades the computational cost of a single update against the accuracy of the gradient approximation.

terms.name: supervised learning
terms.abstract: Supervised learning is the machine learning setting that needs the label values of some data points. That requirement is what sets it apart from other forms of machine learning, such as unsupervised learning or reinforcement learning. Two main types of supervised learning are regression, for a numeric label, and classification, for a label with finitely many values. Empirical risk minimization learns a hypothesis of a hypothesis space that minimizes the average loss on a training set of labeled data points. A label can be obtained from a sensing device, computed, or annotated by a person. These labeling processes typically involve errors, so a recorded label value is a noisy estimate of the true one.
terms.description: A weather station of GeoSphere Austria at Krems an der Donau records the minimum and the maximum temperature of each day. From ten such days, two learning tasks can be built: predicting the maximum temperature of a day from its minimum, and predicting whether the next day is at least two degrees warmer. Both need, for each of the ten days, the value to be predicted, its label. Supervised learning refers to machine learning methods that need the label values of some data points, the ones forming a training set. That requirement sets it apart from the other settings: in unsupervised learning, no such value is available, and the loss is defined through model parameters that summarize the whole dataset; in reinforcement learning, a reward signal measures the usefulness of a prediction instead. Supervised learning methods evaluate the quality of a hypothesis by comparing its prediction against a known label value. Empirical risk minimization learns a hypothesis by comparing its predictions for the data points in a training set with their actual labels. The training set D(train) = ( x(r),y(r) ) r=1m consists of m labeled data points, each with a feature vector x(r) and a label y(r). Among the hypotheses of a hypothesis space H it chooses one that minimizes the average loss on the training set, \[ \widehat{h} \in \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\left(\left( {\mathbf x}^{(r)},y^{(r)} \right),h \right) \text{.} \] The loss of a data point can be evaluated on that data point alone, since its label supplies the value to compare with. The label space Y, the set of values a label can take, decides which of two main types a learning task is: Y = R makes it regression, a discrete label space makes it classification. Both learning tasks can be built from the same data points. Fig. 1 shows two supervised learning tasks, one regression and one classification, obtained from the same data points, the ten days of Krems an der Donau. With the maximum temperature of the day as label, the learning task is regression, and empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss learns the curve of panel (a). The second learning task uses both temperatures of the day as features. Its label is +1 if the next day is at least two degrees warmer and -1 otherwise, so the learning task is classification. The two classes overlap, so no straight line separates them: the same morning can be followed by a warmer or by a cooler day. The label values of data points can be obtained in different ways, such as physical sensing devices, computations, or human annotation. For example, the maximum temperature of a day at Krems can be read from a calibrated thermometer of the weather station. The label value can also be obtained by numerical computations. GeoSphere Austria runs INCA, which computes the temperature across Austria on a grid of one kilometer. INCA starts from the forecast of a numerical weather prediction model and corrects it with the differences between forecast and observation at the surrounding stations, so it returns a temperature value also for a location that has no station. The temperature recordings can be annotated by a person instead, a meteorologist or a panel of local residents. These labeling processes differ in the amount of required resources and in the resulting label quality. Each carries an error of its own, so a recorded label value is a noisy estimate of the true one. The station thermometer has a calibration tolerance. A computed label inherits the error of the equations and of the readings they were given. A resident might misreport temperatures. Human annotation also limits how large the training set can be, since it requires the expert whose judgment is to be reproduced. Crowdsourcing lifts this limit: ImageNet, a dataset of 3.2 million annotated images at the time of its first publication, was assembled by annotators working through a crowdsourcing platform. An annotated label records a judgment rather than a measurement, and two annotators need not return the same value. ImageNet was assembled to limit this disagreement. Several annotators vote on each image, which is kept only on a convincing majority. The number of votes required is fixed per category, from an initial subset of its images.

terms.name: singular value decomposition (SVD)
terms.abstract: The singular value decomposition (SVD) factors any matrix into an orthogonal matrix, a matrix that is zero off its main diagonal, and a second orthogonal matrix. For A ∈ Rm × d it reads A = V Λ Uᵀ, and the nonnegative diagonal entries of Λ are the singular values. In contrast to an eigenvalue decomposition, which only exists for a square diagonalizable matrix, an SVD exists for every matrix. Truncating the SVD after the k largest singular values yields the best approximation by a matrix of rank k, which underlies dimensionality reduction. For linear regression, the SVD of the feature matrix splits the objective into one term per singular value plus an irreducible remainder. The solution with the smallest Euclidean norm divides each component of the label vector along a left singular vector by the matching singular value. The SVD delivers the pseudoinverse, the spectral norm, and the condition number of a matrix.
terms.description: A grayscale photograph with m rows and d columns of pixels is stored as a matrix of m × d intensities, that is, m d numbers. Most photographs can be stored with far fewer numbers: keeping only the k largest of the singular values of that matrix, defined below, costs k (m + d + 1) numbers. The SVD of a matrix A ∈ Rm × d is a factorization of the form \begin{equation} {\mathbf A} = \mathbf{V} {\boldsymbol \Lambda} \mathbf{U}^{\top} \text{,} \end{equation} with orthogonal matrices, whose columns are orthonormal vectors, \[ \mathbf{V} = \big({\mathbf v}^{(1)}, \ldots, {\mathbf v}^{(m)}\big) \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}, \qquad \mathbf{U} = \big( {\mathbf u}^{(1)}, \ldots, {\mathbf u}^{(d)} \big) \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} \text{.} \] The matrix Λ ∈ Rm × d in Eq. (1) is zero off the main diagonal, whose entries Λj,j = λj ≥ 0 are referred to as singular values and ordered as λ1 ≥ λ2 ≥ … ≥ 0. The columns u(j) of U are the right singular vectors and the columns v(j) of V the left singular vectors; both families are orthonormal. Multiplying the factorization by u(j) gives A u(j) = λj v(j). The matrix A therefore maps each right singular vector u(j) to the left singular vector v(j) scaled by the singular value λj (see Fig. 1). In contrast to an eigenvalue decomposition, which only exists for square diagonalizable matrices, an SVD exists for every matrix. The existence of the SVD and its computation follow from the spectral decomposition of the symmetric positive semi-definite matrix AᵀA. That matrix has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors u(j) of Rd, with eigenvalues λj2 ≥ 0, the squares of the singular values. The left singular vectors are then v(j) := A u(j) / λj for λj > 0, completed to an orthonormal basis of Rm for λj = 0. The matrices U, Λ, and V built this way satisfy A = V Λ Uᵀ. If A is itself symmetric and positive semi-definite, its SVD coincides with its eigenvalue decomposition. The largest singular value λ1 equals the spectral norm ‖ A ‖2, and, for a matrix of full rank, the ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value is the condition number κ (A); a matrix of deficient rank has κ (A) = ∞ by convention. Retaining only the k largest singular values yields the truncated SVD \begin{equation} \widehat{{\mathbf A}} := \sum_{j=1}^{k} \lambda_{j} {\mathbf v}^{(j)} \big({\mathbf u}^{(j)}\big)^{\top} \text{,} \end{equation} a matrix of rank at most k. Among all matrices B of rank at most k, the truncation Eq. (2) minimizes the approximation error ‖ A - B ‖F. This property is what makes the truncation useful for storing the photograph of the opening. No matrix of rank at most k is closer to A, so the truncation loses as little as any storage by a rank-k matrix can. It requires only the k largest singular values with their left and right singular vectors, that is, k (m + d + 1) numbers instead of m d (pythondemos/svd.py). Principal component analysis is the same truncation applied to a centered feature matrix X ∈ Rm × d: a linear dimensionality reduction that replaces each feature vector by its coordinates along the k directions of largest variance. The right singular vectors u(j) of X are the eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix (1)/(m) Xᵀ X, whose eigenvalues are λj2/m. Principal component analysis therefore projects each data point onto the leading u(1), …, u(k). The SVD can also be used to analyze and to implement linear regression methods. Consider a feature matrix X ∈ Rm × d, whose r-th row is the feature vector of the r-th data point, and a label vector y ∈ Rm. Linear regression minimizes the squared Euclidean norm ‖ X w - y ‖22 of the residual over the model parameters w. The squared residual norm is the empirical risk minimization objective for the squared error loss, the least squares problem. Let p be the number of nonzero singular values of X, its rank. A component of w along a right singular vector u(j) with j > p leaves X w unchanged, so expanding w = Σj=1p w̃(j) u(j) in the leading right singular vectors loses nothing. With X u(j) = λjv(j) and the orthonormality of the left singular vectors v(j), the objective of linear regression reads \[ \begin{aligned} \left\lVert {\mathbf X} {\mathbf w} - {\mathbf y} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} &= \left\lVert \textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{p} \lambda_{j}\widetilde{w}^{(j)} {\mathbf v}^{(j)} - {\mathbf y} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} &= \sum_{j=1}^{p} \big(\lambda_{j}\widetilde{w}^{(j)} - ({\mathbf v}^{(j)})^{\top}{\mathbf y}\big)^{2} + \sum_{j=p+1}^{m} \big(({\mathbf v}^{(j)})^{\top}{\mathbf y}\big)^{2} \text{.} \end{aligned} \] The objective of linear regression depends on y only through its components (v(j))ᵀy along the left singular vectors. The second sum is the constant, irreducible error from the part of y outside the column space of X. The first sum is minimized termwise at ŵ(j) = (v(j))ᵀy / λj for j ≤ p. In matrix form, this is ŵ = X+ y with the pseudoinverse X+ = U Λ+ Vᵀ, where Λ+ inverts the nonzero singular values. The vector ŵ is the solution of linear regression with the smallest Euclidean norm. A small singular value divides the corresponding component of y by a small number, which is why the condition number of X determines how noise in y enters ŵ. Amplified noise matters because the least squares objective is a proxy: the goal is a small squared error on data points outside the training set (see generalization), and noise amplified into ŵ is carried to every such data point.

terms.name: support vector machine (SVM)
terms.abstract: The support vector machine (SVM) is a binary classification method that learns a linear classifier by regularized empirical risk minimization, combining the hinge loss with a squared-norm penalty term. For a linearly separable training set and sufficiently weak regularization, the solution is the maximum-margin separating hyperplane. This hyperplane is fully determined by the feature vectors closest to it, which are called support vectors. The kernel SVM is obtained by combining the basic SVM with a feature transformation derived from a kernel function.
terms.description: A handwritten digit is recognized from the pixel values of its image, and a text document is sorted by topic from the frequencies of its words. In both tasks a numeric feature vector has to be mapped to a label, and the SVM has been applied to both. The SVM is a binary classification method for data points with feature space X=Rd. In its simplest form, the SVM learns a linear classifier with decision boundary \{ {\mathbf x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}: {\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x} + b = 0 \}. The linear classifier is parameterized by a nonzero vector w ∈ Rd 0 and an offset b ∈ R. The vector w is the normal vector to the decision boundary and the offset b shifts the decision boundary away from the origin. For a data point with feature vector x and label y ∈ -1, +1, the SVM delivers the prediction ŷ = sign(wᵀ x + b). The SVM can be formulated as an instance of regularized empirical risk minimization for learning a linear classifier from a training set that consists of m data points. The model parameters (ŵ, b̂) of the linear classifier are obtained as \begin{equation} (\widehat{{\mathbf w}}, \widehat{b}) = \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{{\mathbf w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}, b \in \mathbb{R}} \underbrace{\frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \max\{0, 1 - y^{(r)} ({\mathbf w}^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} + b)\} + \alpha \left\lVert {\mathbf w} \right\rVert_{2}^{2}}_{:= f({\mathbf w}, b)}\text{.} \end{equation} The SVM objective function consists of the average hinge loss on the training set plus a penalty term α ‖ w ‖22 with regularization parameter α > 0. The penalty term in the SVM problem Eq. (1) is the scaled squared Euclidean norm α ‖ w ‖22, the same penalty term as in ridge regression. It does not involve the model parameter b, which is therefore left unpenalized. In linear regression, the penalty term estimates how much higher the loss is on data points outside the training set than on it (see linear regression), an interpretation that requires the quadratic structure of the squared error loss. For the SVM, the penalty term instead controls the generalization gap: the hinge loss is Lipschitz continuous in w, with a constant given by the Euclidean norm of the feature vector. Adding the penalty term α ‖ w ‖22 to the average hinge loss has three effects: First, it makes the overall objective function in the SVM problem Eq. (1) strongly convex in w, so that its solution ŵ is unique. Second, it controls how much that solution varies if the data points in the training set change. Third, it keeps ‖ w ‖2 small and therefore the margins wide. If the feature vectors in the training set have bounded Euclidean norm, the expectation of the difference between the risk and the empirical hinge loss of the learned linear classifier decreases in proportion to 1/(α m). The solution of the SVM problem Eq. (1) has a geometric meaning when the training set is linearly separable, i.e., there is some choice for (w, b) such that sign(wᵀ x(r) + b) y(r)=1 for r=1, …, m. For a sufficiently small α, the solution of the SVM problem Eq. (1) determines the separating hyperplane that is farthest from the feature vectors in the training set (see Fig. 1). The distance between this hyperplane and the nearest feature vectors, which are precisely the support vectors discussed below, is referred to as the margin and is given by 1/‖ ŵ ‖2. The margin of the learned hyperplane measures robustness against perturbations of the features of a data point. Perturbing a feature vector x by a vector δ changes the score ŵᵀx + b̂ by ŵᵀδ, whose magnitude is at most ‖ ŵ ‖2 ‖ δ ‖2 by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. A data point therefore stays correctly classified under every feature perturbation with ‖ δ ‖2 < γ, as illustrated by the dashed circle around a support vector in Fig. 1. Data points whose feature vectors lie farther from the decision boundary tolerate even larger perturbations: the tolerated radius equals the distance of the feature vector from the decision boundary, which is at least γ and equals γ precisely for the support vectors. Maximizing the margin maximizes this worst-case tolerated radius, so the maximum-margin classifier is the separating classifier that is robust against the largest feature perturbations. The same holds beyond the separable case: the SVM problem Eq. (1) is equivalent to minimizing the hinge loss under the worst case over bounded perturbations of the feature vectors. Every solution of the SVM problem Eq. (1) has a structure that holds whether or not the training set is linearly separable. In particular, \widehat{{\mathbf w}} = \sum_{r=1}^{m} \beta_{r} y^{(r)} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} with expansion coefficients 0 ≤ βr ≤ 1/(2 α m) that are nonzero only for the feature vectors with y^{(r)} (\widehat{{\mathbf w}}^{\top} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} + \widehat{b}) \leq 1. These feature vectors are referred to as support vectors since they entirely determine the SVM solution (ŵ, b̂). Applying a perturbation to any feature vector that is not a support vector leaves ŵ, b̂ unchanged, provided the perturbation is small enough to preserve the strict inequality y (ŵᵀ x + b̂) > 1 (see Fig. 2, whose training set contains an outlier). Like logistic regression and linear regression, the SVM learns the model parameters (w, b) of a linear model. In contrast to logistic regression and linear regression, the SVM objective function f(w, b) is non-smooth because of the hinge loss. However, the hinge loss is the maximum of two affine functions of (w, b) and therefore convex, so the SVM objective function, the sum of its average and the convex penalty term, is convex and the optimization problem Eq. (1) can be solved by convex optimization methods. One such method is subgradient descent, which is obtained from gradient descent by replacing the gradient of the objective function with a subgradient. Starting from an initial choice w(0), b(0) of the model parameters, subgradient descent repeatedly applies the update \[ \big({\mathbf w}^{(t+1)}, b^{(t+1)}\big) = \big({\mathbf w}^{(t)}, b^{(t)}\big) - \eta^{(t)} {\mathbf g}^{(t)} \text{, for } t = 0,1,\ldots \text{,} \] with a step size η(t) > 0 and a subgradient g(t) ∈ ∂ f(w(t), b(t)) of the SVM objective function Eq. (1). Inserting the SVM objective function Eq. (1) into the generic update yields the explicit update \[ \begin{aligned} {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} &= \big(1 - 2 \eta^{(t)} \alpha\big) {\mathbf w}^{(t)} + \frac{\eta^{(t)}}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \beta^{(t)}_{r} y^{(r)} {\mathbf x}^{(r)} \text{,} b^{(t+1)} &= b^{(t)} + \frac{\eta^{(t)}}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \beta^{(t)}_{r} y^{(r)} \text{,} \end{aligned} \] with expansion coefficients β(t)r ∈ [0, 1], for r = 1, …, m. The coefficient β(t)r is nonzero only for data points that satisfy y(r) ( (w(t))ᵀ x(r) + b(t) ) ≤ 1, i.e., data points on which the hinge loss is nonzero or non-differentiable at the current model parameters. Each iteration scales w(t) by the factor 1 - 2 η(t) α (the effect of the penalty term) and adds corrections y(r) x(r) only from these data points. In particular, for the initialization w(0) = 0, every iterate w(t) is a weighted sum Σr=1m βr y(r) x(r) of the feature vectors in the training set. The weighted sum has the form of the expansion of the solution ŵ in the support vectors stated above, built up one iteration at a time. A coefficient of the iterate w(t) is nonzero only for a data point that satisfied y(r) ( (w(t'))ᵀ x(r) + b(t') ) ≤ 1 at some earlier iteration t' < t. For step sizes with 2 η(t') α < 1, such a coefficient stays positive afterwards, since every later iteration rescales it by a positive factor and adds a nonnegative amount. The iterate can therefore also carry feature vectors that are not support vectors of the solution ŵ. For a constant step size η = B/(ρ√(T)) over T iterations, where B bounds the norm of a minimizer of Eq. (1) and ρ the norm of the subgradients used, the SVM objective function at the average of the iterates exceeds its minimum by at most Bρ/√(T). An overly large regularization parameter α makes the SVM underfit: the above expansion of ŵ implies ‖ ŵ ‖2 ≤ ρ/(2α), with ρ the largest Euclidean norm of a feature vector in the training set, so ŵ shrinks toward 0. Consider a training set with unequal class sizes. For sufficiently large α, the predictions approach the constant majority-class prediction sign(b̂) and every data point of the minority class is a misclassified support vector. The training set of Fig. 2 also has unequal class sizes, four data points labeled y = +1 and three labeled y = -1, but with the value α = 1/14 used there, the SVM misclassifies one data point that can be considered an outlier. Increasing the value of α to 50 for that training set shrinks ‖ ŵ ‖2, makes every prediction on the training set equal to +1, and misclassifies all three data points of the minority class. The basic SVM Eq. (1) learns a linear classifier on the feature space X = Rd. It can be generalized to a classification method for data points whose feature vectors lie in an arbitrary feature space X by first applying a feature transformation φ: X → X' with X' = Rd and then learning a linear classifier on the transformed feature vectors. By choosing φ (and d) appropriately, any given training set with distinct feature vectors can be made linearly separable in X', e.g., by mapping each distinct feature vector to its own coordinate axis. A general construction of a feature transformation φ is via a kernel k: X × X → R. In this construction, the transformed feature space is, in general, not Rd but a Hilbert space H, which can be infinite-dimensional (see kernel method). The resulting method is then referred to as a kernel SVM.

terms.name: tabular data
terms.abstract: Tabular data consist of data points that share a common, fixed set of attributes. The measured attributes serve as the features or as the label of a data point. The data points constitute the rows, or records, of a table, and the attributes are its columns. Every row has one cell per column, and the cells within one column hold values of the same attribute. The fixed attribute set separates tabular data from other types of data, such as text or graphs, whose data points carry no common set of attributes.
terms.description: A Finnish Meteorological Institute weather station measures the weather of each day, and the measurements are represented as a table with one row for each day (Fig. 1(a)). The table has four columns, one per attribute of a day: the date, the morning minimum temperature, the precipitation, and the maximum daytime temperature. The date identifies the data point, and the three measured attributes are the candidates for its features and its label. Tabular data consist of data points that share such a common, fixed set of attributes. As the name suggests, tabular data can be stored as a table: the rows of the table are the data points, and the columns of the table are the attributes. In Fig. 1(b), the learning task is to forecast the maximum daytime temperature of a day from its morning minimum temperature. A machine learning method reads the minimum-temperature column as the feature and the maximum-temperature column as the label, while the precipitation column is left unused. It learns a hypothesis from the 366 data points, shown as a scatterplot with the learned curve. The distinct characteristic of tabular data is the rigid shape of a table. Every row contains the same number of cells, one per column, and the cells within one column hold values of the same attribute of the data points. The value range must be defined for each column, and every cell of a column holds a value from that range. The precipitation column of Fig. 1(a), for example, holds a daily amount in millimeters or the special value -1.0, which records that no precipitation was observed. A second, different use of a special value is a marker such as ``N/A'' reserved for an empty cell. Missing data are represented by an empty cell: an attribute that was not recorded for a data point leaves its cell empty, while the table keeps its shape. Data imputation fills such a cell with an estimate computed from the cells that were recorded. The fixed attribute set is what separates tabular data from other data types. For the weather measurements, the station records the same quantities every day, so the attribute set is fixed by the measurement process and shared by every data point. A text, in contrast, is a sequence of tokens whose length varies from data point to data point, and a graph varies in its node and edge sets. Such data points carry no attribute set of their own. One can be imposed, for example the number of occurrences of each word from a fixed word list, but such a set discards the order of the tokens. The table of weather measurements loses nothing in this way, since a day is fully described by its four attributes, while a text with its tokens in another order is a different text. Instead, feature learning methods are developed that map such data points to feature vectors (or embeddings). In database theory, the relational model formalizes a table as a relation. A relation is a set of tuples of attribute values. The relational model also provides the operations, such as selecting rows or joining tables, that database systems use to manipulate tabular data.

terms.name: trusted execution environment (TEE)
terms.abstract: A trusted execution environment (TEE) is a part of a computing system that isolates code and data from other software. Even the operating system cannot directly read or alter its protected memory. Remote attestation can prove to another party which code it runs. Processor features such as Arm TrustZone and Intel SGX provide TEEs on ordinary chips. In machine learning, a TEE protects input feature vectors, learned model parameters and the integrity of the computed prediction. It does not limit what the prediction reveals; differential privacy addresses that problem. Physical and software side channels require additional countermeasures. Compared with fully homomorphic encryption, a TEE runs at near-native speed but replaces a mathematical guarantee with trust in the chip vendor and its hardware.
terms.description: Consider an embedded controller in a refrigerated medicine cabinet. Each minute, it reads a temperature sensor and forms a feature vector x from the current temperature and its recent changes. A learned hypothesis computes the prediction ĥ(x) of whether the cooling system is failing. The controller sits in a sealed metal box with no network cable and no radio. Its only inputs are the sensor cable and the power cable, and its only output is an alarm display. The model parameters ŵ of ĥ and the recorded temperature readings never leave the box. A TEE is the part of the processor that provides the logical isolation. Software outside it cannot directly read or alter its protected code and memory, even if that software is a privileged operating system. The metal enclosure is not the TEE; it is a separate layer that protects the processor against physical probing and fault injection. Most TEEs are a mode of an ordinary processor. Arm TrustZone splits the processor of the controller into two parts. The normal world runs the display software. The secure world runs the prediction code and holds ŵ and the temperature readings. The normal world cannot read the memory of the secure world even with root privileges. Intel SGX provides similar isolation for an enclave inside a process on a server. Remote attestation lets a client verify a signed digest of the enclave's code before it sends any data. The isolation guarantee concerns direct access through software and memory interfaces; information revealed by outputs, side channels and physical attacks requires additional protection. Fig. 1 shows the embedded controller and what each part can see. A TEE protects three assets of a machine learning system. The first is the data: the temperature history is an operational record that the cabinet operator must not disclose or allow an attacker to alter. The second is the learned hypothesis. Its model parameters ŵ are the outcome of training on a costly dataset. An attack that reads them out obtains the hypothesis without the dataset. The third is the integrity of the prediction: nobody can alter the code so that it suppresses an alarm when the cooling system is failing. A TEE does not protect what the prediction reveals. A membership inference attack that only observes predictions is unaffected by it, and differential privacy addresses that part. A TEE also does not, by itself, protect against physical side channels. The processor's current and electromagnetic field depend on the data it processes. A probe held near the chip can recover secret keys from these traces. The same probe recovers the model parameters and the layer structure of an artificial neural network running on an embedded processor, one multiplication at a time. A short electromagnetic pulse or a glitch on the supply voltage can also skip an instruction, e.g., the check that rejects unsigned code. The metal enclosure attenuates the emitted field and blocks the pulse. Tamper sensors erase ŵ when the box is opened. Constant-time code makes the power trace independent of the data. However, server TEEs are also exposed to software and processor-level side channels. The operating system can see the memory access pattern of an enclave. Therefore, machine learning code inside an enclave must be data-oblivious. Its access patterns must not depend on the data. Speculative execution has also leaked enclave memory outright. Two uses of TEEs beyond the sealed box are prediction in the cloud and federated learning. A hospital that rents a server can require an SGX enclave. It first uses attestation to verify the agreed prediction code. It then encrypts its feature vectors for the enclave, so the cloud provider never sees them. In federated learning, a server enclave can provide a hardware-based implementation of secure aggregation. Clients encrypt their model parameters updates for the enclave. It decrypts and sums the updates, while the server operator sees only the sum. Separately, the TrustZone secure world of each phone can protect its local update before transmission; a system can use either protection or combine both. A TEE, fully homomorphic encryption and differential privacy provide different guarantees by different means. Fully homomorphic encryption hides the data during computation without trusting the processor, at a cost of orders of magnitude in time and memory. A TEE obtains near-native speed by trusting the chip vendor, the hardware implementation and the countermeasures against side channels. Differential privacy bounds what the released prediction reveals about any single data point and can be combined with either.

terms.name: test set
terms.abstract: A test set contains data points used to evaluate a hypothesis delivered by a machine learning method. These points are used neither for training nor for model selection. A test set is therefore also called a hold-out set. Under the independent and identically distributed assumption, its average loss is an unbiased estimator of the risk of the learned hypothesis. A concentration inequality relates the accuracy of this estimate to the test set size. The estimate remains valid only if no design choice depends on the test set. Selection based on repeated evaluation converts it into a validation set; overlap with the training set is test set contamination.
terms.description: Consider a machine learning method that uses weather recordings from Krems an der Donau (Austria). It learns a hypothesis ĥ that predicts tomorrow's maximum temperature from today's maximum. A training set is used to learn a hypothesis via empirical risk minimization. A validation set is then used to compare hypotheses from different models, such as a linear model and polynomial regression. Both sets influence the selected hypothesis, so its loss on them is usually smaller than on data points that the method did not use. Assessing ĥ therefore requires data points from neither set. A test set D(test) is a dataset of data points used to evaluate a hypothesis delivered by a machine learning method. Its data points enter neither the training of a model on the training set D(train) nor model selection based on a validation set D(val) (Fig. 1). A test set is therefore also called a hold-out set. Some texts instead use that name for the validation set. For the temperature forecaster, the test set consists of days absent from both other sets. Suppose that ĥ was learned and selected without using D(test). Its test error is the average loss \[ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}^{(\rm test)}|} \sum_{{\mathbf z} \in \mathcal{D}^{(\rm test)}} L\left({\mathbf z},\widehat{h} \right) \text{.} \] Here, L(z,ĥ ) is the loss, a number that quantifies the error on one data point. Under the independent and identically distributed assumption, the points in D(train), D(val), and D(test) are independent draws from the same probability distribution p(z). The test error is then an unbiased estimator of the risk of ĥ. The risk is the expected loss on a data point drawn from p(z) independently of all three sets. The validation error is used to select ĥ, so it tends to understate the risk of the selected hypothesis. The sizes of the three sets are design choices. Under the independent and identically distributed assumption, the test error averages |D(test)| independent loss values. If the loss lies in [0,1], a concentration inequality bounds the difference between test error and risk. For a confidence level δ ∈ (0,1), this difference is at most √(ln(2/δ)/(2 |D(test)|)) with probability at least 1-δ. Solving that bound for |D(test)| gives the test set size a desired difference and confidence level require. The validation set needs a concentration inequality that covers every hypothesis compared during model selection at once, so its required size grows with their number. The training set receives the remaining data points. No fixed rule determines the proportions. Fig. 2 shows a common example: 50 percent for training and 25 percent each for validation and testing. A test error remains a valid risk estimate only if the test set is used once, after all choices are fixed. Using D(test) to compare models converts it into a validation set, and its error into a validation error. Moving any of its data points into the training set is test set contamination. In a machine learning competition, organizers compare models submitted by participants on a common test set. The organizers keep the test labels private and compute each error. Participants cannot use those labels to revise their models. The reported test error can therefore estimate risk, provided that the organizers limit repeated feedback on the same test set.

terms.name: training error
terms.abstract: The training error of a hypothesis is its average loss over the training set, the empirical risk of the hypothesis on the data points used for training. For a hypothesis delivered by empirical risk minimization, it is the smallest empirical risk that any hypothesis of the hypothesis space attains. Because the same data points selected the hypothesis, the training error is often far below the risk, by a gap that grows with the size of the hypothesis space, so a hypothesis with zero training error can have a large risk. Under the independent and identically distributed assumption, the training error of every hypothesis is a noisy estimate of its risk, and empirical risk minimization compares all of them at once, so a generalization guarantee for the empirical risk minimization solution requires the deviation to be small uniformly over the hypothesis space. A training error far below the validation error indicates overfitting, and a large training error indicates underfitting.
terms.description: Twenty of the 1827 days of five years, 2020 to 2024, at the weather station Krems an der Donau (Austria), every 92nd day, are drawn in Fig. 1 as a scatterplot. Each day is a data point: its feature x is the morning minimum temperature, its label y the maximum temperature of the day. Three of the days, drawn in black, form a training set, the days used for training, for two empirical risk minimization-based methods that deliver the hypotheses ĥ(1) and ĥ(2). The hypothesis ĥ(1) is learned by empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss over the hypothesis space of affine maps h(x) = b + w x, the linear model. The dotted bars are its prediction errors on the three days, the differences between the recorded maximum and the value of ĥ(1), and the average of the three squared bars is its training error, 7.91. The second hypothesis ĥ(2) is learned by empirical risk minimization over the hypothesis space of all polynomials of degree at most two. Although the training error of ĥ(2) is zero, and therefore far below that of ĥ(1), it is the worse choice: averaged over all days of the five years, the loss of ĥ(2) is 42.90 against 24.22 for ĥ(1). Holding the intercept of ĥ(1) at the value empirical risk minimization gave it and varying only its slope w leaves the training error a function of one number. Fig. 2 shows it with the risk, the expected loss over the probability distribution of a day, approximated by the average over the five years. The two functions have different minimizers: the training error is smallest at the slope that empirical risk minimization picked, the risk at a smaller slope. At the slope empirical risk minimization picked, the training error is a third of the risk. The training error is an average over the three days that determined the hypothesis; it does not measure the loss on a day outside the training set. The training error Et of a hypothesis ĥ is its average loss over the training set D(train) = z(r)r=1m, \[ E_{t} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\left({\mathbf z}^{(r)},\widehat{h} \right) \text{,} \] i.e., the empirical risk of ĥ on the data points used for learning ĥ. The hypothesis is the output of a training method, a map A that reads in a training set and delivers ĥ = A(D(train)). For a hypothesis delivered by empirical risk minimization, the training error is the smallest empirical risk that any hypothesis of the hypothesis space attains on D(train), since empirical risk minimization minimizes this average. The training error is computed on the same data points that selected ĥ, which limits its use as a measure of quality. The goal of a machine learning method is to learn a hypothesis that incurs a small loss on any data point, also those outside the training set, that is, to minimize the risk introduced above. The training error of the learned hypothesis is often a poor estimator for its risk, because the learned hypothesis has been adapted to the training set by minimizing the training error. A hypothesis with zero training error can therefore have a large risk, as ĥ(2) of Fig. 1 does. The difference between the risk and the training error is the generalization gap. Under the independent and identically distributed assumption, the training error becomes a random variable, as it depends on the randomly generated training set. For one fixed hypothesis h ∈ H, the empirical risk L̂(h|D(train)) is an average of the m loss values L(z(1),h ), …, L(z(m),h ), which are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs. It is therefore the realization of a random variable with expectation L̄ ( h ) and a variance proportional to 1/m. Empirical risk minimization does not evaluate this estimate at one fixed hypothesis: it compares the estimates of all hypotheses in H and picks the smallest. The estimates form the family L̂(h|D(train)) h ∈ H, a stochastic process indexed by the hypothesis space: one random variable for each hypothesis, all realized by the single draw of D(train). The minimizer ĥ of this process is itself a random variable, and its training error Et = L̂(ĥ|D(train)) is the minimum of many noisy estimates, so it is below L̄ ( ĥ ) on average. A guarantee of generalization for the empirical risk minimization solution must therefore hold uniformly over the hypothesis space: if \begin{equation} \sup_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \big| \widehat{L}\big(h|\mathcal{D}^{(\rm train)}\big) - \bar{L} \big( h \big) \big| \leq \epsilon \text{,} \end{equation} then L̄ ( ĥ ) ≤ Et + ε, and the risk of ĥ exceeds the smallest risk in H by at most 2ε. A hypothesis space for which the uniform deviation Eq. (1) falls below any ε with probability at least 1-δ once m is large enough has the uniform convergence property introduced by Vapnik and Chervonenkis (2015). For a finite hypothesis space and a loss with values in [0,1], a union bound over the hypotheses and Hoeffding's inequality give ε = √(ln(2 |H| / δ) / (2 m)). For an infinite hypothesis space, ln |H| is replaced by a measure of its size such as the Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension or the Rademacher complexity. In contrast, the validation error, computed as the average loss on data points not used in the training, is often a much better estimator for the risk of the learned hypothesis. For example, let the data points of the validation set be realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs, independent of the training set. Each summand of the validation error is then the loss on an independent draw from the probability distribution of a data point, whose expectation conditional on the training set is the risk of the learned hypothesis. The expectation of the validation error conditional on the training set is therefore that risk. Moreover, the validation error estimates the risk of the single hypothesis that A delivered, so one Hoeffding bound without |H| suffices for it, and it concentrates around the risk at a rate that depends only on the size of the validation set, not on how the hypothesis was learned. Fig. 3 shows three deviations of a training error from a risk for one year of the Krems record: for one fixed hypothesis, for the hypothesis that empirical risk minimization learns, and the largest deviation over the hypothesis space. The 366 days of the year stand in for the probability distribution of a day, so the risk of a hypothesis is its average loss over the year, and a training set of m days is drawn at random from the year, 300 times for each m ∈ 10, 20, 40, 80. The hypothesis space is the linear model, which consists of all hypothesis maps h(x) = w1 x + w0 with w1, w0 ∈ R. The fixed hypothesis is the one with the smallest risk in the hypothesis space, the hypothesis learned by linear regression from all 366 days; it does not depend on the draw. The empirical risk minimization hypothesis is learned by linear regression from the drawn training set. The largest deviation over the hypothesis space, the uniform deviation Eq. (1), is approximated by the maximum over a grid of 2500 hypotheses around the learned one. Over the repeated draws, the deviation of the fixed hypothesis has mean zero. The training error of the empirical risk minimization hypothesis is below its risk on average, and the largest deviation is several times the standard deviation of the fixed hypothesis' deviation. The gap of the empirical risk minimization hypothesis never exceeds the largest deviation, as the uniform deviation Eq. (1) requires, and both decrease as the training set grows (pythondemos/trainerr.py). The size of the gap L̄ ( ĥ ) - Et depends on the hypothesis space. The first day of each month from January to August 2024 forms a training set of eight days, and the rest of the year is held back. A hypothesis of the linear model learned from the eight days has a training error of 20.36, only slightly below its average squared error of 21.60 on the held-back days: the linear model has two model parameters and can adapt little to the particular eight days. Fig. 4 shows the two errors for polynomials of prescribed maximum degree p = 0, …, 7. Increasing the degree means a larger hypothesis space, a polynomial of degree p being one of degree p+1 with a zero leading coefficient, so the training error never increases with the degree. In contrast, the average loss on the held-back days is smallest at degree one and grows for larger degrees, where the polynomial oscillates between the eight days it was learned from. By comparing the training error of a machine learning method with the resulting validation error, two failures can be detected. A training error far below the validation error indicates overfitting. A large training error indicates underfitting: a hypothesis space too small, or an iterative optimizer that stopped too early, which restricts the effective hypothesis space. Fig. 4 also shows the effect of regularization by model pruning: restricting the hypothesis space by using a small polynomial degree raises the training error a little and lowers the average loss on the held-back days.

terms.name: training
terms.abstract: Training is the process of choosing a useful hypothesis out of a hypothesis space, or model, by solving an optimization problem whose objective function a training method builds from the data points it reads. In supervised learning, the objective function is the average loss over data points whose label values are known, such as the average squared error loss. In unsupervised learning, it measures structure instead, such as the clustering error incurred by a choice of cluster centroids. In reinforcement learning, it is the expected cumulative reward collected by a policy. Training methods differ also in how they access data points: offline methods require the training set up front, while online methods update the hypothesis whenever new data points arrive. Many training methods iterate an operator on the model parameters of a parametric model: a gradient step where the objective function is differentiable, and one sweep of alternating optimization in the k-means and expectation–maximization algorithms. An offline method applies the same operator at every step and stops at a fixed point of it, while an online method applies an operator that the arriving data point changes. These operators make the objective function small on the data points the method is given, and controlling the loss on data points outside the training set is a challenge that no choice of optimization method removes.
terms.description: A shop forecasts daily bread demand from the weather with a linear model. It trains that linear model by gradient descent on a year of past records.
