To let the forecaster follow a changing clientele instead, it trains the same linear model by online gradient descent on each new day's sales: the same model and the same objective function, with a different form of data access. The shop trains in both cases. Training is the process by which a machine learning method picks one hypothesis out of a hypothesis space. The hypothesis space H, or model, is the set of candidate maps the method may choose from. Training selects the single hypothesis ĥ that the method then uses for inference: the training phase learns ĥ, and the inference phase applies ĥ, unchanged, to newly arriving data points to deliver predictions. What makes one candidate better than another is an objective function, so training amounts to solving an optimization problem. Training methods differ in two respects. The first is the objective function. In supervised learning, each data point carries a label, and the objective function is the average loss of a hypothesis over the training set, its empirical risk, such as the average squared error loss in linear regression. In unsupervised learning, no label is given, so the objective function measures a structural quantity instead, such as the clustering error incurred by a choice of cluster centroids in hard clustering. In reinforcement learning, there is no fixed training set at all: the objective function is the expected cumulative reward G collected by a policy that interacts with an environment. The second respect is the form of data access, offline or online. A training method is an algorithm A that reads in a dataset D of data points, constructs the objective function from them together with the chosen model and loss, and delivers the hypothesis making that objective function small, ĥ = A(D). An offline algorithm reads in all data points at once, computes, and delivers ĥ. An online algorithm reads in new data points as they arrive, updating the current hypothesis at each time instant t = 1, 2, … instead of waiting for a complete training set. The hypotheses it produces form a Markov chain, since each one depends on the dataset only through its predecessor and the data point that just arrived (Fig. 1). Inference and online training both act on a newly arriving data point, and that data point plays a different role in each. Inference applies a hypothesis that training has already delivered and leaves it as it is, so the arriving data point supplies only the features to predict from. Online training keeps changing the hypothesis, so the arriving data point supplies the loss that decides the next hypothesis. An online method does both in each round: it commits to a hypothesis and predicts with it, the loss of that hypothesis is then revealed, and the next hypothesis is chosen from the losses revealed so far. For a parametric model, each hypothesis h(w) is fixed by a choice of model parameters w, so training searches over w. Many training methods amount to iterating an operator on those model parameters, \[ {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} = T({\mathbf w}^{(t)}) \text{, for } t = 0,1,\ldots \text{,} \] and the two forms of data access appear here as two forms of the operator. An offline method builds its objective function once, from the whole dataset, so T is fixed: the same map is applied at every step, and training stops at, or near, a fixed point of T, where a further iteration leaves the model parameters unchanged. An online method has no fixed objective function. Its operator reads in the arriving data point, \[ {\mathbf w}^{(t+1)} = T\big({\mathbf w}^{(t)}, {\mathbf z}^{(t)}\big) \text{,} \] so the map changes from step to step, and in general there is no single fixed point to stop at. The model parameters keep changing for as long as new data points arrive. The learned hypothesis ĥ is the one that the final model parameters define. What T does is decided by the shape of the objective function. When the objective function is differentiable in all model parameters at once, T is a gradient step, T(w) = w - η ∇ f(w) with step size η. The form of data access then decides which objective function the gradient is taken of, so a single operator yields three different training methods. Offline empirical risk minimization takes the gradient of the average loss f(w) over the whole training set. When that training set is too large to pass through at every step, stochastic gradient descent replaces ∇ f(w) by the gradient of the average loss over a few data points. Its operator is drawn at random at each step, from a distribution that the training set fixes, so it is fixed in expectation rather than fixed outright. In online learning, there is no training set at all, and online gradient descent takes one gradient step on the loss of the arriving data point alone. Some objective functions arising in training methods can be minimized easily once a subset of the model parameters is held fixed. Then T is one sweep of alternating optimization, a minimization over each subset in turn. The k-means algorithm alternates between assigning each data point to the nearest cluster and recomputing the cluster means. The expectation–maximization algorithm is the probabilistic instance: training a Gaussian mixture model, it alternates between the responsibilities of the mixture components for each data point and the parameters of those components. What separates expectation–maximization from a plain alternation is that each step minimizes a surrogate, a bound on the objective function rather than the objective function itself, which is why the likelihood function cannot decrease. Both are offline. The k-means algorithm reaches a fixed point of its operator after finitely many steps, since every step lowers the objective function and there are finitely many assignments; for expectation–maximization, under a mild continuity condition, the likelihood function converges and every limit point of the iterates is a stationary point of it. Neither is guaranteed to reach the smallest loss available in H: k-means can stop at a local minimum of its objective function, and a stationary point of the likelihood function need not maximize it. A gradient step and a sweep of alternating optimization both make the objective function small on the data points the training method is given, and that is all either of them does. Controlling the discrepancy between the loss on the training set and the loss on data points outside it is one of the main challenges in machine learning, and no choice of optimization method removes it.

terms.name: training set
terms.abstract: A training set is a dataset used to train a model: it consists of data points for which the loss incurred by each candidate hypothesis can be evaluated, so that training methods can pick the hypothesis that performs best on it. Empirical risk minimization, for example, learns the hypothesis minimizing the average loss on the training set, the empirical risk, whose minimum value is the training error. Because the learned hypothesis is picked to perform well on the training set, a small training error can be misleading and result in overfitting. The validation error on a held-back validation set indicates whether the learned hypothesis also predicts well outside the training set.
terms.description: Consider three days of weather recordings: for each day, the morning minimum temperature is the feature and the maximum daytime temperature is the label. The ultimate goal of a machine learning method is to learn a hypothesis (or to train a model) that incurs a small prediction error not only on the data points used for training but on any data point that is typical for the application. The prediction error is measured by some loss function: the loss is a number, typically nonnegative, that quantifies the error of a hypothesis on a single data point, such as the squared difference between the predicted and the true label. The goal is formalized probabilistically as a small risk: the expected loss under the probability distribution from which the data points are drawn (independent and identically distributed assumption). The method must therefore compare the candidate hypotheses from its hypothesis space on data points for which the loss can be evaluated. For example, in regression or classification, the loss can only be computed for data points with a known label. These data points form a dataset referred to as the training set, D(train) = z(r)r=1m. A training method is a map A whose input is the training set and whose output is a learned hypothesis, ĥ = A(D(train)). Training evaluates this map on the given training set. For example, empirical risk minimization minimizes the average loss on the training set, the empirical risk, to learn a hypothesis \[ \widehat{h} \in \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\left({\mathbf z}^{(r)},h \right) \text{.} \] The empirical risk of the learned hypothesis is the training error. Fig. 1 shows a training set of the three days along with two hypotheses learned from it: the linear hypothesis ĥ(1) delivered by empirical risk minimization on the linear model, and a degree-two polynomial ĥ(2) that passes through all three data points and therefore attains a training error of zero. Since ĥ is chosen to make the empirical risk small, the training error is typically smaller than the loss that the same hypothesis incurs on data points outside D(train). A small training error therefore does not guarantee a small loss outside the training set. Fig. 1 illustrates this: the polynomial ĥ(2) attains a training error of zero, the linear hypothesis ĥ(1) does not. The figure shows no data points outside D(train), but it shows that the two curves predict different labels for feature values between and beyond the three training data points. At most one of the two curves can therefore incur a small loss on a new data point with such a feature value, and the training error cannot tell which one (see overfitting). A second subset of data points, the validation set D(val), is therefore held back from model training (Fig. 2): the average loss on D(val), the validation error, evaluates the learned hypothesis on data points it was not trained on. Comparing the two errors diagnoses the machine learning method: if both are small, the learned hypothesis is likely to predict well outside D(train) as well. A small training error paired with a validation error far above it indicates overfitting; one typical cause is a hypothesis space that is too large for the number of data points in D(train). Which data points are contained in D(train) decides what is learned. The choice of the training set therefore matters for trustworthy artificial intelligence: a training set that underrepresents a group of data points can yield a learned hypothesis that incurs a larger loss on that group, a source of unfairness (see fairness).

terms.name: transfer learning
terms.abstract: Transfer learning is the reuse of what was learned on one learning task to solve another learning task. A learning task can be characterized by a probability distribution of data points, and the effectiveness of transfer learning depends on the similarity of the corresponding probability distributions. Task similarity can be encoded as a similarity graph whose edge weights couple the learning tasks at its nodes; transfer learning methods can then be obtained by optimization over this graph.
terms.description: The weather stations Krems an der Donau and Melk in the Wachau valley each record the minimum and the maximum temperature of every day. Predicting the maximum temperature y of a day at one station, the label, from its minimum temperature x, the feature, is a learning task. Each weather station defines a separate learning task. Fig. 1 shows the two tasks side by side, each with a decision tree of depth two, the hypothesis learned from a training set of five labeled days of 2020. A learning task can be characterized by the probability distribution of its data points: at the two stations those distributions are similar. Transfer learning uses such similarity. It couples the learning tasks so that what is learned at one station improves the predictions at the other, and its effectiveness depends on how similar the probability distributions of the coupled tasks are. The coupling in Fig. 1 is implemented by adding a penalty to the objective function of the model training at each station. Let h(1) and h(2) be the hypotheses of the two stations and T a test set of feature values selected at random from the range [-10, 10] of minimum temperatures. Transfer learning then minimizes the sum of the two training errors plus α (1)/(|T|) Σx ∈ T ( h(1)(x) - h(2)(x) )2, the mean squared disagreement of the two hypotheses on the test features. For decision trees, minimizing over one tree while the other is held fixed is a weighted training of that tree on its own days together with the test features labeled by the other tree. Alternating the two minimizations is a block coordinate descent for the coupled problem: an exact minimization over one tree cannot increase the coupled objective function, so the sequence of objective values is nonincreasing. A decision tree is learned greedily, so each step is only an approximate block minimization, and the alternation is a heuristic for the coupled problem rather than a method that solves it. With five labeled days per station, the coupled trees agree on the test features (mean squared disagreement 32.2 → 0.1), and their average error on the held-out days of the two stations falls from 47.4 to 33.5. The coupling of two tasks extends to a collection of learning tasks, one per node i = 1, …, n of an undirected weighted graph G, the similarity graph. A weighted edge i,i' with edge weight Ai,i' encodes the similarity between two learning tasks; a zero weight leaves them uncoupled. Each node i carries a local model, a local dataset, and the local hypothesis h(i) learned from them. Minimizing the sum of the local training errors plus α times the generalized total variation \sum_{\{i,i'\} \in \mathcal{E}} A_{i,i'} d^{(i,i')} \text{,} with d(i,i') a measure of the discrepancy between the local hypotheses h(i) and h(i'), is generalized total variation minimization. The coupling in Fig. 1 is generalized total variation minimization on a graph with two nodes, with the mean squared disagreement on the test features T as the discrepancy measure; this measure applies to any local model, the decision trees included. For local models with model parameters w(i), the squared distance ‖ w(i) - w(i') ‖22 is a common choice, and the network Lasso is the variant with the unsquared distance. Generalized total variation minimization learns all local hypotheses simultaneously and transfers knowledge between well-connected learning tasks, as in federated learning. Fig. 2 shows a similarity graph of nine stations in Lower Austria, with edge weights that fall off with the distance between stations and are kept for the nearest neighbors of each. With five labeled days and a decision tree at every station, generalized total variation minimization with the disagreement on T lowers the average held-out error of the nine stations from 57.0 to 35.9 and the error at eight of them; at the ninth, Wien, whose edges are the weakest of the graph, the coupling raises it slightly. A special case of transfer learning is a node without any labeled data points. Its own training error is absent from the objective, so generalized total variation minimization determines its hypothesis through the generalized total variation alone, from the predictions of its neighbors on the test features. The unlabeled node is the case of semi-supervised learning: it still has data points, and its position in the similarity graph is what lets them be used. A second form of transfer learning places the similarity between a pretraining task and the new one, instead of between the stations of a similarity graph. It adapts a deep net trained on a large dataset to a small one: the features computed by its early layers are kept (see feature learning) and the remaining model parameters are adapted by fine-tuning. When the features useful for the first task are not useful for the second, the adapted hypothesis can have a larger risk than one trained from scratch, which is called negative transfer. The case in which the learning task stays fixed and only the probability distribution of the feature vectors changes is domain adaptation.

terms.name: transformer
terms.abstract: A transformer is an artificial neural network built by composing layers, each of which transforms the features of a data point made up of smaller units, so-called tokens, such as the words of a text or the patches of an image. The feature vectors of the tokens are stacked into a matrix; each layer maps this matrix to one of the same shape, so that layers can be composed freely into a deep artificial neural network. The layers alternate between token mixing, which combines information across tokens, and a position-wise multilayer perceptron, which transforms each token separately.
terms.description: A text consists of words, and an image consists of patches of pixels (see Fig. 1): the data points of many machine learning applications consist of smaller units, so-called tokens. A transformer is an artificial neural network that is built by composing layers, each of which transforms the features of such a token-based data point. The feature vectors (or embeddings) x(1), …, x(n) ∈ Rd of the n tokens are stacked into a matrix X = (x(1), …, x(n))ᵀ ∈ Rn × d. Each layer of the original transformer maps such a matrix to a transformed matrix of the same shape, so that layers can be composed freely into a deep artificial neural network. For example, a transformer that translates a sentence transforms the stacked word embeddings, layer by layer, into feature vectors from which the translated words are predicted; transformers also process images by taking patches as tokens. Contemporary LLMs, such as GPT-3, are transformers trained to predict the next token of a text. The layers of a transformer alternate between two types of transformations of X (see Fig. 2). A token-mixing layer maps X to a new matrix X̃, each row of which is a weighted sum of linear images of the rows of X, with weights that can depend on X itself; the tokens thereby interact. In the original transformer, token mixing is implemented by multi-head attention, whose output for each token is a weighted sum of the value vectors, the rows of X multiplied by a learned matrix. Attention distinguishes transformers from RNNs, which process the tokens of a data point sequentially instead of in parallel. A position-wise multilayer perceptron then transforms each row of X̃ separately. For each of the two transformations, a residual connection adds the input of the transformation to its output, and a subsequent layer normalization standardizes each row of the resulting matrix. The matrices produced by successive layers represent the tokens at increasingly abstract levels. This progression is measured by probing: a simple classifier is trained to predict a chosen property from the output of a single layer, and the depth at which the property becomes predictable locates it in the network. In a language transformer, word-level properties are predictable from the output of early layers. One example is a part-of-speech tag, which marks whether a word is a noun, a verb, or an adjective. Relations between tokens far apart in the text become predictable only in deeper layers. Deep CNNs show the same progression, from edges and textures in early layers to object parts in deeper ones. Vision transformers develop it too: their early layers split attention between nearby and distant patches, while the deeper layers attend across the whole image. In language and vision transformers alike, the most informative representations often arise in the middle layers, whose outputs can outperform those of the final layer as features for other tasks. Whatever the layers represent, computing them is dominated by the token mixing that produces the matrix of each layer, which is computationally expensive. Attention compares every pair of tokens, so its cost grows as n2 with the number n of tokens. This quadratic growth motivates alternative techniques for token mixing. Some transformer variants reduce the number of tokens in deeper layers. Any transformation that combines the rows of X can replace attention: a multilayer perceptron applied across tokens, a fixed Fourier transform, or a state-space layer whose cost is linear in n.

terms.name: transparency
terms.abstract: Transparency is a key requirement for trustworthy artificial intelligence: it names the duties to close the information gaps between the provider of an artificial intelligence system, its deployer, and the persons affected by its predictions. For machine learning methods, transparency is often used interchangeably with explainability: explanations, delivered along with the predictions of a learned hypothesis, let a human user anticipate those predictions. The EU AI Act makes transparency a binding design requirement. Under the Act, the provider must design a high-risk artificial intelligence system so that its deployer can interpret the delivered predictions. Persons interacting with an artificial intelligence system must be informed of that fact. Affected persons may obtain an explanation of decisions based on the predictions delivered by a high-risk artificial intelligence system. The Act also requires documentation of the algorithm design, the training datasets, and the intended use of an artificial intelligence system, as well as a machine-readable marking of synthetic content as artificially generated.
terms.description: Consider a bank that uses an artificial intelligence system to score loan applications. The loan officer sees only the score, and the applicant might not even know that an artificial intelligence system was involved. Transparency names the duties to close such information gaps; it is a fundamental requirement for trustworthy artificial intelligence. In the context of machine learning methods, transparency is often used interchangeably with explainability: explanations, delivered along with the predictions of a learned hypothesis, let a human user anticipate those predictions. Some machine learning methods inherently offer this form of transparency. Classification methods quantify the confidence in an individual prediction via the distance of the feature vector from the decision boundary. A shallow decision tree does not require a separately constructed explanation: presenting the tree as a flow chart of explicit, human-readable decision rules is an explanation of every prediction it delivers (see interpretable machine learning). In the broader scope of AI systems, transparency extends beyond explainability: it includes informing persons that an artificial intelligence system is in use and providing information about the limitations, the overall reliability, and the intended use of the system as a whole. The binding transparency obligations discussed below are those of the EU AI Act; other jurisdictions impose related but distinct duties, e.g., the Colorado Automated Decision-Making Technology Act and the court proceedings State v. Loomis on the use of a proprietary recidivism-risk score in sentencing. The Act distributes its obligations among three roles: the provider that develops an artificial intelligence system, the deployer that uses it, and the persons who interact with the artificial intelligence system or are affected by its output (see deployer). The Act's term output denotes the predictions delivered by a learned hypothesis; the machine learning term prediction is used below. Like interpretability and explainability, which are relative to a specific user or group of users, transparency is relative to its addressee: what must be disclosed depends on the role. Specifically, toward the deployer, the provider must design and develop a high-risk artificial intelligence system so that its operation is sufficiently transparent to enable the deployers to interpret its predictions and use them appropriately. A second example, medical diagnosis, shows the two roles: the provider is, e.g., a company that develops an X-ray analysis tool, and a clinic that uses the tool acts as the deployer. The provider can meet the duty of Art. 13 by designing the tool to disclose to the clinician the confidence level for the predictions delivered by a learned hypothesis. This duty concerns the meaning of the predictions in the context of their use; the AI Risk Management Framework of the US National Institute of Standards and Technology reserves the term interpretability for this contextual meaning. This usage differs from interpretability as the comprehension of the computational process of the method; Art. 13 does not require that comprehension. Toward persons who interact directly with an artificial intelligence system, such as an artificial intelligence-powered chatbot, the provider must design the artificial intelligence system so that these persons are informed of that fact. Providers of AI systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video, or text content must mark such content in a machine-readable format as artificially generated. This marking duty applies whether or not the artificial intelligence system is a high-risk artificial intelligence system; it is waived, e.g., where the artificial intelligence system only performs an assistive function for standard editing. For a deep fake, the deployer must, in addition, disclose visibly that the content is artificially generated or manipulated. A person can be affected by an artificial intelligence system without directly interacting with it. A patient whose diagnosis is supported by an artificial intelligence-based system deals only with the clinician. Nevertheless, the deployer must inform the patient that a high-risk artificial intelligence system is used concerning them. The EU AI Act also grants the affected person a right to explanation: the deployer must, on request, provide a clear and meaningful explanation of the role of the artificial intelligence system in a decision based on its predictions. In credit scoring, for example, a loan applicant faced with an adverse automated decision may obtain from the deployer, under this right, an explanation of the contributing factors, such as income level or credit history, and use it to contest the decision (see Fig. 1). Transparency also encompasses documentation detailing the purpose and design choices underlying the artificial intelligence system. For a high-risk artificial intelligence system, the provider must provide documentation that covers the algorithm design and the datasets used for training. The provider of a general-purpose AI model must additionally publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training. Datasheets for datasets and model cards help practitioners understand the intended use cases and limitations of an artificial intelligence system. Concretely, Fig. 1 locates these obligations in a scatterplot of training set data points together with a learned hypothesis, for the credit-scoring example. The solid curve depicts the learned hypothesis ĥ that the artificial intelligence system applies: it maps the income x of an applicant to a predicted credit score ĥ(x), and a loan is approved when the predicted score exceeds an approval threshold (dotted line). The duty of Art. 13 concerns the use of this map: here, the deployer must be able to state the prediction ĥ(x') for an applicant with income x' (open square) and its distance from the threshold. The filled circles depict the training set D(train) of completed loans, with income as the feature x and credit score as the label y, from which ĥ was learned, e.g., via empirical risk minimization, by minimizing the average loss of the hypothesis over D(train). The documentation of Art. 11 covers both components of this training: the dataset D(train) and the design of the algorithm, including the model and the loss used. Income levels outside the range covered by D(train) (shaded region) are a limitation that the documentation must state, since no estimate of the risk computed from D(train) covers them. The right to explanation of Art. 86 is exercised for a single prediction: the applicant with income x', whose predicted score falls below the threshold, may ask why. One answer is a counterfactual: the smallest change of the feature that flips the decision, the income x'' (open diamond, arrow) at which ĥ reaches the threshold. Fig. 2 summarizes these transparency obligations as information flows between the provider of an artificial intelligence system, its deployer, and the persons exposed to its predictions.

terms.name: trustworthy artificial intelligence (trustworthy AI)
terms.abstract: Trustworthy artificial intelligence (trustworthy AI) names an artificial intelligence system that meets requirements beyond delivering accurate predictions. From an engineering perspective, the ultimate goal of machine learning is to predict the label of any data point accurately, i.e., to learn a hypothesis with small risk. This perspective is too narrow, since a machine learning method is embedded in a sociotechnical system that includes human users. Trustworthy AI therefore formulates additional requirements for the method: human oversight, robustness, privacy, transparency, fairness, societal well-being, and accountability. Guidelines and regulations across the world state these requirements, from the OECD AI Principles to national rules in China and Australia and federal and state rules in the US, and the Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI of the European Commission are one example among them. Their seven key requirements are stated for the artificial intelligence system as a whole, including the people and the organization around the machine learning method inside it. The requirements translate into design choices for the components of empirical risk minimization: the training set, the model, the loss function, and the algorithm. For example, robustness requires a model that contains no hypothesis map that is too sensitive to a small perturbation of the feature vector. Each such requirement is a measurable property of the learned hypothesis or of the method that learned it: a bound on the change of a prediction under a perturbation of the feature vector, the change of the prediction when only a sensitive attribute is flipped, the counterfactual that explains a rejection, or the share of borderline decisions passed to a person.
terms.description: Consider a bank that uses an artificial intelligence system to decide on loan applications. The system applies a hypothesis ĥ, learned from the records of completed loans, to the feature vector x of an applicant, which collects the income, the gender, and further attributes. The loan is approved when the predicted creditworthiness ĥ(x) exceeds a threshold τ. From an engineering perspective, the ultimate goal of a machine learning method is to predict the label of any data point accurately. This goal is formalized as a small risk of ĥ, the expected loss on an applicant drawn from the same probability distribution as the completed loans. This perspective is too narrow. The machine learning method is embedded in a sociotechnical system that includes human users: the applicants whose loans it decides, the loan officers who act on its predictions, and the supervisor who audits the bank. These users rely on the decisions only if the system meets requirements beyond the accuracy of its predictions. A small change of the income must not flip the decision, the gender alone must not flip it either, a rejected applicant must learn why, and a loan officer must be able to overrule the system. Trustworthy AI formulates such requirements for a machine learning method and names an artificial intelligence system that meets them. Such requirements are stated by guidelines and regulations adopted across the world since 2019. Examples are the OECD AI Principles, Australia's AI Ethics Principles, the AI Risk Management Framework of the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, China's Interim Measures for generative artificial intelligence services, and the management-system standard ISO/IEC 42001. These documents name much the same requirements and differ in their legal force. The Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI of the European Commission's High-Level Expert Group are used as the example here, since they enumerate the requirements explicitly. Their seven key requirements (KRs) are human agency and oversight (KR1), technical robustness and safety (KR2), privacy and data governance (KR3), transparency (KR4), diversity, nondiscrimination, and fairness (KR5), societal and environmental well-being (KR6), and accountability (KR7). The accompanying assessment list turns each requirement into questions that the provider and the deployer of the artificial intelligence system answer about their system. These requirements are stated for an artificial intelligence system as a whole, which includes the data pipeline, the user interface, and the organization that operates it, and not only for the machine learning method inside it. KR6 and KR7 concern the purpose and the governance of the system and have no counterpart in the machine learning method. KR1 to KR5, in contrast, translate into design choices for the components of empirical risk minimization: the training set D(train), the model H, the loss function, and an algorithm that minimizes the average loss over D(train). KR2, e.g., requires a model H that contains no hypothesis map that is too sensitive to a small perturbation of the feature vector. Excluding such maps from H is model pruning, one of the three routes that regularization distinguishes. Each of these requirements is a measurable property of the learned hypothesis ĥ or of the method that learned it. Fig. 1 places KR1, KR2, KR4, and KR5 in the credit-scoring example. The horizontal axis is a one-dimensional sketch of the feature vector x: the income, the gender, and the further attributes of an applicant collapsed into one coordinate. The vertical axis is the creditworthiness, the label y. The filled circles are the training set D(train) of m = 5 completed loans, the solid curve a hypothesis ĥ drawn for illustration in place of one learned from D(train), and the dotted line the approval threshold τ = 3.8. The applicant with feature vector x' (open square) obtains the predicted creditworthiness ĥ(x') = 2.94 and is rejected. KR2 asks that a small perturbation of the feature vector changes the prediction little. The perturbation of x' by δ = 0.5 (horizontal arrow) moves the predicted creditworthiness from 2.94 to 3.19 (vertical arrow). The slope of ĥ never exceeds 1.225, so the hypothesis is Lipschitz continuous with that constant: no perturbation by δ changes the prediction by more than 1.225 δ (see robustness). KR2 also covers perturbations of D(train), e.g., by data poisoning, against which the stability of the machine learning method protects. KR5 asks that the decision does not depend on a sensitive attribute s such as gender. The open triangle depicts the same applicant with only the gender flipped, the feature vector x⋆. The predicted creditworthiness rises to ĥ(x⋆) = 3.93, above τ, so the system approves the loan (as a borderline case, it is also passed to the loan officer): the decision depends on the gender, which violates the counterfactual criterion of fairness. The gap ĥ(x⋆) - ĥ(x') = 0.99 measures the violation. It is closed by a design choice for a component of empirical risk minimization: the model (excluding the sensitive attribute and the features correlated with it), the loss function (a penalty term for the gap), or D(train) (resampling the groups). KR4 asks for transparency: the rejected applicant is told that an artificial intelligence system was used and may obtain an explanation. The counterfactual x'' (open diamond), at which ĥ reaches τ, is such an explanation. It is the smallest change of the income, at fixed gender, that flips the decision, and it tells the applicant the income at which the loan would be approved. The gender flip x⋆ also flips the decision, but it is not a change the applicant can make, which is what makes it a violation of KR5 rather than an explanation. KR1 asks that a person can oversee and overrule the decisions. The shaded band marks predicted creditworthiness within ε = 0.3 of τ. Applications in this band are passed to a loan officer, who decides; one of the five loans in D(train) falls into it. A wider band passes more applications to the officer and leaves fewer borderline decisions to the system (see human oversight). Finally, KR3 has no place in the figure, since it concerns the data rather than a prediction: it asks that the records of completed loans, which are personal data, are protected during training and cannot be recovered from ĥ; differential privacy and federated learning are design choices for the algorithm and for D(train) to that end (see data governance). Beyond guidelines, binding law states the same requirements. The EU AI Act is one example: it makes KR1 to KR4 obligatory for a high-risk artificial intelligence system, a class that includes the credit scoring of natural persons. China's Interim Measures bind the providers of generative artificial intelligence services to transparency and nondiscrimination. In the US, individual states legislate. California gives a consumer subject to an automated lending decision a notice, an opt-out, and access to the logic of the decision. Arizona requires a licensed health care provider to review every denial of an insurance claim that artificial intelligence would issue on grounds of medical judgment. These requirements can conflict: closing the gender gap raises the average loss on D(train), and the noise that differential privacy adds to the training makes explanations less precise. Trustworthiness is therefore a set of measured properties that are balanced for the application, not a single number.

terms.name: unsupervised learning
terms.abstract: Unsupervised learning refers to machine learning methods that do not require knowledge of the label of any data point. These methods learn a hypothesis by loss functions that are constructed from the features of data points only. Two important examples of unsupervised learning are clustering and dimensionality reduction. Clustering methods use some notion of clustering error to learn model parameters that encode a cluster structure. Dimensionality reduction methods construct a loss from the reconstruction error.
terms.description: Twenty days at Krems an der Donau are each characterized by two features, the daily minimum and the daily maximum temperature, and nothing else is recorded about them (Fig. 1). Unsupervised learning methods learn a hypothesis map that predicts a label that is not known for any of these data points. For example, the label could be an index that selects one out of two clusters to which the data point belongs. Another label could be the optimal scalar representation of a data point. Formally, an unsupervised machine learning method learns a hypothesis out of a hypothesis space based on an unlabeled dataset D = x(1), …, x(m) of feature vectors x(r) ∈ X, with no label space. The model parameters are typically learned by an instance of empirical risk minimization, minimizing the average loss over the dataset, \[ \widehat{h} \in \mathop{\mathrm{arg min}}_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L\left({\mathbf x}^{(r)},h \right) \text{.} \] What sets unsupervised methods apart from supervised methods, such as linear regression, is the choice of loss function. Two important families of unsupervised methods are obtained by specific constructions of the loss, clustering and dimensionality reduction. The clustering method k-means uses k cluster centroids as model parameters w = w(1), …, w(k). They are learned by minimizing the average clustering error, the loss \[ L\left({\mathbf x},{\mathbf w} \right) = \min_{c = 1, \ldots, k} \left\lVert {\mathbf x} - {{\mathbf w}}^{(c)} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{.} \] Principal component analysis is a dimensionality reduction method that learns a linear feature transformation x ↦ W x together with a reconstruction map z ↦ R z that rebuilds the feature vector from it. Both are model parameters, and for a given R the loss of a data point is its reconstruction error \[ L\left({\mathbf x},\left( {\mathbf W},{\mathbf R} \right) \right) = \left\lVert {\mathbf x} - {\mathbf R} {\mathbf W} {\mathbf x} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \text{.} \] One R is used for the whole dataset, and empirical risk minimization learns it together with W by minimizing the average of this loss. For the learned pair the reconstruction is the orthogonal projection of the feature vector on a subspace of dimension d'. Fig. 1 shows both on the Krems days: the two cluster centroids with the data points assigned to each, and the learned direction with the orthogonal projections that give each day its single number.

terms.name: validation error
terms.abstract: The validation error of a learned hypothesis ĥ, obtained from a machine learning method using some training set, is its average loss over a validation set. The validation set consists of data points that do not belong to the training set used to learn the hypothesis ĥ. When the generation of the data points in the validation set is modeled by independent and identically distributed RVs, the validation error is an unbiased estimator of the risk. If the training set is modeled as random, the learned hypothesis becomes a random variable as well, and the validation error is unbiased conditioned on the learned hypothesis. The validation error describes the performance of a learned hypothesis on data points outside the training set used for model training. It is therefore a more suitable criterion for model selection than the training error. A comparison of the validation error with the training error of a learned hypothesis allows one to diagnose overfitting and underfitting.
terms.description: The weather station Krems an der Donau (Austria) recorded the morning minimum and the maximum temperature of every day from 2020 to 2024, a dataset of 1827 days. Each day is a data point: its feature x is the morning minimum temperature, its label y the maximum temperature of the day. Fig. 1 shows twenty of these data points as a scatterplot. Three of them, drawn in black, form a training set used to learn two hypotheses by empirical risk minimization: the linear hypothesis ĥ(1) over the linear model and the degree-two polynomial ĥ(2) delivered by polynomial regression. The polynomial passes through all three days and incurs a training error of zero, far below the training error 7.91 of ĥ(1). Its average loss over all 1827 data points from 2020 to 2024, however, is 42.90. The usefulness of a hypothesis ĥ = A(D(train)), learned by some machine learning method A from a training set D(train), must be assessed beyond D(train). To this end, ĥ is evaluated on a validation set D(val) that consists of data points outside the training set. The validation error Ev of ĥ is its average loss on the validation set, \begin{equation} E_{v} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}^{(\rm val)}|} \sum_{{\mathbf z} \in \mathcal{D}^{(\rm val)}} L\left({\mathbf z},\widehat{h} \right) \text{,} \end{equation} with L(z,ĥ ) the loss that ĥ incurs on a data point z. Fig. 1 illustrates a validation set of three data points, drawn as red triangles and chosen by a fixed rule to spread across the range of the feature. The dotted bars are the prediction errors of the polynomial on them. The average of the three squared bars is the validation error Eq. (1) of the polynomial, 42.58. This validation error is close to the average squared error loss of ĥ(2) over all 1827 data points, 42.90. A hypothesis with a larger training error can be the better one: the linear hypothesis ĥ(1) has a training error of 7.91 but a validation error of 6.98. What the validation error Eq. (1) estimates is fixed by an independent and identically distributed assumption for the data generation. The data points are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs with a common probability distribution. That probability distribution defines the risk L̄ ( ĥ ), the expectation of L(z,ĥ ) over a data point drawn from it. Each summand of the average Eq. (1) has that expectation, so Ev is the realization of a random variable with expectation L̄ ( ĥ ): for a fixed hypothesis ĥ it is an unbiased estimator of L̄ ( ĥ ). Its variance is the variance of a single loss divided by |D(val)|, i.e., it decreases as |D(val)| grows. In practice, the learned hypothesis ĥ = A(D(train)) is the output of a training method A that reads in a training set D(train). Under the independent and identically distributed assumption, the training set is itself the realization of a random variable, and so is the learned hypothesis ĥ: a different realization of D(train) would have delivered a different hypothesis. The validation error is then unbiased conditioned on the learned hypothesis. The training error has no such property: conditioned on ĥ, the data points of D(train) are no longer independent and identically distributed realizations of the probability distribution of a data point, because ĥ was chosen to make its average loss on them small. If the data points of D(val) and D(train) are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs, then D(val) is independent of ĥ. The conditional expectation of Ev given ĥ is then its risk, \[ \mathbb{E} \big\{ E_{v} \mid \widehat{h} \big\} = \bar{L} \big( \widehat{h} \big) \text{.} \] The loss function L(·,· ), by contrast, is evaluated on one data point. How large must a validation set be for Ev to be close to the risk? The variance computed above gives the typical deviation; a concentration inequality gives a guarantee that holds with a prescribed probability. For a fixed hypothesis ĥ, a loss with values in [0,1], and some confidence parameter δ ∈ (0,1), Hoeffding's inequality gives, with probability at least 1-δ over the draw of D(val), \begin{equation} \big| E_{v} - \bar{L} \big( \widehat{h} \big) \big| \leq \sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2 |\mathcal{D}^{(\rm val)}|}} \text{,} \end{equation} see Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David (2014, Thm. 11.1). The bound Eq. (2) depends on the size of the validation set and on δ alone, not on the hypothesis space H from which ĥ was learned. This is different from controlling the deviation of the training error from the risk. The empirical risk minimization solution was selected by comparing all hypotheses of H on the training set, so a bound like Eq. (2) for the training error of ĥ has to hold for every hypothesis of H at once, and such a bound grows with the size of H. In Fig. 1 the validation set was fixed. A numerical experiment shows how much the validation error varies when the validation set is instead chosen at random. Consider the hypothesis \[ \widehat{h}(x) = 10.47 + 1.05 x \text{,} \] obtained by linear regression from forty data points of the same station record, every ninth day of 2024. The data points of 306 further days of that year, none of them used for training, are collected in a dataset D(pool). In this experiment, the pool is only the collection from which each validation set is drawn at random. It is not a test set D(test), which is kept apart to assess one selected hypothesis and is read once. Fig. 2 shows the mean and the standard deviation of the validation error of ĥ over repeated draws of a validation set of prescribed size from D(pool). The standard deviation decreases with increasing size of the validation set, as the variance computation above predicts: it falls as 1/√(|D(val)|). This is also the form of the bound Eq. (2), though that bound itself does not apply, since the squared error loss takes values beyond [0,1]. Beyond estimating the risk of one hypothesis, the validation error is compared with the training error and across models. A training error far below the validation error indicates overfitting. A validation error close to the training error shows no overfitting; when both are also far above the error that a larger model reaches on the same validation set, the diagnosis is underfitting and the model is too small for the task. The two errors together therefore diagnose a machine learning method and guide its revision, by a larger model in the second case and by regularization, more training data points, or a smaller model in the first. Comparing the validation errors of several candidate models is model selection. A model has no validation error of its own. The phrase validation error of a model is short for the validation error of the hypothesis that A delivers from that model, since Ev is the average loss of a single hypothesis. The selected model is the one whose hypothesis attains the smallest of the compared validation errors. That smallest validation error is biased downward as an estimate of the risk, since the minimum of several noisy estimates lies below the quantity it estimates on average, and a test set D(test) is kept apart for the final assessment. What the validation error costs is data points: a data point held back for D(val) cannot be used for training. What it buys is an estimate that the training error cannot give, computed on data points the training never read. The price of that estimate is paid twice, because it is itself noisy. Its standard deviation falls only as 1/√(|D(val)|), so halving the noise costs four times the data points: on the Krems record a validation set of twenty data points spreads by 4.96 squared degrees around the risk and one of eighty by 2.26. A deviation smaller than that spread cannot be read off one validation set. For the hypothesis of the experiment, learned over the linear model, the training error lies 0.45 squared degrees below the risk, while an average over twenty data points fluctuates by about 5.37. One validation set of that size therefore cannot resolve the overfitting of a linear model at all. It does resolve the overfitting of the degree-nine polynomial regression, whose training error sits far below its risk. Where data points are too few to spend on a validation set of that size, k-fold cross-validation is the usual answer: every data point serves once for validation and otherwise for training, at the cost of learning one hypothesis per fold instead of one in total.

terms.name: validation set
terms.abstract: A validation set consists of data points that have not been used for model training. For a learned hypothesis, the average loss on the validation set, the validation error, indicates how well the hypothesis predicts the labels of data points outside the training set. The validation error is used for model selection: the hypotheses learned by different machine learning methods are compared, and the one with the smallest validation error is selected. The selected hypothesis depends on the validation set, so assessing it requires a test set whose data points entered neither training nor selection. The size of the validation set determines how reliable the validation error is. When data points are scarce, k-fold cross-validation uses each fold of the dataset in turn as validation set and averages the k validation errors.
terms.description: Consider three days of weather recordings: for each day, the morning minimum temperature is the feature and the maximum daytime temperature is the label. Fig. 1 shows a training set D(train) of three such days along with two hypotheses learned from it: the linear hypothesis ĥ(1) delivered by empirical risk minimization on the linear model, and a degree-two polynomial ĥ(2) that passes through all three data points and therefore attains a training error of zero. Three further days, marked by open triangles, were held back from model training: they form a validation set D(val). The validation error of a hypothesis ĥ learned from the training set is its average loss on the validation set, \[ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}^{(\rm val)}|} \sum_{{\mathbf z} \in \mathcal{D}^{(\rm val)}} L\left({\mathbf z},\widehat{h} \right) \text{.} \] Here, L(z,ĥ ) is the loss of ĥ on the data point z. In Fig. 1, the polynomial ĥ(2) attains a training error of zero but a validation error of 17.3, while the linear hypothesis ĥ(1) has a training error of 2.9 and a validation error of 3.0. The comparison of the two validation errors is an instance of model selection: the hypotheses learned by different machine learning methods are compared, and the one with the smallest validation error is selected. In Fig. 1, the hypothesis ĥ(1) is selected. The selected hypothesis depends on D(val): its validation error is the smallest of the compared validation errors, so the validation error of the selected hypothesis is biased downward. Assessing the hypothesis learned from the model that was chosen on the basis of the validation errors requires a third dataset whose data points entered neither training nor selection: the test set D(test). In Fig. 2, the three days of the test set, marked by open squares, yield a test error E(test) = 1.3 for the selected hypothesis ĥ(1). The test error is the only one of the three numbers that was not used to choose anything, so it is not biased by selection. With only three test days, however, it is itself a noisy estimate of the risk of ĥ(1). The validation error is an average of |D(val)| losses, one per validation data point. How closely it tracks the risk of a learned hypothesis therefore depends on the size |D(val)|, and a validation set that is too small gives an unreliable validation error. Take a loss with values in [0,1], a fixed hypothesis ĥ, and a confidence parameter δ in (0, 1) chosen by the user. Hoeffding's inequality then guarantees, with probability at least 1 - δ, that the risk of ĥ lies within an uncertainty band of half-width ε around the measured validation error. The guarantee requires that \[ |\mathcal{D}^{(\rm val)}| \geq \frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2 \epsilon^{2}} \text{.} \] Fig. 3 shows this lower bound as a function of the half-width ε for three values of δ; it holds for any validation error, not only those of the weather example. Narrowing the band is costly: halving ε quadruples the required size. To have the validation error within ε = 0.1 of the risk with δ = 0.1, it suffices to hold back |D(val)| ≥ 150 data points, the point of the dashed curve at ε = 0.1 in Fig. 3, regardless of the hypothesis space and of the size of D(train). The bound covers one fixed hypothesis. A bound that covers the selected hypothesis must hold for all compared hypotheses at once, which requires a larger validation set. The bound can be checked by simulation. Fig. 4 reports how often the validation error of a fixed hypothesis deviates from the risk by more than ε, when the validation set holds exactly the number of data points that the bound requires. The loss used there takes the values 0 and 1 with equal probability, so its variance is the largest a loss with values in [0,1] can have. Each share is measured over 200,000 validation sets. Every measured share stays below its δ, and below δ / 4, so the size the bound requires is larger than the size the measured deviations call for. A validation set eight times smaller does fail the guarantee. At ε = 0.1 and δ = 0.1 the bound asks for 150 data points. With 19 of them, 36 of every 100 validation errors land farther than ε from the risk. A typical machine learning workflow therefore splits the available dataset three ways. A training set learns the hypotheses, a validation set selects among them, and a test set assesses the selected one. The test set is used only once. When data points are scarce, that split is expensive: the bound above asks for 150 data points at ε = 0.1 and δ = 0.1, which a dataset of 200 days cannot spend on validation alone. As a remedy, k-fold cross-validation divides the dataset into k folds. For each fold in turn, it uses that fold as validation set and the other k - 1 folds as training set. Each of the k validation errors is therefore computed on different data points and for a different learned hypothesis. Every fold yields a noisy validation error, an average of the losses over the few data points of the fold, and averaging the k per-fold validation errors produces a more reliable estimate of the risk. For the three training set days and the three validation days of Fig. 1 pooled into one dataset, three folds of two days give per-fold validation errors of 11.21, 2.80, and 3.29, averaging 5.77. Over 300 replicate datasets of six days, the standard deviation of the three-fold average is 14.4, against 55.8 for one split holding back two days. Each fold requires its own training run, k in total instead of the single run of one split. Neither a single split nor k-fold cross-validation avoids the estimation noise arising from using a small validation set. Three validation data points are too few to order two hypotheses reliably. Over 20,000 draws of three validation days, the validation error prefers the hypothesis with the larger risk in 12 of every 100 draws for the pair of Fig. 2, whose risks are 4.29 squared degrees for the line and 23.46 for the polynomial. For two lines whose risks differ by 1.68 squared degrees, it does so in 24 of every 100 draws. The wide risk margin of the selection in Fig. 2 therefore does not make that selection safe; what the validation error of three data points delivers is a preference, not a guarantee.

terms.name: variance
terms.abstract: The variance of a real-valued random variable is the expectation of the squared difference between the random variable and its mean. It quantifies the spread of the probability distribution of the random variable around the mean: a small variance means that realizations concentrate near the mean. The term also refers to the sample variance of a dataset; the two usages are consistent, since the sample variance is the variance of the random variable obtained by drawing a data point uniformly from the dataset. Under the squared error loss, the variance is the smallest risk that a constant prediction of a numeric label can achieve. For a random vector, the variance is the expectation of the squared Euclidean norm of the deviation from the mean. This quantity equals the trace of the covariance matrix of the random vector, i.e., the sum of the variances of its entries.
terms.description: The Helsinki Kaisaniemi weather station recorded seven daily maximum temperatures between 19.6 and 22.2 ∘C on 24--30 August 2026, and every reading lies within two degrees of their average of 20.5 ∘C. How far readings scatter around their average is what the variance measures. The variance of a real-valued random variable y is the expectation E ( y - Ey )2 of the squared difference between y and its expectation Ey, also called its mean. The term is also used to refer to the sample variance of a finite dataset D = y(1), …, y(m) ∈ R. These two usages are consistent. A dataset defines a discrete random variable ỹ(D) = y(I) on the sample space 1, …, m. Here, the index I is chosen uniformly at random, i.e., P(I=r)=1/m for all r=1,…,m, so the probability distribution of ỹ(D) is the empirical distribution of the dataset. The variance of ỹ(D) is precisely the sample variance \[ \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \Big( y^{(r)} - \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r'=1}^{m} y^{(r')} \Big)^{2} \text{,} \] i.e., the average squared deviation of the data points from their sample mean. Fig. 1 depicts the seven Helsinki readings of 24--30 August 2026 as realizations of a real-valued random variable, together with their sample mean and the deviation of each measurement from it. For the seven temperatures of Fig. 1, the sample variance is the number 6.34/7 ≈ 0.91, computed from the readings alone. It estimates the variance of the random variable that generated them, which is a property of its probability distribution and is never observed exactly. The sample variance also serves as a threshold for detecting outliers: a common rule declares a data point an outlier when its squared deviation from the sample mean exceeds nine times the sample variance, i.e., three standard deviations. The reading of 22.2 ∘C deviates by 1.7 ∘C, whose square 2.89 is about three times the sample variance, so the rule keeps every reading. For a random variable with a finite second moment, i.e., E y2 < ∞, the mean is the constant b that minimizes the risk E ( y - b )2. The variance is the smallest value this risk attains, i.e., its minimum at b = Ey: \[ \mathbb{E}\big\{ \big( y - \mathbb{E}\{y\} \big)^{2} \big\} = \min_{b \in \mathbb{R}} \mathbb{E}\big\{ ( y - b )^{2} \big\} \text{.} \] This minimum-risk characterization applies directly to the simplest machine learning problem, predicting a numeric label y without using any features. The hypothesis space for this problem consists of the constant maps h(·) = b with b ∈ R. Each such hypothesis amounts to a single bias term: it delivers the same prediction b for every data point. Given a training set D(train) = y(1), …, y(m) that consists of labels y(r) ∈ R only, empirical risk minimization with the squared error loss amounts to finding the constant that best predicts the label of a data point. The solution b̂ is the sample mean of the labels (see mean), and the training error of the learned hypothesis is the sample variance of the labels. For the temperatures of Fig. 1, the learned hypothesis is the dashed line: b̂ = 20.5 ∘C, with training error equal to the sample variance 0.91 computed above. The variance of the label therefore serves as a baseline: a machine learning method that uses features is useful only if its risk falls below the variance of the label. Variance extends from a real-valued random variable to a random vector x as the expectation of the squared Euclidean norm of the deviation from the mean, E ‖ x - Ex ‖22 = tr (C(x)). The squared Euclidean norm is the sum of the squared deviations of the entries of x, so its expectation is the sum of their variances. The variances of the entries are the diagonal entries of the covariance matrix C(x), and the sum of the diagonal entries is the trace.

terms.name: weighted graph
terms.abstract: A weighted graph is a graph whose edges carry nonnegative numbers, the edge weights, that measure how strongly two nodes are tied. It consists of a finite set of nodes, a set of undirected edges joining pairs of distinct nodes, and a positive weight for each edge; a pair of nodes that is not an edge has weight zero. The weights form the weight matrix A, a symmetric matrix with a zero diagonal that is also the adjacency matrix of the graph, and the sum of a row is the weighted node degree of its node. In machine learning, the nodes are often the data points of a dataset and the weight of an edge is the similarity of two data points, e.g., a Gaussian function of the Euclidean distance between their feature vectors, kept for the k nearest neighbors of each data point. Graph clustering seeks subsets of nodes whose outgoing edges carry little weight. Transfer learning and federated learning use the weights of a graph of learning tasks as the coefficients of a penalty term that couples the hypotheses of neighboring tasks.
terms.description: Consider ten days of the year 2024 at Krems an der Donau, every 37th day from 1 January to 29 November, each a data point with a feature vector x ∈ R2 that holds the morning minimum and the maximum daytime temperature of the day. Two days are similar when their feature vectors are close. A drawing records the similarities: each day is a dot, called a node, two similar days are joined by a line, called an edge, and a number on the edge says how similar the two days are. Fig. 2(a) shows this drawing for the ten days, with an edge between two days whenever one of them is among the three days nearest to the other and a number between 0 and 1 that falls off with the Euclidean distance between them. Nodes, edges, and a number on every edge make a weighted graph. Formally, a weighted graph G = ( V,E ) consists of a finite set of nodes V = 1, …, n, a set E of edges, and an edge weight for each edge. Each edge is an unordered pair i,i' of two distinct nodes, so the graph is an undirected graph without self-loops, and the two nodes of an edge are neighbors of each other. The weight of an edge i,i' ∈ E is a positive number Ai,i' > 0, and a pair of nodes that is not an edge has weight Ai,i' = 0. With this convention, the weights determine the edge set, and they are collected in the weight matrix \begin{equation} {\mathbf A} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} \text{ with entries } A_{i,i'} = A_{i',i} \geq 0 \text{ and } A_{i,i} = 0 \text{ for } i, i' \in \mathcal{V} \text{.} \end{equation} The weight matrix Eq. (1) is a symmetric matrix with a zero diagonal. It is the adjacency matrix of the graph: the entry in row i and column i' is the weight of the edge between i and i', or zero when there is no edge. An unweighted graph is the special case in which every edge has weight 1, so the entries of its weight matrix Eq. (1) are 0 and 1. Fig. 1 shows a weighted graph with four nodes beside its weight matrix. The sum of the weights of the edges at a node is its weighted node degree, \begin{equation} d^{(i)} = \sum_{i' \in \mathcal{V}} A_{i,i'} \text{,} \end{equation} which is the sum of row i of the weight matrix. For an unweighted graph the node degree Eq. (2) counts the neighbors of the node. The Laplacian matrix of the graph is built from the weight matrix and the degrees Eq. (2), and its eigenvectors are what spectral clustering computes. What a weight means is fixed by the application, and two conventions are in use. In a road network, the nodes are intersections, the edges are road segments, and the weight of an edge is the length of the segment or the time needed to travel it. A large weight then means far apart, and the shortest route between two intersections is the path whose weights add up to the smallest value. In machine learning, the weight of an edge usually measures similarity: a large weight means close together. A method that reads a similarity as a length, or a length as a similarity, inverts every conclusion it draws, so the convention must be stated. The graph in Fig. 2(a) uses the similarity convention. The main use of a weighted graph in machine learning is the similarity graph of a dataset D = x(1), …, x(m). Its nodes are the data points, V = 1, …, m with node r standing for x(r), and the weight of an edge measures the similarity of its two data points. For feature vectors in Rd, a common choice is the Gaussian weight \begin{equation} A_{r,r'} = \exp \Big( - \left\lVert {\mathbf x}^{(r)} - {\mathbf x}^{(r')} \right\rVert_{2}^{2} \big/ (2 \sigma^{2}) \Big) \text{,} \end{equation} which is 1 for two identical feature vectors and falls off with their Euclidean distance at a rate set by the width σ > 0. Giving the Gaussian weight Eq. (3) to every pair of data points produces a fully connected graph with m(m-1)/2 edges, whose weight matrix has no zero off the diagonal. A sparse alternative is the k-nearest-neighbor graph: an edge joins r and r' when one of the two data points is among the k nearest data points of the other, it carries the Gaussian weight Eq. (3), and every other pair has weight zero. The width σ and the number k of neighbors are hyperparameters of the construction; a usual choice for σ is the mean distance of a data point to its k-th nearest neighbor. For the ten days at Krems and k = 3, this choice gives σ = 8.27 degrees, and 19 of the 45 pairs of days are edges. Their weights range from 0.11, between 10 August and 16 September, to 0.95, between 16 September and 23 October, and the weighted degrees Eq. (2) from 1.13, on 10 August, to 4.61, on 7 February. Fig. 2(b) shows the weight matrix. A similarity graph turns clustering into a question about the weights. A cluster is a subset C ⊆ V of nodes whose inner edges carry large weights and whose outgoing edges carry small ones. The total weight of the edges that leave the subset, \begin{equation} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}} \sum_{i' \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \mathcal{C}} A_{i,i'} \text{,} \end{equation} is the cut of C. Graph clustering methods such as spectral clustering choose the clusters to make their cuts Eq. (4) small relative to their sizes. For the ten days at Krems, take the seven days with a maximum temperature below 18 degrees as the subset C. Its cut Eq. (4) is 1.92 out of a total edge weight of 13.25: the four edges that leave it are 21 percent of the edges and carry 14.5 percent of the weight. On all 366 days of 2024 and with k = 10, the graph has 2209 edges. The edges between the 186 cold and the 180 warm days carry 3.7 percent of the total weight, and no edge joins a day of January or February with a day of July or August. On a photograph cut into patches, the same construction with the mean color of a patch as its feature vector gives a weighted graph whose clusters are the regions of an image segmentation. A weighted graph also enters empirical risk minimization through a penalty term. In transfer learning and in federated learning, the nodes are learning tasks, each with its own local dataset and a local hypothesis h(i), and the weight Ai,i' states how similar two tasks are. Generalized total variation minimization minimizes the sum of the local training errors plus the generalized total variation \begin{equation} \sum_{\{i,i'\} \in \mathcal{E}} A_{i,i'} d^{(i,i')} \text{,} \end{equation} with d(i,i') a measure of the discrepancy between h(i) and h(i'). The generalized total variation Eq. (5) couples the tasks: an edge with a large weight pulls the two hypotheses at its nodes together, and a zero weight leaves them independent. The network Lasso is the special case with the Euclidean distance between the local model parameters as the discrepancy. Adding a penalty term is one of the three routes that regularization distinguishes, and the weighted graph is where this penalty term is specified. On a similarity graph of labeled and unlabeled data points, the penalty term Eq. (5) with the squared difference (h(x(r)) - h(x(r')))2 as the discrepancy is the Laplacian regularizer of semi-supervised learning. It asks a hypothesis to take similar values on two data points joined by an edge of large weight, which is how the unlabeled data points shape the hypothesis. A graph neural network uses the weights for a third purpose, to combine the feature vectors of the neighbors of each node into a new feature vector of the node.

terms.name: explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)
terms.abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is the subfield of artificial intelligence concerned with making the predictions of machine learning methods understandable to humans. Much of it can be posed as a function approximation problem: a learned hypothesis is explained by a simpler function that a human can comprehend. Explanations differ in what they are made of. One kind reports a score for each feature, the weights of a linear map fitted near the data point (local interpretable model-agnostic explanations) or additive contributions to the prediction (SHapley Additive exPlanations). A counterfactual instead names another feature vector, the closest one whose prediction differs. A concept activation vector states the explanation in a concept the user names, located in the activations inside the trained method. All three are post hoc and treat the learned hypothesis as fixed. The alternative is a hypothesis that needs no separate explanation, reached by restricting the hypothesis space to hypotheses a human comprehends or by regularization that favors such hypotheses. Explainable empirical risk minimization instead keeps the hypothesis space and penalizes deviations from the predictions of one specific user.
terms.description: A bank's artificial intelligence system rejects a loan application, and the applicant asks why. XAI is the subfield of artificial intelligence concerned with making the predictions of machine learning methods understandable to humans. It aims to complement each prediction by an explanation of how it has been obtained. If the machine learning method uses a sufficiently simple hypothesis space, the learned hypothesis may be inherently interpretable and no separate explanation is needed; see interpretable machine learning, discussed further below. The term XAI was popularized by a program of the US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency; in the context of machine learning, the synonymous term explainable machine learning is also used. The underlying property is explainability, which the international terminology standard for artificial intelligence defines for AI systems in general. Much of XAI can be posed as a function approximation problem. A trained hypothesis ĥ: X → Y, e.g., delivered by an opaque deep net, is typically a composition of many nonlinear layers, a function on a high-dimensional feature space X. Explaining ĥ at a data point with feature vector x ∈ X means answering one question about that function in a form a human can comprehend. The examples of explanations below are of three kinds, distinguished by what the explanation is made of: the first approximates ĥ by a simpler function, the second asks where ĥ takes a different value, and the third refers to a concept inside the trained method. The first is a score for each feature of the data point. The scores are the weights of a simpler hypothesis, such as a linear map, that agrees with ĥ near x and comes from a hypothesis space whose hypotheses a user can read, as local interpretable model-agnostic explanations computes them. The second is another feature vector, one whose prediction differs. The third is a concept the user names, located inside the trained method rather than among the features of the data point. All three are post hoc: they treat the learned hypothesis as fixed and construct the explanation after training. The first kind of explanation reports one score per feature, saying how much that feature contributed to the prediction. Local interpretable model-agnostic explanations obtains the scores as the weights of a linear map fitted to ĥ near x; Fig. 1 draws that construction. SHapley Additive exPlanations obtains them by decomposing the prediction into a base value and one contribution per feature, the contributions being Shapley values. The two deliver the same kind of explanation and differ in how its scores are computed. When features are properties of image pixels, the feature scores are a second image of the same size: one relevance score per pixel (see Fig. 2). The class activation map is one construction of such a per-pixel score. The second kind of explanation is a counterfactual. It reports no scores and approximates nothing. It asks instead where ĥ takes a different value, pointing out how the features must be modified for the prediction ĥ(x) to come out differently. A counterfactual identifies the smallest such modification, with closeness measured by a chosen metric (see Fig. 3). For the rejected loan applicant, for example, local interpretable model-agnostic explanations reports which of the applicant's features, such as income and credit history, its local linear approximation assigns the largest weight to in the rejection. A counterfactual instead states the smallest modification of those features that would turn the prediction into an approval. The third kind of explanation refers not to the features of the data point but to a concept the user specifies. Such a concept is defined by a dataset of examples the user supplies. A concept activation vector locates such a concept as a direction in the space of the activations of one hidden layer of an artificial neural network: the normal vector of a decision boundary that separates the supplied examples carrying the concept from those that do not. In contrast to local interpretable model-agnostic explanations and counterfactual explanations, a concept activation vector needs access to the internal computations of a machine learning system. One such internal computation is the activation z = f(x) of a hidden layer in a deep net. A deep net computes ĥ by feeding the activations z to the final layers, which deliver a score s(z) for each label; the prediction ĥ(x) follows from those scores (see concept activation vector). In an image classifier, for example, a user who suspects that photographs are labeled zebra through the concept stripes supplies photographs that show stripes and photographs that do not. The concept activation vector for stripes is then the normal vector of the linear classifier that separates the activations z of the two sets of photographs. How much the concept contributed to the prediction of a zebra photograph is then measured by the directional derivative of the score s along that concept activation vector. The above XAI methods construct an explanation after training, for a learned hypothesis that is already fixed. The alternative is to learn one that needs no separate explanation. Interpretable machine learning does so by admitting only hypotheses a human comprehends directly. The restriction is achieved by manually choosing a hypothesis space that is simple enough, or by regularization that favors hypotheses with specific properties, such as sparsity or predictability. Explainable empirical risk minimization uses regularization but not to that end: it leaves the hypothesis space as it is and delivers explainability to one specific user. That user supplies their own predictions for the data points of a training set, and the penalty term measures the deviation of the predictions of the learned hypothesis from the user predictions. Three aspects of an explanation are studied: whom it serves, how much of the learned hypothesis it covers, and whether it is faithful. How much an explanation achieves depends on who receives it: explainability is measured relative to a specific user. Explanations can be local, concerning a single prediction, or global, characterizing the learned hypothesis as a whole. An explanation must be faithful, i.e., reflect the computation that the learned hypothesis carries out. When the explanation scores the features, this can be tested rather than asserted. A class activation map is faithful for a prediction if flipping the pixels it scores highest changes that prediction more often than flipping as many of the pixels it scores lowest. Perturbing the highest-scoring regions first and recording how quickly the predicted class score falls is the standard form of the test. For the image of Fig. 2 and a linear classifier fitted to images of that kind, flipping the three highest-scoring pixels changes the prediction, while flipping the pixels in the opposite order leaves it unchanged through all 36 of them. The map-guided order also changes the prediction sooner on each of 200 noisy variants of the image. Faithfulness also limits what a post hoc explanation can achieve: one that agreed with the learned hypothesis everywhere would be that hypothesis itself, so a simpler explanation deviates from it somewhere. Two legal instruments explicitly state requirements on XAI.
