Under the general data protection regulation, a person subjected to a decision taken by automated means is entitled to ``meaningful information about the logic involved'' in that decision. Communicating the algorithm itself is not a sufficiently concise and intelligible explanation. Counterfactual information can be appropriate: the extent to which a variation in the personal data would have led to a different result. The second instrument is the EU AI Act, which requires for a high-risk artificial intelligence system that affected persons obtain ``clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure'' (see right to explanation).

terms.name: 0/1 loss
terms.abstract: The 0/1 loss of a classifier on a data point is 1 if the predicted label differs from the true label and 0 if the two agree, so it is the indicator function of a misclassification. Its average over a dataset is the fraction of misclassified data points, which is one minus the accuracy, and its expectation is the probability of a misclassification, whose smallest value over all classifiers is the Bayes risk. For binary classification it depends on the data point only through the margin, and it uses the real-valued hypothesis only through its sign. As a function of the model parameters it is piecewise constant with a zero gradient wherever the gradient exists, and finding the linear classifier with the fewest misclassifications on a training set is NP-hard, so it is not used as the objective function of training. Empirical risk minimization uses a convex surrogate instead, the hinge loss or the logistic loss divided by ln 2, each an upper bound on the 0/1 loss whose minimizers over all functions have the sign of the classifier with the Bayes risk. The 0/1 loss remains the loss by which a classifier is evaluated on a test set.
terms.description: A frost warning for Krems an der Donau is issued in the evening and is either right or wrong the next morning: frost came, or it did not. Counting a wrong warning as 1 and a right one as 0 is the 0/1 loss. In general, consider a data point with features x ∈ X and a label y from a finite label space Y, and a classifier h: X → Y that predicts the label. The 0/1 loss incurred by h on the data point (x, y) is \begin{equation} L^{(0/1)}\left(({\mathbf x}, y),h \right) := \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } h({\mathbf x}) = y \text{,} 1 & \text{if } h({\mathbf x}) \neq y \text{.} \end{cases} \end{equation} It is the indicator function of a misclassification, and it takes the same two values whether the label space holds two elements or many. The average of the 0/1 loss Eq. (1) over a dataset D = (x(1), y(1)), …, (x(m), y(m)) is the fraction of misclassified data points, \begin{equation} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{r=1}^{m} L^{(0/1)}\left(({\mathbf x}^{(r)}, y^{(r)}),h \right) = 1 - \operatorname{acc}(h \mid \mathcal{D}) \text{,} \end{equation} which is one minus the accuracy of h on D. On a training set, the average Eq. (2) is the training error of h under the 0/1 loss, and on a test set it is the error rate reported for a classification method. For data points that are realizations of independent and identically distributed RVs with a common probability distribution, the expectation of the 0/1 loss is the probability that h misclassifies a data point, which is the risk of h under the 0/1 loss. The risk is smallest for the classifier that assigns each x the label value with the largest conditional probability given x, and that smallest risk is the Bayes risk. For binary classification with Y = -1, +1, a classifier is usually built from a real-valued hypothesis h: X → R that predicts ŷ = sign(h(x)). The 0/1 loss Eq. (1) of this classifier depends on the data point only through the margin y · h(x), \begin{equation} L^{(0/1)}\left(({\mathbf x}, y),h \right) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } y \cdot h({\mathbf x}) > 0 \text{,} 1 & \text{if } y \cdot h({\mathbf x}) \leq 0 \text{.} \end{cases} \end{equation} A positive margin is a correct prediction, and a data point on the decision boundary h(x) = 0 counts as misclassified. The margin form Eq. (3) uses h only through its sign, so multiplying h by any positive number leaves the 0/1 loss of every data point unchanged. The 0/1 loss is the natural loss for classification, and empirical risk minimization with it would take the training error Eq. (2) as the objective function to minimize over a hypothesis space H. Two obstacles stand in the way. First, as a function of the model parameters of h, the average 0/1 loss is piecewise constant: it changes only when the decision boundary crosses a data point, and between two such crossings its gradient is zero. Gradient descent and its variants therefore receive no direction of improvement from it, and the average is neither convex nor smooth. Second, the problem is hard even for methods that use no gradient. If some linear classifier classifies every data point of the training set correctly, a linear program finds one. Without that guarantee, finding the linear classifier with the fewest misclassifications on a given training set is NP-hard, and so is finding one whose number of correct predictions is within a fixed factor of the largest achievable. Fig. 1 shows both obstacles in the frost warning of the opening. Each of the m = 365 days of 2024 at Krems is a data point whose single feature x is the lowest temperature of the day and whose label is y = +1 if the lowest temperature of the following day is below 0 ∘C (frost) and y = -1 otherwise. Frost follows 68 of the 365 days. The warning compares the day's lowest temperature with a threshold τ: the hypothesis h(x) = τ - x predicts frost when it is positive, and the single model parameter τ selects a classifier from the hypothesis space of all thresholds. The 0/1 loss of one day is a step in τ, from 1 to 0 at the day's temperature, and the average over the year is a staircase with 195 steps, one at each distinct temperature. Its smallest value, 40/365 = 0.110, is attained by every threshold strictly between 0.2 and 0.3 and between 0.4 and 0.6 ∘C: the set of minimizers is not a single point, and the slope of the staircase is zero at every threshold that is not a jump. A warning that never predicts frost has average 0/1 loss 68/365 = 0.186, and one that always predicts frost has 0.814. Practical classification methods replace the 0/1 loss in empirical risk minimization by a surrogate loss function that is convex in h(x) and an upper bound on the 0/1 loss. The hinge loss max0, 1 - y · h(x), which gives the support vector machine, lies on or above the 0/1 loss for every margin. The logistic loss ln(1 + exp(-y · h(x))), which gives logistic regression, equals ln 2 ≈ 0.69 at margin 0 and is an upper bound only after division by ln 2. Scaling a surrogate so that it passes through 1 at margin 0 is the usual convention when loss functions are compared. Because the surrogate is an upper bound, the risk of any hypothesis under the 0/1 loss is at most its risk under the surrogate, so a hypothesis with a small surrogate risk misclassifies rarely. Both surrogates are also calibrated for classification: for a convex function of the margin that is differentiable at 0 with a negative derivative there, every sequence of hypotheses whose surrogate risk tends to its smallest possible value has a 0/1 risk that tends to the Bayes risk. Over all functions of x, the hinge loss is minimized by the sign of P(y = +1 | x) - 1/2 and the logistic loss by the logarithm of the odds of y = +1, and the sign of either minimizer is the classifier with the Bayes risk. Unlike the 0/1 loss, a surrogate changes when h is multiplied by a positive number, so it depends on the scale of h and not only on its sign. For the frost warning, the average logistic loss divided by ln 2 and the average hinge loss are convex functions of the threshold that lie above the staircase everywhere (Fig. 1). Each has a single minimizer, τ = -0.04 ∘C for the logistic loss and 0.06 ∘C for the hinge loss, and at both the average 0/1 loss is 41/365 = 0.112, one day more than the smallest value of the staircase. At the minimizer of the logistic loss, the average logistic loss divided by ln 2 is 0.405 for h, 0.333 for h/2, and 0.670 for 2h, while the average 0/1 loss is the same for all three. A small average 0/1 loss on the training set is not the goal of training but a means to a small risk, and the two can differ. Fig. 2 shows a training set on which a linear classifier h' misclassifies one data point while a classifier h'' whose decision boundary bends around that data point misclassifies none. A small shift of a feature vector near this decision boundary flips the prediction of h'', so its zero training error does not indicate good generalization; this is overfitting. Restricting the hypothesis space to linear classifiers is a form of regularization, the route that shrinks the hypothesis space.
